--measure names a statistic to summarise, and repeats for more. --level sets the confidence level of the intervals. --workers runs that many replications at once, each in its own process, and gives the same results, because each replication keeps its seed:

# Two statistics at a 99% level, two replications at a time
desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --replications 10 --seed 42 --until 1h --measure tasks.pack.wait_mean --measure resources.packers.utilization_avg --level 0.99 --workers 2

measure                               n          mean    half-width (99%)
tasks.pack.wait_mean                 10         4.505              0.9314
resources.packers.utilization_avg    10         79.53               2.243

Seed 42; replication seeds: 2684470948, 4091952314, 233227757, 3276785861, 3644269654, 1206282609, 3543069911, 3479688010, 877132087, 1244265337
Repeat one replication with: desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --seed <its seed> --until 1h

The means are the same as before. At 99%, the half-width of the mean wait grows from 0.6483 to 0.9314 seconds, because more confidence needs a wider interval.

--stdout prints the run's records as JSON lines, instead of writing to the file's sinks. --drain stops the arrivals at the end time and runs on until every order has left. This run stops the arrivals at 20 seconds, and its last record is the ninth order packed, at 24.789 seconds:

# Every record of a 20-second run that drains, as JSON lines in a file
desflow run experiment/yaml/experiment_shop.yaml --seed 42 --until 20 --drain --stdout > records.jsonl

docs.title: Compare Designs
docs.text:
desflow experiment runs an experiment: here two packers against three, 20 replications of each with the same seeds, with a check that three packers keep the mean wait under 2 seconds. --output names the folder for its files, here results/packers in the current folder. Without it, they go to the folder the file's output names, beside the file:

desflow experiment experiment/yaml/experiment.yaml --output results/packers

Wrote the artifacts and report.md to results/packers
passed: three: tasks.pack.wait_mean max 2, checked 0.5919

The check passed: the upper end of the interval of the mean wait with three packers is 0.5919 seconds, under the bound of 2. The command exits with status 1 when a check fails, so a CI job that runs it fails too. The six files in results/packers hold every value, and report.md compares the designs, as Experiment Results describes. After editing experiment.json by hand, desflow report builds the report again from the files, without running anything:

desflow report results/packers

Wrote results/packers/report.md

docs.title: Fit Measured Times
docs.text:
A packing time in a model comes from measured times. The fitting example holds 40 packing times measured at a bench, for a shop of its own, and desflow fit fits every distribution family to them:

desflow examples get fitting --api yaml
desflow fit fitting/packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --lower 0

40 rows: 40 used, 0 missing, 0 invalid
family            status              AIC  KS stat KS p (approx.)  parameters or reason
exponential       rejected                                         its std is 1.5, the data's is 0.4832: more than 25% apart
normal            fitted            59.33    0.157         0.2504  mean=1.5, std=0.483218 (can draw below the lower bound 0)
lognormal         fitted            57.33  0.09406         0.8385  mean=1.50251, std=0.511854
truncated_normal  fitted            59.25   0.1558         0.2579  mean=1.49836, std=0.48579, low=0
constant          skipped                                          the values are not all equal
uniform           fitted            59.45    0.225        0.02923  low=0.7, high=2.7
triangular *      fitted            56.68   0.1258          0.511  low=0.546332, mode=1.2, high=2.83766
gamma             fitted            56.79   0.1157         0.6165  shape=9.55777, scale=0.15694
weibull           fitted            58.99   0.1502         0.2972  shape=3.33522, scale=1.67203
empirical         fitted                                           values: 40 numbers
* best: triangular

The first line counts the values. Each row is one family: fitted with its AIC, where lower is better, or the reason it was not fitted. The triangular has the lowest AIC, 56.68, and the gamma is within 0.11 of it, so the data cannot tell the two apart. Fitting the Inputs checks what the choice changes.

The other options shape the fit, as Input Fitting describes:

  • --unit names the data's unit, ms, s, min or h, and the settings are written in seconds.
  • --upper is the highest plausible value, and a family that can draw above it is marked.
  • --candidates names the families to try.
  • --bins offers the empirical distribution as a histogram with that many bins.
  • --min-count is the fewest values a family is fitted to.
  • --tolerance is how far a fitted mean and standard deviation may be from the data's, as a share of the data's.
  • --drop-invalid leaves out values that are not numbers or lie outside the bounds, instead of stopping.
  • --out writes the best fit as YAML that a blueprint includes, and --plot draws the data against it as a PNG.
# Three families, a histogram of 8 bins, and the best fit written for the blueprint
desflow fit fitting/packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --upper 10 --candidates triangular,gamma,empirical --bins 8 --min-count 30 --tolerance 0.2 --drop-invalid --out fitting/yaml/packing_fit.yaml --plot packing_fit.png

40 rows: 40 used, 0 missing, 0 invalid
family            status              AIC  KS stat KS p (approx.)  parameters or reason
triangular *      fitted            56.68   0.1258          0.511  low=0.546332, mode=1.2, high=2.83766
gamma             fitted            56.79   0.1157         0.6165  shape=9.55777, scale=0.15694 (can draw above the upper bound 10)
empirical         fitted                                           edges: 9 numbers, counts: 8 numbers
* best: triangular
Wrote fitting/yaml/packing_fit.yaml
Wrote packing_fit.png

The empirical row is now a histogram of 8 bins, and the gamma row is marked because a gamma can draw above 10 seconds. fitting/yaml/packing_fit.yaml is the file the fitting example's blueprint includes, so fitting/yaml/fitting.yaml now draws its packing times from this triangular.

docs.title: Convert Parameters
docs.text:
A gamma takes a shape and a scale, not a mean and a standard deviation. desflow dist converts the measured times' mean of 1.5 seconds and standard deviation of 0.4832 seconds into them:

desflow dist gamma --mean 1.5 --std 0.4832

parameters: shape 9.63671, scale 0.155655
mean 1.5, std 0.4832
variability: low (std / mean 0.322)
with no random generator, every draw is 1.5
YAML: {dist: gamma, shape: 9.63671, scale: 0.155655}
Python: dist="gamma", shape=9.63671, scale=0.155655

The shape and scale are close to the gamma that desflow fit found from the 40 values. The last two lines are the service in a blueprint and in the builder.

Given a family's own parameters, desflow dist converts the other way. Each of these lines prints the family's mean and standard deviation, as in the output above, for each kind of parameter: a rate, a constant's value, a low and a high, and a shape and a scale:

desflow dist exponential --rate 0.4
desflow dist constant --value 4
desflow dist uniform --low 0.7 --high 2.7
desflow dist gamma --shape 9.63671 --scale 0.155655

The shop's arrivals, rate: 0.4, are 2.5 seconds apart on average. A triangular also takes a mode, its most likely value. The one desflow fit found has a mean of 1.53 seconds, close to the measured 1.5:

desflow dist triangular --low 0.55 --mode 1.2 --high 2.84

parameters: low 0.55, mode 1.2, high 2.84
mean 1.53, std 0.481785
variability: low (std / mean 0.315)
with no random generator, every draw is 1.53
YAML: {dist: triangular, low: 0.55, mode: 1.2, high: 2.84}
Python: dist="triangular", low=0.55, mode=1.2, high=2.84

desflow dist alone prints a table of every family with its parameters and a one-line summary, and Choosing Inputs explains the variability line:

desflow dist

docs.title: Set Up an Editor
docs.text:
desflow schema prints the JSON Schema of a blueprint, for the release you installed. An editor that reads it offers the keys as you type and marks a misspelt one:

desflow schema > blueprint.schema.json

Set Up Your Editor names the file in the editor's settings.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Each command reads its file and calls the library function a Python script would call. desflow run loads the model with load_context and runs it once, or calls replicate when --replications is given. desflow experiment calls run_experiment, desflow report calls write_report, and desflow fit reads the column and calls fit_column. desflow dist, desflow schema and desflow examples read the distribution table, the blueprint schema and the list of examples. A command therefore gives the same result as the Python call with the same arguments.

desflow explain takes the most steps. Look at them in order:

Graph. explain builds the graph from what the model declares: its arrivals, tasks, resources, stores, containers and next shares. It builds and runs nothing. Code the model does not declare, such as a hand-written arrival loop or an add_process function, becomes an opaque node.

Rates. Each task's arrival rate comes from flow balance: the rate from its arrivals plus the share of each task that sends work to it. A next function or a hand-written arrival loop makes the rates unknown, because the graph cannot see where the work goes.

Coverage. The formulas hold for a plain network of queues:

  • Each task holds at most one resource.
  • Each queue serves in arrival order, fifo or lifo, which give the same mean wait.
  • Nothing blocks, removes, delays or reorders work by priority.

Anything else marks tasks, and the rate of a marked task is unknown. These mark tasks:

  • A task feature, such as put, patience or fail, marks that task and every task after it.
  • A resource feature, such as queue_limit or breakdowns, marks the tasks that use it and every task after them.
  • A priority queue whose tasks have different priorities marks every task after its tasks. The resource keeps its utilisation but has no wait.
  • An unstable resource marks every task after its tasks. The resource keeps its status.
  • A scenario step, live ingress or an add_process function marks every arrival and every task.

A resource used by a marked task has no supported utilisation, status or wait, and the output names the reason under Not estimated.

Waits. The utilisation ρ is λ ÷ (c × μ): the arrival rate divided by the units times the rate one unit serves. The status follows from it. The wait depends on the units and the input:

  • With no unit limit, the wait is 0.
  • At one unit, the wait comes from Kingman's formula. It is exact when the input is Poisson, and an approximation when one arrival with other gaps feeds the resource's only task.
  • At more than one unit, the wait comes from Erlang C, which needs Poisson arrivals and one exponential service time shared by every task that uses the resource.
  • With any other input or times there is no wait, and the output says to run --verify.

Little's law then gives the queue length and the number in the system. The bottleneck is the resource with the highest supported utilisation. The hints solve the utilisation alone for the units and the arrival rate that reach --target.

Verify. --verify runs the model as one replication does: unpaced, with no ingress or egress, and with the typical statistics. It measures from the end of the warm-up to --until, or to the blueprint's run.until when --until is not given. It compares four measures with the analysis: each resource's utilisation and queue length, the wait of each task that holds one resource, and each arrival's throughput. A measure agrees with the analysis:

  • For one run, when it is within 10% of the analysis, or measures 0 where the analysis gives 0.
  • For replications, when it is within the 95% interval's half-width or 1%, whichever is larger.

A measure is not compared in these cases:

  • The analysis has no value for it.
  • Its resource is unstable.
  • Its wait comes from Kingman's formula as an approximation.
  • For a throughput, the arrival starts no task the graph shows, or its flow passes a marked task or an unstable resource.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Inputs are files. run reads a blueprint, explain a blueprint or a builder file with a module-level SimulationContext, experiment an experiment file, and fit a CSV file. For a Python model, use replicate and run_experiment, as Replications shows.
  • Examples need the network. examples get downloads from GitHub at the installed release's tag. --ref picks another tag or branch.
  • explain --json is experimental. Its shape can change in 1.x, and schema_version changes with it.
  • Exit statuses: 0 on success, 1 on a failure, 2 on a usage error.
    • 1: run or explain cannot load the file, an experiment check fails (its files are still written), fit finds no usable family, or dist has no formula from a mean and a standard deviation for the family.
    • 2: a missing file, an option value that is not valid such as --until abc, a value that is not a number in a fit column, or an experiment file that is not valid.

docs.title: Analyse the Event Log
docs.text: Write a run's events to Parquet, read them back with pyarrow and turn them into an event log: one row for each step an order took, with the entity, the event type, the event, the time and the run. Then find each order's wait and time in the shop, and the run's throughput.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Streaming Out writes records to files.
  • Egress describes the sink, and Records and Telemetry the fields of a record.
  • The analysis uses pyarrow only, with no pandas. Install it with pip install "desflow[parquet]".

docs.title: Write the Events
docs.text:
Add a Parquet sink, ParquetStorageEgress, to the shop. It writes one flat row for each event, in files named events_<8 hex digits>.parquet. The finished event carries a status, as the queued and started events do:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/analyse_the_event_log.yaml:run
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The finished event's value, so every event of a task has a status
    payload: {status: finished}

egress:
  # One flat row per event, in files named events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
  - type: Parquet
    config:
      default_path: ${OUT:-analyse_output}/events.parquet

run:
  until: 120

run_yaml loads it with the folder in OUT, and runs it:

docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log.py:run-yaml
def run_yaml(
    out: Path, blueprint: str = "analyse_the_event_log.yaml"
) -> SimulationContext:
    """Runs the blueprint for two minutes into an empty folder and returns it."""
    shutil.rmtree(out, ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
    with patch.dict(os.environ, {"OUT": str(out)}):  # the folder the blueprint reads
        app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(blueprint)
    app.run()  # until 120, from the blueprint
    return app
docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log.py:run
def shop(out: Path) -> SimulationContext:
    """One packer, orders about every 2 seconds, events written to Parquet in out."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
        # One flat row per event, in files named events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
        .add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/events.parquet"))
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        # The finished event's value, so every event of a task has a status
        return {"status": "finished"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app
docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log_low_level.py:run
def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # The finished event's value, so every event of a task has a status
        env.publish_event(key, {"status": "finished"}, "pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(out: Path) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """One packer, orders about every 2 seconds, events written to Parquet in out."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    # One flat row per event, in files named events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
    env.setup_egress([ParquetStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/events.parquet")])
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env

A run adds files to the folder and never replaces them, so the script empties it before a run.

docs.title: Read Them Back
docs.text:
From here on, the code is the same for every form. pyarrow.dataset reads every file under a folder as one table:

docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log.py:read
def read_events(out: Path) -> Table:
    """Every file the sink wrote under out, as one table of events."""
    return ds.dataset(out, format="parquet").to_table()

One 2-minute run of the shop writes 191 rows in every form: 64 queued events, 64 started and 63 finished, because one order is still being packed when the run ends.

docs.title: Build the Event Log
docs.text:
Each order's three events become the rows of an event log. A queued event is the order's arrival and its wait in the queue, a started event is the start of packing, and a finished event is the end of packing and the order leaving. The files are read in no fixed order, so the rows are sorted by time, and by the order of the statuses where times are equal:

docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log.py:log
# Each status of a task becomes these rows of the log, in this order
ROWS = {
    "queued": [("arrival_departure", "arrival"), ("queue", "waiting_for_packer")],
    "started": [("resource_use", "packing_start")],
    "finished": [("resource_use_end", "packing_end"), ("arrival_departure", "depart")],
}
ORDER = list(ROWS)  # queued, started, finished: the order of an order's events


def event_log(events: Table, run: int = 1) -> Table:
    """The event log: one row for each step an order took, sorted by time.

    The files are read in no fixed order, so the rows are sorted by time and, at the
    same time, by the order of the statuses.
    """
    packing = events.filter(pc.equal(events["task"], "pack_order")).to_pylist()
    packing.sort(key=lambda row: (row["sim_ts"], ORDER.index(row["status"])))
    rows = [
        {
            "entity_id": row["key"],
            "event_type": event_type,
            "event": event,
            "time": row["sim_ts"],
            "run": run,
        }
        for row in packing
        for event_type, event in ROWS[row["status"]]
    ]
    return Table.from_pylist(rows)

The log has 318 rows for 64 orders, and its columns are entity_id, event_type, event, time and run. This is the form Animate a Run takes.

docs.title: Find Waits and Throughput
docs.text:
An order's wait is the time from its arrival to the start of packing, and its time in the shop is the time from its arrival to its departure. Throughput is the number of orders that left in each minute of the run:

docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log.py:waits
def times(log: Table, event: str) -> dict:
    """The time of `event` for each order that reached it."""
    rows = log.filter(pc.equal(log["event"], event))
    return dict(zip(rows["entity_id"].to_pylist(), rows["time"].to_pylist()))


def waits_and_times(log: Table) -> dict:
    """Each order's wait, and its time in the shop if it left before the run ended."""
    arrived = times(log, "arrival")
    started = times(log, "packing_start")
    left = times(log, "depart")
    return {
        order: {
            "wait": round(started[order] - arrived[order], 3),
            "in_shop": round(left[order] - arrived[order], 3)
            if order in left
            else None,
        }
        for order in started
    }


def mean_wait(per_order: dict) -> float:
    """The mean wait of the orders that started packing, in seconds."""
    return pc.mean(pa.array([row["wait"] for row in per_order.values()])).as_py()


def throughput_per_minute(log: Table, seconds: float) -> float:
    """Orders that left the shop in each minute of the run."""
    return len(times(log, "depart")) / (seconds / 60)

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
python analyse_the_event_log.py runs the builder form, writes the files to analyse_output/ and prints the counts below. python analyse_the_event_log_low_level.py does the same with the low-level form, and run_yaml with the blueprint. Each form writes the same events, so each gives the same counts.

The first order waits 0.0 seconds and is in the shop for 1.5 seconds. The mean wait is 1.250 seconds and the longest wait is 3.66 seconds. These come from one 2-minute run of a shop with one packer, not from the busy hour of the tutorials. 63 orders leave in two minutes, a throughput of 31.5 orders a minute. The 64th is still being packed, so it has a wait and no time in the shop.

The analysis and run_yaml are in analyse_the_event_log.py, in the Builder tab.

docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log.py
"""Analyse the Event Log: a run written to Parquet, read back as an event log.

The shop runs for two minutes with one packer and writes its events to Parquet. The
script reads the files with pyarrow, turns each order's three events into the rows of
an event log (entity, event type, event, time, run), and computes each order's wait
and time in the shop and the run's throughput. It uses pyarrow only, no pandas.
python analyse_the_event_log.py writes the files to analyse_output/. `run_yaml`
runs analyse_the_event_log.yaml instead, and analyse_the_event_log_low_level.py is
the low-level API; each writes the same events.
"""

import logging
import os
import shutil
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import patch

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
import pyarrow.dataset as ds
from pyarrow import Table

from desflow import ParquetStorageEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)

RUN_SECONDS = 120


def shop(out: Path) -> SimulationContext:
    """One packer, orders about every 2 seconds, events written to Parquet in out."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
        # One flat row per event, in files named events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
        .add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/events.parquet"))
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        # The finished event's value, so every event of a task has a status
        return {"status": "finished"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def run(out: Path) -> SimulationContext:
    """Runs the shop for two minutes into an empty folder and returns it."""
    shutil.rmtree(out, ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
    app = shop(out)
    app.run(until=RUN_SECONDS)
    return app


def run_yaml(
    out: Path, blueprint: str = "analyse_the_event_log.yaml"
) -> SimulationContext:
    """Runs the blueprint for two minutes into an empty folder and returns it."""
    shutil.rmtree(out, ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
    with patch.dict(os.environ, {"OUT": str(out)}):  # the folder the blueprint reads
        app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(blueprint)
    app.run()  # until 120, from the blueprint
    return app


def read_events(out: Path) -> Table:
    """Every file the sink wrote under out, as one table of events."""
    return ds.dataset(out, format="parquet").to_table()


# Each status of a task becomes these rows of the log, in this order
ROWS = {
    "queued": [("arrival_departure", "arrival"), ("queue", "waiting_for_packer")],
    "started": [("resource_use", "packing_start")],
    "finished": [("resource_use_end", "packing_end"), ("arrival_departure", "depart")],
}
ORDER = list(ROWS)  # queued, started, finished: the order of an order's events


def event_log(events: Table, run: int = 1) -> Table:
    """The event log: one row for each step an order took, sorted by time.

    The files are read in no fixed order, so the rows are sorted by time and, at the
    same time, by the order of the statuses.
    """
    packing = events.filter(pc.equal(events["task"], "pack_order")).to_pylist()
    packing.sort(key=lambda row: (row["sim_ts"], ORDER.index(row["status"])))
    rows = [
        {
            "entity_id": row["key"],
            "event_type": event_type,
            "event": event,
            "time": row["sim_ts"],
            "run": run,
        }
        for row in packing
        for event_type, event in ROWS[row["status"]]
    ]
    return Table.from_pylist(rows)


def times(log: Table, event: str) -> dict:
    """The time of `event` for each order that reached it."""
    rows = log.filter(pc.equal(log["event"], event))
    return dict(zip(rows["entity_id"].to_pylist(), rows["time"].to_pylist()))


def waits_and_times(log: Table) -> dict:
    """Each order's wait, and its time in the shop if it left before the run ended."""
    arrived = times(log, "arrival")
    started = times(log, "packing_start")
    left = times(log, "depart")
    return {
        order: {
            "wait": round(started[order] - arrived[order], 3),
            "in_shop": round(left[order] - arrived[order], 3)
            if order in left
            else None,
        }
        for order in started
    }


def mean_wait(per_order: dict) -> float:
    """The mean wait of the orders that started packing, in seconds."""
    return pc.mean(pa.array([row["wait"] for row in per_order.values()])).as_py()


def throughput_per_minute(log: Table, seconds: float) -> float:
    """Orders that left the shop in each minute of the run."""
    return len(times(log, "depart")) / (seconds / 60)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    folder = Path("analyse_output")
    run(folder)
    log = event_log(read_events(folder))
    per_order = waits_and_times(log)
    print(f"{log.num_rows} rows in the log, for {len(per_order)} orders")
    print(f"mean wait {mean_wait(per_order):.3f} s")
    print(f"throughput {throughput_per_minute(log, RUN_SECONDS):.1f} orders a minute")
docs/snippets/guides/analyse_the_event_log_low_level.py
"""The Analyse the Event Log guide, low-level API: the shop written to Parquet.

The low-level version of the shop in analyse_the_event_log.py: one packer, orders
about every 2 seconds, each event written to Parquet with its status. python
analyse_the_event_log_low_level.py writes the files to analyse_output/ and analyses
them with the functions of analyse_the_event_log.py, which must be beside it.
"""

import itertools
import logging
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    ParquetStorageEgress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)

RUN_SECONDS = 120
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)


def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # The finished event's value, so every event of a task has a status
        env.publish_event(key, {"status": "finished"}, "pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(out: Path) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """One packer, orders about every 2 seconds, events written to Parquet in out."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    # One flat row per event, in files named events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
    env.setup_egress([ParquetStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/events.parquet")])
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env


def run(out: Path) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """Runs the shop for two minutes into an empty folder and returns it."""
    shutil.rmtree(out, ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
    env = shop(out)
    env.run(until=RUN_SECONDS)
    env.teardown()  # writes the last files
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from analyse_the_event_log import (
        event_log,
        mean_wait,
        read_events,
        throughput_per_minute,
        waits_and_times,
    )

    folder = Path("analyse_output")
    run(folder)
    log = event_log(read_events(folder))
    per_order = waits_and_times(log)
    print(f"{log.num_rows} rows in the log, for {len(per_order)} orders")
    print(f"mean wait {mean_wait(per_order):.3f} s")
    print(f"throughput {throughput_per_minute(log, RUN_SECONDS):.1f} orders a minute")

docs.title: Animate a Run
docs.text: Animate a run so each order is seen moving through the shop: arriving, waiting, being packed and leaving.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Analyse the Event Log writes the event log this page animates.
  • vidigi is a separate package that animates a discrete event simulation from its event log. Install it with pip install "vidigi==2.0.0" and the parquet extra of desflow.

docs.title: Build the Log
docs.text:
vidigi takes a pandas table with the columns entity_id, event_type, event and time, as the event log of Analyse the Event Log has them. It recognises the event types arrival_departure, queue, resource_use and resource_use_end. It draws a resource as numbered slots, so the rows of resource_use need a resource_id column. There is one packer, so the slot is 1:

docs/snippets/guides/animate_a_run.py:log
def vidigi_log(out: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The run's event log as a pandas table, with the packer's slot on its use rows."""
    log = event_log(read_events(out)).to_pandas()
    # vidigi draws the packers in numbered slots; there is one packer, so slot 1
    log["resource_id"] = log["event_type"].eq("resource_use").map({True: 1})
    return log

vidigi reads one run at a time, and refuses a log that holds more than one.

docs.title: Place the Events
docs.text:
Each event is drawn at a position, with a label. The event that uses a resource names it, so vidigi draws the packers there:

docs/snippets/guides/animate_a_run.py:positions
# Where each event is drawn: the arrival, the queue, the packer and the exit
POSITIONS = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"event": "arrival", "x": 250, "y": 220, "label": "Arrival"},
        {"event": "waiting_for_packer", "x": 250, "y": 160, "label": "Waiting"},
        {
            "event": "packing_start",
            "x": 250,
            "y": 100,
            "label": "Packing",
            "resource": "packers",
        },
        {"event": "depart", "x": 250, "y": 40, "label": "Shipped"},
    ]
)

docs.title: Animate
docs.text:
animate_activity_log returns a Plotly figure. scenario gives the number of packers to draw, the times are in seconds, and every_x_time_units makes one frame for every 2 seconds:

docs/snippets/guides/animate_a_run.py:animate
def animation(log: pd.DataFrame) -> Figure:
    """The Plotly animation of the run, one frame for every 2 simulated seconds."""
    figure = animate_activity_log(
        log,
        POSITIONS,
        scenario={"packers": 1},  # the number of packers drawn at the packing event
        simulation_time_unit="seconds",
        every_x_time_units=FRAME_SECONDS,
        limit_duration=RUN_SECONDS,
        plotly_height=480,
        override_x_max=400,
        stage_label_offset=30,  # room for the order icon before each label
        override_y_max=260,
        text_size=14,
        entity_icon_size=16,
        gap_between_entities=32,  # clear of the icon size at a phone width
    )
    # Narrow side margins leave the plot wide enough for the labels on a phone
    figure.update_layout(margin={"l": 10, "r": 10})
    return figure

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
make runs the shop into a folder and animates it. It takes the run of any form, because every form of the shop writes the same events:

docs/snippets/guides/animate_a_run.py:make
def make(out: Path, run_shop=run) -> Figure:
    """Runs the shop into out and animates it.

    run_shop is the run of any form: run, run_yaml or the low-level script's run.
    """
    run_shop(out)
    return animation(vidigi_log(out))

The 2-minute run makes 61 frames, named 0, 2, 4 and on to 120, and the figure draws all 64 orders. Passing run_yaml, or the run of analyse_the_event_log_low_level.py, makes the same frames.

figure.write_html("animate_a_run.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn", config={"responsive": True}) saves the figure as a page that fits the width of its window. This is the animation of the script below. Press play, or drag the slider:

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
The script imports the functions of Analyse the Event Log, so keep it in one folder with the files of that page.

Full files docs/snippets/guides/animate_a_run.py
"""Animate a Run: the shop's event log, animated with vidigi.

The script runs the shop of Analyse the Event Log for two minutes, reads its Parquet
files back as an event log, adds the one column vidigi needs beyond it, and animates
the run with vidigi 2.0.0's animate_activity_log: one frame for every 2 simulated
seconds. python animate_a_run.py writes the animation to animate_a_run.html. Every
form of the shop writes the same events, so `make` animates any of them.
"""

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from analyse_the_event_log import RUN_SECONDS, event_log, read_events, run
from plotly.graph_objects import Figure
from vidigi.animation import animate_activity_log

FRAME_SECONDS = 2


def vidigi_log(out: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The run's event log as a pandas table, with the packer's slot on its use rows."""
    log = event_log(read_events(out)).to_pandas()
    # vidigi draws the packers in numbered slots; there is one packer, so slot 1
    log["resource_id"] = log["event_type"].eq("resource_use").map({True: 1})
    return log


# Where each event is drawn: the arrival, the queue, the packer and the exit
POSITIONS = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"event": "arrival", "x": 250, "y": 220, "label": "Arrival"},
        {"event": "waiting_for_packer", "x": 250, "y": 160, "label": "Waiting"},
        {
            "event": "packing_start",
            "x": 250,
            "y": 100,
            "label": "Packing",
            "resource": "packers",
        },
        {"event": "depart", "x": 250, "y": 40, "label": "Shipped"},
    ]
)


def animation(log: pd.DataFrame) -> Figure:
    """The Plotly animation of the run, one frame for every 2 simulated seconds."""
    figure = animate_activity_log(
        log,
        POSITIONS,
        scenario={"packers": 1},  # the number of packers drawn at the packing event
        simulation_time_unit="seconds",
        every_x_time_units=FRAME_SECONDS,
        limit_duration=RUN_SECONDS,
        plotly_height=480,
        override_x_max=400,
        stage_label_offset=30,  # room for the order icon before each label
        override_y_max=260,
        text_size=14,
        entity_icon_size=16,
        gap_between_entities=32,  # clear of the icon size at a phone width
    )
    # Narrow side margins leave the plot wide enough for the labels on a phone
    figure.update_layout(margin={"l": 10, "r": 10})
    return figure


def make(out: Path, run_shop=run) -> Figure:
    """Runs the shop into out and animates it.

    run_shop is the run of any form: run, run_yaml or the low-level script's run.
    """
    run_shop(out)
    return animation(vidigi_log(out))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
        figure = make(Path(folder))
    figure.write_html(
        "animate_a_run.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn", config={"responsive": True}
    )
    print(f"{len(figure.frames)} frames")

docs.title: Check Against Theory
docs.text: Check a model against the queueing formulas, on a queue the formulas describe. A model that agrees is computing what it should. A model that differs has a defect to find.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Queues and Capacity explains utilisation and the waits the formulas give.
  • Checking a Model places this check among the others.
  • Queueing Basics gives the formulas.

docs.title: Build a Queue the Formulas Describe
docs.text:
The M/M/1 and M/M/c formulas hold when the gaps between arrivals and the service times are exponential, every arrival joins one queue and waits until it is served, and nothing changes while the model runs. This shop has one packer, an order every 1.33 seconds on average (rate: 0.75) and a mean packing time of 1 second. Its utilisation is therefore 0.75 × 1 ÷ 1 = 0.75:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/check_against_theory.yaml:shop
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42
  warmup: 2000  # seconds left out of every measure, while the queue fills

arrivals:
  # An order every 1.33 s on average (rate 0.75) with one packer; RATE=1.5 with PACKERS=2
  orders:
    dist: exponential
    rate: ${RATE:-0.75}
    spawn: pack_order

services:
  packing: {dist: exponential, rate: 1}  # 1 second on average

resources:
  packers:
    current_cap: ${PACKERS:-1}
    max_cap: 4

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

run:
  until: 20000
docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory_shop.py:shop
# An order every 1.33 s on average (rate 0.75) with one packer; RATE=1.5 with PACKERS=2
rate = float(os.environ.get("RATE", "0.75"))
packers = int(os.environ.get("PACKERS", "1"))

app = (
    # warmup: seconds left out of every measure, while the queue fills
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42, warmup=2000)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=rate, spawn="pack_order")
    .add_service("packing", dist="exponential", rate=1)  # 1 second on average
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=4)
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

The low-level API has no analysis: explain and analyze read a blueprint or a builder file. Write the model as a builder file to check it.

The highlighted lines of the blueprint are the warm-up and the three numbers the formulas read: the arrival rate, the service rate and the number of packers. The warm-up leaves out the first 2,000 seconds, while the queue fills from empty. RATE and PACKERS set the second case below.

Work out the mean wait by hand first. For one packer it is ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) × the mean service time, where ρ is the utilisation. For several packers it is the Erlang C chance that every packer is busy, divided by (c ÷ the mean service time − the arrival rate):

docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory.py:by-hand
load = rate * service  # packers' worth of work arriving each second
utilisation = load / packers
if packers == 1:
    return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * service  # M/M/1
# M/M/c: Erlang C, the chance that every packer is busy, over (c / service - rate)
last = load**packers / math.factorial(packers) / (1 - utilisation)
busy = last / (sum(load**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(packers)) + last)
return busy / (packers / service - rate)

With one packer at utilisation 0.75, the mean wait is 0.75 ÷ 0.25 × 1 = 3 seconds. With two packers and 1.5 orders a second, it is 1.286 seconds.

docs.title: Verify It
docs.text:
desflow explain gives the same values from the blueprint, and --verify runs the model and compares. Each pair is a value from the formulas and the same measure from the runs. A pair differs by one of two rules:

  • With --replications 10, the model runs ten times. A pair differs when the formula's value lies outside the 95% interval of the runs and is more than 1 percent from their mean.
  • With one run, a pair differs when the two values are more than 10 percent apart.

The 1 percent matters when every run gives the same value, as with constant times. The interval then has a width of 0, and the last order still being packed at the end would count as a difference. This command runs ten replications. A builder file has no run.until, so its command gives the end of each run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow explain check_against_theory.yaml --verify --replications 10

desflow explain check_against_theory_shop.py --verify --replications 10 --until 20000

The low-level API has no analysis: explain and analyze read a blueprint or a builder file. Write the model as a builder file to check it.

Both print the same tables, because they are the same model with the same seed:

Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 0.75/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 0.75/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+--------------------------------------------------+
| resource |    λ | μ | c |    ρ | Wq | L | status |
|----------+------+---+---+------+----+---+--------|
| packers  | 0.75 | 1 | 1 | 0.75 |  3 | 3 | OK     |
+--------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+---------------------+
| c |      ρ | status |
|---+--------+--------|
| 1 |   0.75 | OK     |
| 2 |  0.375 | OK     |
| 3 |   0.25 | OK     |
| 4 | 0.1875 | OK     |
+---------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Hints for utilisation 0.85:
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.75, at most 0.85
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.85 at a request every 1.18 seconds (51 a minute, 0.85 a second)
Verify: 10 runs to 20000 s, seed 42
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| node       | measure      | analysis | measured |        ± | result |
|------------+--------------+----------+----------+----------+--------|
| packers    | utilization  |     0.75 |   0.7508 |  0.00624 | agrees |
| packers    | queue_length |     2.25 |     2.25 |    0.132 | agrees |
| pack_order | wait         |        3 |    2.994 |    0.163 | agrees |
| orders     | throughput   |     0.75 |   0.7514 | 0.004534 | agrees |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
--verify checks the implementation against the queueing analysis where it applies; it does not show that the model is close enough to the real system

Every measure agrees: the utilisation, the queue length Lq = λ × Wq, the mean wait of 3 seconds and the throughput. With two packers at the same utilisation, the wait comes from Erlang C:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
PACKERS=2 RATE=1.5 desflow explain check_against_theory.yaml --verify --replications 10

# Twice the orders and two packers, checked against the formulas
PACKERS=2 RATE=1.5 desflow explain check_against_theory_shop.py --verify --replications 10 --until 20000

The low-level API has no analysis: explain and analyze read a blueprint or a builder file. Write the model as a builder file to check it.

Verify: 10 runs to 20000 s, seed 42
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| node       | measure      | analysis | measured |        ± | result |
|------------+--------------+----------+----------+----------+--------|
| packers    | utilization  |     0.75 |    0.752 | 0.004173 | agrees |
| packers    | queue_length |    1.929 |    1.972 |  0.07398 | agrees |
| pack_order | wait         |    1.286 |    1.312 |  0.04669 | agrees |
| orders     | throughput   |      1.5 |    1.503 |  0.00529 | agrees |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
--verify checks the implementation against the queueing analysis where it applies; it does not show that the model is close enough to the real system

From Python, analyze(verify=True) runs the same check and returns it as explanation.verification. This function prints each pair:

docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory.py:show
def show(explanation):
    """Prints each pair of the verification: the formula's value and the runs'."""
    for c in explanation.verification.comparisons:
        result = "differs" if c.differs else "agrees"
        print(
            f"{c.node} {c.measure}: analysis {c.analytical:.3f}, "
            f"runs {c.measured:.3f} ± {c.half_width:.3f}, {result}"
        )

Each form loads its model from its file and passes the result to show:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory.py:verify
app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(BLUEPRINT)
explanation = app.analyze(verify=True, replications=10)  # until from run.until
show(explanation)
docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory.py:verify-builder
app = load_context(SHOP.parent, SHOP.name)  # a new copy for each run needs a file
explanation = app.analyze(verify=True, until=20000, replications=10)
show(explanation)

The low-level API has no analysis: explain and analyze read a blueprint or a builder file. Write the model as a builder file to check it.

packers utilization: analysis 0.750, runs 0.751 ± 0.006, agrees
packers queue_length: analysis 2.250, runs 2.250 ± 0.132, agrees
pack_order wait: analysis 3.000, runs 2.994 ± 0.163, agrees
orders throughput: analysis 0.750, runs 0.751 ± 0.005, agrees

A context built in a script's own code refuses verify=True, because the runs need a new copy of the model, which only a file can give.

--json prints the same result as JSON, for a script or a CI job outside Python. Each comparison has node, measure, analytical, measured, half_width and differs. With jq -e, this command prints true and exits 0 when no pair differs, and exits 1 when one does:

# Exit with an error when any reading differs from its formula
desflow explain check_against_theory.yaml --verify --replications 10 --json | jq -e '[.verification.comparisons[] | select(.differs)] | length == 0'

The JSON shape is experimental through 1.x, as the Changelog says.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text: Every pair says agrees for the shop above. When one says differs, read it as follows.

docs.title: Read a Difference
docs.text:
A pair that differs on a model the formulas describe points at the model: a wrong rate or unit, a task that holds its resource longer than its service, or a route that sends entities somewhere else.

Chance can also make a pair differ. A short run varies from one run to the next. With replications, each pair's 95% interval misses a correct value about 1 time in 20, so among many pairs one difference is expected now and then. Before looking for a defect, run the check again with more replications, a longer until or another seed.

Agreement shows the program computes what the model on paper says. It says nothing about whether the model is close enough to the real shop, which only a comparison with the shop's own records can show, as Checking a Model does.

docs.title: When the Formulas Do Not Apply
docs.text:
explain estimates a wait only where a formula holds, and gives the reason where none does. Two packers whose packing always takes 1 second have no closed formula:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/check_against_theory_constant.yaml:unsupported
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.5, spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1 s}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 2, max_cap: 4}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

desflow explain check_against_theory_constant.yaml prints the same reason under Not estimated.

docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory.py:unsupported
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.5, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1)
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=2, max_cap=4)
app.task("packing", "packers", name="pack_order")(lambda task_id: {})
packers = app.analyze().resources[0]
print(f"utilisation {packers.utilization}, status {packers.status}")
print(f"wait: {packers.wait_reason}")

The low-level API has no analysis: explain and analyze read a blueprint or a builder file. Write the model as a builder file to check it.

utilisation 0.75, status OK
wait: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times; run --verify to measure it

The utilisation is still known here, because it needs only the rates. The same rule applies to every model. The formulas hold in a plain network of queues: each task holds at most one resource, each queue serves first come, first served, and nothing blocks, removes, delays or reorders work. Anything else takes the formulas out of use, from the part of the model where it happens to the end of the flow:

  • a task's patience, balk, fail, keep, get, put, signal, subscribe, interrupt or on actions, preemption, or several resources held at once: that task and every task after it;
  • a wait other than a single request, such as a wait with two or more requests, or a request that a timeout of the same wait can end: that task and every task after it;
  • a resource's queue_limit, custom type or breakdowns: the tasks that use it and every task after them;
  • an unstable resource: every task after its tasks, though the resource itself keeps its utilisation and status;
  • a priority queue whose tasks have different priorities: its wait, and every task after its tasks;
  • a scenario step that changes a parameter, live ingress, or an add_process function: every arrival and every task;
  • a replayed arrival, a hand-written arrival loop or a next function: every rate they could change.

A task outside what the formulas cover has no rate, so each resource it uses has no utilisation, status or wait. Such a resource is not ranked as the bottleneck. When no resource has a utilisation, explain says that no bottleneck can be named, and why. Each unknown value is printed under Not estimated, with the first reason found.

One value is given but not compared. With one packer and gaps that are not exponential, such as constant or uniform gaps, Kingman's formula gives the wait only approximately, so explain shows it as an estimate. --verify marks that wait and the queue length not compared, because a correct model can differ from an approximation.

--verify still runs such a model and prints what it measures. It compares only the values the analysis gives. Every other row says not compared, with the reason, and a row whose measure did not happen in the run says no reading. The interval from replications is then the check, as the experiments of Checking a Model use it.

The script works out the waits by hand and verifies both the blueprint and the builder file:

docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory.py
"""Check Against Theory: a shop the queueing formulas describe, checked against them.

check_against_theory.yaml, and check_against_theory_shop.py in the builder, are one
packer with exponential gaps and packing times. The script works out the wait by hand,
verifies each form against `explain`'s analysis from Python, and shows a shop the
formulas do not cover, with the reason.
"""

import math
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import SimulationContext, load_context

BLUEPRINT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "yaml" / "check_against_theory.yaml"
SHOP = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "check_against_theory_shop.py"


def by_hand(packers: int, rate: float, service: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """The mean wait in the queue from the M/M/1 and M/M/c formulas."""
    load = rate * service  # packers' worth of work arriving each second
    utilisation = load / packers
    if packers == 1:
        return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * service  # M/M/1
    # M/M/c: Erlang C, the chance that every packer is busy, over (c / service - rate)
    last = load**packers / math.factorial(packers) / (1 - utilisation)
    busy = last / (sum(load**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(packers)) + last)
    return busy / (packers / service - rate)


def show(explanation):
    """Prints each pair of the verification: the formula's value and the runs'."""
    for c in explanation.verification.comparisons:
        result = "differs" if c.differs else "agrees"
        print(
            f"{c.node} {c.measure}: analysis {c.analytical:.3f}, "
            f"runs {c.measured:.3f} ± {c.half_width:.3f}, {result}"
        )


def verify():
    """The blueprint's one packer, verified with 10 runs from Python."""
    app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(BLUEPRINT)
    explanation = app.analyze(verify=True, replications=10)  # until from run.until
    show(explanation)
    return explanation


def verify_builder():
    """The builder file's one packer, verified with 10 runs from Python."""
    app = load_context(SHOP.parent, SHOP.name)  # a new copy for each run needs a file
    explanation = app.analyze(verify=True, until=20000, replications=10)
    show(explanation)
    return explanation


def unsupported():
    """Two packers whose packing always takes 1 second: no formula for the wait."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0)
    app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.5, spawn="pack_order")
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=2, max_cap=4)
    app.task("packing", "packers", name="pack_order")(lambda task_id: {})
    packers = app.analyze().resources[0]
    print(f"utilisation {packers.utilization}, status {packers.status}")
    print(f"wait: {packers.wait_reason}")
    return packers


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"one packer, an order every 1.33 s (rate 0.75): {by_hand(1, 0.75):.3f} s")
    print(f"two packers at 1.5 orders a second: {by_hand(2, 1.5):.3f} s")
    verify()
    verify_builder()
    unsupported()
docs/snippets/guides/check_against_theory_shop.py
"""Check Against Theory: the shop of check_against_theory.yaml as a builder file.

Check it with:
desflow explain check_against_theory_shop.py --verify --replications 10 --until 20000
"""

import os

from desflow import SimulationContext

# An order every 1.33 s on average (rate 0.75) with one packer; RATE=1.5 with PACKERS=2
rate = float(os.environ.get("RATE", "0.75"))
packers = int(os.environ.get("PACKERS", "1"))

app = (
    # warmup: seconds left out of every measure, while the queue fills
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42, warmup=2000)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=rate, spawn="pack_order")
    .add_service("packing", dist="exponential", rate=1)  # 1 second on average
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=4)
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=20000)

check_against_theory.py, in the YAML tab, verifies this file too, with verify_builder.

docs.title: Fit a Distribution
docs.text: Fit a column of your own measured times, such as the gaps between orders in an order log, and load the result into a model.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Fitting the Inputs fits the shop's packing times and checks what the choice changes.
  • Input Fitting describes every option and outcome.
  • Fitting needs the fit extra: pip install "desflow[fit]".

docs.title: Make the Column
docs.text:
A service is fitted to its durations. An arrival is fitted to the gaps between arrivals, not to the times they happened, so turn an order log's times into gaps first:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:gaps
with LOG.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    placed = [
        datetime.fromisoformat(row["placed_at"]) for row in csv.DictReader(handle)
    ]
# An arrival is fitted to the gaps between orders, not to the times themselves
return [
    (later - earlier).total_seconds() for earlier, later in zip(placed, placed[1:])
]

order_log.csv is an illustrative log of 300 orders placed one afternoon, with the time each was placed to a tenth of a second. Write the gaps to a CSV column to fit them with desflow fit instead.

docs.title: Fit It
docs.text:
State the unit and the bounds. The gaps are in seconds and none can be below 0:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:fit
result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics

On the command line, desflow fit gaps.csv --column gap_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --out fitted/orders.yaml does the same. The table for the 299 gaps:

299 rows: 299 used, 0 missing, 0 invalid
family            status              AIC  KS stat KS p (approx.)  parameters or reason
exponential *     fitted             1205  0.03517         0.8404  rate=0.36388
normal            fitted             1487   0.1707      4.359e-08  mean=2.74816, std=2.88857 (can draw below the lower bound 0)
lognormal         skipped                                          lognormal needs every value above 0; 5 are not
truncated_normal  did not fit                                      RuntimeError: Maximum number of function evaluations has been exceeded.
constant          skipped                                          the values are not all equal
uniform           rejected                                         its mean is 12.75, the data's is 2.748: more than 25% apart
triangular        rejected                                         its mean is 7.702, the data's is 2.748: more than 25% apart
gamma             skipped                                          gamma needs every value above 0; 5 are not
weibull           skipped                                          weibull needs every value above 0; 5 are not
empirical         fitted                                           values: 299 numbers
* best: exponential

docs.title: Read the Table
docs.text:
• Skipped families were not fitted, and the reason says why. Here the log's times are given to a tenth of a second, so some orders share a time, and 5 gaps are 0. gamma, weibull and lognormal need every value above 0, so they are skipped.
  • Did not fit means scipy's fit failed. Its message is the reason. Here the truncated normal's search did not settle, because the gaps are far from a normal shape.
  • Rejected families were fitted, but their mean or standard deviation is more than 25% from the data's, or a parameter is out of range. Here uniform and triangular reach far beyond most gaps.
  • Fitted families have an AIC, where lower is better, and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-value, which is approximate. The exponential has the lowest AIC and a p-value of 0.84. Its rate, rate: 0.36388, is one over the mean gap of 2.75 seconds: an order every 2.75 seconds on average. normal fits too, but it can draw below 0.

When two families' AIC are too close to tell them apart, as AIC and the KS Test explains, run the model with each and see whether the answer changes, as Fitting the Inputs does. Read --plot fit.png, or result.plot("fit.png"), as well as the table.

docs.title: Load It
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

Write the best fit with --out, or from Python:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:write
path = Path(folder) / "fitted" / "orders.yaml"
path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
path.write_text(result.yaml(source="order_log.csv, gaps between placed_at"))

and include it. An arrival also needs the task it spawns, so the include names the file and adds spawn:

docs/snippets/yaml/fit_a_distribution.yaml:include
arrivals:
  # The fitted gaps, with the task each order starts added to them
  orders: !include {file: fitted/orders.yaml, spawn: pack_order}

The file:

docs/snippets/yaml/fitted/orders.yaml
# Fitted by desflow fit from order_log.csv, gaps between placed_at: exponential, from 299 values in s, written in seconds.
dist: exponential
rate: 0.36388
docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:load
# The best fit's settings, such as dist="exponential", rate=0.4
.add_arrival("orders", **result.settings())
docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution_low_level.py:load
def params(result) -> SimParameter:
    """One packer, with the fitted arrivals."""
    return SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # The best fit's settings, such as dist="exponential", rate=0.4
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(**result.settings())},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="gamma", shape=4, scale=0.375)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2)},
    )

result.settings("normal") takes another fitted family instead of the best.

docs.title: When Nothing Fits
docs.text:
When every family is skipped, rejected or did not fit, the best is the empirical distribution: the data itself, which a run draws from at random. For many values, a histogram is shorter:

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py:empirical
result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", candidates=["empirical"], bins=10)

On the command line, the same is --candidates empirical --bins 10. An empirical distribution never draws a value outside the data's range, so it cannot produce a gap longer than the longest one in the log.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
Each form fits the gaps and runs the shop for an hour with the fitted arrivals. In that one run, one packer packs 1,302 orders in every form, because each uses the same seed, 42. The scripts read order_log.csv from their own folder, so run them in a clone of the repository:

# The scripts and the order log are in docs/snippets/guides/ of the repository
git clone https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow.git
cd desflow/docs/snippets/guides
python fit_a_distribution.py
python fit_a_distribution_low_level.py

For the blueprint, write fitted/orders.yaml first, with write or desflow fit --out, beside fit_a_distribution.yaml, then run desflow run fit_a_distribution.yaml.

docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution.py
"""Fit a Distribution: the gaps between orders in an order log, fitted and loaded.

order_log.csv is an illustrative log of 300 orders placed one afternoon, with the
time each was placed. The script turns the times into the gaps between orders,
fits them, prints the table of candidates, and runs the shop for an hour with the
fitted arrivals. `write` saves the settings for a blueprint's `!include`.
"""

import csv
import logging
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import SimulationContext, fit_column

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
LOG = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "order_log.csv"


def gaps():
    """The gaps between consecutive orders, in seconds."""
    with LOG.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        placed = [
            datetime.fromisoformat(row["placed_at"]) for row in csv.DictReader(handle)
        ]
    # An arrival is fitted to the gaps between orders, not to the times themselves
    return [
        (later - earlier).total_seconds() for earlier, later in zip(placed, placed[1:])
    ]


def fit():
    """Every family fitted to the gaps."""
    result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", lower=0)
    print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
    return result


def histogram():
    """The empirical alternative: the gaps as a histogram of 10 bins."""
    result = fit_column(gaps(), unit="s", candidates=["empirical"], bins=10)
    return result


def write(result, folder):
    """Writes the best fit where a blueprint includes it."""
    path = Path(folder) / "fitted" / "orders.yaml"
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text(result.yaml(source="order_log.csv, gaps between placed_at"))
    return path


def shop(result) -> SimulationContext:
    """One packer, with the fitted arrivals."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("packing", dist="gamma", shape=4, scale=0.375)
        # The best fit's settings, such as dist="exponential", rate=0.4
        .add_arrival("orders", **result.settings())
        .with_stats("basic")
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_loop(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app = shop(fit())
    app.run(until="1 h")
    finished = app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished"]
    print(f"orders packed in an hour: {finished}")
docs/snippets/guides/fit_a_distribution_low_level.py
"""The Fit a Distribution guide, low-level API: the shop with arrivals fitted to an
order log.

python fit_a_distribution_low_level.py fits the gaps between the orders in
order_log.csv, as fit_a_distribution.py does, and runs the shop for an hour with the
fitted arrivals. It prints the number of orders packed.
"""

import asyncio
import itertools
import queue

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)
from fit_a_distribution import fit


class Count:
    """An egress that counts the orders packed."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.packed = 0

    async def run(self, egress_queue):
        try:
            while True:
                try:
                    for record in egress_queue.get_nowait():
                        value = record["value"]
                        self.packed += value.get("event_type") == "order_packed"
                except queue.Empty:
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            pass


def params(result) -> SimParameter:
    """One packer, with the fitted arrivals."""
    return SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # The best fit's settings, such as dist="exponential", rate=0.4
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(**result.settings())},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="gamma", shape=4, scale=0.375)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2)},
    )


def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(key, {"event_type": "order_packed"}, "pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def run(result, until: float = 3600) -> int:
    """Runs the shop for an hour and returns the number of orders packed."""
    count = Count()
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params(result))
    env.setup_egress([count])
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    env.run(until=until)
    env.teardown()  # waits until the sink has taken every batch
    return count.packed


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"orders packed in an hour: {run(fit())}")

docs.title: Test a Model
docs.text: Write tests for a model that run with pytest and fail when a change breaks it. This page writes three kinds: a functional test of what the model does when an input changes, a unit test of one component on its own, and a back test against results saved from an earlier run.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Checking a Model checks the shop by hand, against observed values and against Little's law.
  • Checking and Validating says what each check proves.
  • The three kinds of test follow the Tests chapter of the HSMA book on discrete event simulation.
  • You need pytest: pip install pytest.

docs.title: Build a Model to Test
docs.text:
A test changes one input and runs the model again, so write the model as a function of its inputs and return the numbers a test reads. This shop takes the number of packers, the order rate and the seed. results runs ten minutes of it. A blueprint reads its inputs from variables, so the YAML form sets them before it loads the blueprint:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/test_a_model.yaml:shop
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: ${SEED:-42}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: "${PACKERS:-2}", max_cap: 10}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: "${RATE:-0.5}", spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

stats: {level: typical, interval: 600}

run:
  until: 600

shop sets the variables and loads the blueprint, and results runs it:

docs/snippets/guides/test_a_model_yaml.py:shop
def shop(packers=2, rate=0.5, seed=42) -> SimulationContext:
    """The blueprint, with its inputs set through the variables it reads."""
    inputs = {"PACKERS": str(packers), "RATE": str(rate), "SEED": str(seed)}
    with patch.dict(os.environ, inputs):  # restored when the blueprint is loaded
        return SimulationContext.from_yaml(BLUEPRINT)


def results(**inputs) -> dict:
    """Runs ten minutes of the shop and returns the orders packed and the mean wait."""
    app = shop(**inputs)
    app.run()  # until 600, from the blueprint
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": readings[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": round(readings[name("wait_mean")], 6),
    }
docs/snippets/guides/test_a_model.py:shop
def shop(packers=2, rate=0.5, seed=42) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with `packers` packers and orders at `rate` a second."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=seed)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=rate)

def pack_order(env, packers, task_id):

docs.title: Write a Functional Test
docs.text:
The tests call only results, so they are the same in the file of every form. A functional test checks that the model behaves as expected when an input changes. Add packers and the mean wait must fall, so run one, two and three packers and compare the three waits:

docs/snippets/guides/test_a_model.py:functional
def test_more_packers_shorten_the_wait():
    """A functional test: change one input and check the output moves the right way."""
    waits = [results(packers=packers)["wait_mean"] for packers in (1, 2, 3)]
    assert waits[0] > waits[1] > waits[2]

The test asserts the direction of the change, not the waits themselves. The waits are 2.055, 0.111 and 0.016 seconds, from one 10-minute run each of this shop, not the busy hour of the tutorials. A test of the direction still passes when a change to the model moves them a little.

docs.title: Write a Unit Test
docs.text:
A unit test checks one component alone. A distribution refuses a rate of 0, which would mean no orders ever. It also refuses a negative time to pack. DistributionConfig raises ValueError for each. pytest.mark.parametrize runs one test for each setting:

docs/snippets/guides/test_a_model.py:unit
@pytest.mark.parametrize(
    "settings",
    [
        {"dist": "exponential", "rate": 0},  # no orders ever
        {"dist": "constant", "value": -1},  # a negative time to pack
    ],
)
def test_a_distribution_that_cannot_happen_is_refused(settings):
    """A unit test: one component, alone, refuses an input that means nothing."""
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        DistributionConfig(**settings)

docs.title: Write a Back Test
docs.text:
A back test checks that the code gives the results an earlier version of it gave, with the same inputs and the same seed. Save the results once, and the test compares every later run with the file:

docs/snippets/guides/test_a_model.py:back
def test_results_match_the_saved_run():
    """A back test: the code reproduces what an earlier version of it produced."""
    assert results() == json.loads(SAVED.read_text())

The saved file holds 319 orders packed and a mean wait of 0.110574 seconds for two packers, written by save_results:

docs/snippets/guides/test_a_model.py:save
def save_results():
    """Saves the results the back test compares with."""
    SAVED.write_text(json.dumps(results(), indent=2) + "\n")

A back test fails on any change to the results, so a failure is either a fault or an intended change. Review the change. If it is intended, run save_results and commit the new file with the change that caused it.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
The back test needs the saved results, so write them once from the folder of the file:

python -c "import test_a_model; test_a_model.save_results()"

pytest collects the test_ functions of a file whose name starts with test_:

pytest test_a_model.py

The YAML form is test_a_model_yaml.py, with test_a_model.yaml beside it, and the low-level form is test_a_model_low_level.py. Each passes the same tests against the same saved file, because the three forms give the same results.
