docs.title: Runnable Examples
docs.text:
Each example is a complete model that you can download with desflow examples get and run, as Get an Example shows. Each is written three ways: as a YAML blueprint, with the builder API and with the low-level API. Its page shows the versions in tabs.

Example What it covers Local Simulation prints events and telemetry, with no container Kafka Digital Twin takes updates from Kafka and publishes events and telemetry to Kafka Fast-Forward to Parquet data generated unpaced at factor=0.0: a week written to Parquet Fast-Forward to Iceberg data generated unpaced at factor=0.0: a day appended to an Iceberg table PostgreSQL writes orders to PostgreSQL and takes updates from a table Redis writes to a Redis Stream and takes updates from Pub/Sub Parquet History, Kafka Live backdated history to Parquet, then live to Kafka Related Records orders and their line items, in two PostgreSQL tables

Each example page says how to download and run it, and which odctl profile from Services for the Examples it needs. desflow examples get prints the extra an example needs, and pip install "desflow[all]" installs every extra, so each example runs once its profile is up.

desflow examples list prints every example in the terminal, with the odctl profile each one needs. The list also has the shop examples, such as stock and breakdowns, which are shown on the page that teaches their feature. desflow examples get NAME downloads the files of the release you installed into NAME/yaml/, NAME/builder/ and NAME/low-level/. --api keeps one version, --dest downloads into another folder, --ref names another tag or branch, such as main, and --force replaces files that are already there:

desflow examples list
desflow examples get local --api yaml --dest work

The second command writes work/local/yaml/local.yaml.

docs.title: Services for the Examples
docs.text:
Every example that needs a broker, a database or an object store gets it from odctl, a separate CLI that manages curated Docker Compose stacks. Install it once:

# With uv
uv tool install "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# Or with pip
pip install "odctl>=1.0,<2"

odctl list -d shows every profile and the ports it publishes. The examples here use five of them: kafka-lite, postgres, valkey, storage and catalog.

docs.title: Starting a Profile
docs.text:
Each example needs at most one odctl profile. Start the profile before you run the example, and stop it afterwards:

Example Start Stop every example that desflow examples marks (no service), such as local, parquet and stock nothing needed kafka, backfill-live odctl up kafka-lite odctl down kafka-lite --volumes postgres, related-records odctl up postgres odctl down postgres --volumes redis odctl up valkey odctl down valkey --volumes parquet with PARQUET_FILESYSTEM=s3 odctl up storage odctl down storage --volumes iceberg odctl up catalog odctl down catalog --volumes

An example's YAML version needs the same profile as its builder version: desflow examples get <name> prints the profile with the run command.

The Kafka and Redis profiles are not named after their service. odctl's one-broker Kafka profile is kafka-lite and its three-broker Kafka profile is kafka-full. odctl runs Valkey in place of Redis, so its Redis profile is valkey. The Kafka examples run on either Kafka profile, because both publish a broker at 127.0.0.1:9092.

docs.title: Endpoints These Profiles Publish
docs.text:
These are the addresses the examples use. Every profile publishes on your machine only, on 127.0.0.1. Use that address rather than localhost, which macOS resolves to the IPv6 address ::1 first, where nothing listens.

Profile Service Address the examples use kafka-lite Kafka, one broker, with the Karapace schema registry 127.0.0.1:9092; schema registry http://127.0.0.1:8081 kafka-full Kafka, three brokers, with the same schema registry 127.0.0.1:9092,127.0.0.1:9093,127.0.0.1:9094; schema registry http://127.0.0.1:8081 postgres PostgreSQL, database odctl postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl valkey Valkey (Redis protocol) redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0 storage S3-compatible object store, bucket odctl-dev http://127.0.0.1:8333, access key user, secret key password catalog Iceberg REST catalog, warehouse s3://warehouse/ http://127.0.0.1:8181

odctl list -d shows every port a profile publishes.

docs.title: Related Records
docs.text:
Related records are rows that belong together across tables. Here every customer order has 1 to 5 line items with random products, prices and quantities, and a total computed from them. The orders and their items are written to two PostgreSQL tables, orders and order_items. Each tab shows the example written one way. In YAML a mapping payload is a constant and cannot hold random values, so the order generator is a Python process in postgres_orders_logic.py, referenced with !python. Call Python from YAML explains how references work. The connection string names odctl, the database that the odctl postgres profile creates, with the user user and the password password.

Look for each order's line items in order_items, with the same order_id as the order's row in orders, and for a total_amount that is the sum of its items.

What It Does

When the run starts, each PostgresEgress creates its table, orders or order_items, and PostgresIngress creates simulation_params, if they do not exist. The run then writes orders and their items until you stop it. Both egresses receive every record. Each keeps only the records whose __table__ key names its table.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: The example needs Docker and the odctl profile postgres, which each Quick Start below starts and stops. Services for the Examples shows how to install odctl.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

cd related-records/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up postgres

# 4. Run it (Ctrl + C to stop)
desflow run postgres_orders.yaml

# 5. Stop its service when finished
odctl down postgres --volumes

docs.title: Change a Parameter Live
docs.text:
While the run goes, raise the arrival rate from a second terminal. The command is the same for every form:

# Change the order arrival rate of the running simulation
docker exec -it postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "INSERT INTO simulation_params (path, value) VALUES ('Shop.arrival.orders.rate', '5.0');"

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
The three tabs write the same records, which a test checks by running each version unpaced. A real run writes each order as a row of orders and each line item as a row of order_items. desflow run postgres_orders.yaml --sample 2 --stdout prints the first two records as JSON lines instead, with no database. They are the one line item of orders-1, then the order itself:

{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":1.276,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":null,"instance":null,"value":{"order_item_id":1,"order_id":1,"product_id":22,"quantity":3,"unit_price":27.56}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":1.276,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":null,"instance":null,"value":{"order_id":1,"customer_id":86,"total_amount":82.68,"status":"pending"}}

This command leaves out the __table__ key that picks each record's table, because only a PostgreSQL sink uses it. It logs a warning that says so. The order's total_amount is its item's quantity times its unit_price.

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/advanced/postgres_orders.yaml
# Orders with random line items, in YAML with one Python function.
#
# Each order arrival builds an order with 1 to 5 items, random prices and
# quantities, and a total computed from them. A mapping payload is a constant and
# cannot hold random values, so the generator is Python in postgres_orders_logic.py
# beside this file, referenced with !python. Everything else is plain YAML.
#
# Two PostgresEgress instances are attached, one per table, and each keeps only the
# records whose __table__ key names its table. Each creates its table at start.
#
# Needs a database: odctl up postgres. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run postgres_orders.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

ingress:
  - type: Postgres
    config:
      connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
      table_name: simulation_params

egress:
  - type: Postgres
    config:
      connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
      tables:
        orders:
          columns:
            order_id: INT
            customer_id: INT
            total_amount: REAL
            status: TEXT
            timestamp: TIMESTAMP
          primary_key: order_id

    config:
      connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
      tables:
        order_items:
          columns:
            order_item_id: INT
            order_id: INT
            product_id: INT
            quantity: INT
            unit_price: REAL
          primary_key: order_item_id

arrivals:
  # No spawn: the process below waits on this arrival itself.
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.0}

processes:
  # Called as order_generator(context, arrival="orders", max_items=5).
  - function: !python postgres_orders_logic.order_generator

"""Python for postgres_orders.yaml: an order generator with random line items."""


def order_generator(context, arrival: str, max_items: int):
    """Publishes an order and its items on every arrival.

    Draws from `context.sampler.rng`, the random number generator seeded by
    `random_seed`, so a seeded run repeats the same orders. The `__table__` key
    names the table each record is written to.
    """
    rng = context.sampler.rng
    order_id = 1
    item_id = 1
    while True:
        # The order's key, such as orders-1, is the record key of all its records
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)

        total = 0.0
        for _ in range(int(rng.integers(1, max_items + 1))):
            price = round(float(rng.uniform(10.0, 50.0)), 2)
            quantity = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
            total += price * quantity
            context.env.publish_event(
                entity.key,
                {
                    "__table__": "order_items",
                    "order_item_id": item_id,
                    "order_id": order_id,
                    "product_id": int(rng.integers(1, 51)),
                    "quantity": quantity,
                    "unit_price": price,
                },
            )
            item_id += 1

        context.env.publish_event(
            entity.key,
            {
                "__table__": "orders",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "customer_id": int(rng.integers(1, 101)),
                "total_amount": round(total, 2),
                "status": "pending",
            },
        )
        order_id += 1

"""
Orders with line items, builder API.

The builder version of `yaml/advanced/postgres_orders.yaml`. Each order arrival
builds an order with 1 to 5 items, random prices and quantities, and a total computed
from them. Two PostgresEgress instances are attached, one per table, and each keeps
only the records whose `__table__` key names its table. Each creates its table at
start.

Needs a database: odctl up postgres. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
Set EXAMPLE_UNTIL to a number of simulation seconds to end the run at that time instead.
"""

import logging
import os

from desflow import PostgresEgress, PostgresIngress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

DSN = "postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl"

ORDERS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_id": "INT",
        "customer_id": "INT",
        "total_amount": "REAL",
        "status": "TEXT",
        "timestamp": "TIMESTAMP",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_id",
}
ORDER_ITEMS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_item_id": "INT",
        "order_id": "INT",
        "product_id": "INT",
        "quantity": "INT",
        "unit_price": "REAL",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_item_id",
}


def order_generator(context: SimulationContext, arrival: str, max_items: int):
    """Publishes an order and its items on every arrival.

    Draws from `context.sampler.rng`, the random number generator seeded by
    `random_seed`, so a seeded run repeats the same orders. The `__table__` key
    names the table each record is written to.
    """
    rng = context.sampler.rng
    order_id = 1
    item_id = 1
    while True:
        # The order's key, such as orders-1, is the record key of all its records
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)

        total = 0.0
        for _ in range(int(rng.integers(1, max_items + 1))):
            price = round(float(rng.uniform(10.0, 50.0)), 2)
            quantity = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
            total += price * quantity
            context.env.publish_event(
                entity.key,
                {
                    "__table__": "order_items",
                    "order_item_id": item_id,
                    "order_id": order_id,
                    "product_id": int(rng.integers(1, 51)),
                    "quantity": quantity,
                    "unit_price": price,
                },
            )
            item_id += 1

        context.env.publish_event(
            entity.key,
            {
                "__table__": "orders",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "customer_id": int(rng.integers(1, 101)),
                "total_amount": round(total, 2),
                "status": "pending",
            },
        )
        order_id += 1


app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_ingress(PostgresIngress(DSN, table_name="simulation_params"))
    .add_egress(PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"orders": ORDERS}))
    .add_egress(PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"order_items": ORDER_ITEMS}))
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.0)
    .add_process(order_generator, arrival="orders", max_items=5)
)

# The simulation time, in seconds, at which the run ends.
# When EXAMPLE_UNTIL is not set, the run goes on until Ctrl + C.
EXAMPLE_UNTIL = float(os.getenv("EXAMPLE_UNTIL") or 0) or None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=EXAMPLE_UNTIL)
examples/low-level/postgres_orders_example.py
"""
Orders with line items, low-level API.

The low-level version of `builder/postgres_orders_example.py` and
`yaml/advanced/postgres_orders.yaml`. It wires `DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`, the
registry and the connectors by hand. With the same seed it publishes the same orders
as the other two.

Needs a database: odctl up postgres. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
Set EXAMPLE_UNTIL to a number of simulation seconds to end the run at that time instead.
"""

import logging
import os

import numpy as np

from desflow import (
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    PostgresEgress,
    PostgresIngress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

DSN = "postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl"

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.0)},
)

ORDERS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_id": "INT",
        "customer_id": "INT",
        "total_amount": "REAL",
        "status": "TEXT",
        "timestamp": "TIMESTAMP",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_id",
}
ORDER_ITEMS = {
    "columns": {
        "order_item_id": "INT",
        "order_id": "INT",
        "product_id": "INT",
        "quantity": "INT",
        "unit_price": "REAL",
    },
    "primary_key": "order_item_id",
}


def order_generator(env, sampler: Sampler, max_items: int):
    """Publishes an order and its items on every arrival.

    The gaps come from the arrival's own random sequence and the order contents from
    `sampler.rng`, as in the builder version, so the two publish the same records.
    """
    rng = sampler.rng
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    order_id = 1
    item_id = 1
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))

        total = 0.0
        for _ in range(int(rng.integers(1, max_items + 1))):
            price = round(float(rng.uniform(10.0, 50.0)), 2)
            quantity = int(rng.integers(1, 4))
            total += price * quantity
            env.publish_event(
                f"orders-{order_id}",
                {
                    "__table__": "order_items",
                    "order_item_id": item_id,
                    "order_id": order_id,
                    "product_id": int(rng.integers(1, 51)),
                    "quantity": quantity,
                    "unit_price": price,
                },
            )
            item_id += 1

        env.publish_event(
            f"orders-{order_id}",
            {
                "__table__": "orders",
                "order_id": order_id,
                "customer_id": int(rng.integers(1, 101)),
                "total_amount": round(total, 2),
                "status": "pending",
            },
        )
        order_id += 1


# The simulation time, in seconds, at which the run ends.
# When EXAMPLE_UNTIL is not set, the run goes on until Ctrl + C.
EXAMPLE_UNTIL = float(os.getenv("EXAMPLE_UNTIL") or 0) or None


def run(until=None, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, strict=False)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_ingress([PostgresIngress(DSN, table_name="simulation_params")])
    env.setup_egress(
        [
            PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"orders": ORDERS}),
            PostgresEgress(DSN, tables={"order_items": ORDER_ITEMS}),
        ]
    )
    sampler = Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, max_items=5))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(until=EXAMPLE_UNTIL)

docs.title: Parquet History, Kafka Live
docs.text: One run writes ten minutes of backdated history to Parquet. It then publishes to Kafka in real time, and this second part is the live tail. Look for the history's Parquet files in data/backfill/, then for the Logical clock reached go-live line in the log, after which records reach Kafka at the pace of the wall clock. Each tab shows the example written one way. The sections after the tabs show the records, and explain why one run is better than two, how the settings fit together and what to get right.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: The example needs Docker and the odctl profile kafka-lite, which each Quick Start below starts and stops. Services for the Examples shows how to install odctl.

docs.title: Run It
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

This example builds the simulation of the Builder tab from a YAML blueprint, with no Python. Until go_live_at the run is unpaced and writes backdated history to Parquet. From go_live_at it is paced in real time and publishes to Kafka.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install "desflow[kafka,parquet]" --with-executables-from "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get backfill-live --api yaml
cd backfill-live/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain backfill_live.yaml

# 4. Start its service
odctl up kafka-lite

# 5. Run it
desflow run backfill_live.yaml

# 6. Stop its service when finished
odctl down kafka-lite --volumes

# 1. Install
pip install "desflow[kafka,parquet]" "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get backfill-live --api yaml
cd backfill-live/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain backfill_live.yaml

# 4. Start its service
odctl up kafka-lite

# 5. Run it
desflow run backfill_live.yaml

# 6. Stop its service when finished
odctl down kafka-lite --volumes

What It Does

Ten minutes of history are written to data/backfill/ within the first second, then the run publishes to sim-events and sim-telemetry in real time for 60 seconds and ends. The history folder is created on the first write, and KafkaEgress creates the two topics when it starts.

logical_start_time: -10m and go_live_at: now are both read against one moment, the time the file is loaded, so they are exactly ten minutes apart. until: 11m then adds one minute of live tail. when: history sends the records stamped before go_live_at to Parquet, and when: live sends the rest to Kafka.

examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py backdates the clock by ten minutes, writes those ten minutes to Parquet in well under a second, then publishes to Kafka in real time for sixty seconds. HISTORY_MINUTES and LIVE_SECONDS set the length of the two halves. A day of history (HISTORY_MINUTES=1440) is about 128,000 events.

# 4. Run it
uv run --no-project --with "desflow[kafka,parquet]" backfill_live_example.py

docs.title: Get Two Details Right
docs.text:
Predicates compare times read from the timestamp. A record carries its logical time as an ISO string with its zone offset, such as +00:00. GO_LIVE_AT is a datetime, and Python cannot compare a string with a datetime, so record["timestamp"] >= GO_LIVE_AT raises a TypeError. Read the string with datetime.fromisoformat and compare the two instants. The comparison is correct whatever zone each side is written in. Cut the go-live instant to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live millisecond counts as live. Take the instant with datetime.now(timezone.utc): a datetime without an offset is read in the run's timezone, else in the zone of logical_start_time, else in UTC, not in the machine's local time.

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/backfill_live.yaml:clock
logical_start_time: -10m
# From here the same run is paced at one simulated second per real second.
go_live_at: now
examples/yaml/backfill_live.yaml:split
egress:
  - type: Parquet
    config:
      default_path: data/backfill/events.parquet
    # Records stamped before go_live_at.
    when: history
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      event_topic: sim-events
      telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
      bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
    # Records stamped at or after go_live_at.
    when: live

A blueprint needs no predicate. when: history and when: live compare each record's timestamp with go_live_at.

examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py:clock
GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

# Records carry their logical time as an ISO string with its zone offset, so the
# predicates that split the two sinks read it as a time and compare instants.
examples/low-level/backfill_live_example.py:clock
GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

Before go_live_at, only batch_size decides when the history is flushed. flush_interval has no effect yet. The interval flush is a simulation process. It starts only if factor is non-zero when the egress is set up. This run starts at factor=0.0, so before go-live, records leave the buffer only when it fills to batch_size. batch_size therefore sets the number of Parquet files. The interval flush starts at go-live, so the live tail also flushes every flush_interval. flush_interval therefore decides how often Kafka receives records. Give each sink its own batch_size and flush_interval to separate those two jobs:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/backfill_live_per_sink.yaml:per-sink
- type: Parquet
  config: {default_path: data/backfill/events.parquet}
  when: history
  batch_size: 200000
- type: Kafka
  config: {bootstrap_servers: 127.0.0.1:9092}
  when: live
  batch_size: 500
  flush_interval: 1.0
docs/snippets/pages/backfill_live.py:per-sink
app.add_egress(parquet, when=is_history, batch_size=200_000)
app.add_egress(kafka, when=is_live, batch_size=500, flush_interval=1.0)
docs/snippets/pages/backfill_live.py:per-sink-low-level
env.setup_egress(
    [parquet, kafka],
    predicates=[is_history, is_live],
    batch_sizes=[200_000, 500],
    flush_intervals=[None, 1.0],  # None: the flush_interval of setup_egress
)

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
The three tabs publish the same records, which a test checks by running each version unpaced. A real run writes the records stamped before go_live_at to Parquet files under data/backfill/, and the rest to sim-events and sim-telemetry. desflow run backfill_live.yaml --sample 4 --stdout prints the first four events as JSON lines instead, unpaced and with no broker:

{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.552,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.552,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"started"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.696,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack_order","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":2.696,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack_order","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"started"}}

Each timestamp is shown as ..., because it changes with every run. It is the start of the history plus sim_ts, so these records are stamped before go_live_at and belong to the history.

During the live tail the run can look as if it has stopped responding. History finishes within the first second of the run. After the Logical clock reached go-live line, the run logs at most one more line, the Kafka producer's connection line, until it shuts down. From go_live_at the run waits on the wall clock, as any live run does. The Logical clock reached go-live line confirms the switch.

Go Live explains why one run replaces two and how logical_start_time, go_live_at and when work together.

docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/backfill_live.yaml
# Backfill then go live in one run, in YAML.
#
# The YAML version of backfill_live_example.py, which --api builder downloads. Until
# go_live_at the clock is detached from the wall clock, so ten minutes of backdated
# shop orders are written to Parquet as fast as the machine allows. From go_live_at
# the run is paced at one simulated second per real second, and the same events go
# to Kafka for one minute.
#
# Needs a broker: odctl up kafka-lite.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run backfill_live.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  # Unpaced to begin with, so the history costs no real time.
  factor: 0.0
  random_seed: 42
  logical_start_time: -10m
  # From here the same run is paced at one simulated second per real second.
  go_live_at: now

egress:
  - type: Parquet
    config:
      default_path: data/backfill/events.parquet
    # Records stamped before go_live_at.
    when: history
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      event_topic: sim-events
      telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
      bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
    # Records stamped at or after go_live_at.
    when: live

# Only batch_size decides when the history is flushed. The interval flush starts at
# go-live, so the live tail also flushes every 10 seconds.
batching:
  batch_size: 2000
  flush_interval: 10.0

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}

arrivals:
  # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {path_id: Shop.service.packing, status: finished}

# The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds.
stats: {level: minimal, interval: 30}

run:
  # Ten minutes of history, then one minute of live tail.
  until: 11m

Scripts live in the examples/ folder of the repository, and the label on the block below is this one's path there.

examples/builder/backfill_live_example.py
"""
Backfill-then-live Example.

One run produces both halves of a tiered dataset. Until `go_live_at` the clock is
detached from the wall clock, so ten minutes of backdated shop orders are written to
Parquet as fast as the machine allows. From `go_live_at` the same run is paced at one
simulated second per real second, and the same events are published to Kafka as they
happen. Doing this in two processes would mean repeating the seed and the start
instant in both, and keeping them in step by hand.
"""

import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from desflow import (
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    KafkaEgress,
    ParquetStorageEgress,
    SimulationContext,
)

# Logging is configured here rather than in a wrapper, because this script is run
# directly. Without it the run produces no output at all.
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = os.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "127.0.0.1:9092")
EVENT_TOPIC = "sim-events"
TELEMETRY_TOPIC = "sim-telemetry"

# How much history to generate, and how long to keep tailing once live. The live half
# costs real time, second for second, so it is short by default.
HISTORY = timedelta(minutes=float(os.getenv("HISTORY_MINUTES", "10")))
LIVE_SECONDS = float(os.getenv("LIVE_SECONDS", "60"))

base_path = os.getenv("DEST_PATH", "data/backfill")

# The go-live instant is now, so everything before it is history and everything after
# it is the live tail. These sit at module scope because the builder below needs them,
# and the builder has to stay at module scope for the decorators to attach to it.
GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

# Records carry their logical time as an ISO string with its zone offset, so the
# predicates that split the two sinks read it as a time and compare instants.


def is_history(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped before the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) < GO_LIVE_AT


def is_live(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped at or after the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) >= GO_LIVE_AT


def history_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
    """Drops telemetry and flattens the event payload, as Parquet needs flat rows."""
    if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
        return None

    if isinstance(data.get("value"), dict):
        data.update(data.pop("value"))

    return f"{base_path}/events.parquet"


# ==========================================
# 1. Infrastructure Builder
# ==========================================
app = (
    SimulationContext(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # Unpaced to begin with, so the history costs no real time.
        factor=0.0,
        random_seed=42,
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
        # From here the same run is paced at one simulated second per real second.
        go_live_at=GO_LIVE_AT,
    )
    .add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(path_router=history_router), when=is_history)
    .add_egress(
        KafkaEgress(
            event_topic=EVENT_TOPIC,
            telemetry_topic=TELEMETRY_TOPIC,
            bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
        ),
        when=is_live,
    )
    # Only batch_size decides when the history is flushed. The interval flush is a
    # simulation process, started only when factor is non-zero as the egress is set up,
    # and this run starts at 0.0. The interval flush starts at go-live, so the live
    # tail also flushes every 10 seconds.
    .with_batching(batch_size=2000, flush_interval=10.0)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)
    # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    # The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds
    .with_stats("minimal", interval=30.0)
)


# ==========================================
# 2. Simulation Logic
# ==========================================
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, context):
    """Returns the flat payload that both sinks receive for a finished task."""
    return {"path_id": "Shop.service.packing", "status": "finished"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_generator(context):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, context, entity=entity))
        task_id += 1


# ==========================================
# 3. Execution
# ==========================================
def run():
    """Generates the history instantly, then tails live for LIVE_SECONDS."""
    os.makedirs(base_path, exist_ok=True)

    try:
        admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, max_tasks=100)
        admin.create_topics(
            topics_config=[
                {"name": EVENT_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
                {"name": TELEMETRY_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
            ]
        )
        time.sleep(2)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Could not explicitly create topics: {e}")

    logger.info(
        "Backfilling from %s to %s into '%s/', then tailing live to Kafka for %.0fs.",
        LOGICAL_START_TIME.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        GO_LIVE_AT.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        base_path,
        LIVE_SECONDS,
    )

    app.run(until=HISTORY.total_seconds() + LIVE_SECONDS)

    logger.info("Run complete. History is in '%s/', the tail is in Kafka.", base_path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

examples/low-level/backfill_live_example.py
"""
Backfill-then-live Example, low-level API.

The low-level version of `builder/backfill_live_example.py`. One run produces both
halves of a tiered dataset. Until `go_live_at` the clock is detached from the wall
clock, so ten minutes of backdated shop orders are written to Parquet as fast as the
machine allows. From `go_live_at` the same run is paced at one simulated second per
real second, and the same events are published to Kafka as they happen.
"""

import logging
import os
import time
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import numpy as np

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    KafkaEgress,
    ParquetStorageEgress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = os.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "127.0.0.1:9092")
EVENT_TOPIC = "sim-events"
TELEMETRY_TOPIC = "sim-telemetry"

HISTORY = timedelta(minutes=float(os.getenv("HISTORY_MINUTES", "10")))
LIVE_SECONDS = float(os.getenv("LIVE_SECONDS", "60"))
base_path = os.getenv("DEST_PATH", "data/backfill")

GO_LIVE_AT = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
# Cut to milliseconds, as timestamps are, so a record stamped in the go-live
# millisecond is live
GO_LIVE_AT = GO_LIVE_AT.replace(microsecond=GO_LIVE_AT.microsecond // 1000 * 1000)
LOGICAL_START_TIME = GO_LIVE_AT - HISTORY

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10)},
)


def is_history(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped before the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) < GO_LIVE_AT


def is_live(record: dict) -> bool:
    """True for records stamped at or after the go-live instant."""
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) >= GO_LIVE_AT


def history_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
    """Drops telemetry and flattens the event payload, as Parquet needs flat rows."""
    if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
        return None
    if isinstance(data.get("value"), dict):
        data.update(data.pop("value"))
    return f"{base_path}/events.parquet"


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """What @app.task does: queued, started, the service time, then finished."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key,
        {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"},
        task="pack_order",
        instance=task_id,
    )
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # counted as in progress
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"},
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            {"path_id": path_id, "status": "finished"},
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run():
    """Generates the history instantly, then tails live for LIVE_SECONDS."""
    os.makedirs(base_path, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, max_tasks=100)
        admin.create_topics(
            topics_config=[
                {"name": EVENT_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
                {"name": TELEMETRY_TOPIC, "partitions": 1},
            ]
        )
        time.sleep(2)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Could not explicitly create topics: {e}")

    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(
        factor=0.0,  # unpaced, so the history costs no real time
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
        go_live_at=GO_LIVE_AT,  # from here, one simulated second per real second
        strict=False,  # a live run goes on when a slow sink makes it fall behind
    )
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(
        [
            ParquetStorageEgress(path_router=history_router),
            KafkaEgress(
                event_topic=EVENT_TOPIC,
                telemetry_topic=TELEMETRY_TOPIC,
                bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
            ),
        ],
        batch_size=2000,
        flush_interval=10.0,
        predicates=[is_history, is_live],  # matched to the providers by position
    )
    # The packers' readings every 30 simulation seconds
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=30.0)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))
    env.process(arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers))

    logger.info(
        "Backfilling from %s to %s into '%s/', then tailing live to Kafka for %.0fs.",
        LOGICAL_START_TIME.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        GO_LIVE_AT.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        base_path,
        LIVE_SECONDS,
    )
    try:
        env.run(until=HISTORY.total_seconds() + LIVE_SECONDS)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    logger.info("Run complete. History is in '%s/', the tail is in Kafka.", base_path)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: Fast-Forward to Iceberg
docs.text:
This example generates a day of a shop's orders at factor=0.0 and appends them to an Apache Iceberg table through an Iceberg REST catalog. Write to Iceberg Tables shows the other catalogs. Each tab shows the example written one way: as a YAML blueprint, with the builder API, or with the low-level API. Ways to write a simulation compares the three.

ParquetStorageEgress writes files and leaves registering them as a table to you. IcebergStorageEgress appends into an Iceberg table instead, so one run ends with a table another engine can query. Look for the day's events as rows of simulation.events, and for the few snapshots that hold them.

Each flush of the buffer is one Iceberg commit. Every commit writes a manifest, a manifest list and a new metadata.json, so query planning slows down as snapshots build up. This example therefore gives the Iceberg egress a large batch_size of its own. At factor=0.0 the buffer is flushed each time it holds 200,000 records, and once more at the end of the run. Each flush adds one snapshot to the table.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: The example needs Docker and the odctl profile catalog, which each Quick Start below starts and stops. Services for the Examples shows how to install odctl.

docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

This example builds the simulation of the builder example in the Builder tab from a YAML blueprint, with no Python. A day of shop orders is generated at factor: 0.0, and each flush of the buffer becomes one Iceberg commit.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install "desflow[iceberg]" --with-executables-from "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get iceberg --api yaml
cd iceberg/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain iceberg.yaml

# 4. Start its service
odctl up catalog

# 5. Run it
desflow run iceberg.yaml

# 6. Stop its service when finished
odctl down catalog --volumes

# 1. Install
pip install "desflow[iceberg]" "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get iceberg --api yaml
cd iceberg/yaml

# 3. Find the bottleneck, with no run
desflow explain iceberg.yaml

# 4. Start its service
odctl up catalog

# 5. Run it
desflow run iceberg.yaml

# 6. Stop its service when finished
odctl down catalog --volumes

What It Does

The run appends a day of lifecycle events to the simulation.events table and ends on its own. With batch_size: 200000 on the egress, the buffer is flushed once per 200,000 records, and each flush is one commit. The day therefore lands in a few snapshots. Without a router, each event is written to default_table as one flat row, and telemetry is left out.

The catalog is contacted on the first write, not when the blueprint is loaded, so a blueprint with a wrong catalog address still loads and fails when the first batch is written.

ICEBERG_URI, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE, S3_ENDPOINT, S3_ACCESS_KEY, S3_SECRET_KEY and S3_REGION override the catalog and credentials.

This version builds the simulation with the builder API (SimulationContext) and writes with IcebergStorageEgress.

# 5. Stop its service when finished

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
The three tabs write the same records, which a test checks by running each version unpaced. A real run appends them as rows of the simulation.events table. desflow run iceberg.yaml --sample 4 --stdout prints the first four events as JSON lines instead, and contacts no catalog:

{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":0.638,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":0.638,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"started"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":0.674,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack_order","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":0.674,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack_order","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"started"}}

Each event becomes one row of the table, and the two fields of value, path_id and status, become columns of their own.

Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level

catalog is a mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, passed to PyIceberg's load_catalog. schemas names a type for each column, so timestamp is created as a timestamp rather than inferred as a string. The ISO time each record carries is converted to a timestamp before the write.

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/iceberg.yaml
# Lakehouse data generation in YAML.
#
# The YAML version of iceberg_example.py, which --api builder downloads. A day of shop
# orders is generated at factor 0, and each flush of the buffer becomes one Iceberg
# commit. Without a router, each event is written to default_table as one flat row
# and telemetry is left out. The catalog is contacted on the first write.
#
# Needs the odctl catalog profile: odctl up catalog. ICEBERG_URI, ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE,
# S3_ENDPOINT, S3_ACCESS_KEY and S3_SECRET_KEY override the catalog and credentials.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run iceberg.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0.0
  random_seed: 42
  # A day before now, so the records are stamped as history.
  logical_start_time: -1d

egress:
  - type: Iceberg
    config:
      # PyIceberg catalog properties, passed to load_catalog.
      catalog:
        name: odctl
        type: rest
        uri: ${ICEBERG_URI:-http://127.0.0.1:8181}
        warehouse: ${ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE:-s3://warehouse/}
        s3.endpoint: ${S3_ENDPOINT:-http://127.0.0.1:8333}
        s3.access-key-id: ${S3_ACCESS_KEY:-user}
        s3.secret-access-key: ${S3_SECRET_KEY:-password}
        s3.region: ${S3_REGION:-us-east-1}
      default_table: simulation.events
      # Pinned rather than inferred, so timestamp is a timestamp, not a string.
      schemas:
        simulation.events:
          sim_ts: double
          timestamp: timestamp
          key: string
          path_id: string
          status: string
    # One commit per flush, sized so a day of events lands in a few snapshots.
    batch_size: 200000

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 2.0, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {path_id: Shop.service.packing, status: finished}

run:
  until: 1 day

This script simulates the shop over a 1-day period. It routes lifecycle events into one Iceberg table. It pins the schema, so the event time is stored as a timestamp. Without the schema, the column would be inferred as a string.

Scripts live in the examples/ folder of the repository, and the label on the block below is this one's path there.

examples/builder/iceberg_example.py
"""
Lakehouse Data Generation Example.

The Iceberg version of `builder/parquet_example.py`. The same fast-forward engine,
but each flush of the buffer becomes one Iceberg commit rather than one Parquet file,
so the run ends with a table another engine can query instead of a folder someone
still has to register.

Every commit writes a manifest, a manifest list and a new `metadata.json`.
`batch_size` on `add_egress` sizes the buffer, so the run produces a handful of
snapshots rather than hundreds.

Requires the odctl `catalog` profile: `odctl up catalog`.
"""

import logging
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import pyarrow as pa

from desflow import IcebergStorageEgress, SimulationContext

# Logging is configured here rather than in a wrapper, because this script is run
# directly. Without it the run produces no output at all.
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    datefmt="%H:%M:%S",
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

NAMESPACE = os.getenv("ICEBERG_NAMESPACE", "simulation")
EVENTS_TABLE = f"{NAMESPACE}.events"

# Pinned rather than inferred. Inference reads the ISO timestamp the environment
# writes as a string, which is not what a consumer of an event table expects.
EVENTS_SCHEMA = pa.schema(
    [
        ("sim_ts", pa.float64()),
        ("timestamp", pa.timestamp("us")),
        ("key", pa.string()),
        ("path_id", pa.string()),
        ("status", pa.string()),
    ]
)


def create_table_router(events_table: str):
    """
    Router Factory: Generates a router returning `namespace.table`, and reshapes
    each event into the pinned schema.
    """

    def table_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
        if data.get("path_id") == "system.simulation.lag_seconds":
            return None

        if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
            return None

        # FLATTEN EVENT INTO THE PINNED COLUMNS
        nested_value = data.pop("value", None)
        if isinstance(nested_value, dict):
            data.update(nested_value)

        # A pinned timestamp column takes a datetime. PyArrow rejects the ISO string
        # the environment writes, so the conversion belongs here.
        data["timestamp"] = datetime.fromisoformat(data["timestamp"])

        return events_table

    return table_router


# ==========================================
# 1. CATALOG CONFIGURATION
# ==========================================
# RestCatalog fetches the catalog configuration as it is constructed, so building
# the client below contacts the catalog when this module is imported. Creating the
# namespace waits longer: the connector does that on its first batch, inside the run.
def build_catalog():
    """Connects to the Iceberg REST catalog from the odctl `catalog` profile."""
    from pyiceberg.catalog.rest import RestCatalog

    return RestCatalog(
        "odctl",
        **{
            "uri": os.getenv("ICEBERG_URI", "http://127.0.0.1:8181"),
            "warehouse": os.getenv("ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE", "s3://warehouse/"),
            "s3.endpoint": os.getenv("S3_ENDPOINT", "http://127.0.0.1:8333"),
            "s3.access-key-id": os.getenv("S3_ACCESS_KEY", "user"),
            "s3.secret-access-key": os.getenv("S3_SECRET_KEY", "password"),
            "s3.region": os.getenv("S3_REGION", "us-east-1"),
        },
    )


router = create_table_router(EVENTS_TABLE)

# The day of backdating this example exists to demonstrate. It sits at module scope
# because the builder below needs it, and the builder has to stay at module scope for
# the decorators further down to attach to it.
LOGICAL_START_TIME = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=1)

# ==========================================
# 2. Infrastructure Builder
# ==========================================
app = (
    SimulationContext(
        sim_id="Shop",
        factor=0.0,
        random_seed=42,
        logical_start_time=LOGICAL_START_TIME,
    )
    .add_egress(
        IcebergStorageEgress(
            catalog=build_catalog(),
            table_router=router,
            schemas={EVENTS_TABLE: EVENTS_SCHEMA},
        ),
        # One commit per flush. Sized so a day of events lands in a few snapshots.
        batch_size=200_000,
    )
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=2.0)
)


# ==========================================
# 3. Simulation Logic
# ==========================================
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, context):
    """
    Returns the exact flat dictionary expected by the table router
    to represent the 'finished' state of the lifecycle.
    """
    return {"path_id": "Shop.service.packing", "status": "finished"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_generator(context):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, context, entity=entity))
        task_id += 1


# ==========================================
# 4. Execution
# ==========================================
def run():
    """Generates 1 day of shop orders instantly, into an Iceberg table."""
    logger.info(
        "Generating historical data mimicking start from "
        f"{LOGICAL_START_TIME.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')}"
    )
    logger.info("Fast-forwarding (factor=0.0)...")

    # The clock detaches and executes 1 day of operations instantaneously
    app.run(until="1 day")

    table = build_catalog().load_table(EVENTS_TABLE)
    logger.info(
        f"Wrote {table.scan().to_arrow().num_rows} rows to '{EVENTS_TABLE}' "
        f"in {len(table.metadata.snapshots)} snapshots at {table.location()}"
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

"""Lakehouse data generation, low-level API.

The low-level version of `builder/iceberg_example.py`. It wires
`DynamicRealtimeEnvironment`, the registry and the connectors by hand rather than
through the builder, which shows what `SimulationContext` does for you.

`factor=0.0` detaches the clock from real time, so a day of shop orders is generated
as fast as the machine allows and committed into an Iceberg table. Each flush of the
buffer is one commit, so `batch_sizes` is what keeps the snapshot count down.

Requires the odctl `catalog` profile: `odctl up catalog`.
"""

import logging
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    IcebergStorageEgress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)
from desflow.utils import time_to_seconds

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
logger = logging.getLogger("iceberg_example")

NAMESPACE = os.getenv("ICEBERG_NAMESPACE", "simulation")
EVENTS_TABLE = f"{NAMESPACE}.events"

# Pinned rather than inferred. Inference reads the ISO timestamp the environment
# writes as a string, which is not what a consumer of an event table expects.
EVENTS_SCHEMA = pa.schema(
    [
        ("sim_ts", pa.float64()),
        ("timestamp", pa.timestamp("us")),
        ("key", pa.string()),
        ("path_id", pa.string()),
        ("status", pa.string()),
    ]
)


def build_catalog():
    """Connects to the Iceberg REST catalog from the odctl `catalog` profile."""
    from pyiceberg.catalog.rest import RestCatalog

    return RestCatalog(
        "odctl",
        **{
            "uri": os.getenv("ICEBERG_URI", "http://127.0.0.1:8181"),
            "warehouse": os.getenv("ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE", "s3://warehouse/"),
            "s3.endpoint": os.getenv("S3_ENDPOINT", "http://127.0.0.1:8333"),
            "s3.access-key-id": os.getenv("S3_ACCESS_KEY", "user"),
            "s3.secret-access-key": os.getenv("S3_SECRET_KEY", "password"),
            "s3.region": os.getenv("S3_REGION", "us-east-1"),
        },
    )


def create_table_router(events_table: str):
    """
    Router Factory: Generates a router returning `namespace.table`, and reshapes
    each event into the pinned schema.
    """

    def table_router(data: dict) -> str | None:
        if data.get("path_id") == "system.simulation.lag_seconds":
            return None

        if data.get("stream_type") != "event":
            return None

        # FLATTEN EVENT INTO THE PINNED COLUMNS
        nested_value = data.pop("value", None)
        if isinstance(nested_value, dict):
            data.update(nested_value)

        # A pinned timestamp column takes a datetime. PyArrow rejects the ISO string
        # the environment writes, so the conversion belongs here.
        data["timestamp"] = datetime.fromisoformat(data["timestamp"])

        return events_table

    return table_router


# The shop starts with 4 packers and has room for 10.
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=2.0)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.2)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """What @app.task does: queued, started, the service time, then finished."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key,
        {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"},
        task="pack_order",
        instance=task_id,
    )
    with packers.request() as req:
        yield req
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"},
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            {"path_id": path_id, "status": "finished"},
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )


def arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run():
    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. SIMULATION SETUP
    # ---------------------------------------------------------
    start_time = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(days=1)
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0, logical_start_time=start_time)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)

    egress = IcebergStorageEgress(
        catalog=build_catalog(),
        table_router=create_table_router(EVENTS_TABLE),
        schemas={EVENTS_TABLE: EVENTS_SCHEMA},
    )

    # One commit per flush, so a day of events lands in a handful of snapshots.
    env.setup_egress([egress], batch_sizes=[200_000], flush_interval=86400)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))

    env.process(arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers))

    run_duration_str = "1 day"
    run_duration_sec = time_to_seconds(run_duration_str)

    logger.info(
        f"Generating historical data from {start_time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')}"
    )
    logger.info("Fast-forwarding (factor=0.0)...")

    try:
        env.run(until=run_duration_sec)
    finally:
        env.teardown()

    table = build_catalog().load_table(EVENTS_TABLE)
    logger.info(
        f"Wrote {table.scan().to_arrow().num_rows} rows to '{EVENTS_TABLE}' "
        f"in {len(table.metadata.snapshots)} snapshots at {table.location()}"
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: Kafka Digital Twin
docs.text:
This example models a shop packing orders. The simulation reads parameter updates from a Kafka topic and publishes events and telemetry to Kafka topics. Each tab shows the example written one way: as a YAML blueprint, with the builder API, or with the low-level API. Ways to write a simulation compares the three.

With KafkaIngress and KafkaEgress in place of the local connectors, the simulation runs as a separate service. Look for the lifecycle events on sim-events and the packers' readings on sim-telemetry, published every 2 simulation seconds. A JSON parameter update sent to sim-config changes the running simulation, and the readings show the change.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: The example needs Docker and the odctl profile kafka-lite, which each Quick Start below starts and stops. Services for the Examples shows how to install odctl.

docs.title: Run It

This example builds the simulation of the builder example in the Builder tab from a YAML blueprint, with no Python. The connectors, the parameters, the task and the telemetry are all declared in the file.

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install "desflow[kafka]" --with-executables-from "odctl>=1.0,<2"

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get kafka --api yaml
cd kafka/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up kafka-lite

# 4. Run it (Ctrl + C to stop)
desflow run kafka.yaml

# 5. In a second terminal, in the same folder, watch and steer it at http://localhost:8080
uv run --no-project --with "desflow[kafka]" --with nicegui ../kafka_dashboard.py

# 6. Stop its service when finished
odctl down kafka-lite --volumes

# 1. Install
pip install "desflow[kafka]" "odctl>=1.0,<2" nicegui

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get kafka --api yaml
cd kafka/yaml

# 3. Start its service
odctl up kafka-lite

# 4. Run it (Ctrl + C to stop)
desflow run kafka.yaml

# 5. In a second terminal, in the same folder, watch and steer it at http://localhost:8080
python ../kafka_dashboard.py

# 6. Stop its service when finished
odctl down kafka-lite --volumes

What It Does

The run keeps going until you stop it. When it starts, KafkaEgress creates sim-events and sim-telemetry if they do not exist. The run then publishes task lifecycle events to sim-events, and the packers' four readings (capacity, in_use, queue_length and utilization) and the task's in_progress to sim-telemetry. It applies parameter updates sent to sim-config.

The dashboard in the Quick Start works with this run unchanged, because it reads the same topics and the same four packer readings.

The blueprint reads the broker address with ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}, so the environment variable KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS overrides it.

docs.title: Change a Parameter Live
docs.text: Step 5 of each Quick Start starts a dashboard at http://localhost:8080. It reads sim-telemetry, and its capacity control sends a new current_cap for the packers to sim-config. KafkaIngress applies the update while the run goes, and the packers' capacity reading on sim-telemetry shows the change. Any producer can send the same update: a JSON message such as {"path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 3} on sim-config.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
The three tabs publish the same records, which a test checks by running each version unpaced. A real run sends the events to sim-events and the telemetry to sim-telemetry. desflow run kafka.yaml --sample 5 --stdout prints the first five events, and the telemetry published between them, as JSON lines instead, unpaced and with no broker:

{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":1.276,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-1","task":"pack_order","instance":0,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"started"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":1.348,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-2","task":"pack_order","instance":1,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"queued"}}

{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":2.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity","value":1}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":2.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use","value":1}

With one packer, orders-1 starts at once and the next orders wait. At 2 simulation seconds the readings show 1 packer in use, 2 orders in the queue and 3 tasks in progress.

Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level

The blueprint wires both Kafka connectors and declares the packers, the packing service, the order arrival and the task. The finished event of each task is the fixed payload. stats: minimal publishes the packers' four built-in readings and the task's in_progress every 2 simulation seconds. with_stats("minimal", interval=2.0) does the same in the builder version, and env.setup_stats in the low-level version.

Files live in the examples/yaml/ folder of the repository, and the label on each block below is its path there.

examples/yaml/kafka.yaml
# Kafka digital twin in YAML.
#
# The YAML version of kafka_example.py, which --api builder downloads: a shop packing
# orders. KafkaIngress reads parameter updates from sim-config, and KafkaEgress
# publishes lifecycle events to sim-events and packer metrics to sim-telemetry.
# KafkaEgress creates its two topics when the run starts.
#
# Needs a broker: odctl up kafka-lite. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
# KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS overrides the broker address.
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run kafka.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

ingress:
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      topic: sim-config
      bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}

egress:
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      event_topic: sim-events
      telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
      bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 10}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 3.0, std: 0.5}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.0, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {path_id: Shop.service.packing, status: finished}

# The packers' readings every 2 seconds, which kafka_dashboard.py shows.
stats: {level: minimal, interval: 2}

This script connects the simulation to Kafka topics and uses Pydantic models to fix the fields and types of the events.

Scripts live in the examples/ folder of the repository, and the label on the block below is this one's path there.

examples/builder/kafka_example.py
"""Kafka Digital Twin, builder API.

Models a shop packing orders with `SimulationContext` and connects the simulation
to Kafka for input and output. `KafkaIngress` reads parameter updates from `sim-config`,
so the running simulation can be steered without restarting it. `KafkaEgress`
publishes lifecycle events to `sim-events` and metrics to `sim-telemetry`, with
Pydantic models that fix the fields and types of the events.

Needs a broker: `odctl up kafka-lite`. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
Set EXAMPLE_UNTIL to a number of simulation seconds to end the run at that time instead.
"""

import logging
import os
import time

from pydantic import BaseModel

from desflow import (
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    KafkaEgress,
    KafkaIngress,
    SimulationContext,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(name)s: %(message)s"
)
logger = logging.getLogger("kafka_example")


# ==========================================
# 1. Event Payload Model
# ==========================================
class TaskEvent(BaseModel):
    """The fields and types of the finished event.

    Pydantic checks them when the model is built, before the event is sent to Kafka.
    """

    path_id: str
    status: str


BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = os.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "127.0.0.1:9092")
# The simulation time, in seconds, at which the run ends.
# When EXAMPLE_UNTIL is not set, the run goes on until Ctrl + C.
EXAMPLE_UNTIL = float(os.getenv("EXAMPLE_UNTIL") or 0) or None

# ==========================================
# 2. Infrastructure Builder
# ==========================================
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_ingress(KafkaIngress(topic="sim-config", bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS))
    .add_egress(
        KafkaEgress(
            event_topic="sim-events",
            telemetry_topic="sim-telemetry",
            bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
        )
    )
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=10)
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=3.0, std=0.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.0)
    # The packers' readings every 2 seconds, which kafka_dashboard.py shows
    .with_stats("minimal", interval=2.0)
)


# ==========================================
# 3. Simulation Logic
# ==========================================
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, context):
    """
    The @task decorator requests the resource and publishes the 'queued'
    and 'started' events. The function adds its own logic and returns the
    finished payload.
    """
    logger.info(f"Task {task_id} started at sim time: {context.env.now:.2f}s")

    # The payload of the finished event, from the Pydantic model
    return TaskEvent(path_id="Shop.service.packing", status="finished").model_dump(
        mode="json"
    )


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def arrival_generator(context):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, context, entity=entity))
        task_id += 1


# ==========================================
# 4. Execution
# ==========================================
def run():
    TOPICS_CONFIG = [
        {"name": "sim-config", "partitions": 1},
        {"name": "sim-telemetry", "partitions": 1},
        {"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 1},
    ]

    logger.info(f"Connecting to Kafka at {BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS}...")
    try:
        admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, max_tasks=100)
        admin.create_topics(topics_config=TOPICS_CONFIG)
        time.sleep(2)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.warning(f"Could not explicitly create topics: {e}")

    print("Simulation started.")
    print("  - Listen to 'sim-telemetry' for system vitals.")
    print("  - Listen to 'sim-events' for task lifecycles.")
    print("  - Send to 'sim-config' to update parameters.")

    app.run(until=EXAMPLE_UNTIL)  # Starts the clock and orchestrates all connectors


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

Scripts live in the examples/ folder of the repository, and the label on the block below is this one's path there.

examples/low-level/kafka_example.py
"""Kafka Digital Twin, low-level API.

The low-level version of `builder/kafka_example.py`, a shop packing orders, with
the environment, registry and connectors wired by hand. Like the builder version, it
creates its topics first with `KafkaAdminConnector`.

Needs a broker: `odctl up kafka-lite`. Runs until interrupted with Ctrl + C.
Set EXAMPLE_UNTIL to a number of simulation seconds to end the run at that time instead.
"""

import logging
import os
import time

import numpy as np
from pydantic import BaseModel

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    KafkaEgress,
    KafkaIngress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(name)s: %(message)s"
)
logger = logging.getLogger("kafka_example")

BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = os.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS", "127.0.0.1:9092")
# The simulation time, in seconds, at which the run ends.
# When EXAMPLE_UNTIL is not set, the run goes on until Ctrl + C.
EXAMPLE_UNTIL = float(os.getenv("EXAMPLE_UNTIL") or 0) or None


# ==========================================
# 1. Event Payload Model
# ==========================================
class TaskEvent(BaseModel):
    """The fields and types of each lifecycle event.

    env.publish_event() takes this Pydantic model in place of a dict, and turns it
    into a dict. KafkaEgress serializes that dict, to JSON or to Avro.
    """

    path_id: str
    status: str


# ==========================================
# 2. Initial System State
# ==========================================
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.0)},  # 1 a second
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=3.0, std=0.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=10)},
)


# ==========================================
# 3. Simulation Logic
# ==========================================
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """Publishes a Pydantic model instead of a dict for each lifecycle event."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key,
        TaskEvent(path_id=path_id, status="queued"),
        task="pack_order",
        instance=task_id,
    )
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # counted as in progress

    with packers.request() as req:
        yield req

        logger.info(f"Task {task_id} started at sim time: {env.now:.2f}s")
        env.publish_event(
            key,
            TaskEvent(path_id=path_id, status="started"),
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)

        # Use the latest service config from the registry
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))

        env.publish_event(
            key,
            TaskEvent(path_id=path_id, status="finished"),
            task="pack_order",
            instance=task_id,
        )
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


# ==========================================
# 4. Execution
# ==========================================
def run():
    TOPICS_CONFIG = [
        {"name": "sim-config", "partitions": 1},
        {"name": "sim-telemetry", "partitions": 1},
        {"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 1},
    ]

    logger.info(f"Connecting to Kafka at {BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS}...")
    admin_connector = KafkaAdminConnector(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS, max_tasks=100
    )
    admin_connector.create_topics(topics_config=TOPICS_CONFIG)
    time.sleep(2)

    # A secured cluster needs more keyword arguments, such as security_protocol="SASL_SSL"
    ingress = KafkaIngress(topic="sim-config", bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS)

    # KafkaEgress uses JsonSerializer by default. To write Avro instead:
    # from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import ConfluentAvroSerializer
    # avro_serializer = ConfluentAvroSerializer(
    #     registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", schema_str=AVRO_SCHEMA
    # )
    # Then pass: topic_serializers={"sim-events": avro_serializer}
    # Generate AVRO_SCHEMA from AvroBaseModel rather than a plain Pydantic model;
    # see Use Avro and Pydantic. TaskEvent above has no .avro_schema().
    egress = KafkaEgress(
        telemetry_topic="sim-telemetry",
        event_topic="sim-events",
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
    )

    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=1.0, strict=False)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_ingress([ingress])
    env.setup_egress([egress])
    # The packers' readings every 2 seconds, which kafka_dashboard.py shows
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=2.0)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42))

    env.process(arrival_generator(env, sampler, packers))

    print("Simulation started.")
    print("  - Listen to 'sim-telemetry' for system vitals.")
    print("  - Listen to 'sim-events' for task lifecycles.")
    print("  - Send to 'sim-config' to update parameters.")

    try:
        env.run(until=EXAMPLE_UNTIL)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        logger.info("Simulation interrupted by user.")
    finally:
        env.teardown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 1.276, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 1.276, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 2.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 4.651, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed', 'shipping': 'standard', 'order_id': 0}}

Each order produces a queued, a started and a finished event. Every event carries the order's key, such as orders-1, with the task's name and instance. The finished event is the task's payload, with the task id added as order_id because of id_field. The capacity reading shows the scenario: one packer, three from 10 seconds, then two from 20 seconds.

# Local simulation in YAML, with no Python and no containers.
#
# The YAML version of local_example.py, which --api builder downloads. This simulation models a shop
# packing orders. ConsoleEgress prints events and telemetry to the terminal.
# A scenario adds packers at 10 seconds and removes one at 20 seconds.
# The run ends on its own after 30 simulation seconds.
#
# Run it from its folder with: desflow run local.yaml

simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

egress:
  - type: Console

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 5}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 3.0, std: 0.5}

arrivals:
  # Each order spawns one pack_order task.
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.0, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the task's finished event. id_field adds the task id as order_id.
    payload: {event_type: order_packed, shipping: standard}
    id_field: order_id

# simulation seconds, as Shop.stats.resources.packers.<reading>.
