"""The Route Records to Topics guide, low-level API: a shop whose records go to three
Kafka topics.

It needs a Kafka broker on 127.0.0.1:9092: start one with `odctl up kafka-lite`. Run it
with `python complex_routing_low_level.py`, beside complex_routing_logic.py; it runs
for one minute.
"""

import itertools
import logging

from complex_routing_logic import create_topics, custom_kafka_router, packed
from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    KafkaEgress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)


def kafka_egress():
    """Sends each record to the topic the router picks."""
    return KafkaEgress(
        bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092",
        topic_router=custom_kafka_router,
    )


def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    stats = env.stats
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(key, packed(task_id), "pack_order", task_id)
        stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def run(until=60.0, factor=1.0, egress=None):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(egress or [kafka_egress()])
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=10)  # readings for shop-telemetry
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    create_topics()  # with a router, KafkaEgress creates no topics
    run()

docs.title: JSON Schema and Protobuf
docs.text:
KafkaEgress writes every record as JSON by default. JSON Schema keeps a record as JSON and checks it against a schema before it is sent. Protobuf sends it as a compact binary message of a class generated from a .proto file. Either way, a consumer can rely on the shape of every record it reads.

Both formats use the Confluent Schema Registry or the AWS Glue Schema Registry, as Avro does. Each topic can have its own serializer, so topics in different formats share one producer.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Use Avro and Pydantic shows the same steps for Avro.
  • Route Records to Topics explains a topic router.
  • The code publishes to Kafka, so start a broker first with odctl up kafka-lite. See Installation for the one-time odctl install. Stop it with odctl down kafka-lite --volumes.
  • Each serializer needs its extra: pip install "desflow[confluent]" for the Confluent Schema Registry, or pip install "desflow[glue]" for the AWS Glue Schema Registry. Both include kafka.

docs.title: JSON Schema
docs.text:
JSON Schema keeps the records as JSON and checks each one against a schema before it is sent. The serializer raises SerializationError for a record that does not match. A deserializer checks each record it reads in the same way.

Registry Serializer Deserializer Confluent Schema Registry ConfluentJsonSchemaSerializer ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer AWS Glue Schema Registry GlueJsonSchemaSerializer GlueJsonSchemaDeserializer

As with Avro, the schema describes the whole record KafkaEgress sends, with your payload as value. The serializer takes it as the JSON string schema_str:

docs/snippets/guides/json_schema_and_protobuf.py:json-schema
from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import ConfluentJsonSchemaSerializer

# The schema describes the whole record KafkaEgress sends, with the order as its value.
json_schema = """{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "key": {"type": "string"},
    "task": {"type": ["string", "null"]},
    "instance": {"type": ["integer", "null"]},
    "sim_ts": {"type": "number"},
    "timestamp": {"type": "string"},
    "value": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "order_id": {"type": "integer"},
        "amount": {"type": "number"}
      },
      "required": ["order_id", "amount"]
    }
  },
  "required": ["key", "sim_ts", "timestamp", "value"]
}"""

json_serializer = ConfluentJsonSchemaSerializer(
    registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", schema_str=json_schema
)

ConfluentJsonSchemaSerializer registers schema_str as you wrote it, under the subject <topic>-value, on the first record of each topic. It checks a schema with no $schema as Draft 2020-12. It registers no references, so its schema must hold every definition it uses, and a $ref points only inside the schema. ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer resolves a $ref to a schema that the writer registered as a reference. Neither fetches a schema from a web address. GlueJsonSchemaSerializer compiles the schema with fastjsonschema when you build it, fetches a $ref to another document at that point, and fills in the default of a property that a record leaves out.

docs.title: Protobuf
docs.text:
Protobuf sends each record as a message of a class that protoc generates from a .proto file. The serializer takes that class as message_type. A deserializer reads every message as the class it is given as message_type.

Registry Serializer Deserializer Confluent Schema Registry ConfluentProtobufSerializer ConfluentProtobufDeserializer AWS Glue Schema Registry GlueProtobufSerializer GlueProtobufDeserializer

The file describes the same record as the JSON schema above:

docs/snippets/guides/shop_record.proto
// The record KafkaEgress sends for an order, as the JSON Schema and Protobuf
// guide publishes it. Generate shop_record_pb2.py from it with the command on that page.
syntax = "proto3";

package com.desflow.shop;

message Order {
  int64 order_id = 1;
  double amount = 2;
}

// `optional` keeps a missing task or instance apart from 0 and "", as null is in JSON.
message ShopRecord {
  string key = 1;
  optional string task = 2;
  optional int64 instance = 3;
  double sim_ts = 4;
  string timestamp = 5;
  Order value = 6;
}

Generate the Python module from it with your own protoc, in the folder that holds the file. This command uses the protoc that grpcio-tools 1.85.0 bundles, which is protoc 35.1:

uvx --from grpcio-tools==1.85.0 python -m grpc_tools.protoc -I. --python_out=. --pyi_out=. shop_record.proto

The command writes shop_record_pb2.py, and shop_record_pb2.pyi, which tells a type checker the fields of the classes. The module checks the protobuf runtime when it is imported and refuses a runtime older than the protoc that wrote it. The header of the file names the oldest runtime that imports it: Protobuf Python Version: 7.35.1. The module in docs/snippets/guides/ therefore needs protobuf 7.35.1 or later. For your own file, use a protoc whose generated header shows a Protobuf Python Version no newer than the protobuf you have installed. protoc 35.x writes 7.35.x.

The serializer takes the generated class:

docs/snippets/guides/json_schema_and_protobuf.py:protobuf
from shop_record_pb2 import ShopRecord

from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import ConfluentProtobufSerializer

# message_type is the class that protoc generated. The serializer registers its file.
protobuf_serializer = ConfluentProtobufSerializer(
    registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", message_type=ShopRecord
)

ConfluentProtobufSerializer registers the file of the class under the subject <topic>-value on the first record of each topic, after the files that it imports. It builds the message from the record dict by field name and drops a key that the file does not have. A 64 bit integer field, such as order_id and instance, comes back from a deserializer as a string, so "order_id": "3" and not 3.

GlueProtobufSerializer takes one more argument, schema_str: the text of the .proto file, because Glue stores the text and protobuf cannot print it from the generated class. The text must declare the same messages, in the same file, as message_type. The Glue classes need desflow[glue] and the rest of the module needs only desflow[confluent], so this function builds the Glue serializers only when it is called:

docs/snippets/guides/json_schema_and_protobuf.py:glue
def glue_serializers():
    """The same two formats for an AWS Glue Schema Registry; they need `desflow[glue]`."""
    from pathlib import Path

    from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import (
        GlueJsonSchemaSerializer,
        GlueProtobufSerializer,
    )

    glue_json = GlueJsonSchemaSerializer(
        registry_name="shop", schema_str=json_schema, region_name="us-east-1"
    )
    # Glue stores the text of the .proto file, so the serializer takes it as schema_str.
    # It must declare the same messages as message_type.
    glue_protobuf = GlueProtobufSerializer(
        registry_name="shop",
        message_type=ShopRecord,
        schema_str=Path(__file__).with_name("shop_record.proto").read_text(),
        region_name="us-east-1",
    )
    return glue_json, glue_protobuf

docs.title: Run the Shop
docs.text:
The router sends each order to one of the two topics, and topic_serializers names the serializer of each topic, as in Avro for Some Topics. In this shop the orders alternate between the formats, so one run shows both. Each form publishes the order record as the finished event of the packing task:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/json_schema_and_protobuf.yaml:egress
egress:
  # Orders as JSON Schema or Protobuf, the rest as JSON
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: 127.0.0.1:9092
      topic_router: !python json_schema_and_protobuf.order_topic_router
      topic_serializers:
        orders-json: !python json_schema_and_protobuf.json_serializer
        orders-protobuf: !python json_schema_and_protobuf.protobuf_serializer

The blueprint names the order record as the task's payload and loads the router and the serializers with !python, as Run the Shop does for Avro.

docs/snippets/guides/json_schema_and_protobuf.py:router
from desflow import KafkaEgress


# A topic router that sends orders to their own topics.
def order_topic_router(data: dict) -> str:
    if data.get("stream_type") == "telemetry":
        return "sim-telemetry"
    if "order_id" in data.get("value", {}):
        # Orders alternate between the two formats, so one run shows both
        return "orders-protobuf" if data["instance"] % 2 else "orders-json"
    return "sim-events"


egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092",
    topic_router=order_topic_router,
    # Orders are JSON Schema or Protobuf; sim-telemetry and sim-events use JSON.
    topic_serializers={
        "orders-json": json_serializer,
        "orders-protobuf": protobuf_serializer,
    },
)

import logging

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, SimulationContext

app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    .add_egress(egress)  # orders as JSON Schema or Protobuf, the rest as JSON
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, entity):
    # The finished event is the order record
    return {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )

    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    topics = ["sim-events", "sim-telemetry", "orders-json", "orders-protobuf"]
    admin.create_topics([{"name": topic} for topic in topics])
    app.run(until="1 min")

def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )

            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id

def shop(sinks: list, factor: float = 1.0) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """The shop, publishing to the sinks given."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(sinks)

    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))

docs.title: Read the Records Back
docs.text:
A consumer of the order topics reads each one with the deserializer of its format. read_order takes the topic and the value of one message, from any Kafka consumer, and returns the record that was sent:

docs/snippets/guides/json_schema_and_protobuf.py:read-back
from desflow.connectors.ingress.kafka import (
    ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer,
    ConfluentProtobufDeserializer,
    MessageDeserializer,
)

# A consumer of the order topics reads each one with the deserializer of its format.
order_readers: dict[str, MessageDeserializer] = {
    "orders-json": ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer(
        registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081"
    ),
    "orders-protobuf": ConfluentProtobufDeserializer(
        registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", message_type=ShopRecord
    ),
}


def read_order(topic: str, payload: bytes) -> dict:
    """Decodes one message of an order topic into the record that was sent."""
    return order_readers[topic].deserialize(topic, payload)

Each deserializer fetches the schema that a message names from the registry on the first message with that id. ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer checks every record against it. ConfluentProtobufDeserializer checks that it is a Protobuf schema, and decodes the message as message_type. For a Glue registry, GlueJsonSchemaDeserializer(registry_name=...) and GlueProtobufDeserializer(registry_name=..., message_type=...) take the place of these two.

docs.title: Registry Connection
docs.text: For a secured registry, every Confluent serializer and deserializer on this page takes the same arguments as the Avro classes: auth, verify, cert, timeout, headers, proxy and max_retries. Registry Connection explains each one.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text: Run desflow run json_schema_and_protobuf.yaml, python json_schema_and_protobuf.py or python json_schema_and_protobuf_low_level.py while kafka-lite is up, after you generate shop_record_pb2.py. In every form, the queued and started events go to sim-events as JSON. Each order goes to orders-json or orders-protobuf, and its serializer registers the schema or the .proto file with the registry on its first send. read_order reads an orders-json message back as the dict that was sent, and an orders-protobuf message as a dict with order_id and instance as strings.

docs/snippets/guides/json_schema_and_protobuf.py
"""The serializers, router and order readers of the JSON Schema and Protobuf page.

The shop at the end publishes each packed order as JSON Schema or Protobuf and every other
record as JSON. It needs a Kafka broker and a schema registry: start both with
`odctl up kafka-lite`, then run `python json_schema_and_protobuf.py`.
shop_record.proto and shop_record_pb2.py, generated from it, must be beside this file.
json_schema_and_protobuf.yaml and json_schema_and_protobuf_low_level.py are the same shop in
YAML and the low-level API, and use the serializers and router of this file.
"""

# Each section carries its own imports, as the page shows it.
# ruff: noqa: E402

from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import ConfluentJsonSchemaSerializer

# The schema describes the whole record KafkaEgress sends, with the order as its value.
json_schema = """{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "key": {"type": "string"},
    "task": {"type": ["string", "null"]},
    "instance": {"type": ["integer", "null"]},
    "sim_ts": {"type": "number"},
    "timestamp": {"type": "string"},
    "value": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "order_id": {"type": "integer"},
        "amount": {"type": "number"}
      },
      "required": ["order_id", "amount"]
    }
  },
  "required": ["key", "sim_ts", "timestamp", "value"]
}"""

json_serializer = ConfluentJsonSchemaSerializer(
    registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", schema_str=json_schema
)


from shop_record_pb2 import ShopRecord

from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import ConfluentProtobufSerializer

# message_type is the class that protoc generated. The serializer registers its file.
protobuf_serializer = ConfluentProtobufSerializer(
    registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", message_type=ShopRecord
)


def glue_serializers():
    """The same two formats for an AWS Glue Schema Registry; they need `desflow[glue]`."""
    from pathlib import Path

    from desflow.connectors.egress.kafka import (
        GlueJsonSchemaSerializer,
        GlueProtobufSerializer,
    )

    glue_json = GlueJsonSchemaSerializer(
        registry_name="shop", schema_str=json_schema, region_name="us-east-1"
    )
    # Glue stores the text of the .proto file, so the serializer takes it as schema_str.
    # It must declare the same messages as message_type.
    glue_protobuf = GlueProtobufSerializer(
        registry_name="shop",
        message_type=ShopRecord,
        schema_str=Path(__file__).with_name("shop_record.proto").read_text(),
        region_name="us-east-1",
    )
    return glue_json, glue_protobuf


from desflow import KafkaEgress


# A topic router that sends orders to their own topics.
def order_topic_router(data: dict) -> str:
    if data.get("stream_type") == "telemetry":
        return "sim-telemetry"
    if "order_id" in data.get("value", {}):
        # Orders alternate between the two formats, so one run shows both
        return "orders-protobuf" if data["instance"] % 2 else "orders-json"
    return "sim-events"


egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092",
    topic_router=order_topic_router,
    # Orders are JSON Schema or Protobuf; sim-telemetry and sim-events use JSON.
    topic_serializers={
        "orders-json": json_serializer,
        "orders-protobuf": protobuf_serializer,
    },
)


from desflow.connectors.ingress.kafka import (
    ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer,
    ConfluentProtobufDeserializer,
    MessageDeserializer,
)

# A consumer of the order topics reads each one with the deserializer of its format.
order_readers: dict[str, MessageDeserializer] = {
    "orders-json": ConfluentJsonSchemaDeserializer(
        registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081"
    ),
    "orders-protobuf": ConfluentProtobufDeserializer(
        registry_url="http://127.0.0.1:8081", message_type=ShopRecord
    ),
}


def read_order(topic: str, payload: bytes) -> dict:
    """Decodes one message of an order topic into the record that was sent."""
    return order_readers[topic].deserialize(topic, payload)


import logging

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, SimulationContext

app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    .add_egress(egress)  # orders as JSON Schema or Protobuf, the rest as JSON
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int, entity):
    # The finished event is the order record
    return {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def orders(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    # With a router, KafkaEgress creates no topics, so create them first
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    topics = ["sim-events", "sim-telemetry", "orders-json", "orders-protobuf"]
    admin.create_topics([{"name": topic} for topic in topics])
    app.run(until="1 min")

"""The JSON Schema and Protobuf guide, low-level API: each packed order publishes
an order record, sent to orders-json as JSON Schema or to orders-protobuf as Protobuf, and
every other record goes to its topic as JSON.

The serializers and the router are those of json_schema_and_protobuf.py, which must be
beside this script, with shop_record.proto and shop_record_pb2.py. It needs a Kafka broker
and a schema registry: start both with `odctl up kafka-lite`, then run
`python json_schema_and_protobuf_low_level.py`.
"""

import itertools
import logging

from json_schema_and_protobuf import egress

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    KafkaAdminConnector,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)


def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # The finished event is the order record
        order = {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}
        env.publish_event(key, order, "pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(sinks: list, factor: float = 1.0) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """The shop, publishing to the sinks given."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(sinks)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    # With a router, KafkaEgress creates no topics, so create them first
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    topics = ["sim-events", "sim-telemetry", "orders-json", "orders-protobuf"]
    admin.create_topics([{"name": topic} for topic in topics])
    env = shop([egress])  # orders as JSON Schema or Protobuf, the rest as JSON
    try:
        env.run(until=60)
    finally:
        env.teardown()

docs.title: Connect to Secure Kafka
docs.text: The Kafka connectors pass any keyword argument they do not use themselves to the Kafka client underneath, so SASL, mTLS, OAuth and AWS IAM work without code of your own. The connectors use aiokafka. KafkaAdminConnector passes its settings to the aiokafka client of each method: the admin client for create_topics, the producer for send_config and the consumer for collect_data. Each setting must be one that client takes.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Egress and Ingress explain the Kafka connectors without security.
  • Every example here connects to a managed or secured cluster. No odctl profile runs a secured broker, so the shop at the end needs a cluster of your own that uses SASL PLAIN, such as Confluent Cloud. To try the connectors locally without security, start a broker with odctl up kafka-lite and see Installation.

docs.title: Confluent Cloud (SASL PLAIN)
docs.text:
The connector setups below are the same for the builder and the low-level API. A blueprint gives the same keys in the connector's config. It names an object such as an SSL context with !python, as Call Python from YAML shows for a serializer. For Confluent Cloud, or any cluster that uses SASL PLAIN or SCRAM, pass security_protocol, sasl_mechanism and the credentials:

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:sasl
egress = KafkaEgress(
    bootstrap_servers="pkc-xxxx.us-east-1.aws.confluent.cloud:9092",
    # Passed as they are to the Kafka client
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="PLAIN",  # or SCRAM-SHA-512
    sasl_plain_username="<YOUR_API_KEY>",
    sasl_plain_password="<YOUR_API_SECRET>",
)

With no topic_router, KafkaEgress creates sim-events and sim-telemetry when it starts, and passes the security settings to the admin client that creates them.

docs.title: On-Premise Cluster (mTLS)
docs.text:
For a cluster that requires mutual TLS, build an SSL context from your certificate files. aiokafka takes only ssl_context, not the certificate paths, so one context serves every connector.

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:mtls
from aiokafka.helpers import create_ssl_context

from desflow import KafkaIngress

ssl_context = create_ssl_context(
    cafile="/path/to/ca.pem",
    certfile="/path/to/service.cert",
    keyfile="/path/to/service.key",
)

ingress = KafkaIngress(
    topic="sim-commands",
    bootstrap_servers="secure-broker.internal.company.com:9093",
    security_protocol="SSL",
    ssl_context=ssl_context,
)

docs.title: AWS MSK (IAM)
docs.text:
Amazon MSK with IAM access control uses sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER" with a token provider. The token comes from the aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-python package, which you install yourself.

aiokafka requires a subclass of aiokafka.abc.AbstractTokenProvider with an async token(). One provider serves every connector.

docs/snippets/guides/kafka_security.py:msk
from aiokafka.abc import AbstractTokenProvider
from aws_msk_iam_sasl_signer import MSKAuthTokenProvider

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector, KafkaEgress

class MSKTokenProvider(AbstractTokenProvider):
    async def token(self):
        # Uses the AWS credentials of your environment, or the EC2 or EKS role
        token, _ = MSKAuthTokenProvider.generate_auth_token("us-east-1")
        return token

msk = dict(
    bootstrap_servers="b-1.my-msk.amazonaws.com:9098",
    security_protocol="SASL_SSL",
    sasl_mechanism="OAUTHBEARER",
)

# KafkaIngress, KafkaEgress and KafkaAdminConnector all use aiokafka
egress = KafkaEgress(
    **msk, topic_router=my_router, sasl_oauth_token_provider=MSKTokenProvider()
)

admin = KafkaAdminConnector(**msk, sasl_oauth_token_provider=MSKTokenProvider())
admin.create_topics([{"name": "sim-events", "partitions": 3}])

The same OAUTHBEARER setting works with a token provider of your own for Okta, Auth0 or another single sign-on provider.

docs.text:

docs.title: Write a Connector
docs.text: Write a connector of your own when a model must read changes from, or write records to, a system that desflow has no connector for. This page writes an egress that writes each event as a row of a CSV file, and an ingress that follows a JSON Lines file of changes. Neither needs a service.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: • Ingress and Egress describe the connectors desflow has and the threads they run on.

docs.title: Write an Egress
docs.text:
An egress subclasses BaseEgress and has one method, async run(queue). desflow runs it on the egress thread's asyncio loop, apart from the simulation. The queue holds batches: each batch is a list of records, in the record shape every sink receives. run takes a batch with get_nowait, and sleeps when the queue is empty so the other connectors on the loop can run:

docs/snippets/yaml/write_a_connector_logic.py:egress
class CsvEgress(BaseEgress):
    """Writes one CSV row per event: its time, key and task, then the payload
    fields that `columns` names."""

    def __init__(self, path: str, columns: List[str]):
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.columns = list(columns)
        self.active_tasks = 0  # teardown waits while a write is in progress

    async def run(self, egress_queue: queue.Queue) -> None:
        with self.path.open("w", newline="") as file:
            writer = csv.writer(file)
            writer.writerow(["sim_ts", "key", "task", *self.columns])
            while True:
                try:
                    batch = egress_queue.get_nowait()
                except queue.Empty:
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # let the other connectors run
                    continue
                self.active_tasks += 1
                try:
                    # A batch also holds telemetry; this sink writes only the events
                    rows = [
                        self._row(record)
                        for record in batch
                        if record["stream_type"] == "event"
                    ]
                    # A file write blocks, so it runs on a worker thread
                    await asyncio.to_thread(self._write, file, writer, rows)
                finally:
                    self.active_tasks -= 1

    def _row(self, record: dict) -> list:
        value = record["value"] if isinstance(record.get("value"), dict) else {}
        fields = [value.get(column) for column in self.columns]
        return [record["sim_ts"], record.get("key"), record.get("task"), *fields]

    @staticmethod
    def _write(file, writer, rows: list) -> None:
        writer.writerows(rows)
        file.flush()

Three rules apply to every egress:

  • Do not block the loop. A write that blocks, such as a file write or a client without async, runs on a worker thread with asyncio.to_thread.
  • Count the writes in progress. At the end of the run, teardown waits for every queue to empty, then waits while the sink's active_tasks is above 0. A batch taken from the queue but not yet written is therefore not lost.
  • Copy before you change a record. Every sink receives the same dictionaries, so a sink that changes one in place changes what the others write. This sink builds new rows.

An error that ends run is logged at ERROR with the connector's name. The sink then takes no more batches, so once its queue is full the simulation waits, and after drain_stall_seconds the run raises RuntimeError, as Egress describes.

docs.title: Write an Ingress
docs.text:
An ingress subclasses BaseIngress and has one method too, async run(queue), which desflow runs on the ingress thread. It puts each change on the queue as a (path, value) pair. parse_change turns a message such as {"path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2} into that pair, with the check the built-in connectors use. The ingress monitor applies what is queued every 0.1 simulation seconds, and the registry checks each value before it stores it (Live Parameters):

docs/snippets/yaml/write_a_connector_logic.py:ingress
class JsonlIngress(BaseIngress):
    """Follows a JSON Lines file and applies each line it adds, such as
    `{"path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2}`."""

    def __init__(self, path: str, poll: float = 0.1):
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.poll = poll

    async def run(self, ingress_queue: queue.Queue) -> None:
        read = 0  # the lines already applied
        while True:
            if self.path.exists():
                # A file read blocks, so it runs on a worker thread
                text = await asyncio.to_thread(self.path.read_text)
                # Only whole lines: a writer may be partway through the last one
                lines = text[: text.rfind("\n") + 1].splitlines()
                for line in lines[read:]:
                    try:
                        ingress_queue.put(parse_change(json.loads(line)))
                    except ValueError as error:  # also a line that is not JSON
                        logger.warning("Skipped a line of %s: %s", self.path, error)
                read = len(lines)
            await asyncio.sleep(self.poll)

A line of the file that is not a change is logged as one WARNING and skipped, as the built-in connectors do, so one bad message does not stop the run. At the end of the run desflow cancels run, so it needs no way to stop.

docs.title: Use Them
docs.text:
A connector of your own goes where a built-in one goes. Each config key is an argument of the class's constructor:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/write_a_connector.yaml:connectors
ingress:
  - type: !python write_a_connector_logic.JsonlIngress
    config: {path: changes.jsonl}

egress:
  - type: !python write_a_connector_logic.CsvEgress
    config: {path: events.csv, columns: [status, event_type]}

The classes are in write_a_connector_logic.py, beside the blueprint. type: !python names the class, and the loader builds it with config as its arguments.

docs/snippets/guides/write_a_connector.py:builder
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.05, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=3)
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=1.0)
    .add_ingress(JsonlIngress("changes.jsonl"))
    .add_egress(CsvEgress("events.csv", columns=["status", "event_type"]))
)

@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

app.run(until=20)
docs/snippets/guides/write_a_connector_low_level.py:low-level
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.05)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
    )
)
env.setup_ingress([JsonlIngress("changes.jsonl")])
env.setup_egress([CsvEgress("events.csv", columns=["status", "event_type"])])
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")

def order(env, number):
    key, path_id = f"orders-{number}", "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", number - 1
    )
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", number - 1
        )
        yield env.timeout(1.5)
    env.publish_event(key, {"event_type": "order_packed"}, "pack_order", number - 1)

def arrivals(env):
    number = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(1.0)
        number += 1
        env.process(order(env, number))

env.process(arrivals(env))
try:
    env.run(until=20)
finally:
    env.teardown()  # writes what is still buffered and stops the threads

The low-level API attaches the same objects with setup_ingress and setup_egress, and teardown waits for the CSV sink to write what is still queued.

The shop is paced at factor: 0.05, so 20 simulation seconds pass in each real second, and the run lasts one second of real time. An ingress reads its source while time passes, and a run at factor: 0 can end before the source is read once.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
Before the run, changes.jsonl holds one line, which sets the packers to 2 units. An order arrives every second from 1 second, and each takes 1.5 seconds, so one packer would fall behind. The ingress applies the change in the first moments of the run, and from then on each order starts when it arrives. The first rows of events.csv:

sim_ts,key,task,status,event_type
1.0,orders-1,pack_order,queued,
1.0,orders-1,pack_order,started,
2.0,orders-2,pack_order,queued,
2.0,orders-2,pack_order,started,
2.5,orders-1,pack_order,,order_packed

orders-2 starts at 2 seconds while orders-1 is still being packed, so the second unit is there. By 20 seconds, 19 orders have arrived and started, and the 18 that arrived by 18 seconds are packed. That is 19 queued, 19 started and 18 order_packed events: 56 rows. All three forms write the same rows.

python write_a_connector.py writes changes.jsonl, runs the YAML and builder forms, and prints the packers' units at the end and the number of rows in events.csv for each. python write_a_connector_low_level.py does the same for the low-level form.

Every form uses the two connectors in write_a_connector_logic.py unchanged. Put it, the blueprint and the scripts in one folder, and run the scripts from there.

"""Python for write_a_connector.yaml: an egress that writes events to a CSV file and
an ingress that follows a JSON Lines file of changes, as the Write a Connector guide
builds them."""

import asyncio
import csv
import json
import logging
import queue
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List

from desflow.connectors.egress.base import BaseEgress
from desflow.connectors.ingress.base import BaseIngress, parse_change

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class CsvEgress(BaseEgress):
    """Writes one CSV row per event: its time, key and task, then the payload
    fields that `columns` names."""

    def __init__(self, path: str, columns: List[str]):
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.columns = list(columns)
        self.active_tasks = 0  # teardown waits while a write is in progress

    async def run(self, egress_queue: queue.Queue) -> None:
        with self.path.open("w", newline="") as file:
            writer = csv.writer(file)
            writer.writerow(["sim_ts", "key", "task", *self.columns])
            while True:
                try:
                    batch = egress_queue.get_nowait()
                except queue.Empty:
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # let the other connectors run
                    continue
                self.active_tasks += 1
                try:
                    # A batch also holds telemetry; this sink writes only the events
                    rows = [
                        self._row(record)
                        for record in batch
                        if record["stream_type"] == "event"
                    ]
                    # A file write blocks, so it runs on a worker thread
                    await asyncio.to_thread(self._write, file, writer, rows)
                finally:
                    self.active_tasks -= 1

    def _row(self, record: dict) -> list:
        value = record["value"] if isinstance(record.get("value"), dict) else {}
        fields = [value.get(column) for column in self.columns]
        return [record["sim_ts"], record.get("key"), record.get("task"), *fields]

    @staticmethod
    def _write(file, writer, rows: list) -> None:
        writer.writerows(rows)
        file.flush()


class JsonlIngress(BaseIngress):
    """Follows a JSON Lines file and applies each line it adds, such as
    `{"path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2}`."""

    def __init__(self, path: str, poll: float = 0.1):
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.poll = poll

    async def run(self, ingress_queue: queue.Queue) -> None:
        read = 0  # the lines already applied
        while True:
            if self.path.exists():
                # A file read blocks, so it runs on a worker thread
                text = await asyncio.to_thread(self.path.read_text)
                # Only whole lines: a writer may be partway through the last one
                lines = text[: text.rfind("\n") + 1].splitlines()
                for line in lines[read:]:
                    try:
                        ingress_queue.put(parse_change(json.loads(line)))
                    except ValueError as error:  # also a line that is not JSON
                        logger.warning("Skipped a line of %s: %s", self.path, error)
                read = len(lines)
            await asyncio.sleep(self.poll)

docs/snippets/guides/write_a_connector.py
"""Write a Connector: an egress that writes events to a CSV file and an ingress that
follows a JSON Lines file of changes.

An order arrives every second and each takes 1.5 seconds to pack, so one packer
falls behind. Before the run, changes.jsonl holds one change that sets the packers to
2. The ingress applies it at the start, and the events go to events.csv. Each
function runs the shop in the current folder, in YAML or in the builder, and
returns the packers' capacity at the end and the rows of events.csv.
write_a_connector_low_level.py is the low-level API.
"""

import csv
import json
import logging
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import SimulationContext

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))  # write_a_connector_logic.py is beside the blueprint
from write_a_connector_logic import CsvEgress, JsonlIngress  # noqa: E402

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
CHANGE = {"path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2}


def _rows():
    with open("events.csv", newline="") as file:
        return list(csv.DictReader(file))


def yaml_form():
    """The blueprint beside the classes."""
    Path("changes.jsonl").write_text(json.dumps(CHANGE) + "\n")
    app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(HERE / "write_a_connector.yaml")
    app.run()
    return app.get_resource("packers").capacity, _rows()


def builder_form():
    """The same shop with the builder."""
    Path("changes.jsonl").write_text(json.dumps(CHANGE) + "\n")
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.05, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=3)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=1.0)
        .add_ingress(JsonlIngress("changes.jsonl"))
        .add_egress(CsvEgress("events.csv", columns=["status", "event_type"]))
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

    app.run(until=20)
    return app.get_resource("packers").capacity, _rows()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for form in (yaml_form, builder_form):
        capacity, rows = form()
        print(
            f"{form.__name__:15} packers: {capacity}, rows in events.csv: {len(rows)}"
        )
docs/snippets/guides/write_a_connector_low_level.py
"""Write a Connector, low-level API: the shop with the CSV egress and the JSON Lines
ingress of write_a_connector_logic.py.

The low-level version of write_a_connector.py. Before the run, changes.jsonl holds one
change that sets the packers to 2. `low_level_form` runs the shop in the current
folder and returns the packers' capacity at the end and the rows of events.csv.
"""

import csv
import json
import logging
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    SimParameter,
)

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))  # write_a_connector_logic.py is beside the blueprint
from write_a_connector_logic import CsvEgress, JsonlIngress  # noqa: E402

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.WARNING, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
CHANGE = {"path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 2}


def _rows():
    with open("events.csv", newline="") as file:
        return list(csv.DictReader(file))


def low_level_form():
    """The same shop with the environment and the resource."""
    Path("changes.jsonl").write_text(json.dumps(CHANGE) + "\n")
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.05)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
        SimParameter(
            sim_id="Shop",
            service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
            resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        )
    )
    env.setup_ingress([JsonlIngress("changes.jsonl")])
    env.setup_egress([CsvEgress("events.csv", columns=["status", "event_type"])])
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")

    def order(env, number):
        key, path_id = f"orders-{number}", "Shop.service.packing"
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", number - 1
        )
        with packers.request() as request:
            yield request
            env.publish_event(
                key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", number - 1
            )
            yield env.timeout(1.5)
        env.publish_event(key, {"event_type": "order_packed"}, "pack_order", number - 1)

    def arrivals(env):
        number = 0
        while True:
            yield env.timeout(1.0)
            number += 1
            env.process(order(env, number))

    env.process(arrivals(env))
    try:
        env.run(until=20)
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # writes what is still buffered and stops the threads
    return packers.capacity, _rows()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    capacity, rows = low_level_form()
    print(f"low_level_form  packers: {capacity}, rows in events.csv: {len(rows)}")

docs.title: Write to Cloud Storage
docs.text: ParquetStorageEgress and JsonlStorageEgress write each batch of records as a file. The same two sinks write to the local disk, Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage: only their filesystem mapping changes. This page writes an hour of a shop's orders to a store you pick, then reads the files back as one table.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Egress explains the two sinks, their file names and their columns.
  • Install the extra: pip install "desflow[parquet]".
  • To write to a cloud, set up its credentials first, as Choose the Store describes, and create the bucket or container the files go to.

docs.title: Choose the Store
docs.text:
A filesystem mapping names the store with type, and its other keys are the arguments of the PyArrow filesystem class of that store. Without credentials in the mapping, each cloud uses its standard settings:

  • s3: the AWS settings, from environment variables such as AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, the files in ~/.aws, or the role the machine runs as.
  • gcs: Google's default credentials, such as those gcloud auth application-default login saves.
  • azure: Azure's default credentials for the storage account that account_name names.

The script keeps one mapping for each store. STORAGE picks one, and STORAGE_BUCKET names the bucket, the container or, for local, the folder:

docs/snippets/guides/cloud_storage.py:stores
import os

# One filesystem mapping for each store; desflow builds it into a PyArrow filesystem
STORES: dict[str, dict] = {
    # The local disk, for a first run
    "local": {"type": "local"},
    # Amazon S3, with the standard AWS settings: environment variables, ~/.aws or a role
    "s3": {"type": "s3", "region": os.getenv("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1")},
    # Google Cloud Storage, with Google's default credentials
    "gcs": {"type": "gcs"},
    # Azure Blob Storage, with Azure's default credentials for the storage account
    "azure": {"type": "azure", "account_name": os.getenv("AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT")},
}

filesystem = STORES[os.getenv("STORAGE", "local")]
bucket = os.getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET", "output")

The Egress table lists the keys each store takes, such as access_key and secret_key for S3, access_token for GCS and account_key or sas_token for Azure. endpoint_override points s3 or gcs at another service, such as SeaweedFS or MinIO.

docs.title: Write the Files
docs.text:
Both sinks take the same mapping. Each writes into its own folder of the bucket, so a reader of one folder reads one format:

docs/snippets/guides/cloud_storage.py:sinks
from desflow import JsonlStorageEgress, ParquetStorageEgress


def storage_sinks(filesystem: dict, bucket: str) -> list:
    """Every event as Parquet and as JSON Lines, in two folders of the bucket."""
    return [
        ParquetStorageEgress(
            default_path=f"{bucket}/parquet/events.parquet", filesystem=filesystem
        ),
        JsonlStorageEgress(
            default_path=f"{bucket}/jsonl/events.jsonl", filesystem=filesystem
        ),
    ]


sinks = storage_sinks(filesystem, bucket)

Each form runs the shop for an hour of simulated time at factor=0.0, so the run takes a few seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/cloud_storage.yaml:egress
egress:
  # Every event as Parquet and as JSON Lines, in two folders of the bucket
  - type: Parquet
    config:
      default_path: ${STORAGE_BUCKET:-output}/parquet/events.parquet
      filesystem: !python cloud_storage.filesystem
  - type: Jsonl
    config:
      default_path: ${STORAGE_BUCKET:-output}/jsonl/events.jsonl
      filesystem: !python cloud_storage.filesystem

The blueprint loads the mapping of cloud_storage.py with !python, so STORAGE picks the store in every form. ${STORAGE_BUCKET:-output} reads the bucket from the same variable.

docs/snippets/guides/cloud_storage.py:shop
import logging

from desflow import SimulationContext


def build_shop(sinks: list) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, writing to the sinks given, as fast as the machine allows."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    )
    for sink in sinks:
        app.add_egress(sink)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int, entity):
        # The finished event is the order record
        return {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def orders(context: SimulationContext):
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

    return app


app = build_shop(sinks)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="1 hour")

shop takes the sinks as an argument, and the script passes it sinks from the Builder file:

docs/snippets/guides/cloud_storage_low_level.py:shop
def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # The finished event is the order record
        order = {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}
        env.publish_event(key, order, "pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(sinks: list, factor: float = 0.0) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """The shop, writing to the sinks given, as fast as the machine allows."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(sinks)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env

docs.title: Read the Files Back
docs.text:
read_events reads every file in a folder as one table, through a PyArrow filesystem of the same store:

docs/snippets/guides/cloud_storage.py:read
def read_events(store, folder: str, format: str = "parquet"):
    """Every file a sink wrote under `folder`, as one table.

    `store` is a PyArrow filesystem, such as pyarrow.fs.S3FileSystem(region="us-east-1").
    """
    import pyarrow.dataset as ds

    # format="json" reads the files of the JSON Lines sink
    return ds.dataset(folder, format=format, filesystem=store).to_table()

Give each run a folder of its own, or clear the folder before a run, because a second run adds its files beside the first run's.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
Run python cloud_storage.py, python cloud_storage_low_level.py or desflow run cloud_storage.yaml. With no variables set, the files go to the folder output on the local disk:

STORAGE=s3 STORAGE_BUCKET=my-bucket python cloud_storage.py

writes them to the bucket my-bucket on S3 instead. In every form, output/parquet and output/jsonl hold one file for each batch, with the same events: the queued and started events of each order, with path_id and status, and its finished event, with order_id and amount. A seeded run writes the same events in every form. Only timestamp differs, because it is the clock time at the start of the run plus the simulation time.

"""The stores, sinks and shop of the Write to Cloud Storage page.

The shop writes an hour of orders as Parquet and JSON Lines files, as fast as the machine
allows. STORAGE picks the store: local (the default), s3, gcs or azure. STORAGE_BUCKET
names the bucket or container, or the folder on the local disk. Run it with
`STORAGE=s3 STORAGE_BUCKET=my-bucket python cloud_storage.py`, with the credentials of
that cloud set up as the page describes.
cloud_storage.yaml and cloud_storage_low_level.py are the same shop in YAML and the
low-level API, and use the store and the sinks of this file.
"""

# Each section carries its own imports, as the page shows it.
# ruff: noqa: E402

import os

# One filesystem mapping for each store; desflow builds it into a PyArrow filesystem
STORES: dict[str, dict] = {
    # The local disk, for a first run
    "local": {"type": "local"},
    # Amazon S3, with the standard AWS settings: environment variables, ~/.aws or a role
    "s3": {"type": "s3", "region": os.getenv("AWS_REGION", "us-east-1")},
    # Google Cloud Storage, with Google's default credentials
    "gcs": {"type": "gcs"},
    # Azure Blob Storage, with Azure's default credentials for the storage account
    "azure": {"type": "azure", "account_name": os.getenv("AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT")},
}

filesystem = STORES[os.getenv("STORAGE", "local")]
bucket = os.getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET", "output")


from desflow import JsonlStorageEgress, ParquetStorageEgress


def storage_sinks(filesystem: dict, bucket: str) -> list:
    """Every event as Parquet and as JSON Lines, in two folders of the bucket."""
    return [
        ParquetStorageEgress(
            default_path=f"{bucket}/parquet/events.parquet", filesystem=filesystem
        ),
        JsonlStorageEgress(
            default_path=f"{bucket}/jsonl/events.jsonl", filesystem=filesystem
        ),
    ]


sinks = storage_sinks(filesystem, bucket)


import logging

from desflow import SimulationContext


def build_shop(sinks: list) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, writing to the sinks given, as fast as the machine allows."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
    )
    for sink in sinks:
        app.add_egress(sink)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int, entity):
        # The finished event is the order record
        return {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def orders(context: SimulationContext):
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

    return app


app = build_shop(sinks)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="1 hour")


def read_events(store, folder: str, format: str = "parquet"):
    """Every file a sink wrote under `folder`, as one table.

    `store` is a PyArrow filesystem, such as pyarrow.fs.S3FileSystem(region="us-east-1").
    """
    import pyarrow.dataset as ds

    # format="json" reads the files of the JSON Lines sink
    return ds.dataset(folder, format=format, filesystem=store).to_table()

"""The Write to Cloud Storage guide, low-level API: the shop writes an hour of orders as
Parquet and JSON Lines files, as fast as the machine allows.

The store and the sinks are those of cloud_storage.py, which must be beside this script.
STORAGE picks the store (local, the default, s3, gcs or azure) and STORAGE_BUCKET the
bucket, container or local folder. Run it with `python cloud_storage_low_level.py`.
"""

import itertools
import logging

from cloud_storage import sinks

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)


def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # The finished event is the order record
        order = {"order_id": task_id, "amount": 19.99}
        env.publish_event(key, order, "pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(sinks: list, factor: float = 0.0) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """The shop, writing to the sinks given, as fast as the machine allows."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(sinks)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    env = shop(sinks)  # Parquet and JSON Lines files in the store STORAGE names
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)
    finally:
        env.teardown()

docs.title: Write to Iceberg Tables
docs.text: IcebergStorageEgress appends records to an Apache Iceberg table through a catalog, so any engine that reads Iceberg, such as Spark, Trino or DuckDB, can query them. This page appends an hour of a shop's orders to the table shop.events through a catalog you pick, then reads the table back.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Egress explains the sink, the columns of a table it creates, and upserts.
  • Install the extra: pip install "desflow[iceberg]". It covers every catalog on this page.
  • The SQLite catalog needs no service. The REST catalog needs odctl up catalog, and the PostgreSQL catalog odctl up postgres. See Installation for the one-time odctl install. Stop a profile with odctl down <profile> --volumes.
  • The Glue catalog needs AWS credentials and an S3 bucket for the table files.

docs.title: Choose the Catalog
docs.text:
catalog is a mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, which desflow passes to PyIceberg's load_catalog on the first write. type picks the kind of catalog, and the optional name key names it. The script keeps one mapping for each catalog, and ICEBERG_CATALOG picks one:

docs/snippets/guides/iceberg_tables.py:catalogs
import os
from pathlib import Path

# The SQLite database and the local table files go in the folder iceberg/
FOLDER = Path("iceberg").resolve()
FOLDER.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# One mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties for each catalog
CATALOGS = {
    # A SQL catalog on SQLite, with no service, for a first run
    "sqlite": {
        "type": "sql",
        "uri": f"sqlite:///{FOLDER}/catalog.db",
        "warehouse": f"file://{FOLDER}/warehouse",
    },
    # The REST catalog of `odctl up catalog`, with the table files on its SeaweedFS
    "rest": {
        "type": "rest",
        "uri": "http://127.0.0.1:8181",
        "warehouse": "s3://warehouse/",
        "s3.endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:8333",
        "s3.access-key-id": "user",
        "s3.secret-access-key": "password",
        "s3.region": "us-east-1",
    },
    # A SQL catalog on the PostgreSQL of `odctl up postgres`, with local table files
    "postgres": {
        "type": "sql",
        "uri": "postgresql+psycopg2://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl",
        "warehouse": f"file://{FOLDER}/warehouse",
    },
    # The AWS Glue Data Catalog, with the table files in S3 and the standard AWS settings
    "glue": {
        "type": "glue",
        "glue.region": "us-east-1",
        "s3.region": "us-east-1",
        "warehouse": os.getenv("ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE", "s3://my-bucket/warehouse"),
    },
}

name = os.getenv("ICEBERG_CATALOG", "sqlite")
catalog = {"name": name, **CATALOGS[name]}

The Glue mapping gives no keys, so PyIceberg uses the standard AWS settings: environment variables such as AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, the files in ~/.aws, or the role the machine runs as. ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE names the S3 folder of the table files. PyIceberg's configuration lists the properties of each catalog.

docs.title: Write the Table
docs.text:
The sink creates the table from the first batch, with a column for each key of the records. Each flush is one commit, and every commit writes new metadata, so the sink gets a large batch of its own:

docs/snippets/guides/iceberg_tables.py:sink
from desflow import IcebergStorageEgress


def iceberg_sink(catalog: dict, table: str = "shop.events") -> IcebergStorageEgress:
    """Every event as a row of `table`, which the sink creates from the first batch."""
    return IcebergStorageEgress(catalog=catalog, default_table=table)


sink = iceberg_sink(catalog)
# One commit per flush, so the sink gets a large batch of its own
BATCH_SIZE = 200_000

Each form runs the shop for an hour of simulated time at factor=0.0. The run flushes once, at its end, so the hour of orders is one commit:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/iceberg_tables.yaml:egress
egress:
  # Every event as a row of shop.events, which the sink creates from the first batch
  - type: Iceberg
    config:
      default_table: shop.events
      catalog: !python iceberg_tables.catalog
    # One commit per flush, so the sink gets a large batch of its own
    batch_size: 200000

The blueprint loads the mapping of iceberg_tables.py with !python, so ICEBERG_CATALOG picks the catalog in every form.

docs.title: Read the Table Back
docs.text:
read_events loads the table through the same catalog and reads every row:

docs/snippets/guides/iceberg_tables.py:read
def read_events(catalog: dict, table: str = "shop.events"):
    """Every row of `table`, as one PyArrow table."""
    from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog

    properties = {key: value for key, value in catalog.items() if key != "name"}
    return (
        load_catalog(catalog["name"], **properties).load_table(table).scan().to_arrow()
    )

A second run appends its rows to the same table. To replace the rows of an earlier run instead, give the sink upsert_keys, as Egress shows.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
Run python iceberg_tables.py, python iceberg_tables_low_level.py or desflow run iceberg_tables.yaml. With no variables set, the catalog is SQLite, and its database and table files go in the folder iceberg. With the catalog profile up,

ICEBERG_CATALOG=rest python iceberg_tables.py

writes through the REST catalog instead. In every form, shop.events gains one snapshot, with a row for each event: the queued and started events of each order, with path_id and status, and its finished event, with order_id and amount. A seeded run writes the same events in every form. Only timestamp differs, because it is the clock time at the start of the run plus the simulation time.

docs.title: Tune Performance
docs.text: Make a run that generates data go as fast as the machine allows, and measure how many records a second it publishes.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• Time and Pacing explains factor.
  • Egress explains batches.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Run at factor: 0, without go_live_at. The run then waits for no wall clock, each event is processed by SimPy's own step, and no lag telemetry is published. A pending go-live keeps the real-time step until it is reached.
  2. Ask only for the statistics you read: minimal reads a few values at each interval, while typical and all add work at every task step, as Statistics explains.
  3. Use the console sink only to look at a run. It writes one line per record. A file or a stream sink costs less per record, and a counting sink almost nothing.
  4. Give a lake sink a large batch_size, such as 10,000, because each batch becomes one file. A stream sink can keep a small one.
  5. After building a large model, gc.freeze() leaves the objects built so far out of garbage collection. In the measurements below it saved about 9 percent.

This shop takes ten orders a second with 25 packers, and has no sink of its own:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/performance_tuning.yaml:shop
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # no wall clock to wait for
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 25, max_cap: 25}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 2 s, std: 0.4 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 10, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# minimal: readings every 10 s, not the costlier task statistics
stats: {level: minimal, interval: 10}

run:
  until: 1 h
docs/snippets/guides/performance_tuning.py:shop
def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """Ten orders a second and 25 packers, with no sink of its own."""
    app = (
        # factor 0: no wall clock to wait for
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=25, max_cap=25)
        .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.4)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=10.0)
        # minimal: readings every 10 s, not the costlier task statistics
        .with_stats("minimal", interval=10)
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_loop(context: SimulationContext):
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id, stats = "Shop.service.packing", env.stats
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(key, {"event_type": "order_packed"}, "pack_order", task_id)
        stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(egress: list) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """Ten orders a second and 25 packers, publishing to the sinks given."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)  # no wall clock to wait for
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(egress)
    # minimal: readings every 10 s, not the costlier task statistics
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=10)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env

At factor: 0 no system.simulation.lag_seconds is published, so the count holds only the shop's own records. With a lag reading every second it would be 3,600 more.

This function adds a counting sink to a model, runs it, and returns the number of records it published and the records published per second, counted from the start of run() to the end of its teardown. A blueprint loads as a context, so the YAML form uses the builder's function. The low-level form adds the sink to the environment and calls the teardown itself:

    """Runs a model with a counting sink: the record count and the records per second."""
    count = Count()
    app.add_egress(count)
    gc.collect()

def throughput(until: float) -> dict:
    """Runs the shop with a counting sink: the record count and the records per second."""
    count = Count()
    env = shop([count])
    gc.collect()
    gc.freeze()  # leave the objects built so far out of garbage collection
    started = time.perf_counter()
    env.run(until=until)
    env.teardown()  # waits until the sink has taken every batch
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - started
    gc.unfreeze()
    return {"records": count.records, "per_second": round(count.records / seconds)}

For one simulated hour, each form returns 108,688 records, at about 100,000 records a second of wall-clock time on the machine below.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
benchmarks/throughput.py in the repository runs one low-level workload, 5,000 simulation seconds of 10 orders a second, at factor: 0 with a fixed seed, and gives the median of seven runs. Each line changes one thing, so the effect of a change is the ratio of two lines. These are from an arm64 Mac (macOS 26) with Python 3.12.13. "Run" is env.run() alone, and "total" adds the teardown, which waits until every sink has taken every batch:

Configuration Run, seconds Total, seconds Records core only, nothing published 0.248 0.248 0 as shipped, counting sink 0.531 1.138 157,771 with 0.21.0's real-time step at factor: 0 0.555 1.164 157,771 with 0.21.0's timestamp 0.555 1.163 157,771 with a lag reading every second, 0.21.0's default 0.535 1.144 162,771 0.21.0: the three lines above together 0.604 1.211 162,771 as shipped, with gc.freeze() after setup 0.485 1.092 157,771 ConsoleEgress, to /dev/null 0.648 1.251 157,771 0.21.0's ConsoleEgress, one log call per record 0.672 1.902 157,771
  • 0.22.0 against 0.21.0: the run takes 0.531 seconds against 0.604, which is 1.14 times faster. The gain comes from three changes: SimPy's own step at factor: 0, a timestamp formatted once per second of the clock (300 against 580 nanoseconds a record), and no lag readings at factor: 0.
  • Console: in the total, which covers the run and the teardown, logging a batch with one call takes 0.11 seconds more than a counting sink. One call per record took 0.76 seconds more. A terminal is slower than /dev/null, so a run that prints to one costs more than this.
  • Teardown: about 0.6 seconds of every total is the teardown. Once the queues are empty, it waits half a second for a file sink to close its last file, so a short run spends most of its time there.

The table below shows where the time of the run "as shipped" goes. It comes from a sampling profile: a thread reads the main thread's stack every 0.2 milliseconds, as py-spy does from outside the process (py-spy needs root on macOS):

Part Share of the run SimPy's scheduler 28 percent publishing a record: the value made JSON-safe 18 percent publishing a record: building it, its timestamp, buffering and flushing 21 percent resource request and release 14 percent drawing samples 9 percent SimPy events and processes 8 percent the model's own generators and the rest 3 percent

A draw through Sampler.sample costs about 360 nanoseconds, against 200 for numpy's Generator.normal alone. A request granted and released costs about 1,760 nanoseconds, and a timeout about 260.

Python versions. The run "as shipped" takes 0.517 seconds on Python 3.11.15, 0.531 on 3.12.13, 0.492 on 3.13.14 and 0.556 on 3.14.6. No version is more than 13 percent faster than another.

PyPy. desflow does not install on PyPy, because orjson, which it depends on, does not support PyPy. With the other dependencies installed by hand, the run "as shipped" took 0.851 seconds on PyPy 3.11.15, 1.6 times slower than CPython 3.12. Drawing samples, which goes through numpy, took 23 percent of a short profile (96 samples), against 9 percent on CPython.

Real sinks. With the same workload, the total was 1.138 seconds with a counting sink, 1.262 with Parquet on the local disk, and 3.558 with Kafka. The Kafka run used the odctl kafka-lite profile on the same machine, with JSON values. A sink that sends over the network can take longer than the model.

Run uv run --all-extras python benchmarks/throughput.py configs to measure your machine, and micro, profile or sinks for the other parts.

docs/snippets/guides/performance_tuning.py
"""The Tune Performance guide: records per second of a model, without its sinks.

python performance_tuning.py prints the records a one-hour run of the shop below
published, and how many a second. `blueprint()` measures performance_tuning.yaml.
"""

import asyncio
import gc
import queue
import time

from desflow import SimulationContext


class Count:
    """An egress that counts the records it receives and keeps none."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.records = 0

    async def run(self, egress_queue):
        try:
            while True:
                try:
                    self.records += len(egress_queue.get_nowait())
                except queue.Empty:
                    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            pass


def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """Ten orders a second and 25 packers, with no sink of its own."""
    app = (
        # factor 0: no wall clock to wait for
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=25, max_cap=25)
        .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.4)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=10.0)
        # minimal: readings every 10 s, not the costlier task statistics
        .with_stats("minimal", interval=10)
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_loop(context: SimulationContext):
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(context.next_instance("pack_order"), entity=order))

    return app


def throughput(app: SimulationContext, until: float) -> dict:
    """Runs a model with a counting sink: the record count and the records per second."""
    count = Count()
    app.add_egress(count)
    gc.collect()
    gc.freeze()  # leave the objects built so far out of garbage collection
    started = time.perf_counter()
    app.run(until=until)
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - started
    gc.unfreeze()
    return {"records": count.records, "per_second": round(count.records / seconds)}


def blueprint(path: str = "performance_tuning.yaml") -> dict:
    """The same measure of the blueprint, which loads as a context."""
    app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(path)  # a context, as the builder makes one
    return throughput(app, until=3600)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(throughput(shop(), until=3600))
