"""The Tune Performance guide, low-level API: records per second of a model, without
its sinks.

python performance_tuning_low_level.py prints the records a one-hour run of the shop
below published, and how many a second.
"""

import gc
import itertools
import time

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)
from performance_tuning import Count

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=10.0)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=2.0, std=0.4)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=25, max_cap=25)},
)


def pack_order(env, packers, sampler, key, task_id):
    path_id, stats = "Shop.service.packing", env.stats
    env.publish_event(
        key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"}, "pack_order", task_id
    )
    stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as unit:
        yield unit
        env.publish_event(
            key, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"}, "pack_order", task_id
        )
        stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        env.publish_event(key, {"event_type": "order_packed"}, "pack_order", task_id)
        stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def orders(env, packers, sampler):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        env.process(pack_order(env, packers, sampler, f"orders-{number}", number - 1))


def shop(egress: list) -> DynamicRealtimeEnvironment:
    """Ten orders a second and 25 packers, publishing to the sinks given."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)  # no wall clock to wait for
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(egress)
    # minimal: readings every 10 s, not the costlier task statistics
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=10)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(orders(env, packers, Sampler(seed=42)))
    return env


def throughput(until: float) -> dict:
    """Runs the shop with a counting sink: the record count and the records per second."""
    count = Count()
    env = shop([count])
    gc.collect()
    gc.freeze()  # leave the objects built so far out of garbage collection
    started = time.perf_counter()
    env.run(until=until)
    env.teardown()  # waits until the sink has taken every batch
    seconds = time.perf_counter() - started
    gc.unfreeze()
    return {"records": count.records, "per_second": round(count.records / seconds)}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(throughput(until=3600))

docs.title: Set Up Your Editor
docs.text: Get completion for the keys of a blueprint as you type, and a mark under a misspelt key or a value of the wrong kind.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• YAML Blueprints describes what a blueprint file is.
  • YAML Keys lists every key the editor will offer.
  • The editor checks the shape of the file against the blueprint JSON Schema. It does not run the model, so desflow run is still what proves a blueprint works.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install Visual Studio Code and the Red Hat YAML extension (redhat.vscode-yaml) version 1.24.0 or later, which is the extension that reads a JSON Schema for a YAML file.

  2. Put this line at the top of the blueprint, or use the setting in step 3 for every blueprint in a folder:

    docs/snippets/yaml/editor_setup.yaml:modeline
    # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/schema/blueprint.schema.json

  3. To cover a folder of blueprints without a line in each file, add the schema to the workspace settings (.vscode/settings.json) with a glob of the files it applies to. The same object holds the tags of step 4:

    docs/snippets/editor/settings.json
    {
  "yaml.schemas": {
    "https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/schema/blueprint.schema.json": "blueprints/*.yaml"
  },
  "yaml.customTags": [
    "!python scalar:string",
    "!include scalar:object",
    "!include mapping:object"
  ]
}

  4. The yaml.customTags entries tell the extension about the tags a blueprint uses. Without them, it marks !python, and an !include written as a mapping, as unknown tags, and it marks a file name given to !include as the wrong type. They go in the same .vscode/settings.json. Your user settings work too.

  5. Open the file and write a key. The editor offers the keys of the section you are in, shows the section's description when you hover over it, and underlines a key it does not know or a value of the wrong kind.

To work offline, or to pin the schema to the version you have installed, write the copy that comes with the package to a file and name that file instead of the address:

desflow schema > blueprint.schema.json

Then use # yaml-language-server: $schema=./blueprint.schema.json as the line, or "./blueprint.schema.json" as the key in yaml.schemas. In the line the path is relative to the blueprint's folder. In yaml.schemas it is relative to the workspace folder, in a single-folder workspace.

The address above always serves the latest release, so it can offer keys that an older install does not have. To pin a release, use its versioned address, https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/<version>/schema/blueprint.schema.json, with <version> the release you installed, which desflow --version prints.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text: Open the blueprint from Full Files in the editor. Its highlighted third line names the schema. Change packers to packer under tasks, and the editor underlines nothing. Resource names are checked by desflow run, as the list below says. Change current_cap to capacity instead, and the editor underlines it as a key it does not know. Run the blueprint with desflow run editor_setup.yaml.

docs.title: What the Editor Cannot Check
docs.text:
The schema describes the shape of one file. desflow run checks the following instead, and reports each with the file and line:

  • The content of a file named by !include.
  • Whether the module and attribute of a !python reference exist.
  • The text of an expression, such as a when condition or an amount.
  • A name that refers to another section, such as a spawn that names a task that is not there, or a resource that is not declared.
  • The rules between the parameters of one distribution, such as a low below a high.

A mapping !include, such as !include {file: fitted/orders.yaml, spawn: pack_order}, is checked as the entry it stands for, so the editor marks file as an unknown key. desflow run reads it correctly.

Where a value is a number, a whole number, true or false, or one of a fixed set of names, a ${VAR} or ${VAR:-default} reference is also accepted.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: The modeline and the yaml.schemas and yaml.customTags settings belong to the yaml-language-server that the extension runs, as its README at version 2.0.0 describes. That README does not say how a tag with both a scalar and a mapping form is written. The source at 2.0.0 shows it: src/languageservice/parser/custom-tag-provider.ts adds one tag for each entry of yaml.customTags, and its own !include is a scalar only. The YAML library the server uses (version 2.8.3, src/compose/compose-collection.ts) then chooses a tag by its name and its kind of node. Without the !include mapping:object entry, a mapping !include is reported as Unresolved tag: !include.

docs.title: Use an AI Assistant
docs.text:
Let an AI coding assistant write, check and run desflow blueprints with the rules of the library in front of it, instead of guessing them.

The skill is a folder, skills/desflow/, in the Agent Skills format that Claude Code and other assistants read. Its SKILL.md gives the assistant the rules assistants get wrong, and tells it how to:

  • pick a way to write the model;
  • write and run a blueprint;
  • check a model before a long run;
  • run a study with a seed, a warm-up and replications, compare designs and fit measured times.

It links to files for every key, every distribution, every connector, every command, every name the package exports, the local example in all three APIs, and the blueprint JSON Schema. The folder is generated from the code, so it lists what the release has.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• YAML Blueprints describes what the assistant writes.
  • Set Up Your Editor holds the schema the assistant also uses.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Install desflow, so the assistant can run the desflow commands that Command Line shows, such as desflow explain and desflow run.

  2. Copy skills/desflow/ into the skills folder of the assistant. Take it from the repository at the tag of the release you installed: v followed by what desflow --version prints. For Claude Code, ~/.claude/skills/desflow/ is for every project and .claude/skills/desflow/ in a project is for that project. With git, these lines copy it for every project:

    # The source of the installed release, which holds the skill
git clone --depth 1 --branch "v$(desflow --version)" https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/desflow /tmp/desflow-src
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills
cp -R /tmp/desflow-src/skills/desflow ~/.claude/skills/desflow

  3. Ask the assistant for a model, such as "write a desflow blueprint for a shop with two packers and a lunch rush, and run it". It reads the skill when the request mentions desflow or a blueprint.

With the GitHub CLI, one command does the copy. gh skill install is a preview command of the GitHub CLI, so it needs gh 2.90.0 or later:

gh skill install jaehyeon-kim/desflow desflow --agent claude-code --scope user

--scope user installs for every project, in your home folder. --scope project, the default, installs for the current project, inside its git repository, so run it from that repository. Another assistant takes its own --agent value, listed in gh skill install --help. Without --agent, gh asks which assistant to install for. When it cannot ask, it installs for GitHub Copilot. At project scope, Copilot uses .agents/skills, a folder several other assistants also read. gh installs the latest release. desflow@v<version> in place of desflow pins one, with <version> the release you installed.

docs.title: Other Ways to Teach an Assistant
docs.text:
• Schema. Give the assistant https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/schema/blueprint.schema.json, or the output of desflow schema, to validate what it writes.
  • Documentation as text. https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/llms.txt is an index of the pages, and https://jaehyeon.me/desflow/latest/llms-full.txt holds all of them in one file.

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
An assistant can still write a model that runs and answers the wrong question. Read the blueprint before you trust its records, and check desflow run ends without an error. The skill asks the assistant to run a study rather than one run, so ask for the 95% interval, and read Trusting Results for what a number from a simulation supports.

A model of the kind the assistant writes for a shop with a lunch rush is the one Changing Demand builds. Its files are in Full Files: run desflow run changing_demand.yaml, python changing_demand.py or python changing_demand_low_level.py.

"""The Changing Demand tutorial: a 20-minute rush, with one packer or two.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. An order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average
(rate 0.4), and every 1.11 seconds (rate 0.9) from 20 to 40 minutes. Every record is
printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits with one packer through the
rush and with a second packer for it. To see only those lines, run:
python changing_demand.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(rush_packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop of First Simulation, with a rush from 20 to 40 minutes."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4)
        # The rush from 20 to 40 minutes: an order every 1.11 s on average (rate 0.9),
        # and rush_packers packers
        .add_scenario(
            [
                {"at": "20 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
                {
                    "at": "20 min",
                    "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
                    "value": rush_packers,
                },
                {"at": "40 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
                {
                    "at": "40 min",
                    "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
                    "value": 1,
                },
            ]
        )
        # Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            # The gap is drawn from the rate in force now
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(rush_packers: int) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour and returns the orders packed and their waits."""
    app = shop(rush_packers)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": r[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("wait_mean")],
        "wait_max": r[name("wait_max")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in (1, 2):
        r = outcomes(packers)
        print(
            f"{packers} in the rush: {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, longest {r['wait_max']:6.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand_low_level.py
"""The Changing Demand tutorial: a 20-minute rush, with one packer or two.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. An order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average
(rate 0.4), and every 1.11 seconds (rate 0.9) from 20 to 40 minutes. Every record is
printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits with one packer through the
rush and with a second packer for it. To see only those lines, run:
python changing_demand_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    run_scenario,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.4)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2)},
)


def schedule(rush_packers):
    """The rush from 20 to 40 minutes, with rush_packers packers.

    During the rush an order arrives every 1.11 s on average (rate 0.9).
    """
    return [
        {"at": 1200, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
        {
            "at": 1200,
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": rush_packers,
        },
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
    ]


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        # The gap is drawn from the rate in force now
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))


def run(rush_packers=1, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Orders packed, and the mean and longest wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    # Each step applies before every other event at its time
    env.process(run_scenario(env, schedule(rush_packers), until=3600))
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(rush_packers: int) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour and returns the orders packed and their waits."""
    r = run(rush_packers).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "finished": r[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("wait_mean")],
        "wait_max": r[name("wait_max")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in (1, 2):
        r = outcomes(packers)
        print(
            f"{packers} in the rush: {r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, longest {r['wait_max']:6.2f} s"
        )

docs.title: Call Python from YAML
docs.text: A blueprint holds configuration as plain YAML. When a simulation needs logic that YAML cannot express, the file can reference a Python object with !python module.attribute in place of a value. This guide covers when to use it, how a reference is found, what each field receives, the setup step, and the errors a reference can give. It then works through the OML hot rolling digital twin, a steel mill model, and ends with a note on security.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
• YAML Blueprints describes the blueprint file.
  • The Related Records example is a complete blueprint with one Python process.
  • Every file on this page is in the repository under docs/snippets/.

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text:
Use !python when a blueprint needs one of these:

  • Field values with logic. Random or weighted choices, fields derived from other fields and state carried from one event to the next are written as a payload function or a process.
  • More than a task can describe. Collecting several entities into one, such as a batch, is written as a process. Routing (next), priorities (priority and queue: priority), stores and containers, several resources per task (resource: [...] and keep), preemption (preempt: true) and breakdowns (breakdown:) are written in plain YAML.
  • Readings other than the built-in statistics. stats: minimal publishes resource, store and container readings, a container's level among them. Use a telemetry function to publish variables and derived metrics.
  • Routing over several destinations, and serializers. A router or an Avro serializer is a Python object.
  • Setup a connector does not do itself, such as topics that only a router knows about.
  • A connector from another package.

A setting that is a value needs no Python. Environment variables, relative times, when: history and when: live, filesystem and catalog mappings, Iceberg schemas and Postgres tables are all plain YAML, as YAML Keys and Egress list. A value can still come from a module when another program already defines it, as the hot rolling twin below reads its broker address from src/config.py.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Loading a blueprint runs the imports it names. !python imports modules, and importing a module runs its top-level code. A blueprint is therefore as trusted as a Python script: load only files you would run as code, in a local or trusted CI workflow.

Every other node is constructed by yaml.SafeLoader. The tag is registered on a subclass of it, so yaml.safe_load elsewhere in the process is unaffected. Only !python and !include are added to YAML. Every other tag, such as !!python/object, is rejected as yaml.safe_load rejects it.

docs.title: How a Reference Is Resolved
docs.text:
!python module.attribute imports module and returns its attribute. The reference can name anything: a function, a class, a dictionary or a constant.

The longest prefix that is a module is imported, and the rest is read as attributes, so pkg.module.func and module.Class.attribute both work. Before anything is resolved, the folder of the YAML file is added to the front of sys.path, unless it is already on it. A module beside the blueprint is therefore found from any working directory. Other modules are found on the normal sys.path, which includes installed packages. ${VAR} is replaced inside a reference too, so !python ${LOGIC}.ticker picks the module from the environment.

Every reference is resolved and checked when the file is loaded, so a wrong reference fails before the run starts, with the file and line.

Field Must be Called as processes[].function a generator function function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts tasks.<name>.payload a callable, or a mapping payload(task_id, context) once per finished task telemetry[].function a callable function(context) every interval egress[].when a callable, or history or live when(record), True to send the record to that sink ingress[].type, egress[].type a class, or a short name type(**config) while the blueprint is built run.before[] a callable before() once, at the start of run() any value under config, simulation or run.until whatever that argument takes not called

docs.title: Processes, Payloads and kwargs
docs.text:
This blueprint keeps the shop in YAML and moves three pieces of logic into Python: a payload that picks each order's delivery, a breaks process with arguments, and a predicate that keeps telemetry off the terminal:

docs/snippets/yaml/hybrid.yaml
# The shop with its logic in Python. YAML keeps the blueprint and the
# experiment; shop_logic.py beside this file holds what YAML cannot express.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console
    # Only events reach the terminal; telemetry is dropped.
    when: !python shop_logic.events_only

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4.0, std: 1.0}

arrivals:
  # An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2)
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order.
    payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery

processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5).
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}

scenario:
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}

run:
  until: 3 min
docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py
"""Python for the blueprints beside it: a payload, a process with arguments, a
predicate, a custom reading, a resource type and a container type."""

from desflow import ContainerBase, ResourceBase


def choose_delivery(task_id: int, context):
    """Picks each order's delivery from the shared generator, so a seed repeats it."""
    delivery = "standard" if context.sampler.rng.random() < 0.9 else "express"
    return {"status": "finished", "order_id": task_id, "delivery": delivery}


def breaks(context, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Waits `every` seconds, then takes every packer off for a break of `duration`."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        context.env.publish_event(f"{resource}-break", {"status": "down"})
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)
        context.env.publish_event(f"{resource}-break", {"status": "up"})


def events_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Egress predicate: keeps events and drops telemetry."""
    return record["stream_type"] == "event"


def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate


class LoggedPackers(ResourceBase):
    """A resource that keeps how long each request waited before it was granted."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.waits = []

    def _do_put(self, request):
        super()._do_put(request)
        if request.triggered:  # the request was granted just now
            self.waits.append(self.env.now - request.time)


class CountedBin(ContainerBase):
    """A container that counts the puts it grants."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.restocks = 0

    def _do_put(self, event):
        granted = super()._do_put(event)
        if event.triggered:
            self.restocks += 1
        return granted

What each reference receives:

  • payload is called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) for every packed order. It draws from context.sampler, the generator seeded by random_seed, so the deliveries repeat with the seed.
  • processes entries are called as function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts. kwargs is how one function serves several resources.
  • when is called with every record and returns True to send it to that sink.

The run shows the delivery that the payload picked and the events of the breaks process:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'status': 'finished', 'order_id': 0, 'delivery': 'standard'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 50.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'packers-break', 'task': None, 'instance': None, 'value': {'status': 'down'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 55.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'packers-break', 'task': None, 'instance': None, 'value': {'status': 'up'}}

A process is written in one of two ways. A bare reference, - !python module.func, is called as func(context). A mapping with function and kwargs is called as func(context, **kwargs). kwargs is what lets a blueprint start a process whose signature is not (context). When the signature differs more, write a small adapter: a generator function that takes the context, picks out what the process needs, and hands over with yield from.

docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling_adapter.py:arrivals
def arrivals(context, product):
    yield from arrival_process(
        context.env,
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )

A process must be a generator function, one that contains yield. The check runs when the file is loaded and looks only at the function, so an adapter that returns a generator instead of yielding from one is rejected. Write adapters with yield from.

docs.title: Routers, Serializers and Connector Classes
docs.text:
A router replaces the default destination of every record. Each router is a function that receives a record:

  • path_router on Parquet and JSONL, and table_router on Iceberg, return the record's destination, or None to drop it.
  • topic_router on Kafka must always return a topic. To drop records before Kafka, give the sink a when predicate.

With a router, records are written as the router leaves them, so flattening events and dropping telemetry become the router's job. Kafka also leaves topic creation to the caller, because only the router knows which topics it uses. The hot rolling twin below sends every record to one of four topics with topic_router: !python routing.custom_topic_router.

A serializer is an object, so it is built in a module and referenced. KafkaEgress takes default_serializer and topic_serializers, for example default_serializer: !python serializers.AVRO, where serializers.py builds a ConfluentAvroSerializer with the registry URL and the schema.

A connector from another package is referenced by class: type: !python my_package.MyEgress. Its config is passed to the constructor, as for a built-in one.

docs.title: Setup with run.before
docs.text:
run.before lists functions called with no arguments, once, at the start of run(). Connectors already create what they write to when they can: Kafka its event and telemetry topics, Postgres the tables under tables, and Parquet and JSONL their folders. run.before is for anything else, such as the five topics the hot rolling twin below creates for its router.

Put such setup in a function rather than at the top of the module. The module is imported when the file is loaded, so its top-level code runs even when the blueprint is loaded and never run.

docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:before
run:
  until: 1 hour
  before:
    - !python routing_logic.make_output_folder

The module beside the blueprint holds the setup function, and the path_router its Jsonl sink uses:

docs/snippets/yaml_build/routing_logic.py
"""Python for docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml: a router and a setup step."""

import os


def daily_path(record: dict):
    """Writes each event under its day; drops telemetry by returning None."""
    if record["stream_type"] != "event":
        return None
    return f"events/day={record['timestamp'][:10]}/events.jsonl"


def make_output_folder() -> None:
    """Called once by run.before, when the run starts, not when the file is loaded."""
    os.makedirs("events", exist_ok=True)

docs.title: Check the Result
docs.text:
A reference that cannot be resolved stops the load with its line. python_error.yaml names shop_logic.missing as the payload of its task, and desflow run python_error.yaml prints:

Error: python_error.yaml:14: !python shop_logic.missing: 'shop_logic' has no attribute 'missing'

A module that exists but fails on one of its own imports is reported with that error, rather than as a missing module.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Lift the OML hot rolling twin. The OML hot rolling digital twin is a steel mill written with the low-level API. Its generator.py builds a SimParameter with three arrivals, three services, three resources, three containers and three variables. It connects Kafka in both directions with a topic router, and starts the processes in sim_logic.py. Those processes take (env, sampler, resource, ...), not a context, and sim_logic.py runs to 262 lines of multi-stage routing, wear and physics.

The configuration moves to YAML. The processes keep their logic, and a small adapter changes only how they are called.

docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling.yaml
# The OML hot rolling digital twin as a blueprint. The parameters and the Kafka
# connectors that generator.py builds in Python are declared here. The processes stay
# in sim_logic.py, and hot_rolling_adapter.py beside this file adapts them.
#
# Place this file and the adapter in sim_control/, then run from there:
#   desflow run hot_rolling.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: HotRolling
  factor: 1.0
  random_seed: 42

ingress:
  # Control commands from the dashboard.
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: !python src.config.KAFKA_BROKER
      topic: !python src.config.TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS

egress:
  # One producer; the router picks one of four topics for every record.
  - type: Kafka
    config:
      bootstrap_servers: !python src.config.KAFKA_BROKER
      topic_router: !python routing.custom_topic_router

arrivals:
  structural: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2}
  microalloyed: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.15}
  high_alloy: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1}

services:
  pass_roughing: {dist: normal, mean: 2.0, std: 0.2}
  pass_intermediate: {dist: normal, mean: 4.5, std: 0.5}
  pass_finishing: {dist: normal, mean: 8.0, std: 1.2}

resources:
  mill_structural: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  mill_microalloyed: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  mill_high_alloy: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}

containers:
  # The wear is the level; current_cap is the most wear a roll can have
  wear_structural: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}
  wear_microalloyed: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}
  wear_high_alloy: {current_cap: 100.0, max_cap: 100.0, level: 0.001}

variables:
  velocity_structural: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}
  velocity_microalloyed: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}
  velocity_high_alloy: {type: abrupt, value: 0.0}

processes:
  # Started in the order generator.py starts them.
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.drift
    kwargs: {product_lines: [structural, microalloyed, high_alloy]}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.monitor
    kwargs: {product_lines: [structural, microalloyed, high_alloy]}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: structural}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: structural}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: microalloyed}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: microalloyed}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.primer
    kwargs: {product: high_alloy}
  - function: !python hot_rolling_adapter.arrivals
    kwargs: {product: high_alloy}

# A reproducible drift experiment, which the dashboard otherwise drives by hand:
# gradual wear on the structural line from 10 minutes.
scenario:
  - at: 10 min
    path: HotRolling.variables.velocity_structural
    value: {type: gradual, value: 0.5, freq: 1}

run:
  before:
    - !python hot_rolling_adapter.create_topics
docs/snippets/hot_rolling/hot_rolling_adapter.py
"""Adapts the hot rolling processes to the calls a blueprint makes.

A blueprint calls every process as `function(context, **kwargs)`. The processes in
sim_logic.py take `(env, sampler, resource, ...)` instead, so each function here
takes the context, picks out what the process needs, and hands over with
`yield from`. Only the wear paths in sim_logic.py change, from `current_cap` to
`level`.
"""

import time
import uuid

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector
from generator import telemetry_monitor
from sim_logic import arrival_process, drift_engine, roll_slab
from src.config import (
    KAFKA_BROKER,
    TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS,
    TOPIC_GROUND_TRUTH,
    TOPIC_LIFECYCLE,
    TOPIC_PREDICTION_REQUESTS,
    TOPIC_TELEMETRY,
)

# The command-line options of generator.py, fixed here.
VARIABLE_PASSES = False
MAX_PASSES = 5


def drift(context, product_lines):
    yield from drift_engine(context.env, product_lines)


def monitor(context, product_lines):
    yield from telemetry_monitor(context.env, product_lines)


def primer(context, product):
    """Rolls a first slab, so the mill does not start dry."""
    yield from roll_slab(
        context.env,
        uuid.uuid4().hex[:8].upper(),
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )


def arrivals(context, product):
    yield from arrival_process(
        context.env,
        product,
        VARIABLE_PASSES,
        MAX_PASSES,
        context.sampler,
        context.get_resource(f"mill_{product}"),
    )


def create_topics():
    """Creates the five topics generator.py creates before it starts."""
    KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers=KAFKA_BROKER).create_topics(
        topics_config=[
            {"name": TOPIC_CONTROL_INGRESS, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_TELEMETRY, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_LIFECYCLE, "partitions": 1},
            {"name": TOPIC_PREDICTION_REQUESTS, "partitions": 3},
            {"name": TOPIC_GROUND_TRUTH, "partitions": 3},
        ]
    )
    time.sleep(2)

What moved. The whole SimParameter moved to the blueprint, with both Kafka connectors and the custom topic router, the seed, the factor and the topic creation. The broker address and the topic names stay in src/config.py, and the blueprint references them. containers and variables carry the wear levels and drift velocities the processes read and write.

What stayed. drift_engine, arrival_process, roll_slab and telemetry_monitor stay in Python, with one change. They read and write the wear at HotRolling.containers.wear_<grade>.current_cap, but a container's current_cap is now its capacity, not its level. Those paths in sim_logic.py and dashboard.py therefore become .level. The adapter is one generator function per process. Each takes the context, picks out the environment, the sampler and the mill resource, and hands over with yield from. The primer slab and the arrival loop are separate entries, so they start in the order generator.py starts them.

What is new. The scenario turns on gradual wear on the structural line at ten minutes. The twin's dashboard does this by hand over Kafka. As a scenario it repeats exactly, and it can still be combined with the dashboard, because both write to the same registry.

docs.title: Learn
docs.text:
Each page here teaches discrete-event simulation (DES), and how desflow does it, to a reader new to both. What Is DES? explains the idea with no maths. The tutorial then builds one model of a packing shop through a whole study, so read its pages in order. The Simulation Concepts pages explain the theory behind the tutorial's steps. If you already know SimPy, see SimPy and desflow. To look up one part of desflow, see the User Guide. To do one task step by step, see How-To.

Group What it covers What Is DES? what a discrete-event simulation is, and how it plays out a system one event at a time, with no maths Tutorial: A First Model a first model of the shop: how many packers it needs, random times and seeds, what a run measures and how a run ends Tutorial: Inputs packing times chosen and fitted from measured data, demand that changes through the day, and a recorded morning replayed Tutorial: Shop Logic stock, priorities, a flow of tasks, waits for signals, patience, interruptions, competing resources and filtered inventory Tutorial: Studies how many runs to trust, comparing designs, parameter sweeps, checking a model, and a complete study from data to recommendation Tutorial: Running Live parameters changed while the model runs, and records streamed out to files Queueing Basics the results of queueing theory that a study uses: utilisation, Little's law, the effect of variation and the bottleneck A Simulation Study every step of a study, from the question to the report Checking and Validating verification, whether the program does what the model on paper says, and validation, whether the model is close enough to the real system Output Analysis how runs become an answer with a stated precision: replications, warm-up, intervals and comparing designs Readiness and Reporting what a model needs before someone else can trust and repeat it, with the published checklists Common Mistakes eight mistakes that give wrong results, in the order they happen in a study

docs.title: What Is Discrete-Event Simulation?
docs.text:
If you have never used simulation, start here. No maths is needed. A simulation plays out "what would happen if" on a computer, one step at a time, instead of guessing from averages.

Think of a packing shop. Orders arrive about every 2 seconds, and a packer takes 1.5 seconds to pack one. Will orders queue in the busy hour? What if a second packer starts at 9:30, or a delivery brings twenty orders at once?

You could answer by watching the shop with a notebook. You would not write something down every second, because most seconds nothing changes. You would write only the moments when something happens: an order arrives, a packer starts on it, the order is packed. Each of those moments is an event, and the notebook is enough to tell you who waited and for how long.

A discrete-event simulation (DES) is that notebook, written by a computer. You describe the shop: how often orders come, how long packing takes, how many packers there are. The computer then plays out the events one after another, with random variation as in real life, and writes down what happens. Because it skips the moments when nothing changes, it plays out a day, or a year, in seconds. Change the description, add a packer or double the orders, and run it again to see the difference.

desflow does this for any system with arrivals, work and limited capacity: a factory, a warehouse, a shop, a support desk, a network. It also sends every event out as a record, to Kafka, a database or files, so the simulation becomes a source of realistic data. The tutorial builds the packing shop step by step, and this page explains the ideas it rests on.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text:
The shop of First Simulation has one packer, orders about every 2 seconds and 1.5 seconds of packing. Its first records show the events:

  • At 2.552 seconds order 1 arrives, finds the packer free and starts at once.
  • At 2.696 seconds order 2 arrives and joins the queue, because the packer is busy.
  • At 4.052 seconds, 1.5 seconds after it started, order 1 is packed, and order 2 starts in the same instant.

Order 2 waited 4.052 − 2.696 = 1.356 seconds. Nothing in the model says so: the wait comes from when the events fell.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
A discrete-event simulation models a system as a series of events. Each event happens at an instant, and between two events nothing changes. The simulation therefore visits only the instants when events happen. It keeps a list of the events to come, in time order. It takes the earliest, moves its clock straight to that instant, and carries the event out. Carrying out an event usually schedules more: when a packer starts on an order, the simulation schedules the end of packing 1.5 seconds later.

Because the clock jumps, a simulated week with a few thousand events takes only the time needed to compute those events, not a week. Two events can fall at the same instant, as order 1 finishing and order 2 starting do. They run by priority and then in the order they were scheduled, as Run Length shows.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
You do not write the event list. desflow runs on SimPy, which keeps the event list and the clock. You describe the arrivals, the work and the resources, and desflow adds the parts of a simulation study that you would otherwise write yourself:

  • Statistics. Waits, queue lengths and utilisation are collected for you, with a warm-up period left out. Statistics explains them.
  • Replications. desflow run --replications repeats a run with different seeds and gives each statistic with a 95% interval. Replications explains it.
  • Experiments. desflow experiment compares designs with the same random numbers, checks them against bounds and observed values, and writes a report. Experiments explains it.
  • Checks against queueing theory. desflow explain works out each resource's utilisation and waits from the model alone, and --verify compares those figures with runs. Command Line shows it.
  • Inputs from data. desflow fit fits measured times to distributions, and desflow dist converts a distribution's parameters. Input Fitting explains it.

To see these events yourself, follow First Simulation. It gives the shop's file in three forms, a YAML blueprint, a builder script and a low-level script, and how to install desflow and run each one. All three forms print the same records.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Read sim_ts, the simulation time of each record. It jumps from 2.552 to 2.696, then to 3.737, 4.02 and 4.052, because nothing happens in between. A run unpaced, with factor: 0, gives the same records in a fraction of a second. A run paced to the wall clock gives them in real time, which is how desflow feeds live data to a system that reads it.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text:
The orders are the entities: the things that flow through the model. Each order arrives, needs a packer, holds the packer while it is packed, and leaves. The packers are a resource: something limited that an entity holds while it is served. When every packer is busy, the next order waits in the resource's queue.

An entity can carry attributes: facts about it that stay with it as it moves. A Flow of Tasks marks each order as express or not when it arrives, and marks it as backordered when it was picked from an empty shelf. A rule reads an attribute as attr.express.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The time an entity spends in a model is of two kinds. An activity is a period of set length, such as the 1.5 seconds of packing. A delay is time spent waiting for something, such as a free packer, and the model does not set its length: it comes from the state of the shop. You describe the activities, and the simulation produces the delays. The wait in the queue is a delay, which is why it is a result and not an input.

Two models with the same average times can have very different waits, because a run of quick arrivals or one slow order holds everyone up. A simulation shows that directly, where an average cannot.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: A desflow model is built from these parts. An arrival starts entities, a service gives the length of an activity, a resource limits how many are served at once, and a task says what an entity does. Model Parts covers each one, Arrivals and Services shows how to set an activity's length, and Task Flow shows how to set and read attributes.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The waits and queue lengths a run reports are delays, so they change when anything about the shop changes: the arrival rate, the packing times, their spread or the number of packers. Queueing Basics explains how, and which results of queueing theory a model can be checked against.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Each order in First Simulation publishes a queued event when it joins the queue, a started event when a packer takes it, and an order_packed event when it is packed. Measuring a Run adds telemetry: the queue length, the utilisation and the waits, published every 10 seconds.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
A model on its own only moves its clock. What makes it useful here is what it publishes. A sink writes each record to a destination, such as a Kafka topic, a database table or an Iceberg table, so the simulation becomes a source of realistic data for whatever reads it.

Whether that data looks real depends on the model being stable. If work arrives faster than the resources can finish it, the queue grows without limit and every later event is delayed more. The records then show waits that grow all day, which no real shop would allow.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Add a sink for each destination. Streaming Out writes the shop's events to files, and Egress lists every sink. Before a long run, check that every resource's utilisation is below 1, as Queues and Capacity shows.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Each record carries the simulation time, the entity's key and what happened. A reader can rebuild every order's path from them, as Checking and Validating does to check a model.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop opens empty in the morning and closes at the end of the day. A question about one day, such as how many orders are still waiting at closing time, has a natural end: the day. A question about the busy hour, such as the mean wait when the shop is running at 1.8 orders a second, is about the shop after its empty start has stopped mattering.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Banks et al.'s lecture notes on output analysis separate two kinds of study:

  • A terminating run has a natural end, and its results over that period are the answer.
  • A steady-state study asks how the shop behaves in the long run. The start of each run is left out as a warm-up, because an empty shop has shorter waits than a busy one.

The kind of study decides how long to run, whether to leave out the start, and how many runs to make.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: The same model can be run either way. A terminating run ends at the end of the day, and End Conditions shows how to close the doors and let the last orders finish. A steady-state study sets a warm-up, as Trusting Results does with its 2 minutes. Run Length shows how to set the end of a run.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A terminating result describes that period, with its empty start included. A steady-state result describes the shop once it is busy, and does not say what happens in the first minutes. Output Analysis explains how to get an interval for either.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Banks et al., Discrete-Event System Simulation, chapter 3, General Principles, read through lecture notes on that chapter.
  • Ingalls, "Introduction to Simulation" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2001), read through its published text.
  • Banks et al.'s lecture notes on output analysis.
  • The explanations are our own.

docs.title: A Simulation Study
docs.text:
Building a model is one step of a simulation study, and often not the largest. This page walks through the whole study, from the question to the report, with the packing shop as the example. Each step says what to produce and names the tutorial page that does it for the shop. The Complete Model runs every step in order.

The steps follow Law's seven-step approach. Two steps are checks: Check the Assumptions checks the conceptual model, and Build and Check the Model checks the programmed model. When either check fails, the study goes back to Ask One Question and Conceptual Model and Data, because the question or the conceptual model may need to change.

Law notes that programming the model is only 25 to 50 percent of the work of a sound study, despite the common view of simulation as a programming exercise.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• how to write a question that a study can answer;
  • what a conceptual model holds, and how to choose the inputs;
  • how AIC and the KS test score a fitted distribution;
  • how the assumptions and the model are checked;
  • how an experiment answers the question;
  • what a report of the study states.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop's question is: how many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds in the busy hour? The measures are the mean wait of an order and how busy the packers are. The question also fixes the period (the busy hour), the system (the packing area, not the whole warehouse) and who decides (the shop manager).

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A study with no well-defined objective cannot say when it is finished, and Law lists this first among the pitfalls. Without a specific question the right level of model detail cannot be set either: every part of the warehouse could be modelled, and nothing says which parts matter.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Write the question and its measures down before building anything. Name the measure as a statistic the model publishes, such as tasks.pack_order.wait_mean, and the value that decides the answer, such as 10 seconds. An experiment file can state the question and check the decision rule, as Comparing Designs does.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Queues and Capacity answers the question: 3 packers. Trusting Results measures the mean wait of an order with 3 packers: 2.32 ± 0.20 seconds, the mean of 40 replications with the half-width of its 95% interval. Those runs use the measured packing times and a 2-minute warm-up, and other pages run the hour in other ways. The whole interval is far below 10 seconds, so the answer holds at this precision.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text:
The shop's conceptual model says what the model includes, the assumptions it makes and the data it needs:

  • Orders arrive one at a time, at a rate that does not change during the hour.
  • A packer takes the next order from one queue, in order, and packs it.
  • Packing takes 1.5 seconds on average. The first model uses a constant 1.5 seconds, and Choosing Inputs replaces it with the times measured at the bench.
  • Pickers, stock and delivery are outside the model.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Law calls this the assumptions document. It is what the people who know the shop check, and what the model is checked against. It also decides how much detail goes in. Law warns against building one model element for each element of the real system: more detail costs run time, can miss the deadline and can hide the factors that matter.

Each input is an estimate until it is measured. For the shop these are the arrival rate and the packing time.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Collect what is known about the system and write the document before writing code. Take the data from the real system where it exists, choose a distribution for each input, and test how much the choice matters. Choosing Inputs compares the candidate distributions, and Fitting the Inputs fits them to measured times. Add detail only when it can change the decision. Model Parts lists the parts a model can have.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model with an input nobody has measured is still usable, as long as the study tests how far the answer depends on it. Parameter Sweeps does this for the arrival rate: with three packers the wait depends strongly on the rate, and with four it does not.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Fitting a distribution to measured times gives a candidate from each family, such as a gamma or a lognormal, and two scores say how well each candidate matches the data. For the shop's 40 packing times, Fitting the Inputs gives the triangular an AIC of 56.68 and the gamma 56.79.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The two scores measure different things:

  • AIC, Akaike's information criterion, scores how likely the data is under the fitted family, with a penalty for each parameter the fit chose: 2k − 2 × the log-likelihood, where k is the number of parameters. Lower is better.
  • KS, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, is the largest gap between the share of the data below a value and the share the family puts below it. Its p-value is the chance of a gap at least that large if the data came from the family.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: desflow fit fits each family to a column of measured values and prints both scores, as Fitting the Inputs shows. Compare the AIC of two families on the same data: only the difference means anything. Use the KS p-value to rule a family out: a small p-value, such as below 0.05, is a reason to reject it.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: By a common guideline, an AIC difference below 2 does not tell two fits apart, so the triangular and the gamma fit the shop's times equally well. When the family was fitted to the same data, the KS p-value is approximate and tends to be too high. A good score therefore does not settle the choice. Run the model with each close candidate and check whether the answer changes, as Fitting the Inputs does.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Ask the shop manager whether arrivals really are steady in the busy hour, and whether a packer ever does anything else. If orders come in a rush at the start of the hour, the first assumption is wrong, and Changing Demand shows the model that follows.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Law calls this step a structured walk-through. It finds wrong assumptions before code depends on them. It also makes the results more credible to the people who will act on them, because they have checked what the model assumes.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Walk the people who know the system through the assumptions document, one line at a time. Record each assumption they confirm, and change the document where they correct it. An experiment file keeps the agreed assumptions, the source of each input and the limits of the model, as The Complete Model does.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: An assumption the owner of the system confirms can go into the model. One they correct sends the study back to the conceptual model, before any code is written.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop's model is built in First Simulation and extended in the tutorials that follow it. Checking a Model checks it: it traces fixed inputs, pushes the inputs to extremes, compares the model with queueing theory and with the real shop, and tests its sensitivity.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A model can run without errors and still be wrong. The checks are of two kinds, which Checking and Validating describes. Verification checks that the program does what the conceptual model says. Validation checks that the model is a good enough picture of the shop for the question.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Verify by reading the trace, working a case by hand, and comparing the statistics with each other. desflow explain --verify compares the model with the queueing formulas where they apply. Validate by comparing the model's results with the real shop's where there is data, and by testing its sensitivity to the inputs. Queueing Basics gives the formulas that check the queue.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model that passes the checks is fit for the question it was checked against, not for every question. A failed check sends the study back to the conceptual model or to the code.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Comparing Designs compares three packers with four. Over 20 replications of each design with the same seeds, a fourth packer cuts the busy hour's mean wait by 2.21 ± 0.31 seconds (the mean difference and the half-width of its 95% interval).

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: An experiment is a set of runs designed to answer the question. One run of each design can show a difference that comes from the random numbers alone. Several replications, with the same seeds for each design, give an interval for the difference.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Decide the run length, the warm-up and the number of replications, then run each design and compute an interval for each measure. Output Analysis explains these choices, and Trusting Results makes them for the shop. desflow experiment runs the designs and the checks from one file.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The interval for the difference, 2.21 ± 0.31 seconds, lies wholly above 0, so the fourth packer shortens the wait at this precision. Whether 2.21 seconds is worth a packer is the shop manager's decision, not the model's.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The Complete Model ends with report.md. It states the comparisons and the checks, the observed comparison, the assumptions, where each input came from, and the limits of the model.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A reader who was not part of the study acts on the report alone. The report must let that reader judge how far to trust the answer, and repeat the study.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: State the answer to the question first, then the evidence for it. Say what the model includes and leaves out, what the inputs were and where they came from, how the model was checked, and how precise each result is. desflow report writes the report from an experiment's results. Readiness and Reporting lists what to include, and Common Mistakes lists the errors that make a study wrong.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A study often repeats. A result that surprises is a reason to check the model again, and a changed question is a reason to change the model. The steps are an order of work, not a one-way path.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Write one question, its measures and the value that decides it, before building anything.
  • Write the assumptions down, and have the people who know the system check them.
  • Choose each input from data where it exists, and test how much the choice matters.
  • Verify the program and validate the model before trusting a result.
  • Answer the question with intervals from replications, and report the answer first, with its limits.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Law, "How to Conduct a Successful Simulation Study" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2003), which gives the seven-step approach. We read the paper in full.
  • Wikipedia: the Akaike information criterion and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.
  • The wording and the shop example are our own.

docs.title: Checking and Validating
docs.text: A model that runs is not a model that is right. This page explains how to check a model in two ways that need different evidence: verification asks whether the program does what the model on paper says, and validation asks whether that model is a good enough picture of the real system for the question. Both are done on the way through a simulation study, and neither is finished by one test. Checking a Model applies every check on this page to the shop. The page's own one-packer cases come from checking_and_validating.py, which asserts each number.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• the difference between verification and validation;
  • how to read a trace and work a case by hand;
  • which statistics must agree with each other, and which formulas a run must match;
  • how to compare a model with the real system, and what to do when they disagree;
  • how sensitivity analysis shows whether an estimate is good enough.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The model on paper says the shop's arrivals, packing times and number of packers. The program is the SimulationContext, the blueprint or the low-level code that runs them. The real shop is the packing area with its own records. Verification compares the program with the model on paper. Validation compares the program's results with the real shop.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Banks et al., as the lecture notes give it, put the difference briefly: verification is building the model correctly, and validation is building the correct model. A model can pass one and fail the other. A program can follow the model on paper exactly, while the model leaves out the thing that makes the real shop slow. A model can also describe the shop well and have a fault in its code.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Name each check by what it compares. The trace, a case worked by hand, the statistics against each other and a formula are verification. A comparison with the real shop and sensitivity analysis are validation. Law adds credibility: a model is credible when the people who will use its results accept them, and walking them through the assumptions earns it.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Checking a Model passes every verification check and finds one disagreement with the shop's observed values. Verification alone would have called the model ready. The study must explain the disagreement before it trusts the model for the decision.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The records of a desflow run are a trace: the record of each event in time order. In First Simulation, order 2 arrives at 2.696 seconds and joins the queue, and starts at 4.052 seconds, the instant order 1 is packed.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: The lecture notes on Banks et al. list three ways to find errors in a program: a trace, a look at whether the output is reasonable under a variety of input settings, and a check of the model by someone else. The trace is the cheapest of the three.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Run a few orders and follow one by hand. It should arrive, wait while every packer is busy, start when a packer is free, and finish after its packing time. Streaming Out shows how to pick one order's records out of a long run.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: An order that starts while every packer is busy, or finishes before its packing time, is a fault in the program. A trace that follows the rules shows only that the cases in it are right, so the next checks test the rest.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Checking a Model runs three packers for 10 seconds, with an order every second and 4 seconds to pack each. Worked by hand, 4 orders finish, 5 are still in the shop, the mean wait is 5 ÷ 7 = 0.714 seconds, the packers are busy 80% of the time and the queue averages 0.8 orders. The run reports the same numbers.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Constant gaps and constant packing times make every number exact, so a difference is a fault, not chance. Cases at the extremes test the logic further: with demand above capacity, the queue must grow for as long as the run lasts, and a model that cannot show this has a fault.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Replace every random input with a constant, run for a short time, and compare each statistic with the answer worked on paper:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/checking_a_model.yaml:fixed
# Three packers; an order arrives every second and takes 4 seconds to pack
resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 3, max_cap: 10}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: constant, value: 1, spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 4}

desflow run checking_a_model.yaml prints the 20 records of the run, which are its trace, then the statistics at 10 seconds.

docs/snippets/tutorials/checking_a_model.py:fixed
def fixed_shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """Three packers, an order every second and 4 seconds to pack each, for 10 s."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=3, max_cap=10)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=4)
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
    )
docs/snippets/tutorials/checking_a_model_low_level.py:fixed
# Three packers; an order arrives every second and takes 4 seconds to pack
FIXED = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=4)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
)

Then run the extremes, where the answer is known without the model. Four cases with one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing, over an hour:

  • One order every 3 seconds: orders arrive at 3, 6 and on to 3,597 seconds, so 1,199 arrive. Each is packed before the next arrives, so none waits, and the packer works 1,199 × 1.5 seconds of the 3,600, which is 49.96%.
  • One order every second: the packer needs 1.5 seconds for each, so it never keeps up. 3,599 orders arrive, 2,399 finish, and 1,200 are in the shop at the end.
  • One order every 10,000 seconds: no order arrives in the hour, so none starts and none finishes.
  • One order a second with 100 packers: a packer is always free, so no order waits.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A run that matches every case worked by hand has the logic of the model on paper. Checking a Model also runs the busy hour at its extremes over 20 replications: one packer finishes 2,318 orders on average against the most possible, 2,320, and ten packers are busy 27.08% of the time against 27% by hand. A difference in any of these cases must be found before any experiment.

docs.title: Check the Statistics Against Each Other
In the Tutorial
docs.text: Measuring a Run reports the queue length, the arrival count and the mean wait of the busy hour separately. By Little's law they must agree: 2.406 orders in the queue on average, against 1.736 orders a second × 1.3817 seconds = 2.399.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Some relations hold for every model that settles, so they test the statistics without any hand calculation. A run measures each statistic separately, so if they disagree, one of them is wrong.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Compare the average queue with the arrival rate times the mean wait, as Queueing Basics shows in each form of the model. Check that the counts in Statistics add up: when no order balks or reneges, the orders started over the whole run are those finished plus those still in the shop. In Measuring a Run, 6,261 started, 6,250 finished and 11 are still in the shop.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Agreement shows the statistics are consistent with each other. It does not show the model is right for the shop: a model with the wrong packing times would agree just as well. Little's law is also weaker for a queue that never settles. Checking a Model finds it roughly holds with one packer, but that queue's mean depends on how long the run lasts.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Checking a Model runs desflow explain --verify on the busy hour of Trusting Results, ten times. The utilisation of 0.9 and the throughput of 1.8 orders a second agree with the runs: 0.9034 and 1.807. The wait has no formula for three packers with measured packing times, so it is not compared.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: For a simple case there is a formula. One packer with exponential gaps and service times at utilisation 0.75 has a mean wait of 4.5 seconds when the service time averages 1.5 seconds. A run of the model, repeated with several seeds, must produce an interval that contains it. A formula tests the part of the model it covers. It cannot test priorities, breakdowns or changing demand, which is why those are the parts to check by hand and against the real shop.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: desflow explain applies the formulas to a model without running it. It gives each resource's utilisation, and the mean wait where a formula applies. desflow explain --verify then runs the model and compares what the runs measure with those values. Where the formulas do not hold, it gives no value, makes no comparison and says why. Queueing Basics shows the command in each form, and Check Against Theory states the rule and how to read a difference.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: This is verification, not validation. It checks that the program agrees with the queueing formulas, and that the model's rates, units and service times are consistent with each other. It does not show that the model is close enough to the real shop.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Checking a Model compares the model with values observed in the shop over 58 minutes of a busy hour: a mean wait of 2.6 seconds and a utilisation of 91%. The values are illustrative. The wait lies inside the model's 95% interval over 20 replications, 2.16 to 2.80 seconds. The utilisation lies outside its interval, 89.70% to 90.96%.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Validation needs evidence from the real system. Law suggests comparing the model's results with the existing system's where there is one, along with a walk-through of the assumptions by the people who know the system, and sensitivity analysis. The lecture notes on Banks et al. describe calibration as a loop: compare the model with the real system, adjust it, compare again. They also give three steps:

  1. Build a model with high face validity: one that looks right to the people who know the system.
  2. Validate the model's assumptions.
  3. Compare input-output behaviour with the real system's data.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Give the model the inputs of a real period and compare its measures with what happened. An experiment places each observed value beside the model's interval, as Experiment Results describes. Check the inputs as well as the outputs: Choosing Inputs and Fitting the Inputs cover the inputs, and Local Replay runs a model on the arrivals of a real trace.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The results need to agree closely enough for the decision, not exactly. A value outside its interval is a disagreement that the study must explain before it trusts the model. The interval covers only the model's spread from run to run, not the error in the shop's own measurement. When the real system does not exist yet, as for a proposed design, there is nothing to compare with, and validity rests on the assumptions and on sensitivity analysis.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Parameter Sweeps changes the shop's arrival rate around its estimate of 1.8 orders a second. With three packers, a rate 6% above the estimate more than doubles the mean wait, from 2.48 to 5.55 seconds, each the mean of 20 replications after a 2-minute warm-up. With four packers, the mean wait is at most 0.35 seconds at every rate in the sweep.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A model has inputs that are estimates. Sensitivity analysis changes them and sees whether the answer changes. It shows which estimates the decision depends on, and so which ones need more data.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Sweep each uncertain input over the range it could take, and run every design at each value with the same seeds. desflow experiment runs a sweep from one file, as Parameter Sweeps shows.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: If a 6% change in the arrival rate changes the decision, the estimate needs more work. If the decision stays the same, the estimate is good enough. For the shop the choice of four packers holds for any demand in the range, while the three-packer wait cannot be predicted well without a better estimate of the rate.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Verification checks that the program does what the model on paper says. Validation checks that the model is close enough to the real system for the decision.
  • Check as you build: after each part is added, run a case with a known answer.
  • Before the experiments, check the statistics against each other and against a formula where one exists.
  • Before the results are used, compare with the real system, or say that no comparison was possible.
  • Write the checks as tests, as Checking a Model does, so they run again after every change. Readiness and Reporting lists what a model needs before its results are trusted, and Common Mistakes lists the errors these checks find.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Banks et al., Discrete-Event System Simulation, chapter 10, read through lecture notes on it: verification and validation, the trace, the reasonableness checks, review by someone else, calibration and the three-step approach.
  • Law, "How to Conduct a Successful Simulation Study" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2003), read through the paper: credibility and the comparison with the existing system.
  • The checks with Little's law, with a formula and with fixed gaps, the extreme-condition tests, the explanations and the shop examples are our own.

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text: Most wrong simulation results come from a short list of mistakes, and most of them are made before the first run. This page explains eight, in the order they happen in a study. Each one shows what the mistake does to the packing shop, why, how to avoid it, and what the result looks like once it is avoided. The checks behind the figures are in common_mistakes.py, which runs each one with the builder and asserts each number the page quotes.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• why a study needs one question, and a model only the detail that question needs;
  • what replacing an input by its mean, or choosing a distribution by habit, does to the waits;
  • why one run, or one run of each design, is not an answer;
  • why a steady-state question needs a warm-up;
  • why the orders of one run cannot give an interval.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: A shop model built to "see what happens" could include the pickers, the stock, the couriers and the breaks. Nothing says which of them matter, so nothing says when the model is finished.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A model with no question grows, and its results cannot be judged, because there is no measure to judge them by.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Write one question before you write the model, with the measure that answers it, such as "how many packers keep the mean wait of the busy hour under 10 seconds?". A Simulation Study shows how to write it.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: With the question written, each part of the model can be judged by whether it changes the answer. The shop's question needs the packers and the orders, and not the couriers.

docs.title: Copying the Real System in Full
In the Tutorial
docs.text: The busy-hour question depends on the arrivals, the packing times and the number of packers. The pickers, the stock and delivery are outside the shop's first model, and A Flow of Tasks adds picking only when a question needs it.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A model with every detail of the real shop takes long to build, is hard to check, and needs data for each detail that nobody collected. More detail can also hide the factors that matter.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Ask of each part: would the answer change if it were different? If not, leave it out. A Simulation Study writes this down as the conceptual model, and lets the question decide how much detail goes in.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A small model that answers the question is easier to check and to explain. A part added later, when a new question needs it, is checked on its own.

docs.title: Replacing a Distribution by Its Mean
In the Tutorial
docs.text: Packing takes 1.5 seconds on average and an order arrives every 2.0 seconds on average, so it is tempting to put those two numbers in as constants. With one packer, constant gaps and constant packing times, the mean wait over 10 replications is 0.00 seconds. With exponential gaps of the same mean and the same packing time, it is 2.45 seconds over the same 10 replications.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Real orders do not come at even gaps, and that variation is what makes a queue. With constant inputs, each order arrives after the last one is packed, so no order ever waits. Kingman's formula shows the same: with no variation in the gaps or the packing times, the wait is zero.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Use the distribution you measured, not its mean. Choosing Inputs compares candidate distributions for the packing time, and Fitting the Inputs fits them to measured times.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model whose waits are near zero while utilisation is high has probably lost its variation. In Choosing Inputs, the same mean packing time gives a mean wait from 1.27 seconds with constant times to 2.37 seconds with exponential ones.

docs.title: Choosing a Normal or Uniform by Habit
In the Tutorial
