docs.text: A normal distribution with a mean of 1.5 seconds and a standard deviation of 1.0 is a tempting packing time. About 6.7% of 100,000 draws from it are below zero.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A time cannot be negative. The model would have to clip the negative draws, which changes the mean, or fail. A uniform distribution has the opposite problem: it gives every value between its ends the same weight, which real times seldom have.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Fit a distribution to the data, and let a goodness-of-fit check and a plot say which family it is. Input Fitting does this, and Fitting the Inputs works an example. A Simulation Study explains the scores.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: With no data, a triangular distribution of the least, most likely and greatest values is a usual stand-in. Law's pitfall 18 warns against using one when data could be collected, because the greatest value is hard to choose and the long right tail of real times matters. Collect the data if you can.

docs.title: Taking One Run as the Answer
In the Tutorial
docs.text: Run the busy hour with three packers 10 times with different seeds. The mean wait of a run ranges from 1.52 seconds, 28% below the mean, to 2.75 seconds, 30% above it, and the mean of the 10 is 2.11 seconds.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: One run is one sample. A report that gave one run alone could be that far off, and it would carry no sign of how far.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Run replications and report the mean with an interval. Output Analysis explains replications and how many to use, and Trusting Results runs them for the shop.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The pages of this site give several figures for the busy hour's mean wait, because each runs it in a different way. Busy Hour Figures lists each figure and how it was run.

docs.title: No Warm-up for a Steady State
In the Tutorial
docs.text: Take one packer and an order about every 1.58 seconds on average. With 1.5 seconds of packing, the packer is busy 1.5 ÷ 1.58 = 95% of the time. Forty runs of 30 minutes from an empty shop give a mean wait of 11.4 ± 2.1 seconds. The formula for the long-run wait of this shop (M/D/1) gives 14.25 seconds, above the whole interval.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A run starts with an empty shop, so the first orders find no queue, and the mean of a short run is biased low. The effect is largest when the shop is nearly full, because the queue then takes longest to reach its usual length.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: For a steady-state question, leave out a warm-up and run long enough. Output Analysis explains how to choose the warm-up, and shows the setting in each form of the model.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Forty runs of 20,000 seconds that each leave out their first 4,000 seconds give 14.2 ± 1.3 seconds. The interval now contains 14.25 seconds, so the bias is gone. Terminating questions do not need a warm-up, because the empty start is part of the question.

docs.title: Comparing Designs With One Run Each
In the Tutorial
docs.text: Packing in 1.45 seconds instead of 1.5 is a real improvement. Over 20 runs of each, with seeds spawned from 1 for the slower design and from 2 for the faster one, the mean wait is 1.99 seconds for the slower design and 1.51 seconds for the faster. Match the runs in order, first with first: in 4 of the 20 matches, the slower design's run had a mean wait at or below the faster design's run.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: In those 4 matches, one run of each design would have said the change did not help. The difference between two single runs is mostly the difference between their random numbers.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Compare designs with the same number of replications each and an interval on the difference. Use common random numbers to reduce the random variation in the difference. Comparing Designs does this on the shop.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: These runs are not paired, so they are not the runs of the paired comparison in Output Analysis, which runs both designs with the seeds spawned from 42. With pairing, the interval of the difference there is ± 0.12 seconds against ± 0.29 seconds without it.

docs.title: Treating One Run's Statistics as Independent
In the Tutorial
docs.text: In the busy hour, an order that waits long is usually followed by another that waits long, because the second waited in the same queue, behind the first.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: The mean wait of one run is a mean of values that depend on each other. The usual interval formula assumes independent values, so an interval built from the orders of one run is too narrow.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Build the interval from the replications, each of which is independent of the others. Output Analysis shows how.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: An interval from replications says how far the mean may be from the true one. An interval from one run's orders claims a precision the run does not have. Checking and Validating lists the checks that catch the other mistakes before a result is reported.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Write one question, and model only what its answer depends on.
  • Use measured distributions, not their means, and not a normal or uniform by habit.
  • Answer with replications and an interval, never with one run.
  • Leave out a warm-up for a steady-state question.
  • Compare designs with the same seeds and an interval on the difference.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Law, "Twenty-Three Critical Pitfalls in Simulation Modeling and How to Avoid Them" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2024), which we read. The list follows its pitfalls.
  • The examples are our own runs.

docs.title: Output Analysis
docs.text: A simulation run gives numbers, and a number from one run is a sample, not the answer. Output analysis is the work of turning runs into an answer with a stated precision. This page explains the ideas with the busy hour of the shop. Trusting Results and Comparing Designs apply them and show the commands.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• whether a question is terminating or steady state, and what each needs;
  • why a run's empty start biases its mean, and how to choose a warm-up;
  • why one run is not enough, and what replications give;
  • how a 95% interval and its half-width are built;
  • how many replications a study needs;
  • which orders a reading covers;
  • why designs are compared with the same random numbers.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: End Conditions treats the shop as terminating: orders stop at 3,600 seconds, and the question is what happens to the work still in the shop. The busy hour of Trusting Results is treated as steady state, because the question is what the shop's waits usually are.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A terminating run ends at a time or an event the system has by nature, and starts from conditions the system really has. A shop that opens empty and closes at the end of the day is terminating: the day's answer is the answer. A steady-state study asks how a system behaves in the long run, after the effect of its starting conditions has gone. The two need different handling of the start of the run and of its length.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Decide which question the study asks, before choosing a run length:

  • Terminating: the start is part of the answer. Run the real opening state, run to the real closing event, and use replications to measure the spread.
  • Steady state: the start is a distortion. Leave out a warm-up, and run long enough that the rest represents the long run.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The same model can be either, because the choice depends on the question and on the system, not on the model. A terminating result describes the period with its start. A steady-state result describes the shop once it has settled, and says nothing about its first minutes.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Trusting Results plots the busy hour from its start. The mean wait so far climbs from 0.46 seconds to about 1.5 seconds in the first two minutes, because the first orders found free packers. After that it moves up and down with no trend.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: The first orders of a run find every packer free, so their waits are shorter than the waits of the hour as a whole. The mean wait of a run is therefore biased low by its start. When the question is the long run, as for the busy hour, this distortion is called initialisation bias. A warm-up is a time at the start of a run whose observations are left out.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Choose the warm-up from evidence, not from habit, in two steps:

  1. Plot a running statistic from the start of the run, such as the queue length or the mean wait so far, and note when it stops climbing. Law's paper shows a plot made with Welch's method for this, in which the warm-up is the time after which the average has levelled off, and advises choosing it conservatively.
  2. Compare a few candidate warm-ups. Run the same replications after each, and check whether a longer warm-up moves the mean by more than its half-width. A candidate passes when it does not.

Then keep the shortest candidate that passes the comparison and covers the climb in the plot. Set it on the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/trusting_results.yaml:warmup
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; 0 keeps everything
warmup: ${WARMUP:-2 min}
docs/snippets/tutorials/trusting_results.py:warmup
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; None keeps everything
SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42, warmup=warmup)
docs/snippets/tutorials/trusting_results_low_level.py:warmup
# Records and statistics start after the first 2 minutes; None keeps everything
WARMUP = 120.0  # seconds, passed to setup_egress in run below

In the low-level API the warm-up is an argument of env.setup_egress, because the sinks are what leave the records out, as Trusting Results shows.

The warm-up resets every statistic once at that time, as Run Length and Statistics describe.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Trusting Results compares warm-ups of 1, 2 and 4 minutes over five seeds. The longer ones move the mean by 0.011 and 0.036 seconds, far less than the half-width of 0.47 seconds, so all pass, and 2 minutes covers the climb. In the run with the seed 42, the warm-up changes the mean wait only from 1.382 to 1.381 seconds: an hour is long enough that its first minutes hardly count. A shorter run, or one that starts far from the usual state, needs the warm-up much more. A warm-up is not a fix for a model that never settles: if utilisation is 1 or more, there is no steady state for a warm-up to find.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: In the busy hour, with the measured packing times and a 2-minute warm-up, 40 replications give a mean wait of 2.32 ± 0.20 seconds: the mean of the 40 values, with the half-width of its 95% interval. The mean waits of the 40 replications range from 1.45 to 4.39 seconds. The one run with the seed 42 measured 1.38 seconds, lower than any of them.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: The waits of orders in one run follow each other: after a busy period, many orders in a row wait long. They are not independent samples, so the usual formula for the spread of an average, which assumes independent samples, gives an interval that is too narrow. Law lists this as a pitfall, along with treating one run as the truth.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
A replication is a run of the same model with its own random stream. It gives one independent value of each statistic. Run several, and take the mean of their values as the estimate:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# 40 runs: the mean wait and the packers' utilisation, each with its interval
desflow run trusting_results.yaml --replications 40 --measure tasks.pack_order.wait_mean --measure resources.packers.utilization_avg
docs/snippets/tutorials/trusting_results.py:replicate
MEASURES = ["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean", "resources.packers.utilization_avg"]


def replications(n=40):
    """Runs the busy hour n times, each after the warm-up, with seeds spawned from 42."""
    return replicate(shop, n, seed=42, until="1 h", measures=MEASURES)
docs/snippets/tutorials/trusting_results_low_level.py:replicate
MEASURES = ["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean", "resources.packers.utilization_avg"]


def model(env, sampler):
    """The busy hour in a given environment: replicate sets the statistics."""
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))


def replications(n=40):
    """Runs the busy hour n times, each after the warm-up, with seeds spawned from 42."""
    shop = LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop")
    return replicate(shop, n, seed=42, until=3600, warmup=WARMUP, measures=MEASURES)

LowLevelModel names the function that builds the model in an environment it is given, and the warm-up is an argument of replicate, because a replication has no sinks.

Replications describes every option. The seeds are spawned from one seed, so the set repeats exactly. Randomness and Seeds explains the streams.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: One run would have given a confident and wrong answer: 1.38 seconds, against 2.32 ± 0.20 over 40 replications. The interval says how precise the estimate is.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Over 40 replications of the busy hour, the mean wait is 2.32 ± 0.20 seconds. The interval runs from 2.12 to 2.52 seconds, and 0.20 seconds is its half-width.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
A 95% interval, in full a 95% confidence interval, is the mean of n replications plus or minus a half-width of t × s ÷ √n, where:

  • s is the standard deviation of the n values.
  • s ÷ √n is the standard error, an estimate of how far the mean itself varies from one set of replications to the next.
  • t is the Student t quantile for n − 1 degrees of freedom, one less than the number of replications. t is about 2.1 for 20 replications and 2.0 for 40, and larger for fewer, because s is then a rougher estimate.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Every replication command prints the mean and the half-width of each measure. --level changes the confidence level: --level 0.9 on the command line, or level=0.9 in replicate. Choose the level before the runs, with the precision the decision needs.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Over many studies, about 95% of the intervals built this way contain the true mean. A 90% interval from the same 40 runs is narrower, ± 0.16 seconds, but misses the true mean more often: 1 study in 10 instead of 1 in 20.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Trusting Results asks for a half-width within 10% of the mean. Utilisation meets it with 5 replications. The mean wait first meets it at 40: its half-width is 21.2% of the mean after 5 replications, 11.0% after 10, 13.0% after 20 and 8.4% after 40.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: There is no fixed number that is enough, such as 30. Waits vary far more from run to run than how busy the packers are, so each output needs its own number of replications, and the study needs enough for the least precise output the decision uses.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Decide the precision each output needs, then run until the least precise output has it. The half-width shrinks with √n, so a half-width k times smaller needs about k² times as many replications. A first set of a few replications suggests how many are needed: 10 replications gave 11.0%, so 10% needs about 10 × (11.0 ÷ 10)² ≈ 12.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: That estimate is a guide, not a promise: 20 replications gave 13.0%, because the half-width of the first set is itself an estimate. Add replications, then read the half-width again. A longer run is the other way to gain precision. It reduces the effect of the start, but its mean is still one sample.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: In End Conditions, the fixed horizon ends at 3,600 seconds with 2,436 orders started, 2,398 finished and 38 in the shop. With a drain, the run ends at 3,656.4 seconds with all 2,436 finished.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A mean is over some orders, and two runs of the same hour can cover different orders. At a fixed horizon, some orders have started and not finished, and the mean wait covers those that started. With a drain, every order admitted finishes, at the cost of running past the hour.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Report the counts beside the means. The warm-up adds a third group: orders that were in the shop when the warm-up ended. An order that started before the warm-up ended and finished after it counts as finished, and its whole wait counts in the wait and service times. It does not count as started. Statistics has the table of which orders each count covers.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Two means over different groups of orders are not comparable. A reader needs the counts to tell whether a difference between two results comes from the shop or from which orders each reading covers.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Comparing Designs runs three packers and four with the same 20 seeds. A fourth packer cuts the busy hour's mean wait by 2.21 ± 0.31 seconds.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Run each design with the same seeds, so that each pair of runs meets the same arrivals and the same service times, and take the difference seed by seed. This is a paired comparison, and the shared random numbers are called common random numbers. The random variation that the two runs of a pair share cancels in their difference. The interval of the differences is therefore narrower than the interval an unpaired comparison of the same runs gives. Law names comparing designs without a sound statistical approach as a pitfall.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
An experiment pairs its designs by seed and reports the difference with its interval, as Comparing Designs shows. The check below shows the effect on 40 runs of the busy hour with 3 packers, 20 packing in 1.5 seconds and 20 packing in 1.45 seconds, with the same 20 seeds. It builds two intervals for the difference of the mean waits from the same runs: one paired by seed, and one that treats the designs as independent.

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow experiment comparing_designs_experiment.yaml

The experiment runs every design with the same seeds and reports each difference paired by seed. It does not build the unpaired interval, which the Builder tab computes for the comparison.

docs/snippets/pages/output_analysis.py:paired
def waits(service: float, n: int = 20) -> list[float]:
    """The mean wait of each replication; the same seed gives the same seeds to every design."""
    runs = replicate(lambda: shop(service), n, seed=42, until=3600, measures=[WAIT])
    return runs.values[WAIT]


def paired_and_unpaired(slow: list[float], fast: list[float]):
    """Half-widths of the difference of the means: paired by seed, and as if independent."""
    n = len(slow)
    paired = interval([a - b for a, b in zip(slow, fast)])
    # Welch's interval: the two designs' variances add, and the degrees of freedom shrink
    va, vb = statistics.variance(slow) / n, statistics.variance(fast) / n
    df = (va + vb) ** 2 / (va**2 / (n - 1) + vb**2 / (n - 1))
    unpaired = t_quantile(0.975, df) * math.sqrt(va + vb)
    return paired, unpaired

replicate takes a LowLevelModel in place of the builder function, as the Replications section above shows. The two functions then work on its values unchanged.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text:
With the seeds spawned from 42, the mean wait of the 20 runs packing in 1.5 seconds is 0.69 seconds longer than that of the 20 runs packing in 1.45 seconds. The paired interval is ± 0.12 seconds and the unpaired one is ± 0.29 seconds, so pairing more than halves the interval here. Common Mistakes runs the same two designs with other seeds and without pairing, so its means differ from these.

Pairing helps only when the designs use the random numbers in the same way. desflow gives each distribution a stream of its own, so adding a step to one design does not shift the numbers the shared steps draw. The comparison report lists any stream that only one design used, because draws from such a stream are not paired. Check that list before trusting a paired interval.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Decide first whether the question is terminating or steady state.
  • For a steady-state question, choose the warm-up from a plot and a comparison of candidates, and report the evidence.
  • Answer with replications, not one run, and give each output as a mean with its half-width.
  • Choose the precision each output needs, and run until the least precise output has it.
  • Say which orders each count covers.
  • Compare designs with the same seeds, and check the list of unpaired streams. Readiness and Reporting lists what a report must contain.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Banks et al., Discrete-Event System Simulation, chapter 11, on output analysis for a single model, read through lecture notes on it. The notes give the interval across replications the same form as the one above.
  • Law, "Twenty-Three Critical Pitfalls in Simulation Modeling and How to Avoid Them" (Winter Simulation Conference, 2024), read through its published text: the output-analysis pitfalls and Welch's method.
  • The explanations are our own.

docs.title: Queueing Basics
docs.text: A queue forms when orders arrive faster than the packers can pack them, even for a short time. How long an order waits depends on more than the averages. This page explains the few results of queueing theory that a simulation study uses. Each one is explained with the packing shop of the tutorial and checked against a run of it. The numbers on this page come from queueing_basics.py, which asserts every one of them.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• how to write the shop as a queueing model, such as M/D/3;
  • how to work out utilisation, and why the queue settles only below 1;
  • what Little's law says, why it holds, and how to check a run's statistics with it;
  • why waits grow fast near full use, and less with several packers;
  • how the spread of the gaps and the packing times lengthens waits;
  • how to find the bottleneck of a network of tasks;
  • how to check a formula against runs of the shop.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text:
A queueing model has three parts: the arrivals, the queue, and the servers that serve them. In the shop, the arrivals are the orders, the queue is the line in front of the packers, and the servers are the packers. In desflow a server is one unit of a resource, so the packers resource with current_cap: 3 has three servers. The diagram shows the three things a model must say: how far apart orders arrive, how long a packer takes, and how many packers there are.

Kendall's notation writes these three things as arrivals/service/servers. The letter c stands for the number of servers. The busy hour of Queues and Capacity is M/D/3: exponential gaps between orders, a constant packing time of 1.5 seconds, and three packers. Each letter names a distribution:

  • M is an exponential distribution. Gaps between orders placed independently of each other are exponential, and such arrivals are called a Poisson flow.
  • D is a constant time, the same for every order.
  • G is any distribution. Measuring a Run packs with 40 measured times, so its shop is M/G/3.

So M/M/1 has exponential gaps, exponential service times and one server. M/D/1 has constant service times instead, and D/M/1 has constant gaps and exponential service times. When a model leaves out the further terms, they have their defaults: the queue has room for any number of orders, the orders come from an unlimited population, and they are served in the order they arrive.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Each formula on this page holds for some models and not others. The notation says which one applies. A wait worked out with the M/M/3 formula for an M/D/3 shop is about twice too long, as Check a Formula Against the Shop measures.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Write the letters for the model before you use a formula: what the gaps are, what the packing times are, and how many units the resource has. desflow explain does the same for each resource. It names the formula it used, or says why none applies. For the busy hour of Queues and Capacity, an M/D/3 shop, it reports "no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times", as the output under Utilisation shows.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model with a letter G, or with several servers and a letter other than M, has no exact formula for its wait. The run of the shop is then the only measure of the wait, and a formula gives at best an approximation to check it against.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text:
Utilisation is the share of time a server is busy. In the busy hour of Queues and Capacity, orders arrive at 1.8 a second and each takes 1.5 seconds to pack. That is 1.8 × 1.5 = 2.7 seconds of packing arriving every second. Three packers share it, so each is busy 2.7 ÷ 3 = 0.9 of the time, or 90%.

In general, utilisation is the arrival rate times the mean service time, divided by the number of servers. Formulas and the desflow explain tables write it with these symbols:

  • λ (lambda) is the arrival rate, 1.8 orders a second.
  • μ (mu) is the service rate of one server, one over the mean service time: 1 ÷ 1.5 = 0.667 orders a second.
  • c is the number of servers, 3.
  • ρ (rho) is the utilisation: ρ = λ ÷ (c × μ) = 1.8 ÷ (3 × 0.667) = 0.9.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Utilisation decides whether the queue settles at all. There are three cases:

  • Below 1, the packers have spare time on average. The queue grows and shrinks, and its average length settles.
  • At exactly 1, the packers have no spare time. The queue does not settle, and it drifts longer over time. The one exception is constant gaps with constant packing times, where each order arrives just as a packer becomes free.
  • Above 1, orders arrive faster than the packers can pack them. The queue grows without limit in every case.

Queues and Capacity runs the busy hour with 1 to 4 packers. One packer (utilisation 2.7) and two (1.35) leave mean waits of 1127.21 and 426.31 seconds, and the waits keep growing with the length of the run. Three packers (0.9) give 1.27 seconds and four (0.675) give 0.20 seconds.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Work out utilisation for each resource before you run the model. desflow explain does it from the model, without running it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
PACKERS=3 desflow explain queues_and_capacity.yaml


Resources
+--------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |   ρ | Wq | L | status    |
|----------+-----+--------+---+-----+----+---+-----------|
| packers  | 1.8 | 0.6667 | 3 | 0.9 |  - | - | CONGESTED |
+--------------------------------------------------------+

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:analyze
def utilisation_before_the_run():
    """The packers of the Queues and Capacity shop, as `desflow explain` works them out."""
    from queues_and_capacity import shop

    packers = shop(3).analyze().resources[0]  # the busy hour with three packers
    return packers.rate, packers.service_mean, packers.servers, packers.utilization


packers: rate 1.8, mean service 1.5 s, units 3, utilisation 0.9

desflow explain and analyze() do not support low-level models, because a low-level model makes its links between arrivals, tasks and resources in SimPy code as it runs. Work out ρ by hand, or explain the YAML or builder form of the model.

The status column is OK below 0.85, CONGESTED from 0.85 and UNSTABLE from 1.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text:
A utilisation of 1 or above means the design needs more capacity, and no run length gives a stable answer. A utilisation below 1 means the queue settles, but not that the wait is short: Waits Near Full Use shows how long it can be at 0.9.

A run measures utilisation too, as utilization_avg, a percentage. Measuring a Run's busy hour measured 86.56%, below the 0.9 of the formula. The formula with that run's own figures gives the same share: 6,250 orders finished in 3,600 seconds is 1.736 a second, and its packing times averaged 1.4954 seconds, so 1.736 × 1.4954 ÷ 3 = 0.865. That hour's random gaps were a little longer than the mean of 1 ÷ 1.8 seconds:

utilisation 0.866 measured, 0.865 from the run's rate and service

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text:
Little's law says that, in a system that settles, the average number of orders in it equals the arrival rate times the average time an order spends in it: L = λ × W. It needs no assumption about the gaps, the packing times or the order of service. It holds for the queue alone, for the packers alone, and for the whole shop.

In the busy hour of Measuring a Run, 6,250 orders finished in 3,600 seconds, so λ = 1.736 orders a second. The mean wait was 1.3817 seconds, so λ × W = 1.736 × 1.3817 = 2.399. The time-weighted average queue length was 2.406 orders. The two figures agree.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The law holds because both sides count the same total. Add up, over the hour, the seconds each order spent in the queue. Counted second by second, the total is the number waiting at each moment, added over 3,600 seconds: L × 3,600. Counted order by order, it is the number of orders times their mean wait: λ × 3,600 × W. The two totals are equal, so L = λ × W.

desflow measures the queue length, the arrival count and the wait separately. If they do not agree, one of them is wrong. That makes the law the first check on a model's statistics, before any result is trusted.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Read the five statistics at the end of a run, and compare L with λ × W for the queue and for the whole shop. The number in the whole shop is the queue plus the orders being packed, and the orders being packed are the three packers times their utilisation. This function does the arithmetic on the readings of any run of the shop:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:littles-law
def littles_law(readings: dict, seconds: float):
    """The arrival rate, then L and lambda x W for the queue and for the whole shop."""
    rate = readings["Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished"] / seconds
    in_queue = readings["Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg"]
    packers = readings["Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity"]
    in_service = (
        packers * readings["Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg"] / 100
    )
    wait = readings["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]
    service = readings["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean"]
    return (
        rate,
        (in_queue, rate * wait),
        (in_queue + in_service, rate * (wait + service)),
    )

Each tab runs the Measuring a Run hour and reads its statistics:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# Utilisation, queue length, mean wait and packing time, and orders finished
desflow run measuring_a_run.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'utilization_avg"|queue_length_avg"|(wait|service)_mean"|orders\.finished"' | tail -5


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization_avg","value":86.56336659179189}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg","value":2.405756864104584}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":1.3816663590146558}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean","value":1.4953759999999972}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished","value":6250}

Put these five values into the arithmetic of littles_law, with 3 packers and 3,600 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:builder
from measuring_a_run import app

app.run(until="1 h")
readings = app.env.stats.readings()

Then littles_law(readings, 3600).

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:low-level
from measuring_a_run_low_level import run

env = run()
readings = env.stats.readings()

Then littles_law(readings, 3600).

All three give the same figures:

arrival rate 1.736 orders a second
queue: L 2.406, lambda x W 2.399
shop: L 5.003, lambda x W 4.995

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: The queue gives 2.406 against 2.399, and the whole shop 5.003 against 4.995. Both agree within 0.3%. The small difference comes from the 11 orders still in the shop when the hour ended: their time counts in L, but their wait is not yet in W. In a long run of a settled shop, a difference of more than a few percent means a statistic is wrong, for example a task that keeps its packer after it finishes. Checking and Validating uses the law as one of its checks.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Parameter Sweeps runs the busy hour with three packers and the measured packing times at four arrival rates, 20 replications each. At 1.6 orders a second (utilisation 0.8) the mean wait is 0.97 seconds. At 1.8 (utilisation 0.9) it is 2.48 seconds. At 1.9 (utilisation 0.95) it is 5.55 seconds. A rise of 6% in the rate more than doubles the wait.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
For one server with exponential gaps and service times (M/M/1), the mean wait in the queue has a closed form: utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation) × the mean service time. With constant service times (M/D/1) it is exactly half. The first part, utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation), grows faster and faster as utilisation nears 1: it is 1 at 0.5, 9 at 0.9 and 19 at 0.95. The bars show this for one packer with a mean packing time of 1.5 seconds:

So a design that only keeps utilisation below 1 is not enough. A shop that is stable can still make orders wait a long time, and a small change in demand changes the wait a great deal.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
The formulas are short enough to compute. These functions are the ones the rest of the page uses:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:theory
def mm1_wait(utilisation: float) -> float:
    """Mean wait in the queue of an M/M/1 queue: utilisation / (1 - utilisation) x service."""
    return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * SERVICE


def erlang_c(units: int, load: float) -> float:
    """The share of arrivals that find all `units` busy, for a load in packers' worth of work."""
    last = load**units / math.factorial(units) / (1 - load / units)
    return last / (sum(load**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(units)) + last)


def mmc_wait(units: int, arrival_rate: float) -> float:
    """Mean wait in the queue of an M/M/c queue: Erlang C divided by (c / service - lambda)."""
    return erlang_c(units, arrival_rate * SERVICE) / (units / SERVICE - arrival_rate)


def kingman_wait(utilisation: float, arrival_cv: float, service_cv: float) -> float:
    """Kingman's formula for the mean wait in a one-server queue."""
    variability = (arrival_cv**2 + service_cv**2) / 2
    return utilisation / (1 - utilisation) * variability * SERVICE

utilisation 0.5: mean wait M/M/1  1.50 s, M/D/1  0.75 s
utilisation 0.75: mean wait M/M/1  4.50 s, M/D/1  2.25 s
utilisation 0.9: mean wait M/M/1 13.50 s, M/D/1  6.75 s
utilisation 0.95: mean wait M/M/1 28.50 s, M/D/1 14.25 s

desflow explain gives the same figure for a one-packer model: for the shop of First Simulation, M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, its Wq column reads 2.25 seconds.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Near full use, the wait depends strongly on the exact arrival rate. Before trusting a wait at a utilisation of 0.9 or more, check how good the estimate of the rate is, as Parameter Sweeps does. A run near full use also needs to be long before its mean wait settles, as Output Analysis explains.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The busy hour has three packers with constant packing at utilisation 0.9. Ten long runs of it give a mean wait of 2.05 seconds, as Check a Formula Against the Shop shows. One packer with constant packing at the same utilisation would make orders wait 6.75 seconds on average, by the M/D/1 formula above. Three packers sharing one queue wait far less at the same utilisation.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: With several packers sharing one queue, an order waits only when every packer is busy. For exponential gaps and service times (M/M/c), the share of orders that find every packer busy is the Erlang C formula. The mean wait in the queue is that share divided by (c ÷ the mean service time − the arrival rate). The erlang_c and mmc_wait functions above compute it.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Compare designs at the same utilisation with the formulas. With a mean packing time of 1.5 seconds, one packer at utilisation 0.8 gives a mean wait of 6 seconds. Three packers at utilisation 0.8 give about 1.6 seconds:

one packer at utilisation 0.8: mean wait 6.0 s
three packers at utilisation 0.8: mean wait 1.62 s

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Pooling packers into one queue shortens the wait at the same load. A design question such as "one fast packer or three slower ones" needs the wait, not only the utilisation. The formula covers exponential times only, so the shop's own runs answer it for other times.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Choosing Inputs runs the busy hour with four candidate packing times, all with a mean of 1.5 seconds. The mean waits are 1.27 seconds with constant times, 1.28 with triangular, 1.35 with the measured times and 2.37 with exponential. The same mean with a wider spread gives a longer wait.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
Kingman's formula gives an approximate mean wait for one server with any distributions. It measures the spread of each input by its coefficient of variation, the standard deviation divided by the mean, called variation for short. The variation is 1 for an exponential distribution and 0 for a constant one. The mean wait is the product of three parts:

  • utilisation ÷ (1 − utilisation), which grows quickly as utilisation nears 1;
  • (arrival variation² + service variation²) ÷ 2, the effect of the spread;
  • the mean service time.

With exponential gaps (variation 1) and constant service (variation 0), the middle part is 0.5. The formula then gives half the M/M/1 wait, which is the M/D/1 result above. Variation in the gaps counts as much as variation in the packing times. When both variations are 0, the formula gives no wait at all.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: The kingman_wait function above computes it. Use it to judge how much the choice of an input distribution matters before you fit one. Choosing Inputs shows how to compare the candidates by running each.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model whose inputs are replaced by their averages has no variation, so it shows no queue while utilisation is below 1. Its waits are too short. Common Mistakes lists this among the errors that distort a result.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Queues and Capacity adds a checker to the shop. Orders arrive at 1.6 a second, every packed order is checked, and a tenth of the checked orders go back to packing. Four packers take 1.5 seconds an order, and one checker takes 0.4 seconds on average.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
In a network of tasks, work reaches a task in two ways: as new work, and as work routed to it from other tasks. The rate into a task is the sum of the two. This is flow balance. For packing, the rate is 1.6 + 0.1 × the rate into packing. Solving for it gives 1.6 ÷ (1 − 0.1) = 1.6 ÷ 0.9 = 1.778 orders a second. Every packed order goes to the checker, so the checker receives the same 1.778.

Each resource's utilisation follows from its rate. The four packers have 1.778 × 1.5 ÷ 4 = 0.667. The checker has 1.778 × 0.4 = 0.711. The resource with the highest utilisation is the bottleneck, here the checker. It is the first to reach full use when demand grows, and adding units anywhere else does not raise the most the shop can handle.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Work out the rate into each task, then each resource's utilisation:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:flow
# Orders arrive at 1.6 a second, and a tenth of the checked orders go back to packing,
# so the rate into packing solves: rate = 1.6 + 0.1 x rate.
flow_rate = 1.6 / (1 - 0.1)
packers = flow_rate * 1.5 / 4  # four packers, 1.5 seconds an order
checker = flow_rate * 0.4  # one checker, 0.4 seconds an order on average
print(f"rate into packing and into checking: {flow_rate:.3f} orders a second")
print(f"utilisation: packers {packers:.3f}, checker {checker:.3f}")

desflow explain does the same from the model and names the bottleneck:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow explain queues_network.yaml

It ends its resource tables with Bottleneck: checkers.

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:flow-explain
from queues_and_capacity import network

explanation = network().analyze()
print(f"desflow explain names the bottleneck: {explanation.bottleneck}")

desflow explain does not support low-level models. Explain the YAML or builder form of the network.

rate into packing and into checking: 1.778 orders a second
utilisation: packers 0.667, checker 0.711
desflow explain names the bottleneck: checkers

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Add capacity at the bottleneck first. Here a second checker lowers the checker's utilisation to 0.356, while a fifth packer leaves the checker at 0.711 and the shop no faster. Rework raises the load on every task it passes through, so a model without it underestimates every utilisation.

docs.title: Check a Formula Against the Shop
In the Tutorial
docs.text: The busy hour with exponential packing times is M/M/3 at utilisation 0.9. The Erlang C formula gives a mean wait of 4.083 seconds. Ten one-hour runs of the shop measure 4.784 ± 1.301 seconds, so the formula lies within the interval of the runs.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A formula and a run that agree check each other. The formula shows that the model is built as intended, and the runs show that the formula applies. A model that disagrees with a formula on a case the formula covers has a fault in its logic or its statistics.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

desflow explain --verify runs the model and compares each measure with the analysis:

PACKING=exponential desflow explain choosing_inputs.yaml --verify --replications 10


Verify: 10 runs to 3600 s, seed 42
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+
| node       | measure      | analysis | measured |        ± | result |
|------------+--------------+----------+----------+----------+--------|
| packers    | utilization  |      0.9 |   0.9066 | 0.008966 | agrees |
| packers    | queue_length |    7.349 |    8.659 |    2.396 | agrees |
| pack_order | wait         |    4.083 |    4.784 |    1.301 | agrees |
| orders     | throughput   |      1.8 |    1.805 |  0.01634 | agrees |
+---------------------------------------------------------------------+

This shop takes the gaps and the packing times as exponential or constant by choice:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:shop
def shop(arrival: dict, service: dict, packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with the given arrival gaps and packing times, and `packers` packers."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    app.add_arrival("orders", **arrival)
    app.add_service("packing", **service)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


# Exponential gaps and times are the M of Kendall's notation, constant ones the D
def exponential(mean: float) -> dict:
    return {"dist": "exponential", "rate": 1 / mean}


def constant(mean: float) -> dict:
    return {"dist": "constant", "value": mean}

This function runs ten replications, each leaving out its first 2,000 seconds, and returns the mean wait with its 95% half-width:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:measure
def measured_wait(arrival: dict, service: dict, packers: int, until: int):
    """Mean wait over 10 runs, with its 95% half-width; each run leaves out its first 2,000 s."""
    result = replicate(
        lambda: shop(arrival, service, packers),
        10,
        seed=42,
        until=until,
        warmup=2000,
        measures=["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
    )
    row = result.summary[0]
    return row["mean"], row["half_width"]

--verify does not support low-level models. replicate runs a LowLevelModel the same way, as Replications shows, and its mean and half-width compare with a formula as in the Builder tab.

The Builder tab's checks compare each formula with the runs, and pass when the formula lies within the interval:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:checks
for rho, figures in ((0.5, (1.50, 1.47, 0.06)), (0.75, (4.50, 4.46, 0.33))):
    arrival = exponential(SERVICE / rho)
    check(
        f"M/M/1 at utilisation {rho}",
        mm1_wait(rho),
        measured_wait(arrival, exponential(SERVICE), 1, 20_000),
        figures,
    )
check(
    "M/M/3 at utilisation 0.8",
    mmc_wait(3, 1.6),
    measured_wait(exponential(1 / 1.6), exponential(SERVICE), 3, 30_000),
    (1.62, 1.64, 0.06),
)
arrival = exponential(SERVICE / 0.75)
check(
    "M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, Kingman",
    kingman_wait(0.75, 1, 0),
    measured_wait(arrival, constant(SERVICE), 1, 20_000),
    (2.25, 2.23, 0.14),
)

M/M/1 at utilisation 0.5: formula 1.50 s, mean of 10 runs 1.47 ± 0.06 s
M/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: formula 4.50 s, mean of 10 runs 4.46 ± 0.33 s
M/M/3 at utilisation 0.8: formula 1.62 s, mean of 10 runs 1.64 ± 0.06 s
M/D/1 at utilisation 0.75, Kingman: formula 2.25 s, mean of 10 runs 2.23 ± 0.14 s

The busy hour itself is M/D/3, which has no exact formula. For one packer, constant service halves the M/M/1 wait. This check compares the M/D/3 runs with half the M/M/3 wait, as an approximation:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:kendall
# The busy hour is M/D/3: exponential gaps (M), constant service (D), three packers.
# The runs are compared with half the M/M/3 wait at this load.
check(
    "M/D/3 at utilisation 0.9, half the M/M/3 wait",
    mmc_wait(3, 1.8) / 2,
    measured_wait(exponential(1 / 1.8), constant(SERVICE), 3, 20_000),
    (2.04, 2.05, 0.13),
)

M/D/3 at utilisation 0.9, half the M/M/3 wait: formula 2.04 s, mean of 10 runs 2.05 ± 0.13 s

These are 10 runs of 20,000 seconds, each without its first 2,000 seconds, not one-hour runs.

Kingman's formula is an approximation, and this check shows where it is not exact. Constant gaps of 2 seconds with exponential service (D/M/1) at utilisation 0.75:

docs/snippets/pages/queueing_basics.py:dm1
mean, half_width = measured_wait(
    constant(SERVICE / 0.75), exponential(SERVICE), 1, 20_000
)
kingman = kingman_wait(0.75, 0, 1)
print(
    f"D/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: Kingman {kingman:.2f} s, mean of 10 runs {mean:.2f} ± {half_width:.2f} s"
)

D/M/1 at utilisation 0.75: Kingman 2.25 s, mean of 10 runs 1.78 ± 0.09 s

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: Where a formula is exact, as for M/M/1 and M/M/c, it lies within the interval of the runs. Half the M/M/3 wait is close for the M/D/3 busy hour. Kingman's formula lies outside the interval for D/M/1: it is accurate near full use and for the cases above, and a rough guide elsewhere. A check that fails on a case the formula covers points to a fault in the model. A check that fails outside the formula's cases says only that the formula does not apply.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Write the model in Kendall's notation first, to know which formulas apply.
  • Work out utilisation for every resource before a run. At 1 or above, the answer is more capacity.
  • Check a run's statistics with Little's law before trusting any result.
  • Expect long waits near full use, and longer ones when gaps or packing times vary.
  • Find the bottleneck with flow balance, and add capacity there first.
  • Check the model against a formula on the cases the formula covers. The simulation answers the cases it cannot: several resources, priorities, breakdowns and changing demand.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Wikipedia: Kendall's notation, Little's law, Kingman's formula, the Erlang C formula and the Jackson network.
  • The explanations and the checks are our own.

docs.title: Readiness and Reporting
docs.text: A model is ready when someone who was not part of the study can see what it answers, how far to trust the answer, and how to repeat it. This page explains what that takes, with the shop's study in The Complete Model as the example. It points to three published checklists written for simulation studies, and shows which parts desflow does for you and which parts only you can write.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
• why readiness is a statement about a decision, not about a model;
  • what the three levels of the Model Readiness Checklist ask for;
  • what a report needs, by the STRESS-DES checklist;
  • what to share so that others can run the model, by the STARS framework;
  • which items desflow records for you, and which only you can write.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop model is ready to say how many packers the busy hour needs: its inputs came from data, its checks passed, its results carry an interval, and a reader can repeat the runs. It is not ready to say anything about a holiday week, whatever its code looks like.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A model is built and checked for one question. The checks of Checking and Validating show it fits that question, with the inputs and the range of conditions it was checked under. Outside them, nothing has been checked.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: Write down the question the model is ready for, as A Simulation Study does, and state the limits of its use. An experiment file keeps them with the runs: The Complete Model lists "One busy hour only; the rest of the day is not modelled" among its limits, and report.md prints them.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A reader who wants to use the model for another question can see at once that it was not built for it. That question needs its own checks before the model answers it.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The shop's study meets most of the first level below. Its replications and warm-up come from Trusting Results, its seeds are fixed, its core logic is checked in Checking a Model, and it is compared with values observed in the shop. The review of the process with the people who know it is the walk-through of Check the Assumptions, which no tool does.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
The open book HSMA: the little book of DES has a chapter, Model Readiness Checklist, that sorts what a model needs into three levels, by the size of the decision:

  • Bronze is the level for small to medium decisions within one organisation. It asks for views of the model running, checks of the core logic, enough replications and a warm-up, a fixed seed, a comparison with the real system, a review of the process with the people who know it, and documentation.
  • Silver is the level for larger or costlier decisions, or for models used across several areas. It adds a formal reporting checklist such as STRESS-DES, documented code, a code review, automated tests, an open licence, version control and a sensitivity analysis.
  • Gold is the level for models that will be reused, adapted or published. It adds:
    • a documentation site and a changelog;
    • identifiers for the authors and an archive of the code;
    • an online environment to run the model in, parallel runs, a web app and an animation;
    • formal methods for the warm-up and the number of replications;
    • tests against historical data.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Choose the level from the decision, then go through its items. Some items cost nothing in desflow, and some need you:

Item In desflow A fixed seed and independent streams random_seed fixes a run, and replicate makes one integer seed for each replication from one seed and records them, so the same call gives the same results and any replication can be repeated alone. See Replications Enough replications, with an interval replicate gives the mean and the half-width of the 95% interval. How many is your decision The designs and the inputs on record An experiment records the compiled parameters of each design and writes its summary, its comparisons, its checks and a report.md. See Experiments A comparison with the real system An experiment can read an observed file and compare it with the model. See Experiment Results. Which data to use is your decision A view of the model running Every event and reading is a record, which you can read or send to a sink. See Egress, Batching and Delivery Core logic checked Yours: Checking and Validating shows the cases to work by hand Assumptions, data sources and limits Yours: they go in the experiment file and the report, and no tool decides them

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A level is met when every item of it is done, not most. An item left out goes into the report as a limit, so that the reader knows which check the model has not had.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: The Complete Model's report.md gives the question, the model and its versions, the assumptions, each input with its fitted parameters and where it came from, the run settings, the counts, the results, the comparisons, the checks and the observed comparison, then the limits and any input with no source. Its Comparisons section answers the question with each difference and its interval: a fourth packer cuts the packing wait by 1.77 seconds, with a half-width of 0.16 seconds.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: A reader acts on the report alone. The reporting checklist STRESS-DES lists what that reader will ask. It has 20 items in six groups: objectives, logic, data, experimentation, implementation and code access. It is by Monks, Currie, Onggo, Robinson, Kunc and Taylor, and the book gives it in its chapter STRESS-DES Reporting.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Answer each group in one short paragraph of the report, in this order, after the answer and its interval:

  • Objectives: the question and the measures, as in Ask One Question.
  • Logic: the conceptual model, with its assumptions and what it leaves out.
  • Data: where each input came from, and how it was fitted or chosen.
  • Experimentation: the run length, the warm-up, the number of replications and the designs compared.
  • Implementation: the software and its version, and the random number streams.
  • Code access: where the code, the data and the seeds are kept.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: report.md answers the objectives, the data and the experimentation from the experiment file, and gives the software versions. The logic beyond the listed assumptions, how the model was checked, and where the code is kept are yours to add. Common Mistakes lists what to look for before you send the report.

docs.title: In the Tutorial
docs.text: Each tutorial page ends with Full Files: every file its runs need, so a reader can repeat them. desflow itself is under the MIT licence and installs from PyPI with a stated version.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: The framework STARS, by Monks, Harper and Mustafee, says what to share so that others can run and reuse a model. The book gives it in The STARS Framework. A model that only its author can run cannot be checked by anyone else.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
STARS separates essential parts from optional ones:

  • Essential: an open licence; a list of the software the model needs, with its versions; free and open software; a minimum of documentation; an identifier for each author; a citation file; a code repository; and an archive that gives the code a permanent identifier.
  • Optional: fuller documentation, a hosted documentation site, an online environment to run the model in, an interface, and a hosted web app.

Keep the blueprint or the Python files, the experiment file and the observed data in one repository, with the desflow version they ran on.

docs.title: What the Result Means
docs.text: A model shared with its essential parts can be run again by a reader, with the same seeds and the same results. That is the strongest evidence a report can give.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Ready is a statement about one decision: write down the question and the limits of the model's use.
  • Choose the readiness level from the size of the decision, and meet every item of it.
  • desflow records the seeds, the intervals, the designs, the inputs and the comparisons. The assumptions, the checks and the limits are yours to write.
  • Report the answer first, with its interval, then the six groups of STRESS-DES.
  • Share the model with an open licence, its software versions and its files.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The open book HSMA: the little book of DES, its chapters Model Readiness Checklist, STRESS-DES Reporting and The STARS Framework. The chapters are under the CC BY-NC-SA licence, so none of their text is copied here. We read the three and link them, and the lists above are our own summaries.
  • Monks, Currie, Onggo, Robinson, Kunc and Taylor, "Strengthening the reporting of empirical simulation studies: Introducing the STRESS guidelines" (Journal of Simulation, 2019).
  • Monks, Harper and Mustafee, "Towards sharing tools and artefacts for reusable simulations in healthcare" (Journal of Simulation, 2024).

docs.title: End Conditions
docs.text:
For an hour the shop now gets an order every 1.43 seconds on average (42 a minute, rate: 0.7). Its one packer takes 1.5 seconds per order, so it packs at most 40 a minute, a little fewer than the 42 that arrive. Orders are still waiting when the hour ends. A report that counts only the orders packed in the hour leaves them out. This page asks: does a fixed horizon answer the same question as closing the doors and packing every order already in the shop?

  • Decision: which way of ending the run the shop's report uses.
  • Measures: the orders started, finished and still in the shop, the mean wait, and the time the run ends.
  • Runs: two runs, each with the seed 42: one stops at the end of the hour, and one stops taking orders then and runs until the last order is packed.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, and every order takes the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • end a run at a fixed time, or close the doors and drain the orders already in the shop;
  • count the orders started, finished and still in the shop;
  • see which orders a mean wait leaves out.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a drain at the end of the run, which packs every order still in the shop, and the counts that show which orders each way of ending leaves out. The shop is the one from First Simulation, busier: one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing.

docs.title: Count Who Is Still There
docs.text:
An end condition decides which entities a run's results describe. These statistics count the orders:

  • flows.orders.started, from the basic level, counts the orders that entered the shop. An order enters when its first task begins, before any queue.
  • flows.orders.finished, from basic, counts the orders that left.
  • flows.orders.in_system, from basic, counts the orders still in the shop.
  • tasks.pack_order.in_progress, from minimal, counts the orders waiting to be packed or being packed.

The model switches on typical, which also keeps the mean wait:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/end_conditions.yaml:watch
# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 2 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions.py:watch
# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions_low_level.py:watch
# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)

A low-level process reports its entities with env.stats.flow_started(arrival) and env.stats.flow_finished(arrival), as the full file below does.

Every order that started is either finished or still in the shop, so started is finished plus in_system. These counts say how many orders a mean wait leaves out.

docs.title: Close the Doors, Then Finish
docs.text:
Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there. A fixed horizon stops the clock at until, whatever is still going on. A drain stops only the arrivals at until and keeps running until every entity in the model has left. In SimPy that is two steps: interrupt the source process, then run until every admitted process has ended. desflow writes both with drain:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/end_conditions.yaml:run
run:
  # No new orders after one hour
  until: 1 h
  # true: pack every order already in the shop before the run ends
  drain: ${DRAIN:-false}

${DRAIN:-false} reads the environment variable DRAIN, so DRAIN=true desflow run end_conditions.yaml runs the drain, as desflow run end_conditions.yaml --drain does.

docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions.py:run
# No new orders after one hour; with drain, pack every order already in the shop
app.run(until="1 h", drain=drain or None)
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions_low_level.py:run
env.run(until=3600)  # no new orders after one hour
if drain:
    # Stop the source, then run until every admitted order has ended
    source.interrupt()
    env.run(until=env.all_of([o for o in orders if o.is_alive]))

env.all_of(...) is SimPy's AllOf: it happens when every order process has ended. SimPy and desflow explains waiting for all events.

source.interrupt() raises an Interrupt inside the source process, which ends its loop. SimPy and desflow explains interrupts.

o.is_alive is true while a process has not ended.

env.now is the clock, which the script reads to report the end time. SimPy and desflow explains the clock.

The stop at until is an event that SimPy schedules with the URGENT priority, so it comes before the other events at that time. A low-level script that stops its own run at an event can do the same with env.schedule(event, URGENT, delay). In a blueprint, the fire action's urgent and after keys do it, as Signals and Waiting shows.

A drain can also take a limit, drain: {limit: 10 min}, so a model that never empties still ends. A stop ends the run as soon as an event or a condition happens. Run Length describes both.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Does a fixed horizon answer the same question as a drain? Not for every order. Each figure here comes from a run with the seed 42: one that stops at the hour, and one that drains after it. The fixed horizon ends at 3,600 seconds with 2,436 orders started, 2,398 finished and 38 still in the shop, one being packed and 37 waiting. The drain ends 56.4 seconds later, at 3,656.4, with all 2,436 finished:

desflow explain shows why so many orders are left, without a run:

desflow explain end_conditions.yaml

Resources
+--------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |    ρ | Wq | L | status   |
|----------+-----+--------+---+------+----+---+----------|
| packers  | 0.7 | 0.6667 | 1 | 1.05 |  - | - | UNSTABLE |
+--------------------------------------------------------+
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: unstable: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts

The packer gets 1.05 seconds of work every second, more than it can do, so the queue grows for as long as orders arrive. The longer the horizon, the more orders it leaves in the shop. A drain packs them all. In Python, context.analyze() gives the same analysis for a builder model. A low-level model has no explain, because its SimPy code makes the links between arrivals, tasks and resources as it runs, so there are none to read.

The mean wait barely moves: 71.70 seconds with the fixed horizon against 71.51 with the drain. An order's wait is measured when its packing starts, and only 37 of the 2,436 orders start packing after the hour.

Each tab prints both runs: the orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait. A record's sim_ts is the time the run ended.

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# Stop at the end time: orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait
desflow run end_conditions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders\.(started|finished|in_system)"|pack_order\.wait_mean"' | tail -4
# Finish the orders in the shop first
DRAIN=true desflow run end_conditions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders\.(started|finished|in_system)"|pack_order\.wait_mean"' | tail -4


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":71.69841183873338}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished","value":2398}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.started","value":2436}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system","value":38}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3656.383,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":71.50563836690414}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3656.383,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished","value":2436}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3656.383,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.started","value":2436}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3656.383,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system","value":0}


python end_conditions.py 2>/dev/null

horizon: ends at  3600.0 s, 2436 started, 2398 finished, 38 left, mean wait 71.70 s
drain  : ends at  3656.4 s, 2436 started, 2436 finished, 0 left, mean wait 71.51 s

python end_conditions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

horizon: ends at  3600.0 s, 2436 started, 2398 finished, 38 left, mean wait 71.70 s
drain  : ends at  3656.4 s, 2436 started, 2436 finished, 0 left, mean wait 71.51 s

A fixed horizon answers a question about a period, such as how many orders the shop packs in an hour. The orders still in the shop at the end are unfinished work, and in_system says how many there are. A drain answers a question about a batch of orders, such as how long the day's orders take to clear. It serves every admitted order, but the run goes on past the hour. Report the counts beside any mean, so a reader knows which orders it covers. Output Analysis explains the two kinds of run, and Statistics describes each count.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A fixed horizon answers a question about a period. A drain answers a question about a batch of orders.
  • started equals finished plus in_system, so these counts show the orders a result leaves out.
  • Report the counts beside any mean, so a reader knows which orders it covers.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/end_conditions.yaml
# The End Conditions tutorial: a fixed horizon against a drain.
# Run it with: desflow run end_conditions.yaml
# With a drain after the hour: DRAIN=true desflow run end_conditions.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.7, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 2 h}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  # No new orders after one hour
  until: 1 h
  # true: pack every order already in the shop before the run ends
  drain: ${DRAIN:-false}
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions.py
"""The End Conditions tutorial: a fixed horizon against a drain.

One packer, an order every 1.43 seconds on average (rate 0.7) and 1.5 seconds of
packing, for an hour. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the
counts and the mean wait with a fixed horizon and with a drain at the end. To see only
those lines, run:
python end_conditions.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop of First Simulation, busier: more orders than one packer can pack."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.7)
        # Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=7200)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(drain: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour, with or without a drain, and returns the counts and the wait."""
    app = shop()
    # No new orders after one hour; with drain, pack every order already in the shop
    app.run(until="1 h", drain=drain or None)
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.{}".format
    return {
        "started": r[name("flows.orders.started")],
        "finished": r[name("flows.orders.finished")],
        "in_system": r[name("flows.orders.in_system")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("tasks.pack_order.wait_mean")],
        "end": app.env.now,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for drain in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(drain)
        label = "drain  " if drain else "horizon"
        print(
            f"{label}: ends at {r['end']:7.1f} s, {r['started']} started, "
            f"{r['finished']} finished, {r['in_system']} left, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/end_conditions_low_level.py
"""The End Conditions tutorial: a fixed horizon against a drain.

One packer, an order every 1.43 seconds on average (rate 0.7) and 1.5 seconds of
packing, for an hour. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the
counts and the mean wait with a fixed horizon and with a drain at the end. To see only
those lines, run:
python end_conditions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

import simpy

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.7)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    env.stats.flow_started("orders")  # the order enters the shop
    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, orders):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    try:
        for task_id in itertools.count():
            yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
            key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
            orders.append(env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id)))
    except simpy.Interrupt:
        pass  # no new orders after the hour


def run(drain=False, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Orders started, finished and still in the shop, and the mean wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=7200)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    orders = []
    source = env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers, orders))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)  # no new orders after one hour
        if drain:
            # Stop the source, then run until every admitted order has ended
            source.interrupt()
            env.run(until=env.all_of([o for o in orders if o.is_alive]))
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(drain: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour, with or without a drain, and returns the counts and the wait."""
    env = run(drain)
    r = env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.{}".format
    return {
        "started": r[name("flows.orders.started")],
        "finished": r[name("flows.orders.finished")],
        "in_system": r[name("flows.orders.in_system")],
        "wait_mean": r[name("tasks.pack_order.wait_mean")],
        "end": env.now,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for drain in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(drain)
        label = "drain  " if drain else "horizon"
        print(
            f"{label}: ends at {r['end']:7.1f} s, {r['started']} started, "
            f"{r['finished']} finished, {r['in_system']} left, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )

docs.title: First Simulation
docs.text:
This tutorial models a shop that receives and packs customer orders: one packer, an order every 2 seconds on average, and 1.5 seconds of packing per order. It answers one question: how long does an order wait with one packer?

  • Decision: how many packers the shop needs, which later pages decide.
  • Measures: the wait of each order, from the moment it joins the queue to the moment packing starts.
  • Runs: one run of the first 20 seconds, with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, and every order takes exactly the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • describe a model as an arrival, a resource and a service time, in YAML, the builder or the low-level API;
  • run it and read the event records it prints;
  • read an order's wait from its queued and started events.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
This page builds the first model of the shop: a simulation called Shop with an orders arrival, a packers resource with one unit, a packing service and a pack_order task, and a sink that prints each record. The following pages extend the same model, one idea per page.

Each step shows the code three ways, in tabs: a YAML blueprint, the Builder (SimulationContext) and the Low-level API (DynamicRealtimeEnvironment and SimPy processes). Choose the tab for your preferred API; all code tabs on the site switch to that API. The three build the same simulation and print the same records. Writing a Model explains how they relate.

Look at the order of the parts: orders arrive, wait in the packer queue and take the packer for 1.5 seconds. The simulation prints a record of each step to the console. The arrival loop and the task read their values from the registry. The steps below explain each of these parts.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Install the core package, which includes the desflow command, as Installation shows.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint needs only the desflow command. Install it with one of these forms, then run the file:

# With uv, the command alone
uv tool install desflow

# Or with pip
pip install desflow

# Run the blueprint
desflow run first_shop.yaml

A builder model is a Python file, so the Python that runs it must be able to import desflow. uv tool install desflow installs the command only. Run the file with one of these forms:

# With uv, outside a project
uv run --with desflow python first_shop.py

# In a uv project, after `uv add desflow`
uv run python first_shop.py

# After `pip install desflow`
python first_shop.py

The pages that follow show the plain python <file>.py form. Run it with whichever form above you use.

A low-level model is a Python file, so the Python that runs it must be able to import desflow. uv tool install desflow installs the command only. Run the file with one of these forms:

# With uv, outside a project
uv run --with desflow python first_shop_low_level.py

# In a uv project, after `uv add desflow`
uv run python first_shop_low_level.py

# After `pip install desflow`
python first_shop_low_level.py

The pages that follow show the plain python <file>.py form. Run it with whichever form above you use.

docs.title: Describe the Shop
docs.text:
In discrete-event simulation (DES), an entity is a thing that moves through the model, here an order. A resource is what an entity needs and may have to wait for, here the packer. A service time is how long an entity holds the resource, and an arrival process sets when entities appear.

In desflow, these are parameters of one simulation. Its name, the sim_id, is Shop here. The shop has a resource called packers with one unit, a service called packing, and an arrival stream called orders.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:shop
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 1.0  # 1 simulated second takes 1 real second
  random_seed: 42  # the same arrival times on every run

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

services:
  # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5}

arrivals:
  # One order every 2 seconds on average; each arrival spawns pack_order
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:shop
app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
