    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:shop
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run

Packing is constant, so every order takes 1.5 seconds and only the arrivals are random. The gaps between orders are drawn from an exponential distribution with a mean of 2 seconds (30 orders a minute on average), rate: 0.5. The seed makes those draws the same on every run, so your trace matches the one below; Randomness and Seeds explains it.

The registry holds the model's live values: the settings that can change while the simulation runs. Each value has a path, such as Shop.arrival.orders.rate or Shop.resources.packers.current_cap. A scenario, or a message from outside the simulation, changes a value through its path, and the run goes on with the new value. Live Changes does it on the shop, and Live Parameters explains how.

docs.title: Say What an Order Does
docs.text:
In DES terms an order queues for the packer, seizes it when it is free, is delayed for the service time, and releases the packer. desflow calls this a task. A task publishes three events: queued when the order joins the queue for the packer, started when the packer starts on it, and a finished event when packing ends. The value of the finished event is the task's payload.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:order
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The value of the finished event
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

spawn: pack_order on the arrival, in the step above, starts the task for every order.

docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:order
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1

@app.task publishes the three events and handles the packer for you. The arrival loop waits for each arrival and starts one pack_order for the order it returns.

docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:order
def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1

These are SimPy constructs. pack_order is a process: a generator function that the environment runs, pausing at each yield until the event it yielded happens. env.timeout(...) is an event that happens after a delay. packers.request() is an event that happens when a packer is free, and leaving the with block releases the packer. env.process(...) starts a process. SimPy and desflow describes what desflow adds to them.

docs.title: Print the Records
docs.text:
A sink, called an egress, receives every record the simulation publishes. ConsoleEgress prints them; Egress lists the others.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/first_shop.yaml:records
egress:
  - type: Console
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop.py:records
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
docs/snippets/tutorials/first_shop_low_level.py:records
SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below

Every event record carries the order's key, orders-1 for the first order, so all the events of one order can be found together. task names the task, and instance counts the task's runs from 0. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: Run It
What You Get and Why
docs.text:
How long does an order wait with one packer? It depends on how many orders are ahead of it, as the same records on a timeline show: each order waits (yellow) until the packer is free, then holds it for 1.5 seconds of packing (blue).

These records come from one run of the first 20 seconds, with the seed 42. orders-1 finds the packer free, so its queued and started events have the same time. orders-2 is the first order that has to wait: it is queued at 2.696 and started at 4.052, when orders-1 finishes. It waits 1.356 seconds. orders-3 arrives while orders-2 is waiting and waits longer, 1.815 seconds, because two orders are ahead of it.

So with one packer, an order that arrives while the packer is busy waits until every order ahead of it has been packed. The wait depends on when orders happen to arrive, which is why the next pages measure it over many orders.

A discrete-event simulation keeps a list of future events, ordered by time. It takes the earliest one, moves the clock to its time, and runs what it triggers, which may add new events to the list: an arrival schedules the next arrival, and a start of packing schedules its end 1.5 seconds later. The trace above is that list, read in order. What Is DES? explains the event list in more detail.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A model has entities that arrive, resources they wait for, and service times that hold them. desflow calls the work an entity does a task.
  • A task publishes queued, started and a finished event, and an order's wait is its started time minus its queued time.
  • The simulation clock jumps from one event to the next, so a run gives the same records at any pace.

docs.title: Busy Hour Figures
docs.text:
The later pages of this tutorial and the concept pages run the busy hour with 3 packers in different ways, so they give different figures for its mean wait. A figure changes with the number of runs, the packing times, the warm-up, the run length and the seeds. The table lists each figure, the pages that give it and how it was run. Every run is one hour at 1.8 orders a second unless the row says otherwise. Two terms in the table need a definition:

  • "Measured times" are the 40 packing times measured at the bench, drawn as an empirical distribution.
  • "Replications" have seeds spawned from 42. A run of 5, 10 or 20 replications uses the first 5, 10 or 20 of the 40 seeds.
Mean wait (s) Pages How it was run 1.27 Queues and Capacity, Choosing Inputs, Queueing Basics, Common Mistakes one run, seed 42, constant packing, no warm-up 1.28 Choosing Inputs, Queueing Basics one run, seed 42, the expert's triangular packing (1 to 2.25 s, mode 1.25), no warm-up 1.35 Choosing Inputs, Queueing Basics, Randomness and Seeds one run, seed 42, measured times in a service named empirical, no warm-up 1.38 Measuring a Run, Trusting Results, Output Analysis, Randomness and Seeds one run, seed 42, measured times in a service named packing, without a warm-up (1.382) or with a 2-minute warm-up (1.381) 2.37 Choosing Inputs, Queueing Basics, Common Mistakes one run, seed 42, exponential packing, no warm-up 2.11 Common Mistakes 10 replications, constant packing, no warm-up 1.99 Common Mistakes 20 replications with seeds spawned from 1, constant packing, no warm-up 2.05 ± 0.13 Queueing Basics 10 replications of 20,000 seconds, constant packing, the first 2,000 seconds left out 2.20 to 2.23 Trusting Results 5 replications, measured times, warm-ups of 1, 2 and 4 minutes 2.25 ± 0.25 Trusting Results, Checking a Model 10 replications, measured times, 2-minute warm-up 2.48 ± 0.32 Trusting Results, Comparing Designs, Parameter Sweeps, Checking a Model, Checking and Validating, Queueing Basics 20 replications, measured times, 2-minute warm-up 2.32 ± 0.20 Trusting Results, Fitting the Inputs, Comparing Designs, Output Analysis, A Simulation Study 40 replications, measured times, 2-minute warm-up 2.33 ± 0.19 Fitting the Inputs 40 replications, the gamma fitted to the measured times, 2-minute warm-up 2.93 ± 0.25 Fitting the Inputs 40 replications, the triangular fitted to the measured times, 2-minute warm-up

The 1.35 and 1.38 seconds come from the same measured times. The two services draw the times in a different order, because each distribution draws from a random number stream named after its registry path, service.empirical or service.packing (Randomness and Seeds explains the streams).

"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, with the SimulationContext builder.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

app = (
    # 1 simulated second = 1 real second; a seed gives the same arrivals every run
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=1.0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
    # Every order takes exactly 1.5 seconds to pack
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # One order every 2 seconds on average
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Requests a packer, waits the packing time, releases the packer.
    # The returned dictionary is the value of the finished event.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        # Waits for the next arrival and returns the new order, keyed orders-1, ...
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until=20)

"""The First Simulation tutorial: the shop, on the low-level API.

One packer, orders arriving about every 2 seconds, and 1.5 seconds of packing per
order. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)
SEED = 42  # the same arrival times on every run


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order: wait for a packer, pack it, release the packer."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        service = env.registry.get_config(path_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(service))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one pack_order for every arrival, keyed orders-1, orders-2, ..."""
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


SINKS = [ConsoleEgress()]  # passed to env.setup_egress in run below


def run(until=20, factor=1.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, strict=False)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(SINKS)

    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)

    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
Most of the pages so far read one number, the mean wait. A run knows much more. This page asks: what does a run tell me?

  • Decision: which numbers to read from a run before acting on it.
  • Measures: five of the numbers the run publishes: the packers' utilisation, the mean queue, the mean and longest wait, and the orders packed.
  • Runs: one run of the busy hour, with the seed 42, starting with an empty shop.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random at 1.8 a second, and the times measured at the bench stand for every packer.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • switch on the built-in statistics at a level;
  • read utilisation, queue length, waits and counts at the end of a run;
  • check the statistics against each other with Little's Law.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds stats: typical, the built-in statistics at the level that includes waits. The model simulates the busy hour with 3 packers from Queues and Capacity, and draws each packing time from 40 times measured at the bench, each equally likely. The model calls this an empirical distribution. Real packing times vary, so these times describe the shop better than the constant 1.5 seconds of the earlier pages; Choosing Inputs explains the distribution and compares it with others.

docs.title: Switch On Statistics
docs.text:
desflow keeps statistics about a run as it goes. It publishes them as telemetry every 10 simulation seconds and once more at the end, so the last value of each statistic is the state at the end of the run. Statistics are off by default, because most runs only generate data. A level switches them on: none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each publishing what the one before it does and more. typical adds each task's mean and maximum wait and service time. Statistics lists what each level adds. Switch on typical:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
stats: typical
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
.with_stats("typical")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:stats
# Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)

The environment keeps the statistics in env.stats. Resources report their own changes. A low-level process has no task for desflow to watch, so the process reports each step itself. It calls env.stats.task_queued, task_started and task_finished with the task's name and instance id, and flow_started and flow_finished when the order enters and leaves the shop. The full file below shows them.

The statistics are telemetry, so they reach every sink, and they can also be read in Python at the end of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/measuring_a_run.yaml:read
# The statistics are telemetry, so every sink receives them
egress:
  - type: Console
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run.py:read
if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until="1 h")
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in app.env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py:read
if __name__ == "__main__":
    env = run()
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")

Every name has the same form, <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there: desflow run measuring_a_run.yaml, python measuring_a_run.py or python measuring_a_run_low_level.py. These are the statistics published at the end of the hour:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length', 'value': 8}

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.queue_length_avg', 'value': 2.405756864104584}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.in_progress', 'value': 11}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished', 'value': 6250}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean', 'value': 1.3816663590146558}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max', 'value': 9.378296391499589}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_mean', 'value': 1.4953759999999972}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.service_max', 'value': 2.7000000000000455}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished', 'value': 6250}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.started', 'value': 6261}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 3600.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.flows.orders.in_system', 'value': 11}

The statistics mean:

  • utilization_avg 86.56: the packers were busy 86.56% of the time. The utilisation statistics are percentages, while desflow explain and --verify give utilisation as a fraction, 0.9 for 90%.
  • utilization 100.0: all three packers were busy at the end.
  • tasks.pack_order.finished: the orders the task finished.
  • flows.orders.finished: the orders that left the shop. The flow is named after the arrival that started them, orders. With one task the two counts are equal.
  • flows.orders.started: the orders that entered the shop, 6,261.
  • flows.orders.in_system: the 11 orders still in the shop when the hour ended. tasks.pack_order.in_progress gives the same 11.

The names use the spelling utilization, and the text uses "utilisation" for the same thing. The mean wait is 1.38 seconds, over the orders that started packing in this one run with the seed 42. End Conditions shows what a run leaves out when it ends.

docs.title: Counts and Averages Over Time
docs.text:
The statistics are of two kinds. A count, such as finished, adds one for each order. An average over time, also called a time-weighted average, such as utilization_avg or queue_length_avg, weighs each value by how long it lasted. Look at the area under the number of busy packers:

desflow adds the area every time the value changes, so the average is exact at any moment. A reading taken now and then, such as every 10 seconds, sees only the value at that instant. The queue in the first five minutes of the hour shows the difference:

The queue rises and falls many times between two readings, and a handful of readings can land on high points by chance. Here the readings average 2.60 orders, while the average over time for the same five minutes is 2.19 orders.

docs.title: Wait and Service
docs.text:
The time each order spends in the shop has two parts, both measured from the task's own events:

  • wait runs from queued to started: the time spent waiting for a packer;
  • service runs from started to the finished event: the time spent being packed.

service_mean is 1.50 seconds and service_max is 2.7 seconds. The 40 measured times have the same mean and the same longest time, so the model draws what it was given. wait_max is 9.38 seconds: one order waited almost seven times as long as the average one.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What does a run tell me? One run of the busy hour, with the seed 42, the measured packing times and no warm-up, tells you that:

  • the packers were busy 86.6% of the time on average;
  • the queue held 2.41 orders on average;
  • an order waited 1.38 seconds on average and 9.38 seconds at most;
  • 6,250 orders were packed.

The numbers check each other. Little's Law says that the average number waiting equals the rate at which orders arrive times the average time each waits. 6,250 orders in 3,600 seconds is 1.74 a second, and 1.74 × 1.38 = 2.40, which matches queue_length_avg, 2.41. The utilisation checks the same way: 1.74 orders a second × 1.50 seconds ÷ 3 packers = 0.87. A set of statistics that fails a check like this one points to a mistake in the model or in how it is read, as Checking and Validating explains.

Statistics describes how each one is computed, and the Statistics reference lists every name each level publishes.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Statistics are off by default. A level, such as typical, switches them on, and the run publishes them as telemetry.
  • An average over time weighs each value by how long it lasted, so it is exact, unlike readings taken now and then.
  • Statistics that fail a check such as Little's Law point to a mistake in the model or in how it is read.

"""The Measuring a Run tutorial: the busy hour, with built-in statistics, builder.

Three packers, orders at 1.8 a second and the measured packing times. Every record,
the statistics included, is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the final
statistics again at the end.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

# The 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip

app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=3, max_cap=10)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8)
    .add_service("packing", dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)
    # Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
    .with_stats("typical")
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until="1 h")
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in app.env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/measuring_a_run_low_level.py
"""The Measuring a Run tutorial: the busy hour, with built-in statistics, low-level.

Three packers, orders at 1.8 a second and the measured packing times. The order
process reports each step to the environment's statistics, which publish them as
telemetry; the script prints the final statistics again at the end.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

# The 40 packing times measured at the bench, in seconds
MEASURED = [
    1.5, 2.5, 2.4, 1.2, 1.3, 1.2, 1.8, 1.4, 2.0, 0.7,
    2.7, 1.4, 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.8, 2.0, 1.4, 1.4, 1.9,
    1.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.1, 0.7, 1.1, 1.2, 0.9, 0.8, 1.5,
    2.1, 1.3, 1.1, 1.7, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8, 2.2, 1.4, 1.1,
]  # fmt: skip

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=MEASURED)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    """One order, which reports each step to the statistics."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.stats.flow_started("orders")  # the order enters the shop
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts, time averages, and the mean and maximum wait and service, every 10 s
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=10)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    env = run()
    # The statistics are telemetry, so the console printed them; read them here too
    for name, value in env.stats.readings().items():
        print(f"{name} = {value}")

docs.title: Queues and Capacity
docs.text:
In its busy hour the shop gets 1.8 orders a second, and packing still takes 1.5 seconds. One packer cannot keep up. This page asks: how many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds?

  • Decision: the number of packers for the busy hour.
  • Measures: the packers' utilisation and the mean wait.
  • Runs: four runs of the hour, one for each number of packers, each with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random at a steady rate, and every order takes the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • work out a resource's utilisation before running the model;
  • read the load, the stability and the bottleneck with desflow explain;
  • choose the fewest packers that keep the mean wait short.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds more orders, then more packers, and desflow explain, which works out the load from the model before it runs. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with the arrival rate of the busy hour and the number of packers as a setting you change between runs.

docs.title: Work Out the Load
docs.text:
Before running anything, work out how busy the packers would be. Utilisation is the share of time a resource is busy:

utilisation = arrival rate × mean service time ÷ number of units

The load is the part above the division: arrival rate × mean service time. Here it is 1.8 orders a second × 1.5 seconds = 2.7, so each second brings 2.7 seconds of packing, enough work for 2.7 packers. One packer would be busy 270% of the time, which is impossible: it falls further behind with every order.

  • With utilisation below 1 a model is stable: the queue rises and falls, but stays bounded.
  • At 1 or above it is not: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts, and every order waits longer than the one before.

The shop needs at least 3 packers, the fewest that bring utilisation below 1: 2.7 ÷ 3 = 0.9. Queueing Basics explains utilisation, and why the queue grows without limit at 1 or above. Each resource in a model has its own utilisation. The one with the highest utilisation is the bottleneck: it decides how long everything waits.

Here is the busy hour. The arrival rate is 1.8 orders a second, and until is one hour of simulation time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_and_capacity.yaml:load
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0  # unpaced: the hour runs in about a second
  random_seed: 42

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.8, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 1 h
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:load
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)  # unpaced
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
# The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack. Each
# order starts the task pack_order.
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8, spawn="pack_order")
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:load
service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
# The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},

A blueprint accepts a duration with a unit wherever it takes a time, such as until: 1 h and value: 1.5 s, and reads a plain number as seconds. factor: 0 runs the hour unpaced: as fast as the computer can, in about a second. Nobody needs to watch this run in real time.

docs.title: Explain the Load
docs.text:
desflow explain does this arithmetic from a YAML or builder model, without running it. It reads three numbers for each resource and works out the fourth:

  • λ (lambda), the arrival rate: rate: 1.8 of arrivals.orders;
  • μ (mu), the service rate, one over the mean service time: value: 1.5 s of services.packing gives 1 ÷ 1.5 = 0.667 orders a second for each packer, one order every 1.5 seconds (40 a minute);
  • c, the number of units: current_cap of resources.packers;
  • ρ (rho), the utilisation: λ ÷ (c × μ).

Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there.

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow explain queues_and_capacity.yaml

The file is queues_and_capacity.yaml from Full Files. Its number of packers comes from the variable PACKERS, which Run It With More Packers sets. With PACKERS not set, the shop has one packer.

docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:explain
def explain(packers: int) -> str:
    """The busy hour with `packers` packers, as `desflow explain` prints it."""
    return render_terminal(shop(packers).analyze())

context.analyze() returns the same analysis as an Explanation, and render_terminal prints it as the command does. desflow explain also loads a builder Python file that defines a SimulationContext at module level.

desflow explain does not support low-level models. It reads which arrival starts which task and which resource each task uses, and a low-level model does not declare those links: its SimPy code makes them as it runs.

For a YAML or builder model, it prints the graph from each arrival, the resources, the utilisation at each number of units the resource allows, and hints:

Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 1.8/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 1.8/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> exit
Resources
+-------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |   ρ | Wq | L | status   |
|----------+-----+--------+---+-----+----+---+----------|
| packers  | 1.8 | 0.6667 | 1 | 2.7 |  - | - | UNSTABLE |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-------------------------+
|  c |      ρ | status    |
|----+--------+-----------|
|  1 |    2.7 | UNSTABLE  |
|  2 |   1.35 | UNSTABLE  |
|  3 |    0.9 | CONGESTED |
|  4 |  0.675 | OK        |
|  5 |   0.54 | OK        |
|  6 |   0.45 | OK        |
|  7 | 0.3857 | OK        |
|  8 | 0.3375 | OK        |
|  9 |    0.3 | OK        |
| 10 |   0.27 | OK        |
+-------------------------+
Bottleneck: packers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: unstable: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts
Hints for utilisation 0.85:
  packers with 4 units: utilisation 0.675, at most 0.85
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 0.85 at a request every 1.76 seconds (34 a minute, 0.5667 a second)

The output has four parts:

  • The tree shows each order starting pack_order, which uses packers, and the flow ending after it.
  • The resources table gives λ (the arrival rate) 1.8 orders a second, μ (the rate one packer serves) 0.667 orders a second, c (the number of packers) 1 and utilisation ρ 2.7. The status is CONGESTED from utilisation 0.85 and UNSTABLE from 1, so it is UNSTABLE. The wait (Wq) and the number in the shop (L) are left blank, and the reason is printed below the tables: the queue grows for as long as the run lasts.
  • The table by units covers 1 to 10 packers, up to max_cap. Three packers are stable but congested at utilisation 0.9.
  • The first hint names 4 as the fewest packers at or below 0.85. The second hint keeps the current number of units. It gives the rate of requests into the resource at which utilisation reaches the target. With one packer, an arrival rate of 0.5667 orders a second, an order every 1.76 seconds (34 a minute), gives utilisation 0.85. In a network, that rate includes the requests that come back for rework, not only new arrivals.

docs.title: Run It With More Packers
docs.text:
The number of packers is the resource's current_cap. Each run sets it once:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_and_capacity.yaml:packers
resources:
  # The number of packers comes from the PACKERS variable, 1 when it is not set
  packers:
    current_cap: ${PACKERS:-1}
    max_cap: 10

${PACKERS:-1} reads the environment variable PACKERS, and uses 1 when it is not set.

docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:packers
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:packers
resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)},

A DynamicResource with a current_cap of 3 behaves like a SimPy resource with three units: a request is granted as soon as any unit is free, so up to three orders are packed at once. Resources describes how it is built and why.

env.run(until=...) runs SimPy's event loop until that time. DynamicRealtimeEnvironment is desflow's form of SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment. A resource's capacity is its number of units.

To read the mean wait, switch on the built-in statistics at the typical level, which keeps the mean wait of every task; Measuring a Run explains the levels.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_and_capacity.yaml:stats
# The mean wait of pack_order, published once an hour and at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:stats
# The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the run and read at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:stats
# The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the environment and read at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

Now run the hour with 1, 2, 3 and 4 packers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

At the end, the run publishes the mean wait as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean, among all its other records. --stdout prints the records as JSON lines, grep keeps the mean wait, and tail -1 keeps its last reading:

# The mean wait with one to four packers
for n in 1 2 3 4; do
  PACKERS=$n desflow run queues_and_capacity.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.wait_mean"' | tail -1
done
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:table
def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    app = shop(packers)
    app.run(until=UNTIL)
    return app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:table
def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    env = run(packers)
    return env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")

docs.title: Waits Near Full Use
docs.text:
With 2 packers, utilisation is 1.35. The queue grows all hour, so the mean wait depends mainly on how long the run was: run two hours and it roughly doubles. With 3 packers, utilisation is 0.9 and the wait settles. With 4 it is 0.675, and almost nobody waits.

A stable model can still wait a long time, because the wait grows much faster than utilisation near 1. Take one packer with exponential gaps and exponential service times: an M/M/1 queue, in the notation that Queueing Basics explains. Its mean wait in the queue is ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) × the mean service time, where ρ is the utilisation. At utilisation 0.95 the factor is 0.95 ÷ 0.05 = 19, and at 0.8 it is 0.8 ÷ 0.2 = 4, so the wait at 0.95 is about 5 times the wait at 0.8. The chart draws the formula for the shop's 1.5-second packing, with the function desflow explain uses:

Variable times make the wait longer still. Bursts of arrivals, or packing times that vary a lot, fill the queue while the average load is moderate, and the queue takes a long time to empty again. Kingman's formula gives the size of the effect for one server: it multiplies the M/M/1 wait by a factor for the spread of the gaps and of the service times. With exponential gaps and constant packing the factor is 0.5, so the shop's constant packing halves the wait. desflow explain uses Kingman's formula for a resource with one unit, and Choosing Inputs measures the wait with constant, triangular, empirical and exponential packing times.

Little's Law checks a run's output. In a model that settles, the mean number of orders waiting is the arrival rate times the mean wait, Lq = λ × Wq, and the number in the shop is L = λ × (Wq + mean service time). desflow explain prints L beside Wq, and Queueing Basics checks the law against runs of the shop.

docs.title: Networks and Bottlenecks
docs.text:
In a network, each task's rate comes from the tasks before it. This version of the shop checks every packed order with one checker, and sends one order in ten back to be packed again:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/queues_network.yaml:network
arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.6, spawn: pack_order}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}
  checking: {dist: exponential, rate: 2.5}  # 0.4 s on average

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 4, max_cap: 10}
  checkers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    next: check_order
  check_order:
    service: checking
    resource: checkers
    payload: {event_type: order_checked}
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    next: {weights: {ship_order: 9, pack_order: 1}}
  ship_order:
    payload: {event_type: order_shipped}
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity.py:network
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.6, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
app.add_service("checking", dist="exponential", rate=2.5)  # 0.4 s on average
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
app.add_resource("checkers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)

@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="check_order")
def pack_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

# Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="checking",
    resource_id="checkers",
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
)
def check_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_checked"}

@app.task()
def ship_order(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_shipped"}

# print(render_terminal(app.analyze())) prints what desflow explain prints
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py:network
NETWORK = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.6)},
    service={
        "packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5),
        # One check takes 0.4 s on average
        "checking": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=2.5),
    },
    resources={
        "packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10),
        "checkers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4),
    },
)
# Each task's service and resource, and the task after it
STEPS = {
    "pack_order": ("packing", "packers", Router("check_order")),
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    "check_order": (
        "checking",
        "checkers",
        Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}}),
    ),
    "ship_order": (None, None, Router(None)),
}


def step(env, sampler, shop, name, entity, counters):
    """One task of an order, then the task its router chooses."""
    service, resource, router = STEPS[name]
    task_id = next(counters[name])
    if resource is None:
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    else:
        env.stats.task_queued(name, task_id)
        with shop[resource].request() as request:
            yield request
            env.stats.task_started(name, task_id)
            config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{service}")
            yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    following = router.choose(Upstream(task_id, entity, {}, {}), env)
    if following is None:
        env.stats.flow_finished("orders")
    else:
        env.process(step(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, counters))

desflow explain does not support low-level models. It reads which arrival starts which task and which resource each task uses, and a low-level model does not declare those links: its SimPy code makes them as it runs.

Every packed order is checked. Packing receives the new orders, 1.6 a second, and also the tenth of the checked orders that come back. Call the rate into packing x: then x = 1.6 + 0.1 × x, which gives x = 1.6 ÷ 0.9 = 1.778 orders a second. desflow explain queues_network.yaml solves this flow balance for every task. This is its output without the hints at the end:

Shop
`-- orders (arrival, rate 1.6/s)
    `-- spawn -> pack_order (task, rate 1.778/s)
        +-- uses packers (resource)
        `-- next (share 1) -> check_order (task, rate 1.778/s)
            +-- uses checkers (resource)
            +-- next (share 0.9) -> ship_order (task, rate 1.6/s)
            |   `-- next (share 1) -> exit
            `-- next (share 0.1) -> pack_order (again)
Resources
+----------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |     λ |      μ | c |      ρ | Wq | L | status |
|----------+-------+--------+---+--------+----+---+--------|
| packers  | 1.778 | 0.6667 | 4 | 0.6667 |  - | - | OK     |
| checkers | 1.778 |    2.5 | 1 | 0.7111 |  - | - | OK     |
+----------------------------------------------------------+
packers by units
+-------------------------+
|  c |      ρ | status    |
|----+--------+-----------|
|  1 |  2.667 | UNSTABLE  |
|  2 |  1.333 | UNSTABLE  |
|  3 | 0.8889 | CONGESTED |
|  4 | 0.6667 | OK        |
|  5 | 0.5333 | OK        |
|  6 | 0.4444 | OK        |
|  7 |  0.381 | OK        |
|  8 | 0.3333 | OK        |
|  9 | 0.2963 | OK        |
| 10 | 0.2667 | OK        |
+-------------------------+
checkers by units
+---------------------+
| c |      ρ | status |
|---+--------+--------|
| 1 | 0.7111 | OK     |
| 2 | 0.3556 | OK     |
| 3 |  0.237 | OK     |
| 4 | 0.1778 | OK     |
+---------------------+
Bottleneck: checkers
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: no closed formula for c > 1 with non-exponential times; run --verify to measure it
  wait at checkers: its input is not one arrival or a Poisson flow, which Kingman's formula needs; run --verify to measure it

The four packers are at utilisation 0.667 and the checker at 0.711, the higher of the two, so the checker is the bottleneck. In the table by units, 3 packers would be at utilisation 0.889, above the checker. So with 3 packers the packers are the bottleneck, and a fourth packer moves the bottleneck to the checker. Relieving a bottleneck makes the next busiest resource the new one. desflow explain estimates neither wait here, and says why: four packers with constant packing have no closed formula, and the checker's input is the packers' output, which is neither one arrival nor a Poisson flow. --verify, in Check Against Theory, measures both.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
To keep a resource stable, lower its utilisation or its variability:

  • more units: a higher current_cap;
  • faster service: a shorter service time;
  • fewer arrivals: a lower rate;
  • less variable gaps or service times, which shorten the wait at the same utilisation.

To test how a consumer of the records copes, do the opposite on purpose. From utilisation 0.85 a resource is congested, with long waits that come and go, and bursts make them longer. Above 1 it is overloaded: its queue, and the lag of everything after it, grows for as long as the overload lasts.

--target sets the utilisation the hints aim for, 0.85 by default. At 1 or above, the hints are for deliberate overload:

desflow explain queues_and_capacity.yaml --target 1.2

The end of its output, the hints:

Hints for utilisation 1.2:
  packers with 2 units: utilisation 1.35, at least 1.2, for deliberate overload
  packers with 1 unit: utilisation 1.2 at a request every 1.25 seconds (48 a minute, 0.8 a second)

With 2 packers the shop runs at utilisation 1.35, above the target of 1.2. With 1 packer, an arrival rate of 0.8 orders a second, an order every 1.25 seconds (48 a minute), gives exactly 1.2.

A scenario step can raise the arrival rate while the model runs and push a resource past full use on purpose. Changing Demand runs such a rush, and its queue grows for as long as the rush lasts.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
How many packers keep the mean wait under 10 seconds? 3 packers, as the mean wait for 1 to 4 packers shows:

With 3 packers the mean wait is 1.27 seconds, from one run of the hour with constant packing and the seed 42. With 2 packers it is over 400 seconds and still growing when the hour ends. The answer is the fewest packers that bring utilisation below 1. At utilisation 0.9 the wait stays under 10 seconds, because the shop's packing time is constant and 0.9 is not yet close enough to 1.

Queueing Basics explains why the wait grows without limit as utilisation reaches 1, as the table shows for 1 and 2 packers. It also gives the formula for several packers sharing one queue. Each term of the utilisation is a live parameter, so a running model can be relieved, or overloaded on purpose, as Live Parameters shows. Statistics describes how the mean wait is measured.

The formulas describe a queue that has settled. A run starts with no orders in the shop, so its early waits are shorter than the settled waits. A live change, such as a rush, makes the waits rise, and they take time to settle again. Trusting Results shows how to leave out a warm-up and how long to run.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Utilisation is the arrival rate times the mean service time, divided by the number of units. Below 1 the queue settles; at 1 or above it grows for as long as the run lasts.
  • Near utilisation 1 the wait grows much faster than the utilisation, and variable times make it longer still.
  • The resource with the highest utilisation is the bottleneck. Relieving it makes the next busiest resource the bottleneck.

"""The Queues and Capacity tutorial: the shop's busy hour, with the builder.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second and each takes 1.5 seconds to pack. `explain` prints
what `desflow explain` prints for the shop. The script runs the hour once for each
number of packers, unpaced, and prints the mean wait of each run. `network` is the
shop with a checker and rework.
"""

from desflow import SimulationContext
from desflow.explain.render import render_terminal

UNTIL = "1 h"  # the busy hour


def shop(packers: int) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop in its busy hour, with `packers` packers."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)  # unpaced
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack. Each
    # order starts the task pack_order.
    app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8, spawn="pack_order")
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)
    # The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the run and read at the end
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    return app


def explain(packers: int) -> str:
    """The busy hour with `packers` packers, as `desflow explain` prints it."""
    return render_terminal(shop(packers).analyze())


def network() -> SimulationContext:
    """The busy shop as a network: packed orders are checked, one in ten packed again."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.6, spawn="pack_order")
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    app.add_service("checking", dist="exponential", rate=2.5)  # 0.4 s on average
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=4, max_cap=10)
    app.add_resource("checkers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="check_order")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    @app.task(
        service_id="checking",
        resource_id="checkers",
        next={"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}},
    )
    def check_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_checked"}

    @app.task()
    def ship_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_shipped"}

    # print(render_terminal(app.analyze())) prints what desflow explain prints
    return app


def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    app = shop(packers)
    app.run(until=UNTIL)
    return app.env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/queues_and_capacity_low_level.py
"""The Queues and Capacity tutorial: the shop's busy hour, on the low-level API.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second and each takes 1.5 seconds to pack. The script runs the
hour once for each number of packers, unpaced, and prints the mean wait of each run.
`run_network` is the shop with a checker and rework.
"""

import itertools

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Router,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    Upstream,
)

UNTIL = 3600  # the busy hour, in seconds


def params(packers: int) -> SimParameter:
    """The shop in its busy hour, with `packers` packers."""
    return SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
        # The busy hour: 1.8 orders a second, more than one packer can pack
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=packers, max_cap=10)},
    )


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, task_id):
    """One order, which reports each step to the statistics."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(packers: int, until=UNTIL, factor=0.0):
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers, unpaced, and returns the environment."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params(packers))
    # The mean wait of pack_order, kept by the environment and read at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    packers_resource = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers_resource))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


NETWORK = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.6)},
    service={
        "packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5),
        # One check takes 0.4 s on average
        "checking": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=2.5),
    },
    resources={
        "packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=4, max_cap=10),
        "checkers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4),
    },
)
# Each task's service and resource, and the task after it
STEPS = {
    "pack_order": ("packing", "packers", Router("check_order")),
    # Nine in ten pass; the tenth is packed again
    "check_order": (
        "checking",
        "checkers",
        Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 9, "pack_order": 1}}),
    ),
    "ship_order": (None, None, Router(None)),
}


def step(env, sampler, shop, name, entity, counters):
    """One task of an order, then the task its router chooses."""
    service, resource, router = STEPS[name]
    task_id = next(counters[name])
    if resource is None:
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    else:
        env.stats.task_queued(name, task_id)
        with shop[resource].request() as request:
            yield request
            env.stats.task_started(name, task_id)
            config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.service.{service}")
            yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        env.stats.task_finished(name, task_id)
    following = router.choose(Upstream(task_id, entity, {}, {}), env)
    if following is None:
        env.stats.flow_finished("orders")
    else:
        env.process(step(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, counters))


def network_orders(env, sampler, shop, counters):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for number in itertools.count(1):
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.stats.flow_started("orders")
        env.process(
            step(env, sampler, shop, "pack_order", f"orders-{number}", counters)
        )


def run_network(until=UNTIL):
    """Runs the network for the hour, unpaced, and returns the environment."""
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(NETWORK)
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    shop = {
        name: DynamicResource(env, "Shop", name) for name in ("packers", "checkers")
    }
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    # Weights draw from the routing task's own sequence, as the builder's do
    STEPS["check_order"][2].rng = sampler.generator("route.check_order")
    counters = {name: itertools.count() for name in STEPS}
    env.process(network_orders(env, sampler, shop, counters))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def mean_wait(packers: int) -> float:
    """Runs the busy hour with `packers` packers and returns the mean wait."""
    env = run(packers)
    return env.stats.readings()["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for packers in range(1, 5):
        print(f"packers {packers}: mean wait {mean_wait(packers):8.2f} s")

docs.title: Randomness and Seeds
docs.text:
Run the busy shop twice, and the orders arrive at different times and take different times to pack. A stochastic model, one that draws random times, behaves this way, but its results are then hard to check or to compare. This page asks: why do runs differ, and how can you reproduce one?

  • Decision: how to set up runs so that a result can be checked and two versions of the model compared.
  • Measures: the times of one order's events, on repeated runs and after a second arrival is added.
  • Runs: runs of one minute: two with no seed, then repeated runs with the seed 42, with and without a second arrival.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random at 1.8 a second, and each packing time is drawn on its own, whatever the others were.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • see why two runs of a stochastic model differ;
  • repeat a run exactly with a seed;
  • add a part to a model without changing the random times of the others.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
This page adds a seed, then a second arrival: returned parcels. The model simulates the busy hour from Queues and Capacity, using its answer of 3 packers. Packing times now vary: 1.5 seconds on average with a standard deviation of 0.5 seconds, drawn from a normal distribution.

This page uses the normal only to get times that vary. Choosing Inputs chooses packing times from data. Common Mistakes explains why a normal is a poor model of a time. This one draws a value below 0 about once in 740 draws, and desflow raises such a draw to its minimum delay, as Distributions says.

docs.title: Run Twice
docs.text:
A simulation draws its random times from a random number stream: a long sequence of numbers that looks random but is computed from a starting value, the seed. The same seed gives the same sequence, and so the same run. A simulation given no seed starts from a new seed each time, so two runs give two different sets of records.

Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there. desflow never runs without a seed. When you give none, it draws one, uses it, and logs it, so any run can be repeated afterwards:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Leave random_seed out of the simulation section and run the blueprint twice. Each run logs its seed with the command that repeats it. Each run draws its own seed, so your number differs from this one:

No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Repeat it with: desflow run randomness_and_seeds.yaml --seed 3166812249

Leave random_seed out of SimulationContext and run the script twice. Each run logs its seed with the argument that repeats it. Each run draws its own seed, so your number differs from this one:

No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Pass random_seed=3166812249 to repeat it.

The low-level API never draws a seed for you: you pass one to Sampler. A Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random, as Arrivals and Services explains. To start from a new seed each run, draw one yourself, for example with secrets.randbelow(2**32), and print it.

docs.title: Fix the Seed
docs.text:
Set the seed once, and every run draws the same numbers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/randomness_and_seeds.yaml:seed
# The same random numbers on every run; leave it out to draw a new seed
random_seed: 42

desflow run randomness_and_seeds.yaml --seed 7 runs with another seed without editing the file; --seed overrides random_seed.

docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds.py:seed
# The same random numbers on every run; leave it out to draw a new seed
SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds_low_level.py:seed
# The same random numbers on every run, passed to Sampler(seed=SEED) in run below
SEED = 42

Repeating a run exactly is called reproducibility. It is what lets you check a result, show it to someone else, and see what a change to the model does on its own. Pick one order and follow it: the twelfth order, orders-12, has these events on every run with the seed 42:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.993, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 6.695, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 8.443, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}

It is queued at 5.993, gets a packer at 6.695 and is packed at 8.443: a wait of 0.702 seconds.

docs.title: Add Returns
docs.text:
Now add returned parcels: one every 5 seconds on average (12 a minute), each recorded as it arrives. They do not use the packers.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/randomness_and_seeds.yaml:returns
arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 1.8, spawn: pack_order}
  # Returned parcels: one every 5 seconds on average
  returns: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: receive_return}

tasks:
  # A return is recorded as it arrives; it does not use a packer
  receive_return:
    payload: {event_type: return_received}
docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds.py:returns
# Returned parcels: one every 5 seconds on average
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


@app.task()
def receive_return(task_id: int):
    # A return is recorded as it arrives; it does not use a packer
    return {"event_type": "return_received"}


@app.arrival_loop("returns")
def return_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        parcel = yield context.wait_for_arrival("returns")
        context.spawn(receive_return(task_id, entity=parcel))
        task_id += 1
docs/snippets/tutorials/randomness_and_seeds_low_level.py:returns
# Returned parcels: one every 5 seconds on average
PARAMS.arrival["returns"] = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


def return_generator(env, sampler):
    """Records each return as it arrives; it does not use a packer."""
    # Once registered, the config draws from sampler.generator("arrival.returns")
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.returns")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"returns-{task_id + 1}"
        value = {"event_type": "return_received"}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="receive_return", instance=task_id)
        task_id += 1

Sampler(seed=SEED) makes one generator per name, sampler.generator("arrival.returns"), from the seed and the name. The registry names each distribution it registers by its path without the sim id, such as arrival.returns. sampler.sample(config) draws from the generator of that name. Your own code can take a sequence of its own the same way.

A task with no service and no resource, such as receive_return, takes no time: it publishes its payload as soon as the arrival starts it.

Run it with the seed 42. orders-12 has the same three events as before, at the same times. Adding an arrival changed nothing for the orders, because each distribution draws from a random number stream of its own, named by its registry path without the sim id. The orders draw from arrival.orders, packing from service.packing, and the new returns from arrival.returns. Look at the two runs side by side:

With one shared stream, the returns would take some of the numbers the orders and packing used to get, and every later time would shift. The name is part of the stream. Renaming a service, an arrival or a task that routes by weights therefore gives it a new stream, and a run with the same seed then gives other results. Busy Hour Figures lists two such runs: the same measured packing times give 1.35 or 1.38 seconds of mean wait, depending on the service's name.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Why do runs differ, and how can you reproduce one? Runs differ because they start their random number streams from different seeds. Repeat a run by supplying the same seed: random_seed: 42 in the blueprint, random_seed=42 on SimulationContext, Sampler(seed=42) in the low-level API, or desflow run --seed 42. With it, the twelfth order waits 0.702 seconds on every run, and still 0.702 seconds after the returns are added.

One stream per input means that two versions of a model run with the same seed see the same arrivals and the same service times wherever they share them. A difference between their results then comes from the change, not from different random numbers. This is called common random numbers (Output Analysis explains it), and it is how two designs are compared fairly. Arrivals and Services describes how each stream is made, and Distributions lists every family with its parameters.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A seed fixes the random numbers, so the same seed gives the same run. A YAML or builder run that was given no seed draws one and logs it, so it can be repeated.
  • Each distribution draws from its own random number stream, named after its registry path, so adding an arrival leaves the other draws as they were.
  • Renaming a service, an arrival or a weighted route gives it a new stream, and the results change with the same seed.

"""The Randomness and Seeds tutorial: the busy shop, seeded, with returns, builder.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second, and three packers pack each in 1.5 seconds on average,
with a standard deviation of 0.5 seconds. Returned parcels arrive every 5 seconds on
average and are recorded as they arrive. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

app = (
    # The same random numbers on every run; leave it out to draw a new seed
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    .add_resource("packers", current_cap=3, max_cap=10)
    # Packing varies: 1.5 seconds on average, with a standard deviation of 0.5
    .add_service("packing", dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.5)
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1.8)
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
)


@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.arrival_loop("orders")
def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
        context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
        task_id += 1


# Returned parcels: one every 5 seconds on average
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


@app.task()
def receive_return(task_id: int):
    # A return is recorded as it arrives; it does not use a packer
    return {"event_type": "return_received"}


@app.arrival_loop("returns")
def return_generator(context: SimulationContext):
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        parcel = yield context.wait_for_arrival("returns")
        context.spawn(receive_return(task_id, entity=parcel))
        task_id += 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(until="1 min")

"""The Randomness and Seeds tutorial: the busy shop, seeded, with returns, low-level.

Orders arrive at 1.8 a second, and three packers pack each in 1.5 seconds on average,
with a standard deviation of 0.5 seconds. Returned parcels arrive every 5 seconds on
average and are recorded as they arrive. Every record is printed to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=1.8)},
    # Packing varies: 1.5 seconds on average, with a standard deviation of 0.5
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=3, max_cap=10)},
)
# The same random numbers on every run, passed to Sampler(seed=SEED) in run below
SEED = 42


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))
        task_id += 1


# Returned parcels: one every 5 seconds on average
PARAMS.arrival["returns"] = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.2)


def return_generator(env, sampler):
    """Records each return as it arrives; it does not use a packer."""
    # Once registered, the config draws from sampler.generator("arrival.returns")
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.returns")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"returns-{task_id + 1}"
        value = {"event_type": "return_received"}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="receive_return", instance=task_id)
        task_id += 1


def run(until=60, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=SEED)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers))
    env.process(return_generator(env, sampler))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

docs.title: Changing Demand
docs.text:
The shop's one packer packs an order in 1.5 seconds, so it can pack 40 orders a minute. Orders usually arrive every 2.5 seconds on average (24 a minute, rate: 0.4). From 20 to 40 minutes a promotion brings an order every 1.11 seconds on average (54 a minute, rate: 0.9), more than one packer can pack. This page asks: what does a 20-minute rush do to waits, and does a second packer for the rush keep them short?

  • Decision: one packer or two during the rush.
  • Measures: the mean and the longest wait over the hour, and the number of orders packed.
  • Runs: two runs of the hour, one with one packer in the rush and one with two, each with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random at each rate, every order takes the same time to pack, and the rush starts and ends exactly on time.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • change the arrival rate and the number of packers at set times with a schedule;
  • measure what a rush that ends does to the waits;
  • choose what to report for an hour that is not steady.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a schedule: changes to the arrival rate and the number of packers at set times. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with packing at a constant 1.5 seconds.

docs.title: Write the Schedule
docs.text:
A schedule is a list of steps. Each step names a registry path, a value and the simulation time at which the value applies. The rush is four steps: the rate and the packers change at 20 minutes and change back at 40. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/changing_demand.yaml:schedule
# The rush from 20 to 40 minutes: an order every 1.11 s on average (rate 0.9),
# and RUSH_PACKERS packers
scenario:
  - {at: 20 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.9}
  - {at: 20 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: "${RUSH_PACKERS:-1}"}
  - {at: 40 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 40 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

${RUSH_PACKERS:-1} reads the environment variable RUSH_PACKERS, so RUSH_PACKERS=2 desflow run changing_demand.yaml runs the second plan.

docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand.py:schedule
# The rush from 20 to 40 minutes: an order every 1.11 s on average (rate 0.9),
# and rush_packers packers
.add_scenario(
    [
        {"at": "20 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
        {
            "at": "20 min",
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": rush_packers,
        },
        {"at": "40 min", "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {
            "at": "40 min",
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": 1,
        },
    ]
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand_low_level.py:schedule
def schedule(rush_packers):
    """The rush from 20 to 40 minutes, with rush_packers packers.

    During the rush an order arrives every 1.11 s on average (rate 0.9).
    """
    return [
        {"at": 1200, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.9},
        {
            "at": 1200,
            "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap",
            "value": rush_packers,
        },
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 0.4},
        {"at": 2400, "path": "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", "value": 1},
    ]

run_scenario is the SimPy process that applies the steps:

docs/snippets/tutorials/changing_demand_low_level.py:run
# Each step applies before every other event at its time
env.process(run_scenario(env, schedule(rush_packers), until=3600))

The steps follow the simulation clock, so the schedule repeats exactly on every run and at any factor. A step applies before every other event at its time: the order that arrives at 20 minutes draws its next gap from the rush rate. Vary Arrivals by Time sets out these boundaries.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What does a 20-minute rush do to waits? With one packer, it builds a queue for the whole rush. In one run of the hour with the seed 42, the mean wait over the hour is 147.74 seconds and the longest 416.75 seconds, more than 6 minutes. A second packer for the rush keeps the mean at 0.74 seconds and the longest at 6.06. Both pack the same 1,978 orders:

Each tab prints both plans: the orders packed, the mean wait and the longest wait.

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# One packer in the rush: orders packed, mean wait and longest wait
desflow run changing_demand.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(finished|wait_mean|wait_max)"' | tail -3
# Two packers in the rush
RUSH_PACKERS=2 desflow run changing_demand.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(finished|wait_mean|wait_max)"' | tail -3


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished","value":1978}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":147.744431867788}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max","value":416.751806252581}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished","value":1978}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":0.7410266248651487}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_max","value":6.063368615320087}


python changing_demand.py 2>/dev/null

1 in the rush: 1978 packed, mean wait 147.74 s, longest 416.75 s
2 in the rush: 1978 packed, mean wait  0.74 s, longest   6.06 s

python changing_demand_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

1 in the rush: 1978 packed, mean wait 147.74 s, longest 416.75 s
2 in the rush: 1978 packed, mean wait  0.74 s, longest   6.06 s

During the rush one packer would need 0.9 × 1.5 = 1.35 seconds of packing every second, more than it has. Orders arrive at 54 a minute and the packer finishes at most 40, so the queue grows by about 14 orders a minute for as long as the rush lasts. An overload that ends is a finite overload. When the rush ends the load falls to 0.4 × 1.5 = 0.6, and the packer works off the queue, here by about 54 minutes. A load that stays at 1 or above is different: its queue grows for as long as the run lasts, and no run length gives a stable mean wait, as Queueing Basics explains.

A finite overload has an answer, but the answer depends on the schedule. A mean over the hour mixes the quiet minutes with the rush, so report the longest wait, or the waits during the rush, beside it. With two packers the rush load is 1.35 ÷ 2 = 0.68 for each packer, below 1, so waits stay short.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A schedule follows the simulation clock, so it repeats exactly on every run and at any pace.
  • An overload that ends builds a queue that clears only after the rush, so the waits stay high for a while.
  • A mean over the hour mixes the rush with quiet minutes, so report the longest wait, or the waits during the rush, beside it.
