docs/snippets/tutorials/live_changes.py
"""The Live Changes tutorial: a label printer jam, written as a scenario, builder.

One packer takes 1.5 seconds to pack an order, and an order arrives every 2.5 seconds
on average (rate 0.4). From 20 to 30 minutes a jammed label printer slows packing to
3 seconds. The events are written to events/ and the ground-truth records of the jam
to labels/, and the script prints the mean waits with and without the jam.
Run it with: python live_changes.py
With the argument live, it sends the jam live: python live_changes.py live
"""

import json
import logging
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import JsonlStorageEgress, LocalIngress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)


def shop(out: Path, jam: bool = True) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop of Changing Demand, writing its events and labels under out."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4)
        # The events, one flat row per event
        .add_egress(JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/events/orders.jsonl"))
        # The ground-truth records only
        .add_egress(
            JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/labels/labels.jsonl"),
            when="labels",
        )
    )
    if jam:
        # The jam: 3 seconds of packing from 20 to 30 minutes, each change recorded
        app.add_scenario(
            [
                {
                    "at": "20 min",
                    "path": "Shop.service.packing.value",
                    "value": 3.0,
                    "record": {"intervention": "printer_jam"},
                },
                {
                    "at": "30 min",
                    "path": "Shop.service.packing.value",
                    "value": 1.5,
                    "record": {"intervention": "printer_fixed"},
                },
            ]
        )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def read_rows(folder: Path) -> list:
    """Every row of every JSONL file the sink wrote to folder."""
    return [
        json.loads(line)
        for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jsonl"))
        for line in path.read_text().splitlines()
    ]


def waits(out: Path) -> dict:
    """The wait of each order, by the time it was queued, in seconds."""
    queued, started = {}, {}
    for row in read_rows(out / "events"):
        if row.get("status") == "queued":
            queued[row["instance"]] = row["sim_ts"]
        elif row.get("status") == "started":
            started[row["instance"]] = row["sim_ts"]
    return {queued[i]: started[i] - queued[i] for i in started}


def mean_wait(by_time: dict, start: float, end: float) -> float:
    """The mean wait of the orders queued from start to end, in seconds."""
    window = [wait for at, wait in by_time.items() if start <= at < end]
    return sum(window) / len(window)


def outcomes(out: Path) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour with and without the jam; returns the labels and mean waits."""
    result: dict = {}
    by_run: dict = {}
    for jam in (True, False):
        folder = out / ("jam" if jam else "baseline")
        shutil.rmtree(folder, ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
        shop(folder, jam).run(until="1 h")
        by_time = by_run[jam] = waits(folder)
        result[jam] = {
            "jam": round(mean_wait(by_time, 1200, 1800), 2),
            "after": round(mean_wait(by_time, 1800, 2400), 2),
        }
    # Both runs meet the same orders, so each order's two waits can be compared
    result["last_longer"] = max(
        at for at, wait in by_run[True].items() if wait > by_run[False][at] + 0.001
    )
    labels = read_rows(out / "jam" / "labels")
    result["labels"] = [
        (row["sim_ts"], row["label"]["intervention"], row["old"], row["new"])
        for row in sorted(labels, key=lambda row: row["sim_ts"])
    ]
    return result


def live(out: Path) -> SimulationContext:
    """The same jam sent live, half a second of wall-clock time after the start."""
    app = shop(out, jam=False)
    app.factor = 0.005
    # Half a wall-clock second after the start, set packing to 3 seconds
    app.add_ingress(LocalIngress(schedule=[(0.5, "Shop.service.packing.value", 3.0)]))
    # Flush every 60 simulated seconds: at this pace the default of 1 s flushes on a
    # timer over and over, and desflow warns about it
    app.with_batching(batch_size=500, flush_interval=60)
    app.run(until="5 min")
    return app


if __name__ == "__main__":
    here = Path("live_changes_output")
    if sys.argv[1:] == ["live"]:
        # python live_changes.py live: the jam sent live instead
        # A run adds files; start empty
        shutil.rmtree(here / "live", ignore_errors=True)
        env = live(here / "live").env
        packing = env.registry.get_config("Shop.service.packing").value
        print(f"packing after the live change: {packing} s")
    else:
        r = outcomes(here)
        for at, name, old, new in r["labels"]:
            print(f"label at {at:6.1f} s: {name}, packing {old} s to {new} s")
        for jam, label in ((True, "with the jam"), (False, "without it")):
            print(
                f"{label:>12}: mean wait {r[jam]['jam']:6.2f} s from 20 to 30 min, "
                f"{r[jam]['after']:6.2f} s from 30 to 40 min"
            )
        print(f"the last order that waits longer is queued at {r['last_longer']:.1f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/live_changes_low_level.py
"""The Live Changes tutorial: a label printer jam, written as a scenario, low-level.

One packer takes 1.5 seconds to pack an order, and an order arrives every 2.5 seconds
on average (rate 0.4). From 20 to 30 minutes a jammed label printer slows packing to
3 seconds. The events are written to events/ and the ground-truth records of the jam
to labels/, and the script prints the mean waits with and without the jam.
Run it with: python live_changes_low_level.py
With the argument live, it sends the jam live: python live_changes_low_level.py live
"""

import copy
import itertools
import json
import logging
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    JsonlStorageEgress,
    LocalIngress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    run_scenario,
)

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.4)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)

# The jam: 3 seconds of packing from 20 to 30 minutes, each change recorded
JAM = [
    {
        "at": 1200,
        "path": "Shop.service.packing.value",
        "value": 3.0,
        "record": {"intervention": "printer_jam"},
    },
    {
        "at": 1800,
        "path": "Shop.service.packing.value",
        "value": 1.5,
        "record": {"intervention": "printer_fixed"},
    },
]


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))


def run(
    out: Path,
    jam: bool = True,
    factor: float = 0.0,
    until: float = 3600,
    ingress=None,
    flush_interval: float = 1.0,
):
    # strict=False lets a paced run fall behind the wall clock without stopping
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor, strict=False)
    # A copy, because a change to the registry changes the parameters it holds
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(copy.deepcopy(PARAMS))
    env.setup_egress(
        [
            # The events, one flat row per event
            JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/events/orders.jsonl"),
            # The ground-truth records only
            JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/labels/labels.jsonl"),
        ],
        labels=[False, True],
        flush_interval=flush_interval,
    )
    if ingress:
        env.setup_ingress(ingress)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    if jam:
        # Each step applies before every other event at its time
        env.process(run_scenario(env, JAM, until=until))
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def read_rows(folder: Path) -> list:
    """Every row of every JSONL file the sink wrote to folder."""
    return [
        json.loads(line)
        for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jsonl"))
        for line in path.read_text().splitlines()
    ]


def waits(out: Path) -> dict:
    """The wait of each order, by the time it was queued, in seconds."""
    queued, started = {}, {}
    for row in read_rows(out / "events"):
        if row.get("status") == "queued":
            queued[row["instance"]] = row["sim_ts"]
        elif row.get("status") == "started":
            started[row["instance"]] = row["sim_ts"]
    return {queued[i]: started[i] - queued[i] for i in started}


def mean_wait(by_time: dict, start: float, end: float) -> float:
    """The mean wait of the orders queued from start to end, in seconds."""
    window = [wait for at, wait in by_time.items() if start <= at < end]
    return sum(window) / len(window)


def outcomes(out: Path) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour with and without the jam; returns the labels and mean waits."""
    result: dict = {}
    by_run: dict = {}
    for jam in (True, False):
        folder = out / ("jam" if jam else "baseline")
        shutil.rmtree(folder, ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
        run(folder, jam)
        by_time = by_run[jam] = waits(folder)
        result[jam] = {
            "jam": round(mean_wait(by_time, 1200, 1800), 2),
            "after": round(mean_wait(by_time, 1800, 2400), 2),
        }
    # Both runs meet the same orders, so each order's two waits can be compared
    result["last_longer"] = max(
        at for at, wait in by_run[True].items() if wait > by_run[False][at] + 0.001
    )
    labels = read_rows(out / "jam" / "labels")
    result["labels"] = [
        (row["sim_ts"], row["label"]["intervention"], row["old"], row["new"])
        for row in sorted(labels, key=lambda row: row["sim_ts"])
    ]
    return result


def live(out: Path):
    """The same jam sent live, half a second of wall-clock time after the start."""
    # Half a wall-clock second after the start, set packing to 3 seconds
    ingress = [LocalIngress(schedule=[(0.5, "Shop.service.packing.value", 3.0)])]
    # Flush every 60 simulated seconds: at this pace the default of 1 s flushes on a
    # timer over and over, and desflow warns about it
    return run(
        out, jam=False, factor=0.005, until=300, ingress=ingress, flush_interval=60
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    here = Path("live_changes_output")
    if sys.argv[1:] == ["live"]:
        # python live_changes_low_level.py live: the jam sent live instead
        # A run adds files; start empty
        shutil.rmtree(here / "live", ignore_errors=True)
        env = live(here / "live")
        packing = env.registry.get_config("Shop.service.packing").value
        print(f"packing after the live change: {packing} s")
    else:
        r = outcomes(here)
        for at, name, old, new in r["labels"]:
            print(f"label at {at:6.1f} s: {name}, packing {old} s to {new} s")
        for jam, label in ((True, "with the jam"), (False, "without it")):
            print(
                f"{label:>12}: mean wait {r[jam]['jam']:6.2f} s from 20 to 30 min, "
                f"{r[jam]['after']:6.2f} s from 30 to 40 min"
            )
        print(f"the last order that waits longer is queued at {r['last_longer']:.1f} s")

docs.title: Streaming Out
docs.text:
The shop of Changing Demand, without the rush, packs orders for an hour. It has one packer, which takes 1.5 seconds to pack an order, and an order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average (24 a minute, rate: 0.4). A team downstream wants a file of the finished orders. This page asks: which records reach the team's files, how does the team find every record of one order, and when are the files complete?

  • Decision: what the file sink receives, and when the team's job may read the folder.
  • Measures: the records each sink receives, the files the file sink writes and the rows in each.
  • Runs: one unpaced run (factor: 0) of the hour with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: the default batch of 500 records.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • send every record to the terminal and only some of them to a file;
  • find every record of one order by its key;
  • know when the files are complete.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds two sinks: ConsoleEgress, which prints every record to the terminal, and JsonlStorageEgress, which writes JSON Lines files. The file sink has a when predicate that passes only the finished orders. Egress, Batching and Delivery describes every sink.

docs.title: Choose What Each Sink Gets
docs.text:
Every sink receives every event and every telemetry record, unless its when says otherwise. when is a function that takes one record and returns True to send it to that sink. This one passes the events whose value says order_packed:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/streaming_out_logic.py:packed
def packed_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Keeps the finished orders: events whose value says order_packed."""
    return (
        record["stream_type"] == "event"
        and record["value"].get("event_type") == "order_packed"
    )

A blueprint names the function with !python module.function, and the module sits beside the blueprint:

docs/snippets/yaml/streaming_out.yaml:sinks
egress:
  # Every event and every telemetry record
  - type: Console
  # The finished orders only, one flat row each
  - type: Jsonl
    config: {default_path: packed/orders.jsonl}
    when: !python streaming_out_logic.packed_only
docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out.py:packed
def packed_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Keeps the finished orders: events whose value says order_packed."""
    return (
        record["stream_type"] == "event"
        and record["value"].get("event_type") == "order_packed"
    )
docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out.py:sinks
# Every event and every telemetry record
.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
# The finished orders only, one flat row each
.add_egress(
    JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/packed/orders.jsonl"),
    when=packed_only,
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out_low_level.py:sinks
env.setup_egress(
    [
        # Every event and every telemetry record
        ConsoleEgress(),
        # The finished orders only, one flat row each
        JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/packed/orders.jsonl"),
    ],
    predicates=[None, packed_only],
)

predicates takes one entry per sink, in the order of the list, and None passes every record. packed_only is the same function as in the Builder tab.

The predicate sees the record as published, so an event's payload is still under value. It checks stream_type first, because a telemetry record's value is a single number. A record that no sink passes is written nowhere.

docs.title: Find One Order's Records
docs.text:
Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there: desflow run streaming_out.yaml, python streaming_out.py or python streaming_out_low_level.py. Every event carries three names. key names the entity, here the order, and the arrival names the orders orders-1, orders-2, and so on. task names the task, and instance names this run of it. The terminal shows the three events of orders-12, each with the same three names:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 26.97, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 28.202, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 29.702, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}

The file sink receives only the last of the three, the order_packed event. Without a router it writes one flat row per event, with the payload's fields beside the record's own:

{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":29.702,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-12","task":"pack_order","instance":11,"event_type":"order_packed"}

To find one order's records among the 4,329 of the hour, print the records as JSON lines with --stdout and keep the lines with its key. --stdout sends the records to the terminal in place of the sinks, so this run writes no files:

desflow run streaming_out.yaml --stdout | grep '"key":"orders-12"'

It prints the three events of orders-12 above, each as the whole record. In the builder and the low-level API, ConsoleEgress(format="json") as the sink prints the same lines.

A reader that joins the files with another source uses key, and one that follows a task through its states uses task and instance. Records and Telemetry lists every field, and What Each Sink Writes shows how each sink lays them out.

docs.title: Read the Files
docs.text:
The file sink writes one file per batch, named after default_path with 8 random hexadecimal digits, such as packed/orders_1a2b3c4d.jsonl. A file, once written, is never changed:

docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out.py:read
def read_files(folder: Path) -> dict:
    """The rows of each file the sink wrote to folder, by file name."""
    return {
        path.name: [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines()]
        for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jsonl"))
    }

The names are random, so the order of the files is not the order of the records. Sort by sim_ts when the order matters. A second run in the same folder adds new files beside the old ones, so the scripts empty packed/ before they run.

docs.title: Know When the Files Are Complete
docs.text:
The model and the sinks finish at different times. The model stops at until. A sink receives records in batches. At factor: 0, a batch is handed over only when it holds 500 records, and the records left over are handed over at teardown, after the model has stopped. Teardown hands over what each sink still holds, then waits until every sink has written it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

desflow run tears the run down when it reaches run.until, and returns once the sinks have finished.

app.run(until="1 h") tears the run down when it reaches the end, and returns once the sinks have finished.

docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out_low_level.py:run
try:
    env.run(until=3600)  # the model stops at 1 hour
finally:
    env.teardown()  # the sinks receive the rest and finish writing

env.run runs SimPy's event loop and stops at until, as SimPy and desflow describes. env.teardown() is desflow's step that hands over the rest and waits for the sinks.

A job that reads the folder while the run is going therefore sees only the full batches. The terminal can show the same effect. On a fast machine the model can finish before the console sink prints its first line, and then every line appears after the log says Tearing down egress connectors. Teardown waits for the sinks to finish writing, and gives up only when they have made no progress for drain_stall_seconds, as Egress describes. Records not written by then are lost, with a warning.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
The rows the file sink writes over the hour, counted by the time each order was packed:

Which records reach the team's files? These figures come from one unpaced run of the hour with the seed 42.

  • The terminal receives every record: 4,299 events (1,434 orders queued, 1,433 started and 1,432 packed) and 30 telemetry records, five statistics read every 10 minutes.
  • The file sink receives only the 1,432 packed orders, one row each, in 3 files of 500, 500 and 432 rows. The two files of 500 were handed over while the model ran. The file of 432 was handed over at teardown, after the model stopped.

The run returns only when teardown has finished, so the team's job should start only after the run has returned. One order's records share its key: orders-12 was queued at 26.97 seconds, started at 28.202 and packed at 29.702.

Each tab gives the files' rows and the records of orders-12:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Run the blueprint in an empty folder, then count the rows of each file it wrote, smallest first:

desflow run streaming_out.yaml > /dev/null 2>&1
for f in packed/*.jsonl; do grep -c . "$f"; done | sort -n


432
500
500

desflow run streaming_out.yaml --stdout | grep '"key":"orders-12"' prints the records of orders-12, as Find One Order's Records shows.

python streaming_out.py 2>/dev/null

3 files, with [432, 500, 500] rows
orders-12: {'stream_type': 'event', 'sim_ts': 29.702, 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'event_type': 'order_packed'}

python streaming_out_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

3 files, with [432, 500, 500] rows
orders-12: {'stream_type': 'event', 'sim_ts': 29.702, 'key': 'orders-12', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 11, 'event_type': 'order_packed'}

A record goes from publish_event to each sink's when test, then into that sink's buffer, then to a queue that a separate thread writes from. The model only fills buffers, so it can finish while the threads are still writing. Teardown is the step that waits for them. Writing records on background threads is one of the things desflow adds to SimPy, as What desflow Changes sets out. Egress, Batching and Delivery shows each stage of that path. Finding one order's records by its key is also how a run is checked by hand, as Read the Trace shows.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Each sink has its own when test, so one run can send different records to different places.
  • A file sink writes in batches, on a separate thread, and the last batch is written at teardown.
  • Read the files only after the run has returned, when teardown has finished.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/streaming_out.yaml

  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42

  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

docs/snippets/yaml/streaming_out_logic.py
"""Python for the Streaming Out blueprint beside it: the file sink's predicate."""


def packed_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Keeps the finished orders: events whose value says order_packed."""
    return (
        record["stream_type"] == "event"
        and record["value"].get("event_type") == "order_packed"
    )
docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out.py
"""The Streaming Out tutorial: the shop's records, to the terminal and to a file, builder.

One packer takes 1.5 seconds to pack an order, and an order arrives every 2.5 seconds
on average (rate 0.4), for an hour. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the
finished orders are written to packed/. The script then prints the files the sink
wrote and one order's row. To see only those lines, run:
python streaming_out.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import json
import logging
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, JsonlStorageEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def packed_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Keeps the finished orders: events whose value says order_packed."""
    return (
        record["stream_type"] == "event"
        and record["value"].get("event_type") == "order_packed"
    )


def shop(out: Path) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop of Changing Demand, without the rush, writing under out."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4)
        # The packers' and the packing task's readings every 10 minutes, as telemetry
        .with_stats("minimal", interval=600)
        # Every event and every telemetry record
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
        # The finished orders only, one flat row each
        .add_egress(
            JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/packed/orders.jsonl"),
            when=packed_only,
        )
    )

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def read_files(folder: Path) -> dict:
    """The rows of each file the sink wrote to folder, by file name."""
    return {
        path.name: [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines()]
        for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jsonl"))
    }


def outcomes(out: Path) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour; returns the rows in each file and the row of orders-12."""
    shutil.rmtree(out / "packed", ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
    shop(out).run(until="1 h")
    files = read_files(out / "packed")
    rows = [row for file_rows in files.values() for row in file_rows]
    return {
        "file_rows": sorted(len(file_rows) for file_rows in files.values()),
        "row": next(row for row in rows if row["key"] == "orders-12"),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    r = outcomes(Path("streaming_out_output"))
    print(f"{len(r['file_rows'])} files, with {r['file_rows']} rows")
    row = {k: v for k, v in r["row"].items() if k != "timestamp"}
    print(f"orders-12: {row}")
docs/snippets/tutorials/streaming_out_low_level.py
"""The Streaming Out tutorial: the shop's records, to the terminal and to a file, low-level.

One packer takes 1.5 seconds to pack an order, and an order arrives every 2.5 seconds
on average (rate 0.4), for an hour. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the
finished orders are written to packed/. The script then prints the files the sink
wrote and one order's row. To see only those lines, run:
python streaming_out_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import json
import logging
import shutil
from pathlib import Path

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    JsonlStorageEgress,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.4)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=1)},
)


def packed_only(record: dict) -> bool:
    """Keeps the finished orders: events whose value says order_packed."""
    return (
        record["stream_type"] == "event"
        and record["value"].get("event_type") == "order_packed"
    )


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        # The key names the order; task and instance name this run of the task
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id))


def run(out: Path):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress(
        [
            # Every event and every telemetry record
            ConsoleEgress(),
            # The finished orders only, one flat row each
            JsonlStorageEgress(default_path=f"{out}/packed/orders.jsonl"),
        ],
        predicates=[None, packed_only],
    )
    # The packers' and the packing task's readings every 10 minutes, as telemetry
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=600)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), packers))
    try:
        env.run(until=3600)  # the model stops at 1 hour
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # the sinks receive the rest and finish writing
    return env


def read_files(folder: Path) -> dict:
    """The rows of each file the sink wrote to folder, by file name."""
    return {
        path.name: [json.loads(line) for line in path.read_text().splitlines()]
        for path in sorted(folder.glob("*.jsonl"))
    }


def outcomes(out: Path) -> dict:
    """Runs the hour; returns the rows in each file and the row of orders-12."""
    shutil.rmtree(out / "packed", ignore_errors=True)  # a run adds files; start empty
    run(out)
    files = read_files(out / "packed")
    rows = [row for file_rows in files.values() for row in file_rows]
    return {
        "file_rows": sorted(len(file_rows) for file_rows in files.values()),
        "row": next(row for row in rows if row["key"] == "orders-12"),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    r = outcomes(Path("streaming_out_output"))
    print(f"{len(r['file_rows'])} files, with {r['file_rows']} rows")
    row = {k: v for k, v in r["row"].items() if k != "timestamp"}
    print(f"orders-12: {row}")

Experiments describes every setting of an experiment, its files and its report, and the rest of the User Guide describes each part of desflow in full. The Kafka Digital Twin example takes live changes from Kafka and sends its records to Kafka.

docs.title: Competing Resources
docs.text:
The shop now picks each order from the shelves before packing it. One picker fetches the order in a second and carries it to the one packing bench, where packing takes 2 seconds on average. The picker could put the order down by the bench and go back for the next one, or stay with it until the bench is free, so the order is never left unattended. This page asks: what does holding one resource while waiting for another cost?

  • Decision: whether the picker stays with each order until the bench is free.
  • Measures: the mean wait for the picker and for the bench, and the share of time the picker is busy.
  • Runs: two runs of the hour, one for each way of working, each with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, one every 2.5 seconds on average (24 a minute), picking always takes exactly one second, and packing times follow an exponential distribution.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • give a task two resources, a picker and a packing bench;
  • keep the first resource for the next task with a handoff;
  • measure what holding one resource while waiting for another costs.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a second resource, the bench, and a handoff. The picking task keeps the picker for the packing task, which gives the picker back once the order is on the bench.

docs.title: Hold One While Waiting for Another
docs.text:
In SimPy a process holds a resource from the moment its request is granted until it releases the resource. It can request a second resource while it holds the first, with nested with blocks. A desflow task does the same in two ways. It can list several resources, resource: [picker, bench], and hold them all while it works. Or it can hand a unit to the next task of its flow with keep, as Several Resources describes. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/competing_resources.yaml:handoff
pick_order:
  service: picking
  resource: picker
  # The picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
  keep: [picker]
  payload: {event_type: order_picked}
  next: pack_order
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: bench
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}

Remove keep: [picker] to run it without the handoff: pick_order then gives the picker back when it finishes, as every task does.

docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources.py:handoff
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="picker",
    # The picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
    keep=["picker"] if keep else None,
    next="pack_order",
)
def pick_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}

@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="bench")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

Without keep, pick_order gives the picker back when it finishes, as every task does.

docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources_low_level.py:handoff
def pick_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, keep):
    status, finished, duration = step(
        env, sampler, key, "pick_order", task_id, "picking"
    )
    status("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pick_order", task_id)
    picker = shop["picker"].request()
    yield picker
    status("started")
    env.stats.task_started("pick_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(duration())
    finished({"event_type": "order_picked"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pick_order", task_id)
    if not keep:
        shop["picker"].release(picker)
        picker = None
    # With keep, the picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
    env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, picker))


def pack_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, picker):
    status, finished, duration = step(
        env, sampler, key, "pack_order", task_id, "packing"
    )
    status("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with shop["bench"].request() as bench:
        yield bench
        status("started")
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        if picker is not None:
            shop["picker"].release(picker)  # the order is on the bench
        yield env.timeout(duration())
        finished({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")

The picker's request is not in a with block, because the next process releases it.

While the order waits for the bench it holds the picker: a partial holding. Nothing grants the picker and the bench together. Each is acquired in turn, and the units already held stay held while the task waits for the next. The picker's busy share includes that waiting time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/competing_resources.yaml:watch
# The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources.py:watch
# The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources_low_level.py:watch
# The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

docs.title: One Order of Acquisition
docs.text: Two orders that each hold one resource and wait for the other wait for ever: a deadlock. If a picking task held the picker and waited for the bench while a wrapping task held the bench and waited for the picker, both could stop. desflow prevents a deadlock by refusing such a model when it is built. Every task, handoffs included, must acquire shared resources in one order, and the error names the two tasks that disagree. Here every order goes picker first, then bench.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What does holding the picker while waiting for the bench cost? Each figure here is a mean from one run of the hour with the seed 42.

  • When the picker puts the order down and goes back, orders wait 0.32 seconds for the picker and 5.89 seconds for the bench, 6.21 seconds in all.
  • When the picker stays with the order, the wait moves to the picker. Orders wait 8.77 seconds for it and only 1.09 seconds for the bench, 9.85 seconds in all. The picker is then busy 82.7% of the time instead of 39.8%, most of it standing by the bench:

Each tab prints both: the picker's busy share and the mean waits, first with the picker freed, then with it kept.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Each order brings 2 seconds of packing on average and arrives every 2.5 seconds on average, so the bench is busy 2 ÷ 2.5 = 80% of the time and the picker 1 ÷ 2.5 = 40%. The bench is the busier of the two, the bottleneck. When the picker waits at the bench, it spends its own time in the bench's queue. So the picker is busy longer than its work needs, and the next order waits for it. Releasing a resource as soon as it is no longer needed keeps the waits where the work is.

Queueing Basics explains utilisation. Several Resources describes several resources, handoffs and the order rule.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A task that holds a resource while it waits for another keeps that resource busy without work.
  • The wait then moves to the resource that is held, and the next order waits for it.
  • Release a resource as soon as it is no longer needed, unless the work requires it to stay.

docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources.py
"""The Competing Resources tutorial: an order keeps the picker until it is on the bench.

One picker, one packing bench, and an order every 2.5 seconds on average. Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits and the picker's busy share
with and without the handoff at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python competing_resources.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(keep: bool = True) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop; with `keep`, an order keeps the picker until it is on the bench."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("picker", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_resource("bench", current_cap=1, max_cap=2)
        .add_service("picking", dist="constant", value=1)
        .add_service("packing", dist="exponential", rate=0.5)
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4)
        # The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="picking",
        resource_id="picker",
        # The picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
        keep=["picker"] if keep else None,
        next="pack_order",
    )
    def pick_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_picked"}

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="bench")
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pick_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(keep: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns each task's mean wait and the picker's busy share."""
    app = shop(keep)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    r = app.env.stats.readings()
    return {
        "pick_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.wait_mean"],
        "pack_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
        "picker_busy": r["Shop.stats.resources.picker.utilization_avg"],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for keep in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(keep)
        label = "keeps the picker" if keep else "frees the picker"
        print(
            f"{label}: wait to pick {r['pick_wait']:6.2f} s, to pack "
            f"{r['pack_wait']:5.2f} s, picker busy {r['picker_busy']:4.1f}%"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/competing_resources_low_level.py
"""The Competing Resources tutorial: an order keeps the picker until it is on the bench.

One picker, one packing bench, and an order every 2.5 seconds on average. Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the waits and the picker's busy share
with and without the handoff at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python competing_resources_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.4)},
    service={
        "picking": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1),
        "packing": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5),
    },
    resources={
        "picker": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2),
        "bench": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=2),
    },
)


def step(env, sampler, key, task, task_id, service):
    """The publish and service-time helpers of one task instance."""
    path_id = f"Shop.service.{service}"

    def status(state):
        value = {"path_id": path_id, "status": state}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    def finished(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    return status, finished, lambda: sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))


def pick_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, keep):
    status, finished, duration = step(
        env, sampler, key, "pick_order", task_id, "picking"
    )
    status("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pick_order", task_id)
    picker = shop["picker"].request()
    yield picker
    status("started")
    env.stats.task_started("pick_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(duration())
    finished({"event_type": "order_picked"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pick_order", task_id)
    if not keep:
        shop["picker"].release(picker)
        picker = None
    # With keep, the picker carries the order and stays with it until it is on the bench
    env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, picker))


def pack_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, picker):
    status, finished, duration = step(
        env, sampler, key, "pack_order", task_id, "packing"
    )
    status("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with shop["bench"].request() as bench:
        yield bench
        status("started")
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        if picker is not None:
            shop["picker"].release(picker)  # the order is on the bench
        yield env.timeout(duration())
        finished({"event_type": "order_packed"})
        env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def order_generator(env, sampler, shop, keep):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pick_order(env, sampler, shop, key, task_id, keep))


def run(keep=True, until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # The mean wait of each task and the picker's busy share, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    shop = {
        "picker": DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "picker"),
        "bench": DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "bench"),
    }
    env.process(order_generator(env, Sampler(seed=42), shop, keep))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(keep: bool) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns each task's mean wait and the picker's busy share."""
    r = run(keep).stats.readings()
    return {
        "pick_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pick_order.wait_mean"],
        "pack_wait": r["Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"],
        "picker_busy": r["Shop.stats.resources.picker.utilization_avg"],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for keep in (False, True):
        r = outcomes(keep)
        label = "keeps the picker" if keep else "frees the picker"
        print(
            f"{label}: wait to pick {r['pick_wait']:6.2f} s, to pack "
            f"{r['pack_wait']:5.2f} s, picker busy {r['picker_busy']:4.1f}%"
        )

docs.title: Filtered Inventory
docs.text:
The shop now sells shirts in three sizes: small, medium and large. Shirts of every size go on one shelf. A new shirt arrives every 10 seconds on average, and a new order also arrives every 10 seconds on average. Each order is for one shirt of a given size. A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes. Half the orders are for medium shirts, but only 4 shirts in 10 are medium. This page asks: which waiting order can use the shirt that arrives, and which orders go unfilled?

  • Decision: whether the shop's mix of shirt sizes is right for its orders.
  • Measures: the orders filled and cancelled for each size, and the shirts left on the shelf.
  • Runs: one run of a working day of 8 hours, with the seed 42, covering only taking shirts from the shelf: packing is left out.
  • Assumptions: shirts and orders of each size arrive at random, each at a steady rate.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • hold items of several kinds on one shelf, in a store;
  • take only an item that matches the order, with a filter;
  • see which orders go unfilled when one kind is short.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a shelf store, and a filter on the order's get that picks a shirt of the order's size. The order task has no resource: it waits only for its shirt, with the Patience of 10 minutes covering that wait.

docs.title: One Shelf of Items
docs.text:
A store holds items, and each item is a value of its own. Here each shirt is a mapping such as {size: M}, and a restock task puts it on the shelf. Stores and Containers describes stores. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:shelf
stores:
  # Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {size: M}
  shelf: {current_cap: 1000, max_cap: 1000}
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:shelf
# Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {"size": "M"}
app.add_store("shelf", current_cap=1000, max_cap=1000)
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:shelf
# Shirts of every size on one shelf, each item a mapping such as {"size": "M"}
stores={"shelf": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1000, max_cap=1000)},

The shirts and the orders arrive from six arrivals, one per size, each with a size attribute:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:arrivals
# A shirt every 10 seconds on average: 3 in 10 small, 4 medium, 3 large
shirts_s: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.03, spawn: restock, attributes: {size: S}}
shirts_m: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.04, spawn: restock, attributes: {size: M}}
shirts_l: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.03, spawn: restock, attributes: {size: L}}
# An order every 10 seconds on average: a quarter small, half medium, a quarter large
orders_s: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.025, spawn: take_shirt, attributes: {size: S}}
orders_m: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.05, spawn: take_shirt, attributes: {size: M}}
orders_l: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.025, spawn: take_shirt, attributes: {size: L}}
docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:arrivals
for size, rate in SHIRTS.items():
    name = f"shirts_{size.lower()}"
    app.add_arrival(name, dist="exponential", rate=rate, attributes={"size": size})
for size, rate in ORDERS.items():
    name = f"orders_{size.lower()}"
    app.add_arrival(name, dist="exponential", rate=rate, attributes={"size": size})

SHIRTS and ORDERS map each size to its rate, as the full file shows.

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:arrivals
arrival={
    **{
        f"shirts_{s.lower()}": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=r)
        for s, r in SHIRTS.items()
    },
    **{
        f"orders_{s.lower()}": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=r)
        for s, r in ORDERS.items()
    },
},

SHIRTS and ORDERS map each size to its rate. Each arrival process passes its size to the task, as the full file shows.

docs.title: Take the Right Item
docs.text:
A plain get takes the oldest item, whatever it is. A get with a filter takes the oldest item the filter accepts and waits while none does. In SimPy this is a FilterStore, whose get takes a function of the item. In desflow the filter is a condition. In it, item.<field> reads a field of the shirt on offer. The condition can also read every name that other conditions read, such as attr.size for the size the order is for:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:take
take_shirt:
  # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
  get: {store: shelf, filter: item.size == attr.size}
  # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
  patience: 10 min
  # Adds the shirt the get took to the finished event
  item_field: shirt
  payload: {event_type: order_filled}

item_field: shirt adds the shirt the get took to the finished event's payload under the key shirt, as id_field adds the task id under the key it names (YAML Keys lists both).

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory.py:take
@app.task(
    # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
    get={"store": "shelf", "filter": "item.size == attr.size"},
    # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
    patience="10 min",
)
def take_shirt(task_id: int, item):
    # `item` is the shirt the get took
    return {"event_type": "order_filled", "shirt": item}

The builder also takes a function of the item, such as "filter": lambda shirt: shirt["size"] == "M".

docs/snippets/tutorials/filtered_inventory_low_level.py:take
def take_shirt(env, shelf, key, size, task_id):
    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="take_shirt", instance=task_id)

    publish({"status": "queued"})
    # Takes the oldest shirt of the order's own size; waits while there is none
    get = shelf.get(filter=lambda shirt: shirt["size"] == size)
    # A customer cancels an order not filled within 10 minutes
    yield get | env.timeout(PATIENCE)
    if not get.triggered:
        get.cancel()  # out of the queue, so it never takes a shirt later
        publish({"status": "reneged"})
        return
    publish({"status": "started"})
    publish({"event_type": "order_filled", "shirt": get.value})

shelf.get(filter=...) is SimPy's FilterStore.get. Cancelling a get that has not succeeded takes it out of the queue, so it never takes a shirt later.

When a shirt arrives, it is offered to the waiting orders one at a time, oldest first, and the first order whose filter accepts it takes it. A medium order waiting at the front does not stop a small order behind it from taking a small shirt, as it would if all orders waited in one line for the next shirt.

patience covers the wait for the get, as it covers a wait for a resource. A get that gives up takes nothing later: the shirt that would have filled it stays on the shelf for the next order.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Which waiting order can use the shirt that arrives? The oldest order of the shirt's size, and no other. In one run of 8 hours with the seed 42, 315 medium orders are cancelled, and no small or large one. Medium orders are half of all orders, but medium shirts are only 4 in 10:

Each tab prints the counts:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

The blueprint publishes its statistics once, at the end of the 8 hours:

docs/snippets/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:stats
# The counts of each arrival's orders, published once, at the end of the 8 hours
stats: {level: basic, interval: 8 h}

# Orders finished for each size, and the orders that gave up waiting
desflow run filtered_inventory.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'orders_[sml]\.finished"|take_shirt\.reneged"' | tail -4


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.take_shirt.reneged","value":315}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_s.finished","value":732}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_l.finished","value":679}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.flows.orders_m.finished","value":1110}

Each flows.orders_<size>.finished is the number of filled orders of that size. tasks.take_shirt.reneged counts the cancelled orders of every size together. A cancelled order leaves its flow without finishing it, so a size's cancelled orders are its flow's started minus finished minus in_system, the orders still waiting at the end. For medium orders that is 1,454 − 1,110 − 29 = 315, all of the cancelled orders.

python filtered_inventory.py 2>/dev/null

size S:  732 filled,    0 cancelled
size M: 1110 filled,  315 cancelled
size L:  679 filled,    0 cancelled

python filtered_inventory_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

size S:  732 filled,    0 cancelled
size M: 1110 filled,  315 cancelled
size L:  679 filled,    0 cancelled

A filtered store works like one shelf with a separate queue for each kind of item. Orders and shirts of each size arrive at their own rates, on average:

Size An order arrives A shirt arrives Small every 40 seconds (1.5 a minute, rate: 0.025) every 33 seconds (1.8 a minute, rate: 0.03) Medium every 20 seconds (3 a minute, rate: 0.05) every 25 seconds (2.4 a minute, rate: 0.04) Large every 40 seconds (1.5 a minute, rate: 0.025) every 33 seconds (1.8 a minute, rate: 0.03)

Medium orders outnumber medium shirts all day: they ask for 0.05 shirts a second and get 0.04, a utilisation of 1.25. So their queue would grow without end if customers did not cancel after 10 minutes. There are more small and large shirts than orders of those sizes, so every small and large order is filled before its customer cancels. The shirts left over, 248 at the end of the run, wait on the shelf, which has room for 1,000.

SimPy and desflow compares stores and containers with SimPy's. Stores and Containers describes filters and cancelled gets.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A filtered store works like one shelf with a separate queue for each kind of item.
  • A kind whose orders outnumber its items has a queue that grows, even when the shelf holds other items.
  • Patience on the wait ends that growth, at the cost of cancelled orders.

docs.title: Full Files
A Flow of Tasks
docs.text:
Until now an order was one task: it was packed and left. A real order is picked from the shelves, packed and shipped. Sometimes an item is out of stock, and sometimes a parcel fails its check and is packed again. This page asks: how do orders move through pick, pack and ship?

  • Decision: how much work to plan for beyond one pick and one pack per order.
  • Measures: two shares: how many orders go to backorder, and how many parcels are packed again.
  • Runs: one run of an hour with the seed 42, from an order's arrival to its shipment, with the supplier modelled only as a delay.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, each picking time is equally likely to be anywhere from 1 to 3 seconds, and packing always takes 1.5 seconds.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • chain tasks so an order is picked, packed and shipped;
  • route a share of the orders to backorder or back to packing;
  • carry an attribute, such as express, through the flow.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text:
This page adds three tasks in a row: pick_order, pack_order and ship_order. It also adds a backorder delay for an order picked while the shelf of boxes from Stock is empty, and an express attribute that each order carries. The shop is set up as follows:

  • It has two pickers and two packers.
  • A regular order arrives every 2.5 seconds on average (24 a minute, rate: 0.4), and an express order every 10 seconds (6 a minute, rate: 0.1).
  • A delivery of 53 boxes comes every 100 seconds, a little more than the orders take.
  • Picking time is uniform from 1 to 3 seconds only to keep the example short. Common Mistakes explains why a real study fits a distribution to measured times instead, as Choosing Inputs does.

Look at the flow first:

docs.title: Chain the Tasks
docs.text:
Choosing where an entity goes next is called routing. In desflow a task names what follows it with next. Tasks and Processes describes tasks. next takes one of three forms:

  • a task name, which always leads there;
  • a list of when rules, each a condition and a task: the first rule that holds wins, and default catches the rest;
  • weights, which Rework shows.

A task with no next ends the order's flow. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:chain
pick_order:
  service: picking
  resource: pickers
  payload: {event_type: order_picked}
  # The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
  next:
    when:
      - {condition: "level.stock == 0", task: backorder}
    default: pack_order

Here the arrival loop passes the context to each task after its id. A task started by next receives the same arguments as the task before it. So every task function in the flow declares context.

docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:chain
# The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
@app.task(
    service_id="picking",
    resource_id="pickers",
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    },
)
def pick_order(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_picked"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:chain
# The first rule that holds wins; default catches the rest
"pick_order": Router(
    {
        "when": [{"condition": "level.stock == 0", "task": "backorder"}],
        "default": "pack_order",
    }
),

A Router takes the same rules as next and returns the name of the task to start. When a task finishes, its process asks the router and starts the next task as a new process, with the same entity:

docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:next
entity.attributes.update(SETS.get(name, {}))
upstream = Upstream(task_id, entity.key, entity.attributes, finished)
following = ROUTES[name].choose(upstream, env, levels={"stock": shop["stock"]})
if following is None:
    env.stats.flow_finished(entity.arrival)  # the order leaves the shop
    return
instance = next(counters[following])
env.process(task(env, sampler, shop, following, entity, instance, counters))

In SimPy terms, a process that starts another process with env.process(...) is how one step leads to the next. SimPy and desflow describes processes.

The rule reads level.stock, the level of the container stock, at the moment picking finishes. Stores and Containers describes containers. Each name in a condition says where its value comes from: level. for a store or container, attr. for the entity's attributes, payload. for the finished task's payload, and registry["..."] for a live parameter. Task Flow lists everything a condition can use.

Every event of every task carries the order's key, orders-1, so one order can be followed through its whole flow. task names the task, and instance numbers its runs. Each task has one counter, shared by its arrivals and by next, so a re-pick after a backorder gets a new id. In the full builder file the arrival loops take the id from context.next_instance("pick_order"), and the low-level file keeps one counters entry per task.

docs.title: Out of Stock
docs.text:
An order picked while the shelf is empty waits for the supplier for a minute, then is picked again. The wait uses no picker or packer, so backorder has a service and no resource: a timed step. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:backorder
backorder:
  # A timed step: a service and no resource, so it starts at once
  service: supplying
  payload: {event_type: order_backordered}
  # Applied to the order's attributes when the step finishes
  set: {backordered: 1}
  next: pick_order
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:backorder
# A timed step: a service and no resource, so it starts at once. `set` is applied
# to the order's attributes when the step finishes.
@app.task(service_id="supplying", set={"backordered": 1}, next="pick_order")
def backorder(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_backordered"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:backorder
"backorder": Router("pick_order"),
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:set
# Applied to the order's attributes when the step finishes
SETS = {"backorder": {"backordered": 1}}

next: pick_order sends the order back to an earlier task. A route back is allowed anywhere in a flow.

docs.title: Rework
docs.text:
One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again. Sending work back to a task it has passed is called rework. weights chooses the next task at random, in proportion to the weights. It draws from the routing task's own random number stream, route.pack_order. So a seeded run repeats, and the choice does not change any other draw:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:rework
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  get: {container: stock, amount: 1}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  # One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again
  next:
    weights: {ship_order: 95, pack_order: 5}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:rework
# One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1},
    next={"weights": {"ship_order": 95, "pack_order": 5}},
)
def pack_order(task_id: int, context: SimulationContext):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:rework
# One parcel in 20 fails its check and is packed again; the generator is set
# in run below
"pack_order": Router({"weights": {"ship_order": 95, "pack_order": 5}}),

The low-level router needs a generator to draw from: ROUTES["pack_order"].rng = sampler.generator("route.pack_order") in run, the stream the builder uses.

docs.title: Carry Attributes
docs.text:
An order is an entity with attributes: values it carries from task to task, such as whether it is express. The arrival gives each new entity its starting attributes, and set on a task changes them when the task finishes, as backorder does with backordered: 1:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/flow_of_tasks.yaml:attributes
arrivals:
  # Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.4, spawn: pick_order, attributes: {express: 0}}
  express: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: pick_order, attributes: {express: 1}}
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks.py:attributes
# Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.4, attributes={"express": 0})
app.add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.1, attributes={"express": 1})
docs/snippets/tutorials/flow_of_tasks_low_level.py:attributes
# Each order starts with the attributes given here, read as attr.<name>
ATTRIBUTES = {"orders": {"express": 0}, "express": {"express": 1}}

Entity(key, arrival, attributes) is the order, created by the arrival process; the full file below shows it.

Attributes are not published. A condition reads them as attr.express, and a payload includes them only when it names them. ship_order names express and backordered, so its finished event carries both. This is orders-172, which was picked while the shelf was empty, backordered, picked again and packed twice:
