docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
How do orders move through pick, pack and ship? Most go straight through, and a few go to backorder or are packed again. The run publishes the finished count of every task at the end, with stats: basic:

Task Finished in the hour pick_order 1,857 backorder 80 pack_order 1,849 ship_order 1,775

4.3% of picks led to backorder (80 of 1,857), and 4.0% of parcels were packed again (74 of 1,849 packs did not lead to a shipment). The weights set 5%, and this one run of the hour, with the seed 42, drew a few fewer.

Flow balance is the rule that, in a flow, each task's arrival rate follows from the rates into it and the routing weights. Every pack leads to a shipment with probability 0.95, so each order is packed 1 ÷ 0.95 = 1.05 times on average, and the packers see 5% more work than there are orders. A rework loop therefore raises utilisation, so it belongs in the load you work out before running. Queueing Basics shows why waits grow quickly near full use. Task Flow describes routing in full.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A task names the task that follows it, by a condition or by weights.
  • In a flow, each task's rate follows from the rates into it and the routing weights.
  • A rework loop adds work to the resources it returns to, so include it in the load you work out before running.

docs.title: Full Files
Interruptions
docs.text:
A quarter of the shop's orders are express, as in Priorities, but now an express order does not wait for the regular order being packed: it takes the packer at once. This page asks: what remains of a regular order's packing when an express order takes its packer, and which way of carrying on keeps regular orders waiting least?

  • Decision: which of three policies a regular order follows when it loses the packer.
  • Measures: the number of preemptions, the mean wait of regular orders, and the orders packed and lost.
  • Runs: three runs of the hour, one for each policy, each with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: both kinds of order arrive at random, and every order takes the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • let express orders take the packer from regular ones;
  • choose what a preempted order does: resume, restart or abandon;
  • interrupt the orders in the shop from outside.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a packer that can be preempted, as Preemption explains, and an on_interrupt policy on regular orders: resume, restart or abandon. It also calls the packer away once, which interrupts the regular orders in the shop. A breakdown interrupts work in the same way, and the Model Breakdowns guide adds one. The shop is the one from Priorities: one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on average (rate: 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate: 0.15).

docs.title: Preemption
docs.text:
Priority so far decided only who goes next. Preemption also stops the work in progress. In SimPy, a request may find every unit of a PreemptiveResource busy. A lower priority value is more urgent. When the request is more urgent than a process holding a unit, the resource takes the unit from the least urgent holder, the one with the highest priority value, and that process receives an Interrupt. In desflow it is preempt: true on a resource whose queue is priority. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:packers
resources:
  # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority, preempt: true}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:packers
# An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
.add_resource(
    "packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True
)
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:packers
# An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
"packers": DynamicResource(
    env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True
),

preempt=True gives the resource SimPy's preemption, and the process that holds a unit receives an interrupt when it is preempted. The code below uses three more SimPy names:

  • release(request) gives back the unit a request holds;
  • env.active_process is the process that is running now;
  • request.cancel() takes a request that has not been granted out of the queue.

Equal priorities do not preempt, so one express order does not take the packer from another.

docs.title: Resume, Restart or Abandon
docs.text:
A preempted or interrupted task first gives back everything it holds and stops waiting for anything, as SimPy's with blocks do on the way out. Its on_interrupt then says what it does:

  • resume, the default: it queues again and, once it has the packer back, packs for the time it had left;
  • restart: it queues again and packs for a new time, drawn from the same seeded stream, as if the work were spoiled;
  • abandon: it ends, and its flow with it, unless on_interrupt_next names a task to go to.

An order that is abandoned when it loses its packer, and goes to be packed by hand:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:interrupt-next
# An order that loses its packer to a rush order is packed by hand instead
on_interrupt: abandon
on_interrupt_next: pack_by_hand
docs/snippets/pages/interrupt_next.py:builder
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    # An order that loses its packer to a rush order is packed by hand instead
    on_interrupt="abandon",
    on_interrupt_next="pack_by_hand",
)
def pack(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "packed"}
docs/snippets/pages/interrupt_next.py:low-level
def pack(env, sampler, packers, counts):
    request = packers.request(priority=1)
    try:
        yield request
        yield env.timeout(
            sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config("Shop.service.packing"))
        )
        counts["packed"] += 1
    except simpy.Interrupt:
        # An order that loses its packer to a rush order is packed by hand instead
        env.process(pack_by_hand(env, sampler, counts))
    finally:
        packers.release(request)

In the low-level API the process catches the Interrupt and starts the process that packs by hand.

The task publishes preempted (or interrupted) when it loses the packer, and resumed when it has it again. A preempted record names the express order that took the packer (preempted_by, its entity key) and the time the regular order had held it (usage_since):

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:policy
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  priority: 1
  # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
  on_interrupt: ${POLICY:-resume}
  payload: {event_type: order_packed}

${POLICY:-resume} reads the environment variable POLICY, so POLICY=restart desflow run interruptions.yaml runs the second policy.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:policy
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    priority=1,
    # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
    on_interrupt=policy,
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:policy
def pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy):
    """Packs one order; when it loses the packer, it follows `policy`."""
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    shop["running"].setdefault(task, []).append(env.active_process)
    shop["keys"][env.active_process] = key
    remaining, started = None, False
    while True:
        request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            yield request
            status = "resumed" if started else "started"
            publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": status})
            if started:
                env.stats.task_resumed(task, task_id)
            else:
                env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
            started = True
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            publish({"event_type": "order_packed" if priority else "express_packed"})
            env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            request.cancel()
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            if since is not None:
                # resume serves what is left; restart draws a new packing time
                remaining = (
                    remaining - (env.now - since) if policy == "resume" else None
                )
            preempted = isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted)
            if preempted:
                value = {
                    "status": "preempted",
                    "resource": "packers",
                    "preempted_by": shop["keys"].get(interrupt.cause.by),
                    "usage_since": interrupt.cause.usage_since,
                }
            else:
                value = {"status": "interrupted", "cause": interrupt.cause}
            publish({"path_id": path_id, **value})
            env.stats.task_interrupted(task, task_id, preempted=preempted)
            if policy == "abandon":
                env.stats.task_dropped(task, task_id)
                shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
                del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
                return
    shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
    del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)

The process catches simpy.Interrupt. For a preemption, its cause is SimPy's Preempted. The process gives back its request and requests the packer again. on_interrupt writes that loop for you. SimPy delivers an interrupt as an URGENT event, which End Conditions explains.

The statistics count each preempted, interrupted and resumed. A resumed order's wait is the sum of its waits, and its packing time is the total time it was packed:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:watch
# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

docs.title: Interrupt a Task
docs.text:
Preemption is one source of interrupts, and a model can send others. An interrupt names a task. Every instance of that task that is running, waiting or being served receives an interrupt with the given cause, and follows its on_interrupt. A where condition, such as attr.order == 3, limits the interrupt to the instances for which the condition holds. Here the packer is called away at 31 minutes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml:interrupt
scenario:
  # The packer is called away at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
  # waiting or being packed, is interrupted
  - {at: 31 min, interrupt: {task: pack_order, cause: called away}}

A task can carry the same interrupt, applied when it finishes.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions.py:interrupt
def called_away(context: SimulationContext):
    """The packer is called away at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield context.env.timeout(1860)
    context.interrupt("pack_order", cause="called away")

app.add_process(called_away)

context.interrupt(task, where=None, cause=None) returns how many instances it reached. It never reaches the instance that calls it.

docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py:interrupt
def called_away(env, shop):
    """The packer is called away at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield env.timeout(1860)
    for process in list(shop["running"].get("pack_order", [])):
        process.interrupt("called away")

process.interrupt(cause) is SimPy's. The model keeps its own list of the processes it may interrupt.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
What remains of a regular order's packing when an express order takes its packer? Each figure here comes from one run of the hour with the seed 42.

  • With resume, the time it had left remains. After 344 preemptions, regular orders wait 8.12 seconds on average.
  • With restart, nothing remains: each preempted order packs again from the start. Preemptions rise to 393, and the mean wait triples to 25.33 seconds.
  • With abandon, the order is lost. 314 orders are lost, 312 to preemption and 2 to the call at 31 minutes. The 1,293 packed orders wait only 3.60 seconds on average, because every interrupted order leaves the queue.

The call at 31 minutes reaches every regular order in the shop at that moment: 3 under resume, 23 under restart, whose longer queue holds more orders, and 2 under abandon:

Each tab prints all three policies: the orders packed, preempted and called away (interrupted), the mean wait and the mean packing time.

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# The resume policy: orders preempted, called away and packed, mean wait and packing time
desflow run interruptions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(preempted|interrupted|finished|wait_mean|service_mean)"' | tail -5
# The restart policy
POLICY=restart desflow run interruptions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(preempted|interrupted|finished|wait_mean|service_mean)"' | tail -5
# The abandon policy
POLICY=abandon desflow run interruptions.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(preempted|interrupted|finished|wait_mean|service_mean)"' | tail -5

python interruptions.py 2>/dev/null

resume : 344 preempted, 3 called away, 1607 packed, mean wait  8.12 s, mean packing 1.50 s
restart: 393 preempted, 23 called away, 1606 packed, mean wait 25.33 s, mean packing 1.69 s
abandon: 312 preempted, 2 called away, 1293 packed, mean wait  3.60 s, mean packing 1.50 s

python interruptions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

resume : 344 preempted, 3 called away, 1607 packed, mean wait  8.12 s, mean packing 1.50 s
restart: 393 preempted, 23 called away, 1606 packed, mean wait 25.33 s, mean packing 1.69 s
abandon: 312 preempted, 2 called away, 1293 packed, mean wait  3.60 s, mean packing 1.50 s

Under restart the packer spends part of its time on packing that is thrown away, so it does more work for the same orders. The mean time packed rises from 1.50 to 1.69 seconds, and the load nears what one packer can do. Waits then grow fast, as Queueing Basics explains. resume loses no work, so its waits are close to those of plain priority. abandon looks best only because the mean leaves out the orders it lost. So report their count beside it. Priority and Preemption describes preemption, and Tasks and Processes the task's steps.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Preemption gives an urgent task the resource at once, and the task it takes it from must wait.
  • resume loses no work. restart throws work away and adds load, so waits grow fast near full use.
  • abandon looks best only because the mean leaves out the lost orders, so report their count beside it.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/interruptions.yaml
# The Interruptions tutorial: express orders take the packer from regular ones.
# Run it with: desflow run interruptions.yaml
# With restart instead of resume: POLICY=restart desflow run interruptions.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority, preempt: true}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.45, spawn: pack_order}
  express: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.15, spawn: pack_express}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 1
    # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
    on_interrupt: ${POLICY:-resume}
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  pack_express:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0
    payload: {event_type: express_packed}

scenario:
  # The packer is called away at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
  # waiting or being packed, is interrupted
  - {at: 31 min, interrupt: {task: pack_order, cause: called away}}

# Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 1 h

"""The Interruptions tutorial: express orders take the packer from regular ones.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on
average (rate 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate 0.15). Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints what preemption did to regular orders
under each policy at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python interruptions.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(policy: str = "resume") -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, where a regular order follows `policy` when it loses the packer."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
        .add_resource(
            "packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue="priority", preempt=True
        )
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.45)
        .add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.15)
        # Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="packing",
        resource_id="packers",
        priority=1,
        # What a regular order does when it loses the packer
        on_interrupt=policy,
    )
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=0)
    def pack_express(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "express_packed"}

    for arrival, task, name in (
        ("orders", pack_order, "pack_order"),
        ("express", pack_express, "pack_express"),
    ):

        def loop(context: SimulationContext, arrival=arrival, task=task, name=name):
            while True:
                entity = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(context.next_instance(name), entity=entity))

        app.arrival_loop(arrival)(loop)

    def called_away(context: SimulationContext):
        """The packer is called away at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
        waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
        yield context.env.timeout(1860)
        context.interrupt("pack_order", cause="called away")

    app.add_process(called_away)
    return app


def outcomes(policy: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what preemption did to regular orders."""
    app = shop(policy)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "preempted": readings[name("preempted")],
        "interrupted": readings.get(name("interrupted"), 0),
        "finished": readings[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": readings[name("wait_mean")],
        "service_mean": readings[name("service_mean")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for policy in ("resume", "restart", "abandon"):
        r = outcomes(policy)
        print(
            f"{policy:<7}: {r['preempted']} preempted, {r['interrupted']} called away, "
            f"{r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, mean packing {r['service_mean']:4.2f} s"
        )
docs/snippets/tutorials/interruptions_low_level.py
"""The Interruptions tutorial: express orders take the packer from regular ones.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on
average (rate 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate 0.15). Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints what preemption did to regular orders
under each policy at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python interruptions_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import itertools
import logging

import simpy
from simpy.resources.resource import Preempted

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={
        # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express
        "orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.45),
        "express": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.15),
    },
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}


def pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy):
    """Packs one order; when it loses the packer, it follows `policy`."""
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    shop["running"].setdefault(task, []).append(env.active_process)
    shop["keys"][env.active_process] = key
    remaining, started = None, False
    while True:
        request = shop["packers"].request(priority=priority)
        since = None
        try:
            yield request
            status = "resumed" if started else "started"
            publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": status})
            if started:
                env.stats.task_resumed(task, task_id)
            else:
                env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
            started = True
            if remaining is None:
                remaining = sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id))
            since = env.now
            yield env.timeout(remaining)
            publish({"event_type": "order_packed" if priority else "express_packed"})
            env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            break
        except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
            request.cancel()
            shop["packers"].release(request)
            if since is not None:
                # resume serves what is left; restart draws a new packing time
                remaining = (
                    remaining - (env.now - since) if policy == "resume" else None
                )
            preempted = isinstance(interrupt.cause, Preempted)
            if preempted:
                value = {
                    "status": "preempted",
                    "resource": "packers",
                    "preempted_by": shop["keys"].get(interrupt.cause.by),
                    "usage_since": interrupt.cause.usage_since,
                }
            else:
                value = {"status": "interrupted", "cause": interrupt.cause}
            publish({"path_id": path_id, **value})
            env.stats.task_interrupted(task, task_id, preempted=preempted)
            if policy == "abandon":
                env.stats.task_dropped(task, task_id)
                shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
                del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
                return
    shop["running"][task].remove(env.active_process)
    del shop["keys"][env.active_process]
    env.stats.flow_finished(arrival)


def order_generator(env, sampler, shop, arrival, policy):
    config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.arrival.{arrival}")
    for task_id in itertools.count():
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        key = f"{arrival}-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, shop, arrival, key, task_id, policy))


def called_away(env, shop):
    """The packer is called away at 31 minutes: every regular order in the shop,
    waiting or being packed, is interrupted."""
    yield env.timeout(1860)
    for process in list(shop["running"].get("pack_order", [])):
        process.interrupt("called away")


def run(policy="resume", until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts of preemptions and resumptions, and the mean wait and service, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    shop = {
        # An express order takes the packer from a regular one being packed
        "packers": DynamicResource(
            env, "Shop", "packers", queue="priority", preempt=True
        ),
        "running": {},
        # The key of the order each process packs, for the `preempted_by` of a record
        "keys": {},
    }
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, shop, "orders", policy))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, shop, "express", policy))
    env.process(called_away(env, shop))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(policy: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what preemption did to regular orders."""
    readings = run(policy).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        "preempted": readings[name("preempted")],
        "interrupted": readings.get(name("interrupted"), 0),
        "finished": readings[name("finished")],
        "wait_mean": readings[name("wait_mean")],
        "service_mean": readings[name("service_mean")],
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for policy in ("resume", "restart", "abandon"):
        r = outcomes(policy)
        print(
            f"{policy:<7}: {r['preempted']} preempted, {r['interrupted']} called away, "
            f"{r['finished']} packed, "
            f"mean wait {r['wait_mean']:5.2f} s, mean packing {r['service_mean']:4.2f} s"
        )

docs.title: Patience
docs.text:
The shop now gets an order every 1.43 seconds on average (42 a minute, rate: 0.7). Its one packer packs one every 1.5 seconds (40 a minute), so orders arrive faster than they can be packed. A real customer does not wait for ever: one whose order has not started within 30 seconds cancels it. The courier also leaves at the hour, so the shop takes no new orders in the last five minutes. This page asks: which orders leave or refuse to join, and what does that do to the wait of the others?

  • Decision: which figures the shop reports for an hour in which customers may leave.
  • Measures: the orders that leave the queue or refuse to join, and the mean and longest wait of the packed orders.
  • Runs: two runs of the hour, one with a patience of 30 seconds and one without, each with the seed 42.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, every order takes the same time to pack, and every customer has the same patience.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • let an order leave the queue after waiting too long;
  • stop orders joining near closing time;
  • count the orders that left or never joined.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a patience and a balk condition to the packing task. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing, but with an order every 1.43 seconds on average.

docs.title: Leave After a Wait
docs.text:
An entity that leaves a queue after waiting too long reneges. In SimPy it waits for whichever comes first, the unit or a timeout, with the | of two events (an AnyOf), then checks which one happened. In desflow it is the task's patience: how long the task may wait before it leaves the queue and publishes reneged. The patience covers the task's wait, then its resource, then its get from a store or container. It counts waiting time only, and pauses while the task is served. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/patience.yaml:patience
# A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
patience: ${PATIENCE:-30 s}

${PATIENCE:-30 s} reads the environment variable PATIENCE, 30 seconds when it is not set, so PATIENCE="1 h" desflow run patience.yaml runs the hour with no limit that matters. patience takes seconds, a duration, or an expression such as attr.patience, so each order can bring its own.

docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py:patience
# A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
patience=patience,

patience is 30 here, in seconds. It also takes a duration, as in YAML: patience="30 s". A distribution's parameters in the builder take seconds only.

docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py:patience
# A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
yield request | env.timeout(patience)
if not request.triggered:
    # Leaving the with block takes the request out of the queue
    publish("reneged")
    env.stats.task_reneged("pack_order", task_id)
    return

request | env.timeout(patience) is SimPy's AnyOf: it happens when either event does. request.triggered is true once the unit is granted. Leaving the with block takes a waiting request out of the queue at once, so the packer is never granted to an order that has gone. SimPy and desflow describes events and conditions.

A reneged order publishes reneged in place of started and its finished event, and adds nothing to the wait statistics, because it was never served.

--stdout prints the run's records as JSON lines, one record per line, instead of sending them to the blueprint's sinks. So grep can pick out one kind of record. These are the first two orders that leave:

desflow run patience.yaml --stdout | grep '"reneged"' | head -2

{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":215.107,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-143","task":"pack_order","instance":142,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"reneged"}}
{"stream_type":"event","sim_ts":215.363,"timestamp":"...","key":"orders-144","task":"pack_order","instance":143,"value":{"path_id":"Shop.service.packing","status":"reneged"}}

Both orders were queued 30 seconds earlier, at 185.1 and 185.4 seconds, and left when their patience ran out. In the builder and the low-level API, ConsoleEgress(format="json") as the sink prints the same lines.

A grant and a patience can fall at the same instant: the packer finishes the previous order at exactly the moment the next order's 30 seconds run out. desflow then does what plain SimPy does: the outcome depends on which of the two events was scheduled first. The Add Reneging and Balking guide shows both cases.

docs.title: Refuse to Join
docs.text:
An entity that does not join a queue at all balks. In SimPy it is an if before the request. In desflow it is the task's balk, a condition checked before the task joins the queue. When the condition holds, the task publishes balked and never requests the resource. Here t, the simulation time, stops new orders in the last five minutes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/patience.yaml:balk
# The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
balk: t >= 3300
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py:balk
# The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
balk="t >= 3300",
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py:balk
# The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
if env.now >= 3300:
    publish("balked")
    env.stats.task_balked("pack_order", task_id)
    return

The condition reads the names every expression reads, such as attr.<name> for the order's own attributes and level.<name> for a store or container. Task Flow lists them.

A resource can refuse an order too. With a queue_limit, the resource refuses a request made while that many requests already wait, and the task balks, as Queue Limit describes.

docs.title: Count Who Left
docs.text:
With statistics at basic and above, each task publishes how many instances reneged and balked, as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.reneged and .balked, once the first one happens. typical adds the mean and longest wait of the orders that were served:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/patience.yaml:watch
# Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience.py:watch
# Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/patience_low_level.py:watch
# Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)

A low-level process counts its own outcomes with env.stats.task_reneged(task, instance) and env.stats.task_balked(task, instance), as the full file below does.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Which orders leave or refuse to join, and what does that do to the others? Each figure here comes from one run of the hour with the seed 42. With a patience of 30 seconds, 69 orders leave the queue during the hour, and the mean wait of the packed orders falls from 72.16 seconds to 14.57 seconds. No packed order waits more than 30 seconds. In both runs the 194 orders that arrive in the last five minutes refuse to join. The wait of each packed order over the hour shows why:

Each tab prints both runs: the orders packed, reneged and balked, and the mean wait.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A patience of an hour is longer than any wait, so no order reneges, and the run publishes no reneged count.

# Orders packed, given up and turned away, and the mean wait
desflow run patience.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(finished|reneged|balked|wait_mean)"' | tail -4
# A patience of an hour
PATIENCE="1 h" desflow run patience.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_order\.(finished|reneged|balked|wait_mean)"' | tail -4


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished","value":2173}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.balked","value":194}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.reneged","value":69}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":14.567032849554375}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.finished","value":2242}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.balked","value":194}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":72.1639978932148}


python patience.py 2>/dev/null

patience 30 s: 2173 packed, 69 reneged, 194 balked, mean wait 14.57 s
patience none: 2242 packed, 0 reneged, 194 balked, mean wait 72.16 s

python patience_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

patience 30 s: 2173 packed, 69 reneged, 194 balked, mean wait 14.57 s
patience none: 2242 packed, 0 reneged, 194 balked, mean wait 72.16 s

Orders arrive at 42 a minute and bring 0.7 × 1.5 = 1.05 seconds of packing each second, more than one packer can do. So without patience the queue grows, and every order waits longer than the one before. Patience removes the orders that have waited longest, so the queue stays short for the rest. The shop packs 69 fewer orders, and every order it packs waits less. The mean wait of packed orders leaves out the orders that left. So report the reneged and balked counts beside it. Queueing Basics explains why a queue grows without limit above utilisation 1. Statistics describes what each count measures.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Patience removes the orders that have waited longest, so the others wait less.
  • The mean wait of packed orders leaves out the orders that left.
  • Report the reneged and balked counts beside the mean wait.

"""The Patience tutorial: orders leave after waiting too long, and none join near closing.

One packer, an order every 1.43 seconds on average (rate 0.7) and 1.5 seconds of
packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints what happened
to the orders with a patience of 30 seconds and with none at the end. To see only those
lines, run:
python patience.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(patience: float = 30) -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop, where a customer waits at most `patience` seconds."""
    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # An order every 1.43 s on average (0.7 a second): more than one packer packs
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.7)
        # Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )

    @app.task(
        service_id="packing",
        resource_id="packers",
        # A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
        patience=patience,
        # The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
        balk="t >= 3300",
    )
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context: SimulationContext):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def outcomes(patience: float) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what happened to the orders, and the mean wait."""
    app = shop(patience)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        outcome: readings.get(name(outcome), 0)
        for outcome in ("finished", "reneged", "balked", "wait_mean")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for patience, label in ((30, "30 s"), (3600, "none")):
        result = outcomes(patience)
        print(
            f"patience {label:>4}: {result['finished']} packed, "
            f"{result['reneged']} reneged, {result['balked']} balked, "
            f"mean wait {result['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )

"""The Patience tutorial: orders leave after waiting too long, and none join near closing.

One packer, an order every 1.43 seconds on average (rate 0.7) and 1.5 seconds of
packing. Every record is printed to the terminal, and the script prints what happened
to the orders with a patience of 30 seconds and with none at the end. To see only those
lines, run:
python patience_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 1.43 s on average (0.7 a second): more than one packer packs
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.7)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)


def pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, patience):
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(status):
        value = {"path_id": path_id, "status": status}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    # The courier leaves at the hour, so the last 5 minutes take no new orders
    if env.now >= 3300:
        publish("balked")
        env.stats.task_balked("pack_order", task_id)
        return
    publish("queued")
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
    with packers.request() as request:
        # A customer cancels an order not started within 30 seconds
        yield request | env.timeout(patience)
        if not request.triggered:
            # Leaving the with block takes the request out of the queue
            publish("reneged")
            env.stats.task_reneged("pack_order", task_id)
            return
        publish("started")
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        value = {"event_type": "order_packed"}
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, patience):
    arrival = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(arrival))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, patience))
        task_id += 1


def run(patience=30, until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    # Counts of finished, reneged and balked orders, and the mean wait, at the end
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, patience))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def outcomes(patience: float) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns what happened to the orders, and the mean wait."""
    readings = run(patience).stats.readings()
    name = "Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.{}".format
    return {
        outcome: readings.get(name(outcome), 0)
        for outcome in ("finished", "reneged", "balked", "wait_mean")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for patience, label in ((30, "30 s"), (3600, "none")):
        result = outcomes(patience)
        print(
            f"patience {label:>4}: {result['finished']} packed, "
            f"{result['reneged']} reneged, {result['balked']} balked, "
            f"mean wait {result['wait_mean']:5.2f} s"
        )

Add Reneging and Balking shows the same two decisions in a shop example, with ties and how to check that every order is accounted for.

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text:
A quarter of the shop's orders are now express: the customer paid for speed. With one packer and an order every 1.67 seconds on average (36 a minute), an order waits about 5 seconds on average. This page asks: can express orders jump the queue? And what does that cost the others?

  • Decision: whether the packer serves express orders first or every order in order of arrival.
  • Measures: the mean wait of express orders and of regular orders.
  • Runs: two runs of the hour, one for each queue order, each with the seed 42, then runs at two lower arrival rates.
  • Assumptions: both kinds of order arrive at random at steady rates, and every order takes the same time to pack.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • serve a resource's queue by priority instead of in order of arrival;
  • give express orders priority over regular ones;
  • measure what priority costs the orders that wait longer.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds an express arrival, whose task has priority: 0, while regular orders keep priority: 1. It also makes the packer serve its queue by priority. The shop is the one from First Simulation, with one packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on average (27 a minute, rate: 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (9 a minute, rate: 0.15).

docs.title: Order the Queue
docs.text:
Which waiting entity a resource serves next is its queue discipline. The usual one is first in, first out (FIFO). Others are last in, first out (LIFO), and service by priority. Look at four requests that join a queue while the packer is busy, and the order each discipline serves them in:

SimPy has a PriorityResource for the priority discipline, and a PriorityStore for items. In desflow every resource has a queue: fifo (the default), lifo or priority. Under priority the lowest number goes first, and requests with the same priority are served first in, first out. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml:queue
resources:
  # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py:queue
# The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue=queue)
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:queue
# The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue=queue)

docs.title: Give Express Orders Priority
docs.text:
Each task gives its requests a priority. Express orders get 0, so they are served before any regular order that is waiting. Regular orders get 1:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml:priority
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 1
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  pack_express:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0  # served before any regular order that is waiting
    payload: {event_type: express_packed}

Here each task has a fixed number. A priority can also be an expression that reads the entity's attributes, such as priority: attr.priority, so each order gets its own. Task Flow describes attributes. A priority on a task whose resource does not have queue: priority is refused when the file loads. So to run the shop under fifo, remove queue: priority and both priority lines.

docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py:priority
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(1))
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

# Served before any regular order that is waiting
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(0))
def pack_express(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "express_packed"}

rank gives each task its priority under priority, and no priority under fifo, because a priority on a resource with another queue order is refused when the run starts. A task's priority can also be an expression, such as priority="attr.tier", or a function of the task id and the entity's attributes, such as priority=lambda task_id, attributes: attributes["tier"], so each order gets its own. The priority can come from the attributes because they exist before the order joins the queue. The payload does not exist yet.

docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:priority
# Express orders are served before any regular order that is waiting
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py:request
# Under fifo and lifo the priority is ignored
with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:

In the low-level API each request carries its priority. A resource whose queue is fifo or lifo ignores it, so the same code runs under every queue order.

Both kinds of order use the same packer, so they share one queue. The built-in statistics keep a separate mean wait for each task: Shop.stats.tasks.pack_express.wait_mean and Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. Statistics describes them.

docs.title: Starvation
docs.text:
Priority has a price. A regular order is served only when no express order is waiting, so every express order that arrives while it waits pushes it back. The price grows quickly as the shop gets busier.

Run the hour once with the seed 42 at each of three total arrival rates, with a quarter of the orders express each time. In YAML, the variables ORDERS_RATE and EXPRESS_RATE set the two rates. When they are not set, a regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds (27 a minute, 0.45) and an express order every 6.67 seconds (9 a minute, 0.15). This command runs 30 orders a minute in all (0.5 a second):

ORDERS_RATE=0.375 EXPRESS_RATE=0.125 desflow run priorities.yaml 2>&1 | grep wait_mean

ORDERS_RATE=0.4125 EXPRESS_RATE=0.1375 runs 33 a minute (0.55). The mean wait of a regular order is 2.50 seconds at 30 orders a minute, 3.98 seconds at 33 a minute and 6.94 seconds at 36 a minute (0.6). Express orders wait less than a second on average at all three rates. If express orders alone kept the packer busy, regular orders would never be served at all: they would starve.

desflow explain shows how busy the packer is at the default 36 orders a minute, without a run:

desflow explain priorities.yaml

Resources
+--------------------------------------------------------+
| resource |   λ |      μ | c |   ρ | Wq | L | status    |
|----------+-----+--------+---+-----+----+---+-----------|
| packers  | 0.6 | 0.6667 | 1 | 0.9 |  - | - | CONGESTED |
+--------------------------------------------------------+
Not estimated:
  wait at packers: a priority queue serves its tasks in a different order from first come, first served; run --verify to measure it

At utilisation 0.9 the packer is CONGESTED: orders often wait in a long queue, so the order in which it is served matters. explain gives no wait here, because its formulas assume first come, first served. The runs above measure the waits instead. In Python, context.analyze() gives the same analysis for a builder model. A low-level model has no explain, because its SimPy code makes the links between arrivals, tasks and resources as it runs, so there are none to read.

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
Can express orders jump the queue? Yes, and the regular orders pay for it. Each tab prints the mean wait of each kind of order, under fifo, then under priority:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

The fifo run is the blueprint without queue: priority and without the two priority: lines, saved as priorities_fifo.yaml, because a priority on a fifo resource is refused when the run starts.

# First come, first served: the mean wait of each kind of order
desflow run priorities_fifo.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_(order|express)\.wait_mean"' | tail -2
# Express orders first
desflow run priorities.yaml --stdout | grep -E 'pack_(order|express)\.wait_mean"' | tail -2


{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":5.315772740238626}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_express.wait_mean","value":5.844909407947519}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean","value":6.937041396955051}
{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":3600.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.pack_express.wait_mean","value":0.8410706363544268}


python priorities.py 2>/dev/null


fifo     pack_express mean wait  5.84 s
fifo     pack_order   mean wait  5.32 s
priority pack_express mean wait  0.84 s
priority pack_order   mean wait  6.94 s


python priorities_low_level.py 2>/dev/null


fifo     pack_express mean wait  5.84 s
fifo     pack_order   mean wait  5.32 s
priority pack_express mean wait  0.84 s
priority pack_order   mean wait  6.94 s

In one run of the hour with the seed 42, under priority, express orders wait 0.84 seconds on average instead of 5.84. Regular orders pay for it: 6.94 seconds instead of 5.32.

Priority does not make the packer faster, so it cannot remove waiting. It only decides who waits. Weighted by how many orders of each kind arrive, the mean wait is 0.75 × 5.32 + 0.25 × 5.84 = 5.45 seconds under fifo and 0.75 × 6.94 + 0.25 × 0.84 = 5.41 seconds under priority: almost the same total, shared out differently. Both queue orders keep the packer busy the same share of the time, 0.6 × 1.5 = 0.9 (utilisation). Every order takes the same time, so the queue holds the same number of orders on average under both, and Little's Law turns that number into the same mean wait over all orders. Resources describes how the queue orders requests. Plain SimPy's PriorityResource, which SimPy and desflow shows, serves these requests in the same order, ties included. The tests check the order in all three APIs (SimPy Compatibility).

Items can be ranked too: a priority store returns the parcel with the lowest priority first, as Stores and Containers describes. A resource's priority decides which request is served, and a store's priority decides which item is taken.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Every resource has a queue order: fifo (the default), lifo or priority. Under priority the lowest number goes first.
  • Priority does not make the packer faster. It only decides who waits, so the mean wait over all orders hardly changes.
  • The orders that lose priority pay for it, and their price grows quickly as the shop gets busier.

docs.title: Full Files
docs.text:
Full files YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/priorities.yaml
# The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones.
# Run it with: desflow run priorities.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 42

resources:
  # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 4, queue: priority}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express;
  # ORDERS_RATE and EXPRESS_RATE set other rates
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: "${ORDERS_RATE:-0.45}", spawn: pack_order}
  express: {dist: exponential, rate: "${EXPRESS_RATE:-0.15}", spawn: pack_express}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 1
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
  pack_express:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0  # served before any regular order that is waiting
    payload: {event_type: express_packed}

# The mean wait of each task at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 h}

egress:
  - type: Console

run:
  until: 1 h
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities.py
"""The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones, builder.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on
average (rate 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate 0.15). Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the mean wait of each kind of order
under each queue order at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python priorities.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, SimulationContext

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)


def shop(queue: str = "priority") -> SimulationContext:
    """The shop with the packer's queue in `queue` order."""

    def rank(value):
        # A priority counts only under the priority order, and the other orders
        # refuse one, so under fifo the tasks have none
        return value if queue == "priority" else None

    app = (
        SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
        .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
        # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express
        .add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.45)
        .add_arrival("express", dist="exponential", rate=0.15)
        .with_stats("typical", interval=3600)  # the mean wait of each task
        .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    )
    # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=4, queue=queue)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(1))
    def pack_order(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    # Served before any regular order that is waiting
    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", priority=rank(0))
    def pack_express(task_id: int):
        return {"event_type": "express_packed"}


    def loop(arrival, task):
        def generator(context: SimulationContext):
            task_id = 0
            while True:
                order = yield context.wait_for_arrival(arrival)
                context.spawn(task(task_id, entity=order))
                task_id += 1

        return generator

    app.arrival_loop("orders")(loop("orders", pack_order))
    app.arrival_loop("express")(loop("express", pack_express))
    return app


def mean_waits(queue: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns the mean wait of each task."""
    app = shop(queue)
    app.run(until="1 h")
    readings = app.env.stats.readings()
    return {
        task: readings[f"Shop.stats.tasks.{task}.wait_mean"]
        for task in ("pack_express", "pack_order")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for queue in ("fifo", "priority"):
        for task, wait in mean_waits(queue).items():
            print(f"{queue:<8} {task:<12} mean wait {wait:5.2f} s")
docs/snippets/tutorials/priorities_low_level.py
"""The Priorities tutorial: express orders go before regular ones, low-level.

One packer and 1.5 seconds of packing. A regular order arrives every 2.22 seconds on
average (rate 0.45), and an express order every 6.67 seconds (rate 0.15). Every record
is printed to the terminal, and the script prints the mean wait of each kind of order
under each queue order at the end. To see only those lines, run:
python priorities_low_level.py 2>/dev/null
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
)

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)

PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    arrival={
        # An order every 1.67 s on average in all (0.6 a second), one in four express
        "orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.45),
        "express": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.15),
    },
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=1.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=4)},
)
# Express orders are served before any regular order that is waiting
TASKS = {"orders": ("pack_order", 1), "express": ("pack_express", 0)}


def pack(env, sampler, packers, arrival, key, task_id):
    task, priority = TASKS[arrival]
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task=task, instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued(task, task_id)
    # Under fifo and lifo the priority is ignored
    with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started(task, task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        event = "express_packed" if arrival == "express" else "order_packed"
        publish({"event_type": event})
    env.stats.task_finished(task, task_id)


def order_generator(env, sampler, packers, arrival):
    config = env.registry.get_config(f"Shop.arrival.{arrival}")
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(config))
        key = f"{arrival}-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, packers, arrival, key, task_id))
        task_id += 1


def run(queue="priority", until=3600, factor=0.0):
    env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=factor)
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])
    env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=3600)  # the mean wait of each task
    # The packer serves the lowest priority first, the oldest first among equals
    packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers", queue=queue)
    sampler = Sampler(seed=42)
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, "orders"))
    env.process(order_generator(env, sampler, packers, "express"))
    try:
        env.run(until=until)
    finally:
        env.teardown()
    return env


def mean_waits(queue: str) -> dict:
    """Runs one hour and returns the mean wait of each task."""
    readings = run(queue).stats.readings()
    return {
        task: readings[f"Shop.stats.tasks.{task}.wait_mean"]
        for task in ("pack_express", "pack_order")
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for queue in ("fifo", "priority"):
        for task, wait in mean_waits(queue).items():
            print(f"{queue:<8} {task:<12} mean wait {wait:5.2f} s")

docs.title: Process Interaction
docs.text:
Packed orders now wait for a courier, who comes every 10 minutes and takes every order that is waiting. An order that waits too long goes by post instead, which costs more and takes longer. This page asks: when does a waiting order resume, and how long must it be allowed to wait so that most orders go by courier?

  • Decision: how long a packed order may wait for the courier: 5 minutes or 8.
  • Measures: the orders sent by courier and by post, and the mean wait for dispatch.
  • Runs: two runs of an 8-hour day, one for each limit, each with the seed 42, up to the moment each order leaves the shop: the courier's trip and the post are left out.
  • Assumptions: orders arrive at random, every order takes the same time to pack, and the courier is always on time.

docs.title: What You Will Learn
docs.text:
This page shows how to:

  • fire a signal from one process and wait for it in another;
  • wait for the first of a signal and a time limit;
  • measure how a limit splits the orders between two outcomes.

docs.title: What You Add
docs.text: This page adds a signal, courier_left, that the courier fires as it leaves, and a dispatch task that waits for either the signal or its limit, whichever comes first. The shop is the one from First Simulation: one packer, an order every 2 seconds on average and 1.5 seconds of packing.

docs.title: A Signal
docs.text:
So far a process has waited for time, a resource or an item. Processes can also wait for each other. In SimPy one process yields an event, and another process succeeds it, which marks the event as happened. Every process waiting for the event then resumes. desflow gives such an event a name and calls it a signal. A signal is declared once, and a task fires it when the task finishes. The signal can fire again later, and each firing wakes every process that is waiting for it at that moment:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:signal
signals:
  # Fired by the courier as it leaves with every order that waits for it
  - courier_left
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:signal
# Fired by the courier as it leaves with every order that waits for it
app.add_signal("courier_left")
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:signal
# Fired by the courier as it leaves with every order that waits for it
"courier_left": Signal(env, "courier_left"),

Signal holds one pending SimPy Event. wait() returns it. fire(value) succeeds it and puts a fresh one in its place. So a process that starts waiting after a firing waits for the next firing. SimPy and desflow describes events.

The courier arrives every 10 minutes, and its task fires the signal with its payload. Save the files from Full Files in one folder and run the commands there:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:courier
# A courier every 10 minutes
couriers: {dist: constant, value: 10 min, spawn: collect}
docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:collect
collect:
  payload: {event_type: courier_left}
  # Fires courier_left with this payload, so every waiting order resumes
  signal: courier_left
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:courier
# A courier every 10 minutes
.add_arrival("couriers", dist="constant", value=600)
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:collect
# Fires courier_left with this payload, so every waiting order resumes
@app.task(signal="courier_left")
def collect(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "courier_left"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:courier
# A courier every 10 minutes
"couriers": DistributionConfig(dist="constant", value=600),
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:collect
def collect(env, shop, key, ids):
    """Fires courier_left with the payload, so every waiting order resumes."""
    task_id = next(ids["collect"])
    payload = {"event_type": "courier_left"}
    publish(env, key, "collect", task_id, payload)
    env.stats.task_finished("collect", task_id)
    shop["courier_left"].fire(payload)
    env.stats.flow_finished("couriers")
    yield env.timeout(0)

docs.title: Wait for the First of Two
docs.text:
A packed order waits for the courier or for its limit. SimPy waits for the first of several events with a | b, an AnyOf. desflow's wait does the same with any, whose branches each have a name, here courier and limit. After the wait, wait.<branch>.done says whether that branch happened, so next can route on it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:dispatch
dispatch:
  # The courier's departure, or the limit, whichever comes first
  wait:
    any:
      courier: {signal: courier_left}
      limit: {timeout: "${LIMIT:-5 min}"}
  payload: {event_type: dispatched}
  # wait.courier.done is true when the courier came before the limit
  next:
    when: [{condition: wait.courier.done, task: by_courier}]
    default: by_post

"${LIMIT:-5 min}" reads the environment variable LIMIT, 5 minutes when it is not set, so LIMIT="8 min" desflow run process_interaction.yaml runs the longer limit.

docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:dispatch
@app.task(
    # The courier's departure, or the limit, whichever comes first
    wait={
        "any": {"courier": {"signal": "courier_left"}, "limit": {"timeout": limit}}
    },
    # wait.courier.done is true when the courier came before the limit
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "wait.courier.done", "task": "by_courier"}],
        "default": "by_post",
    },
)
def dispatch(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "dispatched"}
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction_low_level.py:dispatch
def dispatch(env, shop, key, ids):
    task_id = next(ids["dispatch"])
    publish(env, key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("dispatch", task_id)
    # The courier's departure, or the limit, whichever comes first
    courier = shop["courier_left"].wait()
    done = yield env.any_of([courier, env.timeout(shop["limit"])])
    publish(env, key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("dispatch", task_id)
    publish(env, key, "dispatch", task_id, {"event_type": "dispatched"})
    env.stats.task_finished("dispatch", task_id)
    # The courier came before the limit when its event is in the AnyOf's value
    task = "by_courier" if courier in done else "by_post"
    env.process(send(env, key, task, ids))

env.any_of([...]) is the AnyOf. Its value holds the events that happened, so courier in done is the YAML's wait.courier.done.

The task publishes queued when it starts waiting and started when the wait ends, so its wait statistics measure the time waiting for the courier:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:watch
# How many orders went each way, and the mean wait for dispatch, at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 8 h}
docs/snippets/tutorials/process_interaction.py:watch
# How many orders went each way, and the mean wait for dispatch, at the end
.with_stats("typical", interval=8 * 3600)

docs.title: What You Get and Why
docs.text:
When does a waiting order resume? It resumes when the courier leaves, if the courier leaves within the order's limit, and at the limit otherwise. Each figure here comes from one run of the 8-hour day with the seed 42. With a limit of 5 minutes, 6,952 orders go by courier and 7,020 by post. With a limit of 8 minutes, 11,005 go by courier and 2,872 by post, and the mean wait for dispatch rises from 225.3 to 288.2 seconds. How long must an order be allowed to wait? Of the two limits, 8 minutes is the one at which most orders go by courier, 79% of them. At 5 minutes, fewer than half do:

Each tab prints both runs: the orders sent by courier and by post, and the mean wait for dispatch.

desflow run process_interaction.yaml --stdout | grep -E '(by_courier|by_post)\.finished"|dispatch\.wait_mean"' | tail -3
# A limit of 8 minutes
LIMIT="8 min" desflow run process_interaction.yaml --stdout | grep -E '(by_courier|by_post)\.finished"|dispatch\.wait_mean"' | tail -3

{"stream_type":"telemetry","sim_ts":28800.0,"timestamp":"...","path_id":"Shop.stats.tasks.dispatch.wait_mean","value":288.1526479841932}

python process_interaction.py 2>/dev/null

limit 5 min: 6952 by courier, 7020 by post, mean wait  225.3 s
limit 8 min: 11005 by courier, 2872 by post, mean wait  288.2 s

python process_interaction_low_level.py 2>/dev/null

limit 5 min: 6952 by courier, 7020 by post, mean wait  225.3 s
limit 8 min: 11005 by courier, 2872 by post, mean wait  288.2 s

Orders are packed at random moments, so the time from packing to the next courier is spread evenly over the 10 minutes between couriers. A limit of 5 minutes catches the courier for half the orders, and a limit of 8 minutes for 8 in 10. The runs show these shares: 49.8% and 79.3% of the orders go by courier. Every waiting order resumes at the same firing, so the courier takes them all at once. These shares come from one run, and Replications explains how runs with other seeds would give each share an interval.

SimPy and desflow shows the plain SimPy forms. Signals and Waiting describes every kind of wait, and Wait for One or All shows ties and failures.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A signal wakes every task waiting for it at once.
  • A wait for the first of two events resumes at whichever comes first: here the courier or the limit.
  • The share of orders that catch the courier follows from the limit and the time between couriers.
