docs.title: Reserved Payload Keys
docs.text:
Some keys of a record's value belong to desflow, not to the data. They are the keys that start and end with two underscores around a name of at least one character, such as __table__ or __stream__, in an event's value or in a telemetry value that is a mapping. A sink handles them in one of two ways:

  • A sink that routes by such a key uses it and removes it. PostgresEgress writes the record to the table its __table__ names, and RedisEgress to the stream its __stream__ names.
  • Every other sink drops every such key, and logs one warning per key the first time it meets it. These sinks are KafkaEgress, the Parquet, JSON Lines and Iceberg sinks, and ConsoleEgress.

The warning names the sink and the key:

KafkaEgress drops the payload key '__table__': keys that start and end with two underscores are reserved for desflow, and only a sink that routes by one, such as PostgreSQL's __table__ or Redis's __stream__, uses it. Rename the key to keep it as data.

The record itself is not changed, so a PostgreSQL sink on the same run still finds its __table__. A sink drops the keys before its router sees the record, so a Kafka topic_router or a storage path_router cannot route by such a key. PostgresEgress and RedisEgress drop only their own routing key, so any other such key reaches their rows as data. Rename a key such as __source__ to source to keep it as data.

docs.title: What Each Sink Writes
docs.text:
Every sink receives the events and telemetry above, and a when: labels sink receives the labels instead. What each writes differs:

Sink Writes ConsoleEgress one line per record: [TEL], [EVT] or [LBL], followed by the record without stream_type. Each batch is one INFO log call, so only a batch's first line carries the logging format's prefix KafkaEgress the record as JSON, without stream_type unless include_stream_type=True; the message key is path_id for telemetry and key for an event. A label goes to event_topic with no key RedisEgress the record as JSON in one payload field, with any __stream__ key removed ParquetStorageEgress, JsonlStorageEgress, IcebergStorageEgress without a router, one flat row per event or label, with an event's value mapping unpacked into columns, and no telemetry; with a router, each record as the router leaves it PostgresEgress an event or telemetry record whose value is a mapping, written to the table its __table__ key names; the key is removed. The sink adds sim_ts and timestamp to the row, and for an event key as event_id, task and instance, or for telemetry path_id, as Egress describes. A label is written as the columns sim_ts, timestamp, path, old, new and label, the last three as JSON text

In a flat row, a finished event's columns are its task's payload only. The queued and started rows of a task carry path_id and status. Its finished row has them null unless the payload holds them. Egress describes the file sinks.

docs.title: Statistic Names
docs.text: Every name the built-in statistics publish, at each level, generated by running the statistics in the code. Statistics explains the levels and how each value is computed. Each level publishes the names of the levels before it, and the new ones listed under it. <sim_id> is the simulation's id, <name> a resource, store or container, <task> a task, and <arrival> the arrival that started a flow's entities.

docs.title: YAML Keys
docs.text:
Every key a blueprint file takes, generated from the JSON Schema that ships with desflow. YAML Blueprints explains how a file is read. Set Up Your Editor shows how to have your editor complete and check these keys as you type.

Each section below is a top-level key. A table lists the keys that an entry of it takes, and a section follows for each entry nested in it. Where a value is a number, a whole number, true or false, or one of a fixed set of names, a ${VAR} or ${VAR:-default} reference is also accepted, and a duration such as 5 min is accepted where the type says Duration.

docs.title: simulation
docs.text:
Type: mapping. Required.

The simulation section: the arguments of SimulationContext.

logical_start_time and go_live_at take now, a signed duration from now such as -1d or -10m, an ISO datetime, or a !python datetime. Both read the same now, the moment the file is validated, so -10m and now are exactly ten minutes apart. now and a time without an offset are read in timezone, an IANA name, UTC by default.

strict makes a paced step raise RuntimeError when the run is more than factor seconds behind the wall clock; it is False here and never checked at factor 0. environment is a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment the run is built on.

Key Type Default sim_id text required factor number 1.0 random_seed integer none timezone text none logical_start_time Time none go_live_at Time none warmup number or Duration none initial_time number or Duration 0.0 lag_interval number or Duration none strict boolean false environment !python reference none

docs.title: resources
docs.text:
Type: mapping of names to Resource. Optional.

A resources entry: its capacity, the order its queue is served in, whether a request of a lower priority value preempts a user, how many requests may wait, the class it is built from, and how it breaks down.

current_cap defaults to 1 and max_cap to current_cap, so {} is a resource of one unit. .inf makes a resource with no limit. type is a !python subclass of ResourceBase.

Key Type Default current_cap number none max_cap number none queue text "fifo" preempt boolean false queue_limit integer none type !python reference none breakdown Breakdown none

docs.title: Breakdown
docs.text:
A resource's breakdown: the time to each failure, the repair time, and whether the tasks being served are interrupted or finish.

Key Type Default time_to_failure Distribution required repair Distribution required work interrupt or finish "interrupt"

docs.title: containers
docs.text:
Type: mapping of names to Container. Optional.

A containers entry: its capacity, the largest level, its starting level and the class it is built from.

current_cap defaults to max_cap, and with neither the container has no limit; .inf is no limit too. max_cap defaults to current_cap. type is a !python subclass of ContainerBase.

Key Type Default current_cap number none max_cap number none level integer or number 0 type !python reference none

docs.title: stores
docs.text:
Type: mapping of names to Store. Optional.

A stores entry: how many items it holds, whether it serves by priority, the items it holds when the run starts, and the class it is built from.

current_cap defaults to max_cap, and with neither the store has no limit; .inf is no limit too. max_cap defaults to current_cap. A capacity is a whole number or .inf. items are returned in the order given; a priority store's items are [priority, item] pairs. type is a !python subclass of StoreBase, which sets its own order, so it cannot be given with priority.

Key Type Default current_cap number none max_cap number none priority boolean false items list of any value type !python reference none

docs.title: services
docs.text:
Type: mapping of names to Distribution. Optional.

A services entry: a distribution family and its parameters.

Time-valued parameters (mean, std, low, mode, high, scale, value, and an empirical's values and edges) take seconds or a duration such as 5 min; rate is a number per second.

Key Type Default dist text required rate number none mean number or Duration none std number or Duration none low number or Duration none value number or Duration none high number or Duration none mode number or Duration none shape number none scale number or Duration none values list of number or Duration none weights list of number none edges list of number or Duration none counts list of number none

An arrivals entry: a distribution, or a replay of recorded rows, the task it spawns, and the attributes each entity it starts carries.

An arrival's replay: the rows of a local file, each one arrival at its time.

path is a CSV or Parquet file, relative to the blueprint; time its column of times; unit ms, s, min or h from the start of the run, or timestamp for a date and time read from simulation.logical_start_time; fields the columns each entity carries, or all; on_invalid error or skip for a row with no valid time.

docs.text: Type: mapping. Optional.

docs.title: signals
docs.text:
Type: mapping of names to SignalSpec or list of names. Optional.

A signals entry in the mapping form: {closing: {once: true, on: [...]}}.

once makes the signal fire once, as SimPy's Event does; on lists actions run when the signal fires, as a task's on lists actions run when it ends.

Key Type Default once boolean false on list of OnEntry

docs.title: OnEntry
docs.text:
One entry of an on: list: exactly one of a fire, spawn or interrupt action, or a path with a value as a scenario step sets a registry value.

Key Type Default fire FireAction none spawn SpawnAction none interrupt InterruptAction none path text none value None none

docs.title: FireAction
docs.text:
An on: fire action: fire signal with a literal value, or with the outcome from copies from a signal or a task. urgent and after fire a one-shot signal ahead of the other events at its time, or later, as SimPy's env.schedule(event, priority, delay) does.

Key Type Default signal text required value None none from text none urgent boolean false after number or Duration none

docs.title: SpawnAction
docs.text:
A spawn: key or an on: spawn action: start task as a new entity, after an optional delay.

Key Type Default task text required after number or Duration none

docs.title: InterruptAction
docs.text:
An interrupt on a task or a scenario step: interrupt every running instance of task whose where condition holds, with cause.

Key Type Default task text required where text none cause None none

docs.title: tasks
docs.text:
Type: mapping of names to Task. Optional.

A tasks entry, built with SimulationContext.task.

payload is the value of the finished event: a mapping, or a !python function called as payload(task_id, context). id_field adds the task id to a mapping payload under that key, item_field adds the item its store get took, and attributes adds the named entity attributes. A task with a service and no resource is a timed step; one with neither, and no get, emits its payload as soon as it is spawned.

priority is a number or an expression such as attr.priority, for a resource whose queue is priority. patience is seconds, a duration such as 30 s or an expression; balk is a condition checked before the task joins the queue. resource is one resource or a list, acquired in the order listed; keep hands units to the next task. on_interrupt is resume, restart or abandon, and interrupt interrupts the running instances of a task when this one finishes. wait is what the task waits for first: a signal, a child task, a timeout or a condition, or any or all of several. signal names a signal the task fires when it finishes. fail is a condition checked after the service: when it holds the task publishes failed with fail_reason, and goes to on_fail. get and put take from and add to a store or container. next is a task name, when rules or weights. set gives the entity attribute values when the task finishes.

Key Type Default service text none resource text or list of text none payload mapping or !python reference required id_field text none item_field text none attributes list of text priority number or text none patience number or text or Duration or expression none balk text none get TransferStep none put TransferStep none next text or Next none set mapping wait SignalWait or TaskWait or TimeoutWait or ConditionWait or AnyWait or AllWait or AtLeastWait or RequestWait or GetWait or PutWait or RunningWait none signal text none fail text none fail_reason text none on_fail text none keep list of text preempt boolean true on_interrupt resume or restart or abandon "resume" on_interrupt_next text none interrupt InterruptAction none spawn SpawnAction none subscribe mapping none on list of OnEntry

docs.title: TransferStep
docs.text:
A task's get or put: one container with an amount, or one store.

amount is a number or an expression such as payload.quantity, and 1 when it is left out. priority is for a put into a priority store, lowest served first, and 0 when it is left out. Text is an expression such as attr.priority; any other value is used as written: a number, a list (which orders element by element, as a tuple does), a mapping, null, a date or a bool. filter is a condition for a store get, such as item.size == attr.size, where item.<field> reads the item offered: the get takes the oldest item that matches. wait: false makes the get or put and does not wait for it: the task goes on at once.

Key Type Default container text none store text none amount number or text 1.0 priority None 0.0 filter text none wait boolean true

Key Type Default when list of Rule default text none weights mapping of names to number none

docs.title: telemetry
docs.text:
Type: list of Telemetry. Optional.

A telemetry entry: custom readings published every interval seconds.

docs.text:

A processes entry: a generator function and extra keyword arguments.

The function is called as function(context, **kwargs) when the run starts.

Key Type Default function !python reference required kwargs mapping

docs.title: scenario
docs.text:
Type: list of ScenarioStep. Optional.

A scenario entry: at simulation time at, set path to value, publish a ground-truth record of record, or both.

at is seconds from the start of the run, or a duration such as "10 min". A step with a record publishes a ground-truth record, stream_type: label, with the path, the value before and after, and the record mapping, to the sinks with when: labels only. A step with an interrupt interrupts the running instances of a task, as a task's interrupt does.

Key Type Default at number or Duration required path text none value None none record mapping none interrupt InterruptAction none

docs.text:
Type: list of Connector. Optional.

An ingress entry: a connector type and its constructor arguments.

type is a short name such as Kafka, or a !python class for a connector from another package.

Key Type Default type short name or !python reference required config mapping

docs.text:
Type: list of EgressConnector. Optional.

An egress entry, with the per-provider options of add_egress.

when is history, live, labels or a !python function taking one record. history sends the records stamped before simulation.go_live_at, and live sends the records stamped at or after it. labels sends the ground-truth records of scenario steps with a record, and nothing else.

Key Type Default type short name or !python reference required config mapping when history or live or labels or !python reference none batch_size integer none flush_interval number none

docs.text:

docs.title: stats
docs.text:
Type: Stats or level name. Optional.

The stats section: the built-in statistics level and how often to publish.

Written as a level alone (stats: basic) or as a mapping (stats: {level: all, interval: 60}). The interval is in seconds or a duration such as 5 min.

Key Type Default level none or minimal or basic or typical or all required interval number or Duration 10.0

docs.text:
Type: mapping. Optional.

The run section.

before lists !python functions called with no arguments before the run starts, for setup such as creating topics or tables. stop ends the run before until at the next firing of a signal, {signal: name}, or when a condition first holds, {condition: ...}. drain, true or {limit: 1 h}, stops the arrivals at until and runs on until no entity is left in the model.

Key Type Default until number or Duration none before list of !python reference stop mapping of names to text none drain boolean or Drain false on_unhandled_failure stop or continue "continue"

docs.text:
A run.drain mapping: the longest a drain may run after until.

Key Type Default limit number or Duration none

docs.title: SimPy and desflow
docs.text:
desflow is built on SimPy, a Python library for discrete-event simulation. SimPy provides the event list, the clock, processes and resources, and desflow keeps all of them. This page teaches the SimPy constructs one at a time, each on the packing shop in plain SimPy with no desflow in it. A low-level desflow model is ordinary SimPy code with a few additions, which Coming from SimPy lists.

The code is plain SimPy 4.1.2, the version desflow is tested against. We confirmed each statement about a construct against SimPy's source in that version (core.py, events.py, rt.py and the resources package). Every function below runs as a script in the docs tests, and its output is the one shown.

docs.title: Environment and the Event List
docs.text:
An Environment holds the clock, env.now, and the event list. The list is ordered by time, then by priority, then by the order in which events were scheduled. Two events at one time therefore run in the order they were scheduled, unless one has the higher priority (URGENT is 0 and NORMAL is 1, and the lower number runs first). What Is DES? explains why the clock jumps from event to event, and Run Length shows how the order matters at the end of a run.

env.timeout(delay) is an event that SimPy schedules delay seconds from now, and a negative delay raises ValueError. env.step() takes the earliest event, moves the clock to its time and runs the event's callbacks. env.peek() gives the time of the next event, or infinity when none is left. env.run(until=...) calls step until the time or the event you give it. The function below schedules two timeouts in the wrong order and steps through them.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:event_list
def event_list():
    """Two events scheduled out of order are processed in time order."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    env.timeout(2.6)  # order 2 arrives
    env.timeout(1.5)  # order 1 is packed
    seen = []
    while env.peek() != math.inf:  # peek is the time of the next event
        seen.append((env.peek(), env.now))
        env.step()  # take the earliest event, move the clock to its time
    return seen, env.now

Each pair is the time of the next event and the clock before the step. The event at 2.6 was scheduled first, but the list is ordered by time, so the event at 1.5 comes first and the clock ends at 2.6.

event list: [(1.5, 0), (2.6, 1.5)], clock at 2.6

In desflow, env is a DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, which is a SimPy environment with pacing added. In the builder, env.run(until=...), env.step() and env.peek() are app.run(until=...), app.step() and app.peek(). In YAML, the end time is run.until.

docs.title: Events and Callbacks
docs.text:
An event is something that happens once. It starts pending. It becomes triggered when succeed(value) or fail(exception) is called, which schedules it. It becomes processed when the environment takes it from the list and runs its callbacks. A callback is a function that takes the event, and callbacks run in the order they were added. A process that yields an event waits on it by adding its own resume function to the callbacks, so one event can wake any number of processes. Calling succeed twice raises RuntimeError, and a failed event that nothing handles stops the run with its exception.

In the shop, several parts of the model wait for an order to be packed. Here a callback and two couriers wait on one event, and the packer triggers it at 1.5 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:events
def events():
    """An event is triggered once, and its callbacks and waiting processes run when it is processed."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packed = env.event()
    log = []
    packed.callbacks.append(
        lambda event: log.append(f"callback at {env.now}: {event.value}")
    )

    def courier(name):
        value = yield packed  # every process waiting on the event resumes with its value
        log.append(f"{name} at {env.now}: {value}")

    env.process(courier("courier 1"))
    env.process(courier("courier 2"))

    def packer():
        yield env.timeout(1.5)
        packed.succeed("order 1")  # triggers the event, which schedules it for now

    env.process(packer())
    env.run()
    return log, (packed.triggered, packed.processed, packed.ok)

The callback was added first, so it runs first, and both couriers resume at the same instant with the event's value. The last line shows the three states after the run: triggered and processed are both true, and ok is true because the event succeeded.

callback at 1.5: order 1
courier 1 at 1.5: order 1
courier 2 at 1.5: order 1
triggered, processed, ok: (True, True, True)

In desflow, a signal is an event that tasks wait for and fire, such as a restock. Signal is its low-level form, add_signal its builder form and signals: its YAML form. A failed event that nothing handles stops a SimPy run, and the low-level API keeps that. By default the builder and YAML publish a failed record and go on (on_unhandled_failure: continue). With on_unhandled_failure: stop they stop the run, as SimPy does. Failures explains both.

docs.title: Processes and Waiting for a Process
docs.text:
A process is a Python generator that SimPy runs: each yield hands SimPy an event, and the process resumes when that event is processed. env.process(generator) starts one. The process is itself an event, which triggers when the generator returns, with the return value. So a process can wait for another by yielding it, and it receives the other's return value. If the child raises an exception, the exception is raised in the parent at its yield.

The shop below takes an order every 2 seconds. Each order starts a pack process and waits for it, and pack takes 1.5 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:processes
def processes():
    """A process is a generator; yielding another process waits for it and returns its value."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    log = []

    def pack(order):
        yield env.timeout(1.5)
        return f"order {order} packed"

    def shop():
        for order in (1, 2):
            yield env.timeout(2)  # time to the next arrival
            result = yield env.process(pack(order))  # wait for the child
            log.append((env.now, result))

    env.process(shop())
    env.run()
    return log

The first order arrives at 2 and is packed at 3.5. The second arrives 2 seconds after the first was packed, at 5.5, and is packed at 7.0.

[(3.5, 'order 1 packed'), (7.0, 'order 2 packed')]

In desflow, a task is a process, and @app.task and @app.arrival_loop write the common ones. A task waits for another task with wait: {task: ...} in YAML, wait={"task": ...} or yield context.call(...) in the builder, and reads the child's last payload as its value. A process you write yourself runs through add_process, which is an extension point.

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text:
process.interrupt(cause) raises simpy.Interrupt inside the process, at the yield where it waits. The cause is any object, and the process reads it as interrupt.cause. The interrupt is scheduled as URGENT, so it takes effect before any other event at that time. A process that catches the exception may wait again, for the same event or a new one. A process that has ended, or the process itself, cannot be interrupted, and interrupt raises RuntimeError.

Here a packer is interrupted for a break at 1.0 seconds, in the middle of a 1.5 second packing. It works out how much is left, takes the break, and finishes.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:interrupts
def interrupts():
    """A packer is interrupted at 1.0 s and finds how much of the 1.5 s packing is left."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    log = []

    def packer():
        left = 1.5
        while left > 0:
            started = env.now
            try:
                yield env.timeout(left)
                left = 0
            except (
                simpy.Interrupt
            ) as interrupt:  # raised inside the process, at its yield
                left -= env.now - started
                log.append((env.now, interrupt.cause, left))
                yield env.timeout(0.5)  # the break
        log.append((env.now, "packed", 0))

    process = env.process(packer())

    def supervisor():
        yield env.timeout(1.0)
        process.interrupt("break")  # the cause is any object

    env.process(supervisor())
    env.run()
    return log

The packer is interrupted at 1.0 with 0.5 seconds left, rests for 0.5, and finishes the rest at 2.0.

[(1.0, 'break', 0.5), (2.0, 'packed', 0)]

In desflow, on_interrupt: resume, restart or abandon on a task chooses what happens to the work in progress. This code does what resume does. interrupt: sends an interrupt. Interruptions uses all three.

docs.title: Waiting for One or All
docs.text:
a | b is an event that triggers when the first of a and b is processed, and a & b is one that triggers when both are. They are the AnyOf and AllOf classes, and env.any_of(events) and env.all_of(events) build them from a list. The value is a ConditionValue. It holds the events that had been processed when the condition is processed, so event in result tells you which ones, and result.todict() gives their values.

A courier below waits for an order to be packed or for 1 second to pass, whichever is first. Then it waits for the packing and for another 3 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:conditions
def conditions():
    """`|` waits for the first of several events, `&` for all of them."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    log = []

    def courier():
        packed = env.timeout(2.0, value="packed")
        limit = env.timeout(1.0, value="limit")
        first = yield packed | limit  # AnyOf: holds every event processed so far
        log.append((env.now, packed in first, limit in first))
        both = yield packed & env.timeout(3.0)  # AllOf: waits for both
        log.append((env.now, len(both.todict())))

    env.process(courier())
    env.run()
    return log

At 1.0 the limit was processed and the packing was not, so the courier stopped waiting. The second wait ends at 4.0, when the timeout created at 1.0 triggers, and both events are in its value.

[(1.0, False, True), (4.0, 2)]

In desflow, wait: {any: ...} and wait: {all: ...} in YAML and wait={"any": ...} in the builder wait on named branches of signals, tasks and timeouts. Wait for One or All shows ties and failures.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
A Resource(env, capacity) has capacity units, one by default. request() returns an event that triggers when a unit is free, and requests are served in the order they arrive. Used in a with block, a request is released when the block ends, and a request still waiting at that point is cancelled. count is the units in use, users the granted requests and queue the waiting ones.

Three orders arrive at 0 and the shop has one packer. Each waits for the one before it.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:resource
def resource():
    """Three orders at 0 s and one packer: each waits in the queue for the one before."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packers = simpy.Resource(env, capacity=1)
    log = []

    def order(name):
        with packers.request() as request:  # leaving the block releases the packer
            yield request
            log.append((name, env.now))
            yield env.timeout(1.5)

    for name in "ABC":
        env.process(order(name))
    env.run()
    return log

[('A', 0), ('B', 1.5), ('C', 3.0)]

PriorityResource takes a priority with each request: the lowest number is served first, and requests with the same priority are served in arrival order. In the shop below, the packer is busy with an order at 0. A standard order arrives at 0.5 and an express order at 1.0, and the express order is served first.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:priority
def priority():
    """The packer is busy at 0 s; a lower priority number is served first, ties in arrival order."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packers = simpy.PriorityResource(env, capacity=1)
    log = []

    def order(name, priority, arrives):
        yield env.timeout(arrives)
        with packers.request(priority=priority) as request:
            yield request
            log.append((name, env.now))
            yield env.timeout(1.5)

    env.process(order("first", priority=1, arrives=0))
    env.process(order("standard", priority=1, arrives=0.5))
    env.process(order("express", priority=0, arrives=1.0))
    env.run()
    return log

[('first', 0), ('express', 1.5), ('standard', 3.0)]

PreemptiveResource adds preemption: a request whose priority number is lower than a current user's, made with preempt=True (the default), takes that user's unit. The user is interrupted, and interrupt.cause is a Preempted object with by, usage_since and resource. The preempted process does not get the unit back, so it must request again if it wants to continue. Below, an express order arrives at 1.0 and interrupts a standard order that has used the packer since 0.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:preemptive
def preemptive():
    """An express order takes the packer from a standard one, which is interrupted."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    packers = simpy.PreemptiveResource(env, capacity=1)
    log = []

    def standard():
        with packers.request(priority=1) as request:
            yield request
            try:
                yield env.timeout(1.5)
                log.append(("standard packed", env.now))
            except simpy.Interrupt as interrupt:
                cause = interrupt.cause  # a Preempted object
                log.append(("standard preempted", env.now, cause.usage_since))

    def express():
        yield env.timeout(1.0)
        with packers.request(priority=0) as request:  # preempt=True is the default
            yield request
            yield env.timeout(1.0)
            log.append(("express packed", env.now))

    env.process(standard())
    env.process(express())
    env.run()
    return log

[('standard preempted', 1.0, 0), ('express packed', 2.0)]

In desflow, DynamicResource is all three: queue: fifo is Resource, queue: priority is PriorityResource, and preempt: true with it is PreemptiveResource. It also follows a capacity in the registry. Resources and Priority and Preemption explain them.

docs.title: Containers and Stores
docs.text:
A Container(env, capacity, init) holds a quantity, such as boxes on a shelf. put(amount) waits while there is no room, and get(amount) waits until enough is held. level is the quantity held now. Waiting requests are served in order, so a large get at the head holds back smaller ones behind it. Here the packer needs 3 boxes while the shelf holds 2, so it waits for a delivery of 5 at 4 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:container
def container():
    """A shelf holds a quantity of boxes: a get for 3 waits until a put makes them available."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    shelf = simpy.Container(env, capacity=10, init=2)
    log = []

    def packer():
        yield shelf.get(3)
        log.append(("took 3 boxes", env.now, shelf.level))

    def delivery():
        yield env.timeout(4)
        yield shelf.put(5)  # the waiting get is served as the boxes arrive

    env.process(packer())
    env.process(delivery())
    env.run()
    return log

The get is served as the delivery arrives, and the shelf then holds 4 of the 7 boxes.

[('took 3 boxes', 4, 4)]

A Store holds distinct items rather than a quantity. put(item) waits while it is full, and get() waits while it is empty and returns the oldest item. A FilterStore lets get take a function that picks the first item it accepts. A PriorityStore returns the smallest item first, and PriorityItem(priority, item) wraps items that cannot be compared. The three below hold the shop's parcels, which differ in size and in urgency.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:stores
def stores():
    """A store holds distinct items; the filtered and priority kinds change which one a get returns."""
    env = simpy.Environment()
    parcels = simpy.Store(env)
    by_size = simpy.FilterStore(env)
    by_urgency = simpy.PriorityStore(env)
    got = {}

    def run():
        for name, size in (("p1", "small"), ("p2", "large"), ("p3", "small")):
            yield parcels.put(name)
            yield by_size.put((name, size))
        yield by_urgency.put(simpy.PriorityItem(2, "standard"))
        yield by_urgency.put(simpy.PriorityItem(1, "express"))
        got["store"] = yield parcels.get()  # first in, first out
        got["filter"] = yield by_size.get(
            lambda item: item[1] == "large"
        )  # first match
        got["priority"] = (yield by_urgency.get()).item  # smallest priority first

    env.process(run())
    env.run()
    return got

{'store': 'p1', 'filter': ('p2', 'large'), 'priority': 'express'}

In desflow, a task's put and get use these: put: {container: stock, amount: 2} for a container, and get: {store: parcels, filter: ...} for a filtered store. A store declared with priority: true is a PriorityStore. Stores and Containers and Stock explain them.

docs.title: Real-time Environment
docs.text:
RealtimeEnvironment(factor) is an environment whose clock follows the wall clock: a step of one time unit takes factor seconds of real time. With strict=True, the default, step raises RuntimeError when the model falls behind the wall clock by more than factor seconds. Set strict=False to let it catch up instead. sync() restarts the real-time reference from the present. Here one simulated second takes 0.2 seconds of real time, so a run of 2 simulated seconds takes at least 0.4 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/simpy_and_desflow.py:realtime
def realtime():
    """One simulated second takes 0.2 wall-clock seconds; the run lasts at least 2 x 0.2 s."""
    env = simpy.rt.RealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.2)  # strict=True is the default

    def packer():
        yield env.timeout(2)

    env.process(packer())
    started = time.monotonic()
    env.run()
    return env.now, time.monotonic() - started

clock 2, wall clock at least 0.4 s: True

SimPy's factor is fixed when the environment is made. desflow's environment can switch to real time during a run, as the Clock and pacing row of What desflow Changes shows. Time and Pacing explains it.

docs.title: Coming from SimPy
docs.text:
If you have written a SimPy model, you already know most of what desflow needs. This page takes a plain SimPy model in the structure most tutorials teach and shows where each part goes in desflow. Nothing you know is lost: a desflow model is SimPy underneath. SimPy and desflow teaches each SimPy construct, and the last two sections of this page list what desflow changes and the form each construct takes in desflow.

The structure comes from the open book HSMA: the little book of DES by Dan Chalk, Sammi Rosser and Amy Heather, which teaches SimPy to health-service modellers. Its chapter The Recommended Structure for DES Models splits a model into four classes: a class of global parameters, an entity class, a model class and a trial class. We read that chapter and the chapter on running large numbers of scenarios. The book's text is under CC BY-NC-SA, so none of it is copied here. The code below is our own. It models the packing shop and follows the same four-class shape.

docs.title: Four Classes
docs.text:
Look at the table for where each class goes. The sections after it explain each row on the shop.

In a plain SimPy model In desflow The global parameters class: arrival and packing times, packers, run length, number of runs Arguments of add_arrival, add_service and add_resource, which are registry paths a run can change, and add_variable (variables in YAML) for values of your own The entity class: the thing that moves through the model, with the facts it remembers An entity with attributes, and statistics that record each order's wait and service for you The model class: one run, with its environment, resources, arrival generator and journey generator SimulationContext, with @app.arrival_loop for the arrival generator and @app.task for the journey The trial class: a loop that builds a model for each run number and collects one result per run replicate, which runs a model n times from spawned seeds and gives an interval over the runs

docs.title: Global Parameters
docs.text:
In the usual structure one class holds every number the model reads, and the model reads them as G.packers. This is the shop's.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:globals
class G:
    """Global parameters: read as G.packers, never instantiated."""

    arrival_mean = 2.0  # seconds between orders
    pack_time = 1.5  # seconds to pack an order
    packers = 1
    run_length = 3600  # seconds
    runs = 10

In desflow these numbers are arguments of the parts they describe:

In G In the builder arrival_mean = 2.0 add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5), an order every 2 seconds on average pack_time = 1.5 add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5) packers = 1 add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=10) run_length and runs arguments of run and replicate, because they belong to the run and not to the system a number of your own, such as a conveyor speed add_variable, or variables in YAML

Each value is stored in a registry under a path such as Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, and the model reads the registry whenever it needs the value. So a value can change while the run goes on, from a scenario or a connector, which a value in G cannot. Each change is checked before it is applied. Live Parameters lists the paths.

docs.title: Entity Class
docs.text:
The entity class is what travels through the model. Here an order carries its number and the time it waited.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:entity
class Order:
    """The entity: what travels through the model, and what it remembers."""

    def __init__(self, order_id):
        self.id = order_id
        self.wait = 0.0

In desflow an arrival creates an entity for you, and attributes on the arrival give it starting facts, such as attributes={"express": 0}. A task can read them to decide what comes next, and change them when it finishes. You do not store the wait yourself: the task records when the order queued, started and finished, and the statistics report the mean wait and service time of every task. Task Flow explains attributes.

docs.title: Model Class
docs.text:
The model class is one run. Its constructor makes the environment and the resources, one generator creates the arriving orders, and another is the journey of one order.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:model
class Model:
    """One run of the shop."""

    def __init__(self, run_number):
        self.env = simpy.Environment()
        self.random = random.Random(run_number)
        self.packers = simpy.Resource(self.env, capacity=G.packers)
        self.waits = []

    def generate_orders(self):
        order_id = 0
        while True:
            order_id += 1
            self.env.process(self.pack_order(Order(order_id)))
            yield self.env.timeout(self.random.expovariate(1 / G.arrival_mean))

    def pack_order(self, order):
        arrived = self.env.now
        with self.packers.request() as request:
            yield request
            order.wait = self.env.now - arrived
            self.waits.append(order.wait)
            yield self.env.timeout(G.pack_time)

    def run(self):
        self.env.process(self.generate_orders())
        self.env.run(until=G.run_length)
        return statistics.mean(self.waits)

In desflow, SimulationContext is that class. It makes the environment, which is a SimPy environment, and the resources from the add_ calls, so the constructor of your own class has nothing left to do. The arrival generator is @app.arrival_loop, and the journey is @app.task, which requests the resource, waits, holds it for the service time and releases it. The task replaces the pack_order method above, and it also publishes queued, started and a finished event as records. If the journey is more than one task, a task names the next one, as A Flow of Tasks shows.

docs.title: Trial Class
docs.text:
The trial class runs the model once for each run number and keeps one result per run. Here the run number also seeds the random generator, so each run differs and each can be repeated.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:trial
class Trial:
    """The runs of one design: one result for each."""

    def run_trial(self):
        return [Model(run).run() for run in range(G.runs)]

In desflow this loop is replicate. It runs the model n times, gives each run its own seed spawned from one seed, reads the statistics at the end of each run, and returns the interval for each measure you name. You do not write the loop, the seeding or the interval. Replications explains the options, and Trusting Results uses it on the shop.

docs.title: Shop in desflow
docs.text:
Here is the whole shop in desflow, with the trial loop beside it. The model is one function that builds a context, and the loop is one call.

docs/snippets/pages/coming_from_simpy.py:desflow
def shop() -> SimulationContext:
    """The same shop: parameters in the registry, the entity and the statistics built in."""
    app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0)
    app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=1 / 2.0)
    app.add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=1.5)
    app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=1, max_cap=10)
    app.with_stats("typical", interval=3600)

    @app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers")
    def pack_order(task_id):
        return {"event_type": "order_packed"}

    @app.arrival_loop("orders")
    def order_generator(context):
        task_id = 0
        while True:
            order = yield context.wait_for_arrival("orders")
            context.spawn(pack_order(task_id, entity=order))
            task_id += 1

    return app


def trial():
    """The trial loop is `replicate`: one seed for each run, and an interval over the runs."""
    result = replicate(
        shop, 10, seed=42, until=3600, measures=["tasks.pack_order.wait_mean"]
    )
    return result.summary[0]

Four parts of the desflow version have no line in the SimPy one:

  • context.wait_for_arrival("orders") waits for the gap to the next order, drawn from the orders arrival's distribution, and returns the new order as an entity.
  • entity=order hands that order to the task, so every record of the task carries the order's key, such as orders-1. Without it the task starts an entity of its own.
  • The dictionary the task returns is the payload of its finished event, so {"event_type": "order_packed"} is published as a record.
  • with_stats("typical", interval=3600) switches on the built-in statistics, such as the mean wait that replicate reads, and publishes them every hour of simulated time.

Builder API describes each call, and Statistics lists the levels.

Both versions run 10 times for one hour from an empty shop, so the two answers estimate the same thing. Each line of the output below gives the mean wait over the 10 runs and the half-width of its 95% interval. The two versions use different random numbers, so the values differ, but the check in the script asserts that they agree within their intervals. This shop is not the busy hour of the tutorials: it has one packer and an order every 2 seconds on average, so its mean wait differs from theirs.

plain SimPy: mean wait 2.30 ± 0.20 s over 10 runs
desflow:     mean wait 2.45 ± 0.27 s over 10 runs

What you take with you is the SimPy you wrote. A model can still be a SimPy generator inside desflow, through the Low-level API, and it keeps the SimPy constructs it uses. What you leave behind is the code around it: the parameters class, the result bookkeeping and the trial loop. What you gain is records, pacing, live parameters and the checks on Output Analysis.

docs.title: What desflow Changes
docs.text:
desflow keeps SimPy's event list, clock, processes and resources. It changes the six things in the table:

Part In SimPy In desflow Clock and pacing Environment runs without waiting; RealtimeEnvironment(factor, strict=True) follows the wall clock and raises RuntimeError when the model falls behind one class, DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, does both: factor=0 runs without waiting, go_live_at switches to real time partway through a run (SimPy's factor cannot change once set), logical_start_time gives every record a date and time, and falling behind is reported as telemetry; strict raises RuntimeError as SimPy's does, with the defaults that Strict Pacing gives; sync() is SimPy's, and resume_pacing() also moves the simulation anchor after a pause; advance(until) runs a started run in segments, as repeated env.run(until=...) does Processes generators started with env.process the same, and the builder adds @app.task, @app.arrival_loop, @app.telemetry_loop and add_process, which write the common ones for you Random times none built in: a model calls random or NumPy itself ten named distributions with checked parameters, drawn by a Sampler from the current values each time; each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, made from the run's seed and its registry path Resources Resource, Container and Store keep the capacity they were created with: it has no setter, so assigning a new one raises AttributeError (SimPy 4.1). Resource serves requests in the order they arrive, and PriorityResource by priority DynamicResource, DynamicContainer and DynamicStore follow a capacity in the registry, and a resource that shrinks lets busy units finish. A resource serves its queue fifo, lifo or by priority, equal priorities first in, first out. run() builds the stores and containers a model declares, and tasks put to and get from them Parameters Python variables, changed only by the model's own code a registry of named paths, changed by connectors, scenarios or processes, with each change checked Output whatever the model prints or logs events and telemetry with a fixed shape, written to Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, files or Iceberg on background threads

docs.title: Each Construct in desflow
docs.text:
Each row names a construct, its form in the three ways of writing a model, and the group of conformance checks on SimPy Compatibility that runs it in plain SimPy and in all three forms and compares the results. A construct with no native form in one of the three is marked as a difference there, with the reason.

SimPy construct YAML Builder Low-level Checks Environment: run, step, peek, now run.until app.run(until=), app.step(), app.peek() env.run(until=) Run Control timeout a task with service and no resource @app.task(service_id=...) yield env.timeout(delay) Events and Processes Events and callbacks signals:, on: add_signal, on= Signal, event.callbacks.append(fn) Events and Processes Processes and waiting for one wait: {task: ...} wait={"task": ...}, context.call(...) yield env.process(child()) Events and Processes Interrupts interrupt:, on_interrupt context.interrupt(...), on_interrupt= process.interrupt(cause) Interrupts and Preemption AnyOf, AllOf wait: {any: ...}, wait: {all: ...} wait={"any": ...}, wait={"all": ...} yield a \| b, yield a & b Wait for One or All Resource, PriorityResource resource: packers, queue: priority @app.task(resource_id=...), add_resource(queue=...) with packers.request() as req: yield req Resources PreemptiveResource preempt: true, queue: priority add_resource(queue="priority", preempt=True) DynamicResource(queue="priority", preempt=True) Interrupts and Preemption Container put and get with container and amount put={"container": ...}, get={"container": ...} yield stock.put(2), yield stock.get(1) Stores and Containers Store, FilterStore, PriorityStore put and get with store, filter, priority: true put={"store": ...}, get={"store": ..., "filter": ...} parcels.get(filter=...) Stores and Containers RealtimeEnvironment simulation.factor, simulation.strict SimulationContext(factor=, strict=) DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=) Run Control

!python and add_process run SimPy code you write yourself. They are extension points, so a construct that has no native form in YAML or the builder is not covered by using them. User Guide pages that build on SimPy name the parts they use in their How It Works section, starting with Arrivals and Services.

docs.title: SimPy Compatibility
docs.text:
Every modelling feature of SimPy 4.1.2, 98 in all, with its status in YAML, the builder and the low-level API: native and checked, or a difference kept by design. A native feature is checked by conformance tests that run a plain SimPy 4.1.2 model and the same model in all three APIs, and compare event times, outcomes and balances. The page is generated from tests/conformance/register.yaml, the list the tests read, so a feature is native here only with its checks.

96 features are native and checked in all three APIs, and 2 are differences kept by design. The last section lists those and one more, strict pacing at factor 0, which is not a SimPy feature of its own.

The low-level API is SimPy with a few classes added, so most SimPy features work in it; SimPy and desflow explains how the two fit together. Where desflow differs from SimPy on purpose, the difference is listed under the table.

The sections are numbered by kind. C1 to C7 are SimPy's core operations, such as events, conditions, interrupts, resources and stores. S1 to S3 are support features desflow builds from those operations: breakdowns, schedules and replay. SimPy has no single call for them, so their conformance tests compare with the same behaviour written in plain SimPy.

Section Operations native in all three APIs C1: Events and Processes 18 C2: Wait for One or All 6 C3: Interrupts and Preemption 4 C4: Resources 12 C5: Stores and Containers 20 C6: Run Control 21 C7: Patience 2 S1: Breakdowns 1 S2: Schedules 1 S3: Replay 1 Differences Kept by Design 3 differences

Under each feature, API details opens to show its SimPy construct, its form in YAML, the builder and the low-level API, and the conformance tests that check it.

docs.title: C1: Events and Processes
docs.text:
Waiting a fixed time, events a task can fire or fail, including an event that triggers once, and processes: starting one, with or without a delay and without waiting for it, waiting for it, reading its return value or its failure, being told when it ends, running actions when an event happens, and inspecting an event, a process or the running process while it runs.

Timed wait: A task waits a set or sampled time, such as the time packing takes, before it goes on.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.Timeout
  • YAML: a task with service and no resource
  • Builder: @app.task(service_id=...) with no resource
  • Low-level: yield env.timeout(delay)
  • Checks: test_c1_timed_wait
  • Taught on: Timed wait

Signal event success and value: One task fires a named signal with a value, and every task waiting for it wakes up and reads that value.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.Event.succeed(value)
  • YAML: signals: [restocked], signal: restocked on the firing task and wait: {signal: restocked}
  • Builder: add_signal, @app.task(signal=...), wait={"signal": ...}, or context.signal(name).fire(value)
  • Low-level: Signal(env, name): yield signal.wait() and signal.fire(value)
  • Checks: test_c1_signal_event_success_and_value
  • Taught on: Signal event success and value

Signal event failure: A signal fires as a failure, and every task waiting for it fails with the same reason.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.Event.fail(exception)
  • YAML: a failing task with signal; its waiters fail with its reason
  • Builder: the same, or context.signal(name).fail(reason)
  • Low-level: signal.fail(reason); waiters receive SignalFailed
  • Checks: test_c1_signal_event_failure
  • Taught on: Signal event failure

Start and wait for a process: A task starts a child flow, such as an inspection, and waits until it ends.

API details
  • SimPy: yield env.process(child())
  • YAML: wait: {task: inspect}
  • Builder: wait={"task": "inspect"}, or yield context.call("inspect")
  • Low-level: yield env.process(child())
  • Checks: test_c1_start_and_wait_for_a_process
  • Taught on: Start and wait for a process

Process return value: The task that waited for a child flow reads what the child produced.

API details
  • SimPy: a process's return value
  • YAML: wait.inspect.value.<field>, the last payload of the child flow
  • Builder: the same, or the value of context.call(...)
  • Low-level: value = yield env.process(child())
  • Checks: test_c1_process_return_value
  • Taught on: Process return value

Process failure: A failure inside a child flow reaches the task waiting for it, which can handle it or fail in turn.

API details
  • SimPy: an exception raised in a process reaches the process that waits for it
  • YAML: fail, fail_reason and on_fail on a task; a failure no on_fail handles fails the waiting task
  • Builder: the same, and a function that raises fails its task
  • Low-level: try: yield env.process(child()) and except
  • Checks: test_c1_process_failure, test_c1_process_failure_handled_by_on_fail
  • Difference: By default (on_unhandled_failure is continue) a failure no task waits for ends the entity's flow in YAML and the builder, publishes failed and is counted, and the run goes on; under on_unhandled_failure of stop it stops the run, matching SimPy and the low-level API, where an exception nobody handles stops the run.
  • Taught on: Process failure

Event inspection: A condition reads whether a signal has fired, whether it succeeded, and its value.

API details
  • SimPy: Event.triggered, .processed, .ok, .value
  • YAML: signal.<name>.count, .ok and .value in a condition
  • Builder: context.signal(name).wait() and its SimPy attributes, or the signal's count, ok and value
  • Low-level: the same attributes of SimPy events and Signal
  • Checks: test_c1_event_inspection
  • Taught on: Event inspection

Process inspection: After a wait, a task reads whether a child flow has finished, whether it succeeded, and its value.

API details
  • SimPy: Process.is_alive, .triggered, .ok, .value
  • YAML: wait.<branch>.done, .ok and .value after the wait
  • Builder: the process context.spawn and context.call return
  • Low-level: the process env.process returns
  • Checks: test_c1_process_inspection
  • Taught on: Process inspection

Wait for a shared condition: A task waits until a condition on the model's state holds, such as stock reaching 5.

API details
  • SimPy: a loop over a fresh "changed" event
  • YAML: wait: {condition: level.stock >= 5}
  • Builder: wait={"condition": "level.stock >= 5"}
  • Low-level: env.watch_changes(check), or a SimPy loop
  • Checks: test_c1_wait_for_a_shared_condition
  • Taught on: Wait for a shared condition

The running process: process.name, process.instance and process.target read the running task's name, instance id and what it waits on now, as SimPy's active process, its name and its target.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment.active_process, events.Process.name, events.Process.target
  • YAML: process.name, process.instance, process.target in a condition
  • Builder: context.env.active_process; .name and .target on a process
  • Low-level: env.active_process.name, .target
  • Checks: test_c1_active_process, test_c1_process_name, test_c1_process_target
  • Taught on: The running process

Start a flow without waiting for it: A task spawns another task as a new entity, keyed <task>-n, with the spawning entity's key in attr.parent, and goes on without waiting.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment.process
  • YAML: spawn: {task: courier}
  • Builder: @app.task(spawn=...), or context.spawn(generator)
  • Low-level: env.process(generator)
  • Checks: test_c1_start_a_process_without_waiting_for_it, test_c1_start_a_process_without_waiting_for_it_drain
  • Taught on: Start a flow without waiting for it

One-shot event: A one-shot signal fires once, as SimPy's Event does: it does not re-arm, a wait after the firing resumes at once, and a second firing is refused.

API details
  • SimPy: events.Event
  • YAML: signals: {closing: {once: true}}
  • Builder: add_signal(name, once=True)
  • Low-level: Signal(env, name, once=True)
  • Checks: test_c1_one_shot_event, test_c1_one_shot_event_fired_twice
  • Taught on: One-shot event

Actions when an event happens: An on: list runs actions when a signal fires or a task ends: fire a signal (copying another outcome), spawn a flow, interrupt a task, or set a value, as SimPy's callbacks, trigger and defused failures.

API details
  • SimPy: events.Event.callbacks, events.Event.trigger, events.Event.defused
  • YAML: on: [{fire: {signal, from}}, {spawn: {...}}] on a task or a signal
  • Builder: on=[...] on @app.task and add_signal
  • Low-level: event.callbacks.append(fn), ev.trigger(other), ev.defused = True
  • Checks: test_c1_callbacks, test_c1_trigger_from_another_event, test_c1_trigger_from_another_event_failure, test_c1_defused_failure, test_c1_drain_waits_for_an_on_spawn, test_c1_drain_waits_for_a_signals_on_actions, test_c1_drain_waits_through_a_balking_next, test_c1_drain_waits_through_a_chain_of_firings, test_c1_process_signal_fire_is_not_counted, test_c1_on_spawn_upstream_after_each_end, test_c1_losing_child_flow_fire_after_left_is_not_counted
  • Taught on: Actions when an event happens

Failure nobody handles: Under on_unhandled_failure: stop a task, child flow or one-shot signal failure nobody handles stops the run, as SimPy; under continue, the default, it is defused and the run goes on.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment.run
  • YAML: run: {on_unhandled_failure: stop}
  • Builder: run(on_unhandled_failure=...) or start(on_unhandled_failure=...)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure=...)
  • Checks: test_c1_failure_nobody_handles, test_c1_failure_nobody_handles_continue, test_c1_failure_nobody_handles_losing_child_flow
  • Taught on: Failure nobody handles

Timeout value: A wait timeout carries a value the waiter receives, as SimPy's env.timeout(delay, value).

API details
  • SimPy: events.Timeout(delay, value)
  • YAML: wait: {timeout: {after: 40 s, value: ...}}
  • Builder: the same mapping in wait=
  • Low-level: env.timeout(delay, value)
  • Checks: test_c1_timeout_value
  • Taught on: Timeout value

Wait for a process already running: A running wait holds until the running instances of a task on the waiter's entity, and the entities it spawned, all end, as SimPy's yield process.

API details
  • SimPy: yield process
  • YAML: wait: {running: {task: charge, where: ...}}
  • Builder: the same in wait=, or yield a process from context.spawn or call
  • Low-level: yield process
  • Checks: test_c1_wait_for_a_process_already_running, test_c1_wait_for_a_process_that_has_ended, test_c1_wait_for_a_process_that_fails, test_c1_wait_for_a_process_two_instances, test_c1_wait_for_a_process_that_hands_on, test_c1_wait_for_a_process_that_it_spawned, test_c1_wait_for_a_process_abandoned_in_a_child_flow
  • Taught on: Wait for a process already running

Start a process after a delay: A spawn with after starts the new entity that long after the task finishes, as SimPy's start_delayed.

API details
  • SimPy: util.start_delayed
  • YAML: spawn: {task: courier, after: 3 s}
  • Builder: spawn={"task", "after"}, or context.spawn(generator, delay=3)
  • Low-level: simpy.util.start_delayed(env, generator, 3)
  • Checks: test_c1_start_a_process_after_a_delay, test_c1_start_a_process_after_a_delay_at_a_tie, test_c1_start_a_process_after_a_delay_refuses_zero
  • Taught on: Start a process after a delay

Be told when an event happens: A subscribe interrupts the task when an event happens, carrying the event and its value, as SimPy's subscribe_at.

API details
  • SimPy: util.subscribe_at
  • YAML: subscribe: {task: charger}
  • Builder: @app.task(subscribe=...), or context.subscribe(event)
  • Low-level: simpy.util.subscribe_at(event)
  • Checks: test_c1_be_told_when_an_event_happens, test_c1_be_told_when_an_event_happens_after_the_subscriber_ended
  • Taught on: Be told when an event happens

docs.title: C2: Wait for One or All
docs.text:
Waiting for the first of several events, or for all of them, as SimPy's AnyOf and AllOf conditions do, with conditions inside conditions, a rule of your own such as at least some of them (SimPy's condition with a count rule), a condition over no events, and a request, put or get as one of the events.

Wait for one event: A task waits for whichever of several events happens first, such as a delivery or a time limit.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.AnyOf, a | b
  • YAML: wait: {any: {stock: {signal: restocked}, limit: {timeout: 3}}}
  • Builder: wait={"any": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield a | b
  • Checks: test_c2_wait_for_one_event, test_c2_wait_for_one_event_two_at_one_instant
  • Difference: Losing signal, timeout and condition branches are dropped when the wait ends; losing child flows keep running, as SimPy leaves processes running.
  • Taught on: Wait for one event

Wait for all events: A task waits until every one of several events has happened.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.AllOf, a & b
  • YAML: wait: {all: {...}}
  • Builder: wait={"all": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield a & b
  • Checks: test_c2_wait_for_all_events, test_c2_wait_for_all_events_with_a_failing_branch
  • Taught on: Wait for all events

Nested and mixed conditions: A wait nests any, all and at_least to any depth, as SimPy's conditions combine with & and |.

API details
  • SimPy: events.Condition, &, |
  • YAML: wait: {all: {look: {task: inspect}, either: {any: {...}}}}
  • Builder: wait={"all": {...}} with nested groups
  • Low-level: yield (a | b) & c
  • Checks: test_c2_nested_and_mixed_conditions, test_c2_nested_condition_with_a_failing_member, test_c2_nested_condition_holds_leaves_of_an_untriggered_group
  • Taught on: Nested and mixed conditions

A condition with a custom rule: at_least: n of several branches is done when n of them are, as SimPy's Condition with a count rule.

API details
  • SimPy: events.Condition(env, evaluate, events)
  • YAML: wait: {at_least: 2, of: {...}}
  • Builder: wait={"at_least": 2, "of": {...}}
  • Low-level: Condition(env, lambda evs, c: c >= 2, [...])
  • Checks: test_c2_condition_with_a_custom_rule, test_c2_custom_rule_equal_to_the_branch_count_is_all, test_c2_custom_rule_two_at_one_instant, test_c2_custom_rule_with_a_failing_member
  • Taught on: A condition with a custom rule

A condition over no events: An empty any or all is accepted and succeeds at once with an empty value, as SimPy does.

API details
  • SimPy: events.AnyOf(env, []), events.AllOf(env, [])
  • YAML: wait: {any: {}} or wait: {all: {}}
  • Builder: wait={"any": {}}
  • Low-level: env.any_of([])
  • Checks: test_c2_condition_over_no_events
  • Taught on: A condition over no events

Request, put or get as a wait branch: A request, get or put can be a wait branch; a won request holds its unit through the service, and a losing branch is cancelled.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.base.Put, resources.base.Get, events.AnyOf
  • YAML: wait: {request: packers}, wait: {get: {store: parcels}}, wait: {put: {store: ...}}
  • Builder: wait={"request": "packers"} or wait={"get": {...}}
  • Low-level: yield req | env.timeout(3)
  • Checks: test_c2_request_as_a_wait_branch, test_c2_get_as_a_wait_branch, test_c2_put_as_a_wait_branch, test_c2_a_wait_branch_on_a_missing_store_is_refused, test_c2_wait_branch_in_a_failing_all, test_c2_request_wait_branch_cleaned_on_renege, test_c2_request_wait_branch_reused_across_a_resume_in_the_wait, test_c2_request_wait_branch_kept_across_a_resume_in_the_service, test_c2_abandon_during_a_wait_with_a_won_branch_is_clean, test_c2_request_wait_branch_reacquired_after_a_preemption, test_c2_a_get_granted_as_the_wait_ends_counts_as_won, test_c2_a_request_granted_as_the_wait_ends_counts_as_won
  • Difference: A request, get or put branch that is granted at the instant its wait ends, after the condition was processed, counts as won, and the task keeps its unit or item, as SimPy's if not event.triggered: event.cancel() leaves a granted event. A SimPy waiter that ignores such an event, because it is not in the condition's value, keeps the unit held or loses the item.
  • Taught on: Request, put or get as a wait branch

docs.title: C3: Interrupts and Preemption
docs.text:
Interrupting a task while it waits or while it is in service, and a higher-priority request taking a resource unit from a lower-priority user, with the cause that tells the user who took it and since when it held it.

Interrupt while waiting: Another task or a scenario step interrupts a task while it is still in a queue.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.Process.interrupt while the process waits for a request
  • YAML: interrupt: {task: waiter} on a scenario step or a task; on_interrupt on the task
  • Builder: context.interrupt("waiter"); @app.task(on_interrupt=...)
  • Low-level: process.interrupt(cause), caught as simpy.Interrupt
  • Checks: test_c3_interrupt_while_waiting
  • Taught on: Interrupt while waiting

Interrupt during service: A task is interrupted while it holds a resource, and resumes, restarts or abandons its work.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.Process.interrupt while the process holds a unit
  • YAML: on_interrupt: resume, restart or abandon
  • Builder: @app.task(on_interrupt=...)
  • Low-level: except simpy.Interrupt, then request again
  • Checks: test_c3_interrupt_during_service, test_c3_two_interrupts_at_one_instant
  • Taught on: Interrupt during service

Priority preemption: A more urgent request takes a resource unit away from a less urgent user, who is interrupted.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.PreemptiveResource
  • YAML: resources.<name>.preempt: true with queue: priority; preempt: false on a task opts out
  • Builder: add_resource(..., queue="priority", preempt=True)
  • Low-level: DynamicResource(..., queue="priority", preempt=True) and request(priority, preempt=True)
  • Checks: test_c3_priority_preemption, test_c3_priority_preemption_equal_priorities, test_c3_two_preemptions_at_one_instant, test_c3_preemption_tie_between_users, test_c3_priority_preemption_low_level
  • Taught on: Priority preemption

Preemption cause: A task that loses its unit to a more urgent request learns who took it and since when it had held the unit.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.Preempted
  • YAML: preempted_by and usage_since in the preempted record
  • Builder: the same record
  • Low-level: simpy.Interrupt.cause is a Preempted with by, usage_since and resource
  • Checks: test_c3_preemption_cause, test_c3_preemption_record_shape, test_c3_preemption_by_a_process_that_is_not_a_task
  • Taught on: Preemption cause

docs.title: C4: Resources
docs.text:
Requesting and releasing resource units, in order of arrival or of priority, with a default capacity of one unit or no limit, reading the count, users and queue, limiting the waiting line, cancelling a request before or after its grant, holding several resources at once, and resources of your own classes.

Ordinary request and release: A task takes one unit of a resource, such as a packer, waits in line if none is free, and gives it back when done.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.Resource
  • YAML: resource: packers on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(resource_id="packers")
  • Low-level: with packers.request() as req: yield req
  • Checks: test_c4_ordinary_request_and_release
  • Taught on: Ordinary request and release

Priority request: Waiting requests are served by priority, the lowest number first, instead of in order of arrival.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.PriorityResource
  • YAML: queue: priority on the resource and priority on a task
  • Builder: add_resource(..., queue="priority") and @app.task(priority=...)
  • Low-level: DynamicResource(..., queue="priority") and request(priority=...)
  • Checks: test_c4_priority_resource_request, test_c4_priority_request_with_mixed_preempt_flags
  • Difference: Equal priorities are served first in, first out, as in SimPy; desflow also offers fifo and lifo queues, under which a request's priority is ignored.
  • Taught on: Priority request

Cancel before a grant: A task leaves the queue before it is served, so it never takes a unit.

API details
  • SimPy: Request.cancel() before it is granted
  • YAML: patience, or an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: request.cancel(), or leaving the with block
  • Checks: test_c4_cancel_before_a_grant, test_c4_renege_ahead_of_a_preempting_request
  • Taught on: Cancel before a grant

Cancel after a grant: A task that already holds a unit stops early and gives the unit back.

API details
  • SimPy: Request.cancel() after the grant releases nothing; Resource.release(request) does
  • YAML: an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon gives the unit back
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: request.cancel() releases nothing; resource.release(request)
  • Checks: test_c4_cancel_after_a_grant
  • Taught on: Cancel after a grant

Hold several resources: A task holds more than one resource at once, taken in a fixed order, and can hand them to the next task.

API details
  • SimPy: nested requests, each held while the next is awaited
  • YAML: resource: [picker, bench], acquired in that order; keep hands units to the next task
  • Builder: @app.task(resource_id=["picker", "bench"], keep=[...])
  • Low-level: nested with blocks
  • Checks: test_c4_hold_several_resources, test_c4_keep_hands_a_unit_to_the_next_task
  • Difference: A model whose tasks acquire two resources in opposite orders is refused when it is built, because those tasks could each wait for ever; SimPy runs it. Two requests under one all wait are made together, so another task that acquires the two one after the other, in either order, is refused too.
  • Taught on: Hold several resources

Resource capacity defaults to 1: A resource declared with no capacity has one unit, and a capacity of infinity makes a resource that never queues.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.Resource(capacity=1)
  • YAML: resources: {packers: {}}; current_cap: .inf for no limit
  • Builder: add_resource("packers"); current_cap=float("inf") for no limit
  • Low-level: DynamicResource(env, sim_id, name) with no registry entry; CapacityConfig(current_cap=float("inf")) for no limit
  • Checks: test_c4_default_capacity, test_c4_resource_with_no_capacity_limit
  • Taught on: Resource capacity defaults to 1

Resource count, queue and users: A condition or a script reads how many units are held, which requests hold them and which wait.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.Resource.count, .queue and .users
  • YAML: users.<resource> and queue.<resource> in a condition, such as balk: queue.machine >= 2
  • Builder: get_resource(name).count, .users and .queue
  • Low-level: resource.count, .users and .queue, the list of waiting requests in service order
  • Checks: test_c4_count_queue_and_users, test_c4_users_and_queue_in_conditions, test_c4_a_condition_is_not_checked_between_the_steps_of_one_call
  • Difference: A lifo queue serves the newest request first, which SimPy has no counterpart of.
  • Taught on: Resource count, queue and users

Release event and its request: Giving a unit back returns an event that holds the request it released and is triggered at once.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.Release.request
  • YAML: implicit: a task releases its units when it ends
  • Builder: get_resource(name).release(request)
  • Low-level: resource.release(request) returns a DynamicRelease whose request is the request
  • Checks: test_c4_release_event
  • Taught on: Release event and its request

Usage since: A granted request records the time its unit was granted, and a preemption report carries it.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.Request.usage_since
  • YAML: usage_since in the preempted record
  • Builder: get_resource(name).users[i].usage_since, and the preempted record
  • Low-level: request.usage_since
  • Checks: test_c4_usage_since
  • Taught on: Usage since

Default request priority 0: A request that names no priority has priority 0, so it ties with priority 0 and goes ahead of priority 1.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.PriorityRequest(priority=0)
  • YAML: a task with no priority on a queue: priority resource
  • Builder: @app.task(resource_id=...) with no priority
  • Low-level: request() with no priority
  • Checks: test_c4_default_priority
  • Taught on: Default request priority 0

A waiting line with a limit: A resource refuses a request when a set number of requests wait already, and a task that is refused balks.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.SortedQueue(maxlen)
  • YAML: queue_limit: 5 on the resource
  • Builder: add_resource(..., queue_limit=5)
  • Low-level: DynamicResource(..., queue_limit=5): request() raises RuntimeError
  • Checks: test_c7_queue_limit, test_c7_queue_limit_on_the_second_of_two_resources, test_c7_queue_limit_fails_a_request_wait_branch, test_c7_a_type_with_its_own_queue_limit_balks_before_queued, test_c7_a_preempted_request_wait_balks_when_the_line_is_full, test_c7_a_interrupt_while_a_preempted_request_waits_leaves_no_stale_request, test_c7_a_preempted_request_wait_reneges_when_the_patience_runs_out, test_c7_a_preempted_request_wait_targets_the_resource_while_it_asks_again
  • Difference: A task whose first resource refuses it publishes balked with the resource before it publishes queued, which SimPy has no counterpart of.
  • Taught on: A waiting line with a limit

Subclass a resource to change its rules: A resource of your own class changes when a request is granted, how the waiting line is kept and what a request or release does.

API details
  • SimPy: resources.resource.PreemptiveResource
  • YAML: type: !python module.Class on the resource
  • Builder: add_resource(..., type=Class)
  • Low-level: a subclass of ResourceBase, built as Class(env, sim_id, name)
  • Checks: test_c4_custom_resource_type
  • Taught on: Subclass a resource to change its rules

docs.title: C5: Stores and Containers
docs.text:
Putting and getting items in a store and amounts in a container, with capacity limits or none, priority items of any orderable type, filtered gets, cancelled puts and gets, the order of puts and gets at the same time, reading what a store holds and its put and get queues, a put or get that the task does not wait for, and stores and containers of your own classes.

Bounded store put: A task adds an item to a store, and waits when the store is full.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.Store.put
  • YAML: put: {store: parcels} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(put={"store": "parcels"})
  • Low-level: yield parcels.put(item)
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_store_put
  • Taught on: Bounded store put

Bounded store get: A task takes an item from a store, and waits when the store is empty.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.Store.get
  • YAML: get: {store: parcels} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
  • Low-level: item = yield parcels.get()
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_store_get
  • Taught on: Bounded store get

Equal-time puts and gets: When items are added and taken at the same moment, waiting tasks are served in the same order as in SimPy.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.Store, one waiting get granted per trigger
  • YAML: get: {store: parcels} and put: {store: parcels} on tasks
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
  • Low-level: yield parcels.put(item), item = yield parcels.get()
  • Checks: test_c5_equal_time_puts_and_gets_follow_simpy_store, test_c5_equal_time_puts_and_gets_as_tasks
  • Difference: While a get with a filter waits, the store grants as SimPy's FilterStore does, looking at every waiting get each time. Once no filtered get waits, it grants one get per trigger, as Store does, where FilterStore goes on to the next. With filtered and unfiltered gets in one queue, gets at the same instant can therefore resume in a different order than in FilterStore; each get receives the same item.
  • Taught on: Equal-time puts and gets

Bounded quantity put: A task adds an amount to a container, such as boxes to stock, and waits when there is no room.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.container.Container.put
  • YAML: put: {container: stock, amount: 2} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(put={"container": "stock", "amount": 2})
  • Low-level: yield stock.put(2)
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_quantity_put
  • Taught on: Bounded quantity put

Bounded quantity get: A task takes an amount from a container, and waits until there is enough.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.container.Container.get
  • YAML: get: {container: stock, amount: 1} on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"container": "stock", "amount": 1})
  • Low-level: yield stock.get(1)
  • Checks: test_c5_bounded_quantity_get
  • Taught on: Bounded quantity get

Priority item storage: Items in a store come out by priority, the lowest number first, instead of in the order they went in.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.PriorityStore
  • YAML: stores.<name>.priority: true and a put with priority
  • Builder: add_store(..., priority=True) and put={"store": ..., "priority": ...}
  • Low-level: DynamicStore(..., priority=True) with simpy.PriorityItem
  • Checks: test_c5_priority_item_storage
  • Difference: Equal priorities come out in put order in the builder and YAML, which add a rising put order to the priority; a plain SimPy PriorityStore gives no order among equal priorities.
  • Taught on: Priority item storage

Filtered retrieval: A task takes only an item that matches a condition, such as a parcel for its own area.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.store.FilterStore.get(filter)
  • YAML: get: {store: parcels, filter: item.area == attr.area}
  • Builder: get={"store": "parcels", "filter": ...}, a condition or a function of the item
  • Low-level: parcels.get(filter=lambda item: ...)
  • Checks: test_c5_filtered_retrieval
  • Difference: A priority store takes no filter, because SimPy has no store that both ranks and filters.
  • Taught on: Filtered retrieval

Cancel store get: A task stops waiting for an item, for example when its patience runs out.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Get.cancel()
  • YAML: patience on a task with a store get
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"store": ...}, patience=...)
  • Low-level: get.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_store_get
  • Taught on: Cancel store get

Cancel quantity get: A task stops waiting for an amount from a container.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Get.cancel()
  • YAML: patience on a task with a container get
  • Builder: @app.task(get={"container": ...}, patience=...)
  • Low-level: get.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_quantity_get
  • Taught on: Cancel quantity get

Cancel store put: A task stops waiting for room in a full store.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.base.Put.cancel()
  • YAML: an interrupt with on_interrupt: abandon while the put waits
  • Builder: the same
  • Low-level: put.cancel()
  • Checks: test_c5_cancel_store_put
  • Taught on: Cancel store put
