docs.title: C6: Run Control
docs.text:
Starting a run from a given time and state, reading the current time, ending it at a time, at an event or on a condition and reading the value that ended it, draining it, running it in segments, stepping through it one model event at a time, scheduling an event with a priority, an environment class of your own, and the pace of the run: its factor, strict pacing and syncing with the wall clock.

Initial time: The simulation clock starts at a given time instead of 0.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment(initial_time=...)
  • YAML: simulation.initial_time
  • Builder: SimulationContext(..., initial_time=100)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(initial_time=100)
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_time
  • Taught on: Initial time

Initial resources: Each resource starts with a given number of units.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.resources.resource.Resource(capacity=...)
  • YAML: resources.<name>.current_cap
  • Builder: add_resource(name, current_cap=2, ...)
  • Low-level: CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, ...)
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_resources
  • Taught on: Initial resources

Initial inventory: Containers start with a given level, and stores with given items.

API details
  • SimPy: Container(init=...); items in a Store
  • YAML: containers.<name>.level and stores.<name>.items
  • Builder: add_container(..., level=6) and add_store(..., items=[...])
  • Low-level: ContainerConfig(level=6) and DynamicStore(..., items=[...])
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_inventory
  • Taught on: Initial inventory

Initial entity state: Each arriving entity, such as an order, starts with given attributes.

API details
  • SimPy: the attributes a process starts with
  • YAML: arrivals.<name>.attributes
  • Builder: add_arrival(..., attributes={...})
  • Low-level: the values a process is started with
  • Checks: test_c6_initial_entity_state
  • Taught on: Initial entity state

Stop at a time: The run ends at a given simulation time.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.run(until=...)
  • YAML: run.until
  • Builder: app.run(until=...)
  • Low-level: env.run(until=...)
  • Checks: test_c6_stop_at_a_time
  • Taught on: Stop at a time

Stop at an event: The run ends when a given event happens, such as a closing signal, even before its end time.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.run(until=event)
  • YAML: run.stop: {signal: closing} beside run.until
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop={"signal": "closing"}), a signal's name, or a function returning an event
  • Low-level: env.run(until=event)
  • Checks: test_c6_stop_at_an_event, test_c6_stop_at_an_event_at_the_same_instant_as_until
  • Difference: When the stop and until fall at the same time, until ends the run first, as SimPy's own until would.
  • Taught on: Stop at an event

Explicit stop condition: The run ends as soon as a condition on the model's state holds.

API details
  • SimPy: env.run(until=event) with a process that succeeds the event when the condition holds
  • YAML: run.stop: {condition: level.stock >= 5}
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop={"condition": "..."})
  • Low-level: env.watch_changes(check) and env.run(until=event)
  • Checks: test_c6_explicit_stop_condition
  • Taught on: Explicit stop condition

Stop arrivals and drain: New arrivals stop, and the run goes on until everything already in the model has finished.

API details
  • SimPy: interrupt the source, then env.run(until=env.all_of(entities))
  • YAML: run.drain: true or {limit: 1 h}; desflow run --drain
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., drain=True), or context.stop_arrivals()
  • Low-level: source.interrupt(), then env.run(until=env.all_of(processes))
  • Checks: test_c6_stop_arrivals_and_drain, test_c6_stop_arrivals_and_drain_with_a_limit
  • Taught on: Stop arrivals and drain

Step one event: The run advances one event at a time, so a script can watch each step.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.step()
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .step()
  • Builder: app.start(), app.step(), app.close()
  • Low-level: env.step()
  • Checks: test_c6_step_one_event
  • Difference: A blueprint has no stepping key; its context, from from_yaml, steps as a builder context does.
  • Taught on: Step one event

Inspect next event time: A script reads when the next event will happen without running it.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.peek()
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .peek()
  • Builder: app.peek()
  • Low-level: env.peek()
  • Checks: test_c6_inspect_next_event_time
  • Taught on: Inspect next event time

A step processes only the model's events: step() and peek() count the events of the model, not the statistics, flush, lag, ingress and watcher processes that desflow adds, so a script steps a model as it would step it in SimPy. Inside run() the step processes every event, desflow's own included, because SimPy's run() calls step() for each event in its one queue.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.step() and peek()
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).start(), then .step() and .peek(); processes: entries are model events
  • Builder: app.start(), app.step(), app.peek(); add_process functions are model events
  • Low-level: env.step() and env.peek()
  • Checks: test_c6_step_counts_model_events, test_c6_step_counts_model_events_in_arrival_models, test_c6_step_with_a_live_capacity_change, test_c6_step_with_a_task_that_has_on_actions, test_c6_run_after_steps_gives_the_records_of_one_run, test_c6_finish_after_steps_that_reached_until, test_c6_finish_after_steps_to_until_with_statistics_due_there
  • Difference: With only desflow's own events left, step() raises EmptySchedule and peek() gives infinity, but the queue is not empty: run() and finish() still process those events.
  • Taught on: A step processes only the model's events

Value of a run stopped at an event: run() returns the value of the event that stopped it, and raises the exception of a stop that failed. The value is a signal's payload for a stop on a signal, True for a condition, and the event's own value for a function. It is None when until or a drain ends the run, or when until and the stop are due together. A stop on a signal that fails raises SignalFailed, the exception the failed event carries, which is what SimPy raises. The run closes before it returns, so the sinks have their records.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.core.Environment.run(until=event)
  • YAML: SimulationContext.from_yaml(path).run() returns the value; desflow run exits with an error when the stop failed
  • Builder: app.run(until=..., stop=...) and app.finish() return the value
  • Low-level: env.run(until=event)
  • Checks: test_c6_run_value
  • Taught on: Value of a run stopped at an event

Current time: t is the simulation clock, read in a condition or an expression, so a route or a balk can depend on the current time.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment.now
  • YAML: t in a condition, such as t < 110
  • Builder: context.env.now
  • Low-level: env.now
  • Checks: test_c6_current_time
  • Taught on: Current time

Schedule an event with a priority: env.schedule(event, priority, delay) puts an event on the queue, and a fire action with after fires a one-shot signal that many seconds from now, as SimPy's schedule does.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment.schedule
  • YAML: fire: {signal: s, after: 5 s} on a signal with once: true
  • Builder: {"fire": {"signal": "s", "after": 5}} in on=, or context.env.schedule(event, priority, delay)
  • Low-level: env.schedule(event, priority, delay)
  • Checks: test_c6_schedule_with_a_priority, test_c6_fire_with_after_is_not_counted_by_a_drain, test_c6_fire_twice_with_after_is_refused_as_a_one_shot_signal
  • Taught on: Schedule an event with a priority

Urgent and normal event priorities: An urgent event is processed before the normal events at its time, as SimPy's URGENT and NORMAL order them; urgent: true on a fire action resumes the waiters first.

API details
  • SimPy: events.URGENT, events.NORMAL
  • YAML: fire: {signal: s, urgent: true} on a signal with once: true
  • Builder: {"fire": {"signal": "s", "urgent": True}} in on=, or simpy.events.URGENT in context.env.schedule
  • Low-level: env.schedule(event, URGENT)
  • Checks: test_c6_fire_with_urgent_and_after, test_c6_fire_urgent_and_after_need_a_one_shot_signal
  • Taught on: Urgent and normal event priorities

Run in segments: advance(until) runs a started run to a time or an event and returns with the run open, and finish() runs on to the end; the segments give the records of one run. resume_pacing() paces again from now after a pause.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment.run, called again
  • YAML: app = SimulationContext.from_yaml(file), then app.start(), app.advance(until) and app.finish()
  • Builder: app.start(), app.advance(until), app.finish()
  • Low-level: env.run(until=), called again; env.resume_pacing()
  • Checks: test_c6_stopped_and_resumed_run, test_c6_run_in_segments, test_c6_advance_refuses_what_a_segment_cannot_do, test_c6_segments_with_stop_and_drain_give_the_records_of_one_run, test_c6_step_after_a_segment_processes_its_event_as_simpy_does, test_c6_advance_to_an_event_and_on, test_c6_finish_raises_a_failed_stop_that_advance_reached, test_c6_advance_to_events_adds_one_internal_event_to_the_queue, test_c6_resume_pacing
  • Taught on: Run in segments

Subclass the environment: A subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment runs the model, so an override of step or schedule sees its events, as a subclass of SimPy's Environment does.

API details
  • SimPy: core.Environment
  • YAML: simulation: {environment: !python module.Env}
  • Builder: SimulationContext(environment=Env)
  • Low-level: class Env(DynamicRealtimeEnvironment)
  • Checks: test_c6_environment_subclass, test_c6_environment_subclass_in_run
  • Taught on: Subclass the environment

Real-time factor: factor sets how many real seconds one simulation second takes, so a run paces to the wall clock, as SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment does.

API details
  • SimPy: rt.RealtimeEnvironment(factor)
  • YAML: simulation.factor
  • Builder: SimulationContext(factor=)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=)
  • Checks: test_c6_real_time_factor
  • Taught on: Real-time factor

Strict pacing: With strict on, a paced step more than factor seconds behind the wall clock raises RuntimeError, as SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment(strict=True) does.

API details
  • SimPy: rt.RealtimeEnvironment.strict
  • YAML: simulation.strict
  • Builder: SimulationContext(strict=True)
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(strict=True)
  • Checks: test_c6_strict_raises_when_behind
  • Taught on: Strict pacing

Strict by default: The low-level environment is strict unless strict=False is passed, as SimPy's is; the builder and YAML default to off.

API details
  • SimPy: rt.RealtimeEnvironment(strict=True)
  • YAML: simulation.strict, default false
  • Builder: SimulationContext(strict=False), the default
  • Low-level: DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(strict=True), the default
  • Checks: test_c6_strict_default
  • Taught on: Strict by default

API details
  • SimPy: rt.RealtimeEnvironment.sync
  • YAML: not in YAML: app.start(), then app.env.sync()
  • Builder: app.env.sync() after start(); the builder syncs once when it builds a strict run
  • Low-level: env.sync()
  • Checks: test_c6_sync_catches_up
  • Taught on: Sync with the wall clock

docs.title: C7: Patience
docs.text:
Customers who give up after waiting too long (reneging) and customers who do not join a queue that is too long (balking).

Reneging: A customer leaves the queue after waiting longer than their patience.

API details
  • SimPy: simpy.events.AnyOf of a request and a timeout
  • YAML: patience: 3 min on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(..., patience=180)
  • Low-level: yield req | env.timeout(patience), then req.triggered
  • Checks: test_c7_reneging, test_c7_reneging_tie_timeout_scheduled_after_the_grant, test_c7_reneging_tie_timeout_scheduled_before_the_grant, test_c7_reneged_request_leaves_the_queue, test_c7_patience_pauses_during_service
  • Taught on: Reneging

Balking: A customer does not join the queue at all when a condition holds, such as the queue being too long.

API details

  • YAML: balk: <condition> on a task
  • Builder: @app.task(..., balk="...")
  • Low-level: an if before the request
  • Checks: test_c7_balking, test_c7_a_balk_condition_gives_back_the_unit_the_task_kept
  • Taught on: Balking

docs.title: S1: Breakdowns
docs.text:
A resource that fails and is repaired, with the work it interrupts.

Breakdown and repair: A resource fails from time to time and is repaired, interrupting the work it was doing.

API details

  • Builder: add_breakdown(resource, time_to_failure={...}, repair={...}, work=...)

docs.title: S2: Schedules
docs.text:
A schedule of times at which an arrival rate or a capacity changes during a run.

Finite schedules: Arrival rates or capacities change at set times during the run.

API details

  • YAML: scenario steps with at, path and value
  • Builder: add_scenario(steps) or add_step(at, path=..., value=...)

docs.title: S3: Replay
docs.text:
Arrivals read from a local CSV or Parquet file instead of drawn at random.

Local replay: Arrivals come from rows in a local CSV or Parquet file instead of a random distribution.

API details

  • YAML: arrivals.<name>.replay: {path, time, unit, fields, on_invalid}
  • Builder: add_arrival_replay(name, source, ...)

docs.title: Differences Kept by Design
docs.text:
• A run with no until (SimPy: core.Environment.run() returns when no event is left): A run with a sink or an ingress connector and no until runs for ever, because a live run has no end: the connectors keep events coming. Give it an until, with a drain when it should finish its work, or a stop that is sure to happen, or stop it with Ctrl+C.
  • Strict pacing at factor 0 (SimPy: rt.RealtimeEnvironment(factor=0, strict=True) raises once the wall clock has moved): An unpaced run has no wall clock to fall behind, so SimPy's check at factor 0 would raise on the first step of every unpaced script. strict is never checked at factor 0, also before go_live_at. Taught on: Strict pacing at factor 0
  • Capacity 0 (SimPy: resources.resource.Resource(capacity=0) raises ValueError, and so do Store and Container): A resource, store or container may have a capacity of 0, at the start or later, because its capacity changes during a run: a shift with no packers, a shelf that is closed. At capacity 0 a resource grants no request, and a store or container accepts no put, until the capacity rises; a get still takes what a store or container holds.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text:
Each page here describes one part of desflow: what it does, how to use it, how it works and its limits. Read a page when you need that part. To learn DES and desflow from the start, follow Learn instead. To do one task step by step, see How-To.

Group What it covers How desflow Works how desflow is built: the parts that run a model, why each exists, and how a run moves through them Writing a Model the three ways to write a model: a YAML blueprint, the builder API and the low-level API Model Parts the parts a model is made of: arrivals and services, input fitting, task flow, and stores and containers Tasks and Processes tasks, processes, the signals they wait for, and failures Resources priority and preemption, tasks that hold several resources, and resource types of your own Time and Pacing the simulation clock, pacing against real time, and how long a run lasts Results what a run measures, replications and experiments Live Runs and Connectors parameters that change during a run, and the connectors that bring changes in and write records out

docs.title: How desflow Works
docs.text:
This page shows how desflow is built: the parts that run a model, why each one exists, and how a run moves through them. Each part links to the How It Works section that describes it in full.

One run moves through the parts of desflow like this:

Whichever way a model is written, it builds one environment, and one run goes the same way from there. The environment holds the registry of live parameters, and the resources, stores and containers follow it. Ingress connectors change registry values from outside while the run goes on. Tasks and other processes publish events and telemetry, and egress connectors write them to their sinks on a thread of their own. The registry paths, the records, the batching and the connectors are therefore the same in all three ways.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
desflow is built on SimPy. SimPy gives the event list, the clock, processes and resources, and desflow keeps all of them. SimPy leaves seven things to the modeller, and each part of desflow adds one of them:

Left to the modeller in SimPy What desflow adds Read the code around a model: a class of parameters, an entity class, a model class and a loop over runs three ways to write a model, each built on the one below Writing a Model one pacing factor, fixed when the environment is made one environment that runs history at full speed, then switches to the wall clock Time and Pacing random times, drawn by the model's own code ten checked distributions, each with a random stream of its own Arrivals and Services parameters that only the model's code changes a registry of named paths that connectors, scenarios and processes change during a run Live Parameters resources, stores and containers that keep the capacity they were made with resources, stores and containers whose capacity follows the registry Resources output, which the model prints or logs records of a fixed shape, written to sinks on a thread of their own Egress statistics, replications and confidence intervals statistics collected during the run, replications, experiments and explain Built-in Statistics

Coming from SimPy compares each change with plain SimPy.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Each part is described in full on its own page. In short:

Part How it works Read Writing a model A YAML blueprint, the builder and the low-level API are layers. from_yaml makes the calls a builder script makes, and the builder's run() makes the calls a low-level script writes by hand. YAML Blueprints, What run() Does Environment and pacing DynamicRealtimeEnvironment is SimPy's RealtimeEnvironment with the registry, the connectors and the statistics added. It runs without waiting at factor: 0 and switches to real time at go_live_at. Time and Pacing Random times A distribution reads its parameters at each draw, so a change applies from the next draw. Each one has its own random stream, made from the run's seed and its registry path. Arrivals and Services Registry Every live value sits under a dot path, such as Shop.service.packing.mean. Each update is checked before it is stored. Live Parameters Resources, stores and containers Each waits on its registry path, so its capacity changes during a run. A resource that shrinks lets its busy units finish. Resources, Stores and Containers Threads, ingress and egress The SimPy thread runs the model. Ingress and egress run their connectors on threads of their own, each on an asyncio loop, so a network wait never stalls a simulation step. Time and Pacing, which also compares these queues with the waiting lines of the model; Ingress, Egress, Write a Connector Measurement and explain One statistics object collects readings while the run goes on. Replications run the model again for each seed and give a Student t interval. desflow explain applies queueing formulas to the model before anything runs. Built-in Statistics, Replications, Experiments, Command Line

docs.title: Live Runs and Connectors
docs.text: A live run changes its parameters while it runs and sends its records out as they happen. Three parts do this: the registry of live parameters, the ingress connectors that change them, and the egress connectors that write the records. The diagram on How desflow Works shows how one run moves through them.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• Live parameters sit in the registry under named paths, such as Shop.service.packing.mean. An arrival rate, a number of packers or a stock level can change while the run goes on.
  • Ingress connectors bring those changes in from outside: from Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL or a local schedule.
  • Egress connectors, or sinks, write the records the run publishes: to the console, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet or JSON Lines files, or Iceberg tables.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Live Parameters: how to name a parameter, the ways to change it, how to record what a change was for, and what happens to a value once it arrives.
  • Ingress: each source connector, the message it reads, how to send one, and when the change lands.
  • Egress: each sink, how to choose which records each one gets, and how records travel from a task to a sink.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
• A value that should change during a run is a registry path, such as a service's mean or a resource's capacity, or a variables entry for any other value.
  • An ingress entry in YAML, or add_ingress in the builder, adds a source of changes.
  • An egress entry, or add_egress, adds a sink.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: A run uses three threads. The ingress thread runs the sources, which put (path, value) pairs on a queue, and the ingress monitor applies them to the registry every 0.1 simulation seconds. The SimPy thread runs the model, which follows each change: a distribution uses the new parameters from its next draw, and a resource changes its capacity. Each record the model publishes goes into a buffer for each sink, and the egress thread writes full batches to the sinks. Time and Pacing shows the threads and the queues between them.

docs.title: Egress, Batching and Delivery
docs.text: An egress connector, or sink, writes the records a run publishes: to the console, Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL, Parquet or JSON Lines files, or Iceberg tables. This page shows each sink, how to choose which records each one gets, and how records travel from a task to a sink.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A run publishes three kinds of record: events, such as a task's queued, started and finished; telemetry, single values such as the statistics; and labels, the ground-truth records of what a scenario changed. Every sink receives every event and every telemetry record, unless its when says otherwise. Labels go only to sinks that ask for them. Records and Telemetry shows each record's shape and what each sink writes.

The tutorial page Streaming Out teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Each sink is listed under egress in a blueprint with its type and config, attached with add_egress in the builder, or passed to env.setup_egress in the low-level API. In the builder snippets below, app is a SimulationContext.

In a blueprint, type is one of the short names below, or a !python class from another package. A connector's module is imported only when a blueprint names it, so a blueprint that uses Kafka does not need the PostgreSQL driver. Parquet and JSON Lines are the exception: they import PyArrow when they start writing. A missing package stops the load with its line and the pip install command.

type Class Extra Console ConsoleEgress none Kafka KafkaEgress kafka Parquet ParquetStorageEgress parquet Jsonl JsonlStorageEgress parquet Iceberg IcebergStorageEgress iceberg Postgres PostgresEgress postgres Redis RedisEgress redis

config holds the constructor's arguments. Settings that Python takes as objects are plain values there: a Parquet or JSON Lines filesystem is a mapping with type: local, s3, gcs or azure, and an Iceberg catalog is a mapping of PyIceberg properties. A Postgres tables mapping creates its tables when the run starts. Each table maps to columns, a mapping of column name to SQL type, and an optional primary_key. An ISO time string bound for a timestamp or date column of Iceberg or PostgreSQL is converted before the write. YAML Keys lists the keys of an egress entry.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
ConsoleEgress has two formats. The default, log, logs each batch at INFO level with one call, one line per record:

  • Each line starts with [EVT] for an event, [TEL] for telemetry or [LBL] for a label.
  • desflow run prints these lines as they are. Its other log lines start with the time, level and logger name.
  • In a script, the logging format the script sets, such as the time and level, starts only the first line of each batch.

One call per batch is much faster than one call per record. In the measurements on Tune Performance, a run that logged each record with its own call took about 50 percent longer in total.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:console-egress
- type: Console
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:console-egress
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress())

The low-level API passes the same ConsoleEgress() to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

With format="json", ConsoleEgress writes each record to stdout as one JSON line instead: the record as published, with its stream_type. Another program can then read the records. It writes at any log level, because the records are output, not a log. Python's logging writes to stderr by default, so the log stays apart from the records, and a pipe such as | jq .key reads only the records. In a blueprint it is type: Console with config: {format: json}. desflow run --sample and --stdout print through it in place of the file's sinks, as YAML Blueprints describes.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:console-json
# One JSON line per record on stdout, stream_type included
- type: Console
  config: {format: json}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:console-json
# One JSON line per record on stdout, stream_type included
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(format="json"))

The low-level API passes the same ConsoleEgress(format="json") to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

A consumer can check each line against the record schema: EventPayload, TelemetryPayload and LabelPayload are the Pydantic models of the three stream types, as Records and Telemetry describes:

docs/snippets/pages/record_schemas.py:validate
# The model of each stream type; a record with a missing or mistyped field raises
SCHEMAS = {"event": EventPayload, "telemetry": TelemetryPayload, "label": LabelPayload}
for line in printed.getvalue().splitlines():
    record = json.loads(line)
    SCHEMAS[record["stream_type"]].model_validate(record)

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
KafkaEgress sends events to event_topic and telemetry to telemetry_topic, keyed by the record's key or path_id. Kafka sends all records with one key to one partition, so all events of one entity stay in order. KafkaEgress creates both topics when the run starts, with one partition each, if they do not exist. With a topic_router, it creates none. Route Records to Topics sends records to other topics, and Connect to Secure Kafka connects to a cluster that uses SASL, mTLS, OAuth or AWS IAM.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:kafka-egress
- type: Kafka
  config:
    bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
    event_topic: sim-events
    telemetry_topic: sim-telemetry
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:kafka-egress
app.add_egress(
    KafkaEgress(
        bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092",
        event_topic="sim-events",
        telemetry_topic="sim-telemetry",
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same KafkaEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: Parquet and JSON Lines
docs.text:
ParquetStorageEgress and JsonlStorageEgress write each batch as a file of its own, on a local disk, S3-compatible storage, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage, through PyArrow. Without a path_router, each event is one flat row in default_path, with its value mapping unpacked into columns, and telemetry is left out.

A Parquet file has a column for every key of any row in its batch, and a mapping value becomes a struct column. A later batch can change the columns:

  • A key that first appears in a later batch adds a column to the later files. A reader that combines the columns of all the files reads it as null in the earlier rows.
  • An integer column that a later batch gives a float becomes a double in the later files.
  • A nested key that first appears later is dropped, because the first batch with a mapping value fixes the keys of its struct column.

A batch that cannot be written is logged at ERROR, and the sink goes on with the next one.

File names. default_path, and any path a path_router returns, is a file name prefix, not a folder. Each batch is written as a file of its own, <stem>_<8 hex digits><extension>, in the path's folder, so output/events.parquet gives files such as output/events_1a2b3c4d.parquet. Give the extension in the path: output/events gives files with none. The folder is created on the first write.

Columns of a finished event. A task's queued and started events carry path_id and status. Its finished event's value is the task's payload only. So in a finished event's row, path_id and status are null unless the payload has them. The Parquet example adds them to its payload for that reason.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:storage-egress
# Parquet files on the local disk, output/events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
- type: Parquet
  config:
    default_path: output/events.parquet
# JSON Lines files on S3-compatible storage, here SeaweedFS from odctl; a mapping
# becomes PyArrow's S3FileSystem
- type: Jsonl
  config:
    default_path: warehouse/events.jsonl
    filesystem:
      type: s3
      access_key: user
      secret_key: password
      endpoint_override: 127.0.0.1:8333
      scheme: http
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:storage-egress
# Parquet files on the local disk, output/events_<8 hex digits>.parquet
app.add_egress(ParquetStorageEgress(default_path="output/events.parquet"))

# JSON Lines files on S3-compatible storage, here SeaweedFS from odctl
seaweedfs = fs.S3FileSystem(
    access_key="user",
    secret_key="password",
    endpoint_override="127.0.0.1:8333",
    scheme="http",
)
app.add_egress(
    JsonlStorageEgress(default_path="warehouse/events.jsonl", filesystem=seaweedfs)
)

The low-level API passes the same sinks to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

Read the files back as one table with pyarrow.dataset, which reads every file in the folder:

docs/snippets/pages/file_sink.py:read
def read_events(folder="output"):
    """Every file the sink wrote under `folder`, as one table."""
    import pyarrow.dataset as ds

    # format="json" reads the files of a JsonlStorageEgress the same way
    return ds.dataset(folder, format="parquet").to_table()

A second run adds its files beside the first run's, so reading the folder then counts both runs. Give each run a folder of its own, or clear the folder before a run.

Filesystems. filesystem is a PyArrow FileSystem object, or a mapping that desflow builds into one when the run starts. The mapping's type picks the class, and its other keys are the arguments of that class:

type PyArrow class Credentials local (the default) LocalFileSystem none s3 S3FileSystem access_key and secret_key; without them, the standard AWS settings gcs GcsFileSystem anonymous: true; or access_token with credential_token_expiration; without them, Google's default credentials azure AzureFileSystem account_name, always; with it account_key, or sas_token (pyarrow 20.0.0 or later), or client_id, client_secret and tenant_id (pyarrow 21.0.0 or later); with account_name alone, Azure's default credentials

An endpoint_override that starts with http:// or https:// also sets scheme, for s3 and gcs, unless scheme is given. azure has no endpoint_override: blob_storage_authority and blob_storage_scheme point it at an emulator such as Azurite. For gcs, credential_token_expiration is an ISO 8601 time, quoted or not, which desflow converts to UTC, and retry_time_limit is a number of seconds, because YAML has no duration type. A key whose value is empty is left out. PyArrow has AzureFileSystem from 16.0.0, the release the parquet extra requires. sas_token and the client credentials need the later releases the table names. PyPI's pyarrow wheels for Windows include it only from 24.0.0.

The same two sinks write to Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage when filesystem is a mapping. Write to Cloud Storage runs a shop against each store, from start to end:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/storage_backends.yaml:cloud
# Parquet files on Google Cloud Storage, with Google's default credentials
- type: Parquet
  config:
    default_path: my-bucket/events.parquet
    # type: gcs makes PyArrow's GcsFileSystem; without credentials it uses Google's default ones
    filesystem:
      type: gcs
# JSON Lines files on Azure Blob Storage, with Azure's default credentials
- type: Jsonl
  config:
    default_path: my-container/events.jsonl
    # type: azure makes PyArrow's AzureFileSystem; without a key it uses Azure's default credentials
    filesystem:
      type: azure
      account_name: myaccount
docs/snippets/pages/storage_backends.py:cloud
# Parquet files on Google Cloud Storage, with Google's default credentials
cloud.add_egress(
    ParquetStorageEgress(
        default_path="my-bucket/events.parquet",
        filesystem={"type": "gcs"},
    )
)
# JSON Lines files on Azure Blob Storage, with Azure's default credentials
cloud.add_egress(
    JsonlStorageEgress(
        default_path="my-container/events.jsonl",
        filesystem={"type": "azure", "account_name": "myaccount"},
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same sinks to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
RedisEgress appends each record to a Redis Stream with XADD, as one payload field holding the record as JSON. A __stream__ key in the record's value picks the stream, and is removed before writing.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:redis-egress
# XADD to the events stream, unless a record's value names another in __stream__
- type: Redis
  config:
    url: redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0
    stream_name: events
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:redis-egress
# XADD to the events stream, unless a record's value names another in __stream__
app.add_egress(
    RedisEgress("redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0", stream_name="events")
)

The low-level API passes the same RedisEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgresEgress inserts records into a table in batches. It writes only the records whose value is a mapping, and the labels on a labels sink, each label as sim_ts, timestamp, path, old, new and label. A record's row is its value, changed in four ways:

  • The record's sim_ts, timestamp, key (as event_id) and path_id are added, and replace fields of the same name.
  • Its task and instance are added too, but a value field of the same name keeps its own value.
  • Keys with no matching column are dropped.
  • A __table__ key sends the record only to the sink whose table_name matches.

The connection string names odctl, the database that the odctl postgres profile creates, with the user user and the password password.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:postgres-egress
- type: Postgres
  config:
    connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
    table_name: orders
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:postgres-egress
dsn = "postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl"
app.add_egress(PostgresEgress(dsn, table_name="orders"))

The low-level API passes the same PostgresEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

By default a record whose key already exists is skipped. upsert_keys updates that row instead, for a model that changes rows it wrote earlier, such as an order moving from packed to shipped. The key columns need a unique index. An update sets only the columns the record carries, and within one flush the last record for a key wins.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:postgres-upsert
- type: Postgres
  config:
    connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
    table_name: orders
    upsert_keys: [order_id]
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:postgres-upsert
app.add_egress(PostgresEgress(dsn, table_name="orders", upsert_keys=["order_id"]))

The low-level API passes the same PostgresEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: Iceberg
docs.text:
IcebergStorageEgress appends records to an Apache Iceberg table through a catalog. One flush is one commit, so this sink needs a large batch_size of its own: every commit writes new metadata, and many small commits slow down queries.

A table the sink creates takes its columns from the records:

  • The first batch gives a column for every key that has a value in some row.
  • A key that is null in every row waits for a batch that gives it a value, because Iceberg has no null type. An example is task in a low-level event published without one.
  • A key that first appears in a later batch is added as an optional column, unless the table is named in schemas, which keeps the columns it gives.

A batch the table refuses is logged at ERROR.

Catalogs. catalog is a PyIceberg Catalog object, or a mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties that desflow passes to load_catalog on the first write. The mapping's optional name key names the catalog. Each catalog below has a test that writes through it:

Catalog type Tested against REST rest the odctl catalog profile SQL on SQLite sql the unit tests, with a database file SQL on PostgreSQL sql the odctl postgres profile Glue glue Floci, an AWS emulator, not AWS itself

The properties of each catalog are listed in PyIceberg's configuration. Write to Iceberg Tables runs a shop through each catalog, from start to end.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:iceberg-egress
# A mapping of PyIceberg catalog properties, here the REST catalog of odctl.
# One commit per flush, so this sink gets a large batch of its own
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.events
    catalog:
      name: odctl
      type: rest
      uri: http://127.0.0.1:8181
      warehouse: s3://warehouse/
      s3.endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8333
      s3.access-key-id: user
      s3.secret-access-key: password
      s3.region: us-east-1
  batch_size: 200000
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:iceberg-egress
catalog = RestCatalog(
    "odctl",
    uri="http://127.0.0.1:8181",
    warehouse="s3://warehouse/",
    **{
        "s3.endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:8333",
        "s3.access-key-id": "user",
        "s3.secret-access-key": "password",
        "s3.region": "us-east-1",
    },
)
# One commit per flush, so this sink gets a large batch of its own
app.add_egress(
    IcebergStorageEgress(catalog=catalog, default_table="sim.events"),
    batch_size=200_000,
)

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, and gives its batch size in batch_sizes, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

A SQL catalog on SQLite needs no service, so it suits a first run. Its database file and the table files are under one folder:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/storage_backends.yaml:sqlite
# The catalog's database and the table files are under the folder iceberg/
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.events
    # The folder iceberg/ must exist before the run
    catalog:
      name: local
      type: sql
      uri: sqlite:///iceberg/catalog.db
      warehouse: file://${PWD}/iceberg/warehouse
docs/snippets/pages/storage_backends.py:sqlite
# The catalog's database and the table files are under the folder iceberg/
folder = Path("iceberg").resolve()
folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
catalog = {
    "name": "local",
    "type": "sql",
    "uri": f"sqlite:///{folder}/catalog.db",
    "warehouse": f"file://{folder}/warehouse",
}
app.add_egress(IcebergStorageEgress(catalog=catalog, default_table="sim.events"))

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, as Low-level API shows.

upsert_keys upserts on key columns instead of appending. A seeded model rerun over the same window writes rows with the same keys, so the upsert replaces those rows instead of duplicating them. An upsert reads the matching rows first, replaces whole rows, never deletes, and needs pyiceberg 0.9.0 or later.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:iceberg-upsert
- type: Iceberg
  config:
    default_table: sim.orders
    upsert_keys: {sim.orders: [order_id]}
    catalog:
      name: odctl
      type: rest
      uri: http://127.0.0.1:8181
      warehouse: s3://warehouse/
  batch_size: 200000
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:iceberg-upsert
app.add_egress(
    IcebergStorageEgress(
        catalog=catalog,
        default_table="sim.orders",
        upsert_keys={"sim.orders": ["order_id"]},
    ),
    batch_size=200_000,
)

The low-level API passes the same IcebergStorageEgress to env.setup_egress, in its list of sinks, and gives its batch size in batch_sizes, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

docs.title: Choose What Each Sink Gets
docs.text:
Every sink receives every event and telemetry record. when narrows that down:

  • A function taking one record and returning True to send it to this sink, in the builder or as !python in a blueprint.
  • history and live, in a blueprint: the records stamped before simulation.go_live_at, and the rest, as Clocks and Pacing describes.
  • labels: the ground-truth labels, and nothing else. No other sink receives a label, so data and labels always reach different sinks. Live Parameters describes them.
YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/batching.yaml:egress
egress:
  # Small and often for this sink; the other uses the defaults
  - type: Console
    batch_size: 50
    flush_interval: 0.5
  # Only the records stamped before go_live_at
  - type: Console
    when: history
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:every-sink
app.add_egress(stream).add_egress(lake)  # both receive every record
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:when
# A record's timestamp is an ISO string with its zone offset, so read it as a time
hot_from = datetime.now(timezone.utc)


def is_hot(record) -> bool:
    return datetime.fromisoformat(record["timestamp"]) >= hot_from


app.add_egress(stream, when=is_hot)  # hot tail
app.add_egress(lake, when=lambda r: not is_hot(r))  # cold history
app.add_egress(audit)  # no predicate: everything

setup_egress takes the functions in predicates, one for each sink by position, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

A labels sink gets the ground-truth labels and nothing else:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:sinks
egress:
  # The data under test: events and telemetry, and no label
  - type: Console
  # The labels only, for a scorer that checks what a detector found
  - type: Jsonl
    config: {default_path: labels/labels.jsonl}
    when: labels
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:labels
app.add_egress(stream)  # events and telemetry, never a label
app.add_egress(audit, when="labels")  # ground-truth labels, and nothing else

labels in setup_egress marks each labels sink with True, by position, as Batch Size and Flush Interval shows.

A file sink such as this one writes one file per batch under labels/, such as labels/labels_1a2b3c4d.jsonl. A run's warmup applies to every sink: none receives a record or telemetry stamped before it. Run Length describes it.

docs.title: Batch Size and Flush Interval
docs.text:
A sink receives records in batches. A batch is handed over when it holds batch_size records, or when flush_interval simulation seconds have passed, whichever comes first. At factor: 0, the timer does not start until a go_live_at switches the run to real time, because simulation time is not tied to the wall clock before then.

Setting Default Set with batch_size 500 with_batching, or per sink on add_egress flush_interval 1.0 simulation seconds with_batching, or per sink on add_egress max_queued_batches 2000 with_batching drain_stall_seconds 30.0 seconds with_batching

with_batching sets the defaults, and each sink can have its own size and interval. A stream sink needs small, frequent batches to keep latency down. A file or lake sink needs large ones, because each batch becomes one file, and for Iceberg one commit.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/batching.yaml
# The delivery settings of the Egress page, as a blueprint.
# Run it with: desflow run batching.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  # A day of history at factor 0, then 1 simulated second per real second from now;
  # when: history and when: live split the records at this instant
  logical_start_time: -1d
  go_live_at: now

# Defaults for every egress, the arguments of with_batching
batching:
  batch_size: 500
  flush_interval: 1.0
  max_queued_batches: 2000
  drain_stall_seconds: 30

egress:
  # Small and often for this sink; the other uses the defaults
  - type: Console
    batch_size: 50
    flush_interval: 0.5
  # Only the records stamped before go_live_at
  - type: Console
    when: history

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 1}

run:
  until: 60
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:defaults
app.with_batching(
    batch_size=5_000,  # records per batch
    flush_interval=1.0,  # simulation seconds; not used at factor=0
    max_queued_batches=2_000,  # a full queue makes the simulation wait
    drain_stall_seconds=30.0,  # how long teardown waits for a queue that stopped
)
docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:per-sink
app.with_batching(batch_size=500, flush_interval=1.0)  # the default for every sink
app.add_egress(stream, batch_size=50, flush_interval=0.5)  # small and often
app.add_egress(lake, batch_size=200_000)  # large files, the default interval

The lists are matched to the sinks by position, and None means the default:

docs/snippets/pages/batching.py:low-level
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.setup_egress(
    [stream, lake],
    batch_size=500,  # defaults for every provider
    flush_interval=1.0,
    predicates=[None, lambda r: r["stream_type"] == "event"],  # by position
    batch_sizes=[50, None],  # None: the default
    flush_intervals=[0.5, None],
    labels=[False, False],  # True makes a provider a labels sink
    warmup=None,  # simulation seconds before which no provider gets a record
)

setup_egress also takes lag_monitor_interval, the simulation seconds between system.simulation.lag_seconds records. Its default, "auto", is off at factor 0 and 1.0 simulation seconds otherwise. A run that goes live starts it at the go-live instant. None or 0 turns it off. The builder and YAML set it with lag_interval, as Clocks and Pacing describes.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A published record goes through the same steps for each sink:

  1. publish_event, publish_telemetry or publish_label builds the record as a plain dictionary.
  2. Each sink tests it once. A labels sink takes only labels, and only a labels sink takes a label. No sink takes a record stamped before the warm-up. Then the sink applies its when.
  3. The record goes into that sink's buffer. When the buffer reaches batch_size, or the sink's timer fires, the buffer is handed to the sink's queue as one batch.
  4. The egress thread takes batches from each queue and writes them with the sink's connector.

A connector is a class with one method, async run(queue), so a sink desflow does not have takes one class to write: Write a Connector shows how.

Each sink has its own buffer and its own queue. All sinks run as tasks on one thread, so a sink that waits with await does not hold up the others. A sink that blocks the thread holds up every sink, as a Kafka sink does while its serializer waits for a schema registry. Memory holds each sink's buffer and the batches waiting in its queue. A record that several sinks take is stored once. A queue holds at most max_queued_batches batches. When it is full, the simulation waits for room, so a sink that cannot keep up slows the run instead of building a backlog. When a queue stays full for drain_stall_seconds, the sink has stopped consuming, and the run raises RuntimeError rather than losing records.

Teardown flushes every buffer, then waits for the queues to drain. It keeps waiting while they shrink, and gives up only when they have not shrunk for drain_stall_seconds. Records still queued then are lost, and a warning names the sinks that held them.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A slow sink slows the run. The run slows on purpose: otherwise a backlog would build that teardown would have to throw away.
  • Size or interval, whichever comes first. The effective batch is the smaller of batch_size and what arrives in one flush_interval, so a large size with a short interval never fills. A warning says so once, after one sink has flushed on its timer 20 times in a row with less than a quarter of its batch_size.
  • A labels sink receives only labels, and a data sink never receives one. A label sent to a Kafka sink goes to its event_topic with no key.
  • Records matching no sink are not written anywhere, which is how when drops them.
  • At factor: 0, records leave a buffer only when it is full and at teardown.

docs.title: Ingress
docs.text: An ingress connector brings parameter changes into a running simulation from outside: from Kafka, Redis, PostgreSQL or a local schedule. This page shows each connector, the message it reads, how to send one, and when the change lands.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
An ingress connector listens to a source while the run goes on. Every message it reads is one change: a registry path and its new value, the same two names a scenario step uses. The change reaches the registry, and the simulation follows it, as Live Parameters describes. Four ingress connectors bring changes in. The seven connectors described on Egress write records out:

The tutorial page Live Changes teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Each connector is attached with add_ingress in the builder, passed to env.setup_ingress in the low-level API, or listed under ingress in a blueprint with its type and config. In a blueprint, type is one of the short names below, or a !python class from another package. config holds the constructor's arguments. A connector's module is imported only when a blueprint names it. A missing package stops the load with its line and the pip install command. YAML Keys lists the keys of an ingress entry.

Connector type Source Message Extra LocalIngress Local a schedule in the code (delay in wall-clock seconds, path, value) none KafkaIngress Kafka a topic a JSON object {"path": ..., "value": ...} kafka RedisIngress Redis a Pub/Sub channel the same JSON object redis PostgresIngress Postgres a table, polled a row with the columns path and value, the value as JSON text postgres

docs.title: Local Schedule
docs.text:
LocalIngress applies changes after set delays in wall-clock seconds from the start of the run. It suits a local run. For a change at an exact simulation time, use a scenario step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:local-ingress
# 10 wall-clock seconds after the start, set the packers capacity to 3
- type: Local
  config:
    schedule:
      - [10.0, Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, 3]
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:local-ingress
# 10 wall-clock seconds after the start, set the packers capacity to 3
app.add_ingress(
    LocalIngress(schedule=[(10.0, "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)])
)

The low-level API passes the same LocalIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
KafkaIngress consumes a topic and reads each message as a JSON object with path and value, or through a deserializer of your own, such as Avro, JSON Schema or Protobuf, as Use Avro and Pydantic and JSON Schema and Protobuf show. Connect to Secure Kafka connects it to a secured cluster.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:kafka-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from the sim-config topic
- type: Kafka
  config:
    topic: sim-config
    bootstrap_servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS:-127.0.0.1:9092}
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:kafka-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from the sim-config topic
app.add_ingress(KafkaIngress(topic="sim-config", bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092"))

The low-level API passes the same KafkaIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

KafkaAdminConnector.send_config(topic, path, value) sends one such message. The Kafka example listens on sim-config, and this sets its number of packers:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint has no sender of its own. Send the message from Python, as the Builder tab shows, or from any Kafka client, as below.

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters_kafka.py
"""Sets the packers capacity of the running Kafka example.

`KafkaAdminConnector.send_config` publishes `{"path": ..., "value": ...}` to the
topic `KafkaIngress` reads, `sim-config` in the example. Call `set_packer_capacity(3)`
while the example runs.
"""

import asyncio

from desflow import KafkaAdminConnector


def set_packer_capacity(value: int) -> None:
    admin = KafkaAdminConnector(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    asyncio.run(
        admin.send_config("sim-config", "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", value)
    )

The sender does not depend on how the model is written: use the function the Builder tab shows.

From any Kafka client, the message is the JSON object itself:

docs/snippets/pages/ingress_senders.py:kafka
async def send_with_kafka(rate: float) -> None:
    """A JSON object with path and value, to the topic KafkaIngress reads."""
    from aiokafka import AIOKafkaProducer

    producer = AIOKafkaProducer(bootstrap_servers="127.0.0.1:9092")
    await producer.start()
    try:
        message = {"path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": rate}
        await producer.send_and_wait("sim-config", json.dumps(message).encode())
    finally:
        await producer.stop()

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
RedisIngress subscribes to a Pub/Sub channel and reads each message as the same JSON object.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:redis-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from a Pub/Sub channel
- type: Redis
  config:
    url: redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0
    channel_name: simulation_params
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:redis-ingress
# Reads {"path": ..., "value": ...} messages from a Pub/Sub channel
app.add_ingress(
    RedisIngress(
        "redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0", channel_name="simulation_params"
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same RedisIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

docs/snippets/pages/ingress_senders.py:redis
async def send_with_redis(rate: float) -> None:
    """The same JSON object, published to the channel RedisIngress subscribes to."""
    import redis.asyncio as redis

    client = redis.from_url("redis://user:password@127.0.0.1:6379/0")
    message = {"path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": rate}
    await client.publish("simulation_params", json.dumps(message))
    await client.aclose()

With the Redis example running, valkey-cli sends one from a shell:

# Change the order arrival rate of the running simulation
docker exec -it valkey valkey-cli --user user --pass password PUBLISH simulation_params '{"path": "Shop.arrival.orders.rate", "value": 10.0}'

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
PostgresIngress polls a table, simulation_params by default, every poll_interval seconds, 2 by default. It creates the table when it is missing, with the columns id, path, value, is_applied and created_at. It applies the rows in two steps:

  1. At the start, it applies the latest applied value of each path, so a restarted run resumes from the last settings.
  2. At each poll, it applies every row whose is_applied is false and marks it true, so the table keeps the history of every change.

value is read as JSON, and as plain text when it is not JSON.

The connection string names odctl, the database that the odctl postgres profile creates, with the user user and the password password.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml_build/connectors.yaml:postgres-ingress
# Applies new rows (path, value) of simulation_params, checking every 2 seconds
- type: Postgres
  config:
    connection_dsn: postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl
    table_name: simulation_params
    poll_interval: 2.0
docs/snippets/pages/connectors.py:postgres-ingress
# Applies new rows (path, value) of simulation_params, checking every 2 seconds
app.add_ingress(
    PostgresIngress(
        "postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl",
        table_name="simulation_params",
        poll_interval=2.0,
    )
)

The low-level API passes the same PostgresIngress to env.setup_ingress, in its list of connectors, as Low-level API shows.

docs/snippets/pages/ingress_senders.py:postgres
async def send_with_postgres(rate: float) -> None:
    """A row in the table PostgresIngress polls; value is JSON text."""
    import asyncpg

    conn = await asyncpg.connect("postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/odctl")
    try:
        await conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO simulation_params (path, value) VALUES ($1, $2)",
            "Shop.arrival.orders.rate",
            json.dumps(rate),
        )
    finally:
        await conn.close()

With the PostgreSQL example running, psql adds one from a shell:

# Change the order arrival rate of the running simulation
docker exec -it postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "INSERT INTO simulation_params (path, value) VALUES ('Shop.arrival.orders.rate', '5.0');"

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The connectors run on the ingress thread, apart from the simulation. Each reads its source, turns every message into a (path, value) pair with one shared check, and puts it on a queue. A SimPy process, the ingress monitor, applies everything queued every 0.1 simulation seconds:

At factor: 1.0, 0.1 simulation seconds take 0.1 real seconds, so a change lands within 0.1 seconds of arriving. The simulation time it lands at depends on when it arrives, so two runs with the same seed and the same messages can differ. A change that must land at an exact simulation time needs a scenario step.

A connector is a class with one method, async run(queue), so a source desflow does not have takes one class to write: Write a Connector shows how.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A bad message is skipped. A message that cannot be decoded, that is not an object, or that lacks a non-empty path or a non-null value is logged as one WARNING line and skipped, and the run goes on. A PostgreSQL row like that is marked applied, so it is read once. A path the model does not have is a warning from the registry.

  • Old keys get a hint. Before 0.21.0, Kafka read path_id, and Redis and PostgreSQL read param_path and param_value. A message with the old keys is skipped with a line that says so, such as this one, which parse_change gives for a Kafka message written for 0.20.0:

    Skipped a Kafka ingress message: expected a non-empty path and a non-null value, got {'path_id': 'Shop.arrival.orders.rate', 'value': 1.0}; path_id, param_path and param_value were renamed to path and value in desflow 0.21.0

  • Old PostgreSQL columns. A table created before 0.21.0 has the columns param_path and param_value. Reading it fails with an error line that gives the two statements to rename them:

    ALTER TABLE simulation_params RENAME COLUMN param_path TO path;
ALTER TABLE simulation_params RENAME COLUMN param_value TO value;

  • LocalIngress follows the wall clock, so at factor: 0 an unpaced run can end before its first change.

  • Ingress needs an until. The ingress monitor repeats for as long as the run lasts, so a run with ingress needs until or Ctrl+C, as Run Length explains.

docs.title: Live Parameters: SimulationRegistry
docs.text: Every parameter of a run can change while the run goes on: an arrival rate, a number of packers, a stock level. This page shows how to name a parameter, the ways to change it, how to record what a change was for, and what happens to a value once it arrives.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Every run has one SimulationRegistry, at env.registry. It maps dot-notation paths, such as Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, to the values the simulation reads. A scenario, an ingress connector or a process changes a parameter by updating its path, and the simulation follows the change without restarting. Changing a parameter takes three steps:

The tutorial page Live Changes teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: Find the Path
docs.text:
A path is the sim_id, the kind of parameter, its name and the field:

Declared with Paths an arrival or a service <sim_id>.arrival.<name>.<parameter> and <sim_id>.service.<name>.<parameter>, one per scalar parameter of its family: .rate for an exponential, .mean and .std for a normal, .low, .mode and .high for a triangular, and so on; an empirical has none a resource <sim_id>.resources.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap a container <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level a store <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap a variable <sim_id>.variables.<name>

Arrivals and Services lists each family's parameters. An update to a path that does not exist, including a parameter the family does not take, is logged as a warning and ignored, so a misspelt path changes nothing.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint's paths follow from the names it declares, as the table above shows. To list them, load it with SimulationContext.from_yaml and call compile_parameters(), as the Builder tab does.

compile_parameters() returns the SimParameter a SimulationContext will register, which shows the names to use:

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:compile
print(app.compile_parameters())

You register the parameters yourself, and read a value with registry.get(path).value:

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:paths
params = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=3.0, std=0.5)},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=5)},
    containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=40)},
    variables={"conveyor_speed": 1.5},
)
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(params)
# Registered paths include:
#   Shop.arrival.orders.rate
#   Shop.service.packing.mean, Shop.service.packing.std
#   Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, Shop.resources.packers.max_cap
#   Shop.containers.stock.current_cap, .max_cap and .level
#   Shop.variables.conveyor_speed
print(env.registry.get("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap").value)  # 2

docs.title: Send a Value
docs.text:
Each source of a change suits a different job and lands at a different moment:

Source Use it for Lands at a scenario: YAML scenario, builder add_scenario, low-level run_scenario an experiment that must repeat exactly the exact simulation time given LocalIngress a local run with changes after set wall-clock delays a wall-clock delay from the start KafkaIngress, RedisIngress, PostgresIngress an operator or another program steering a running model when the message arrives a process calling env.registry.update a change that depends on the state of the simulation when the process makes it

Ingress gives the message each connector reads. A process changes a value directly:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint's process function, listed under processes, calls the same registry.update on context.env.registry, as Processes shows.

A builder process calls the same registry.update on context.env.registry, as Processes shows.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:update
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)  # applied
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 9)  # stored as 5, the max_cap
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.std", -1.0)  # refused, the old 0.5 stays
env.registry.update("Shop.resources.lath.current_cap", 3)  # no such path: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.service.packing.rate", 2.0)  # normal has no rate: ignored
env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 150)  # stored as 100, the capacity

docs.title: Script an Experiment
docs.text:
A blueprint's scenario lists changes, each with the simulation time it applies at. Here a second packer starts at 30 seconds. From one minute, orders arrive twice as fast: the average gap between orders falls from 5 seconds to 2.5 seconds (rate from 0.2 to 0.4). The extra packer leaves at two minutes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/scenario.yaml
# The first blueprint with a scripted experiment: a second packer starts at 30 s.
# From 1 min, orders arrive twice as fast: the average gap falls from 5 s to 2.5 s
# (rate 0.2 to 0.4). The extra packer leaves at 2 min. Every change lands at
# exactly that simulation time, on every run.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0
  random_seed: 1

egress:
  - type: Console

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 3}

services:
  packing: {dist: normal, mean: 4 s, std: 1 s}

arrivals:
  # An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2), 2.5 s from 1 min
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}

# The packers' capacity and queue every 10 seconds, to see each change land
stats: minimal

scenario:
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 2}
  - {at: 1 min, path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate, value: 0.4}
  - {at: 2 min, path: Shop.resources.packers.current_cap, value: 1}

run:
  until: 3 min

add_scenario takes the same steps as a list of mappings, as Vary Arrivals by Time shows.

run_scenario takes the same steps as a list of mappings, and runs as a SimPy process, as Vary Arrivals by Time shows.

The builder and the low-level API take the same steps, as a list of mappings. Vary Arrivals by Time shows one schedule in each API.

A scenario is not a connector. It is a SimPy process that waits on the simulation clock, so each step lands at exactly its at, on every run and at any factor, including 0. Its steps follow these rules, and Vary Arrivals by Time shows each case:

  • A step applies before every other event at its time, so an arrival gap drawn at that moment uses the new value.
  • Steps at the same time apply in the order written.
  • A step at or after until never applies.
  • Every path of a blueprint's scenario is checked against the model's registry when the file loads, so a misspelt path stops the load with its line. The builder checks its paths when the run starts.

LocalIngress waits on the wall clock instead, and an unknown path is only logged when it is due. A scenario and an ingress connector can run together, so a scripted baseline can run while an operator changes values over Kafka. When both change the same path, the later write wins.

docs.title: Record What a Change Was For
docs.text:
A detector or an agent that watches the data is scored against what really happened. A scenario step with a record publishes a ground-truth record of it: stream_type: "label", with the step's path, the value before (old) and after (new), and the step's record mapping as label. A step can have a record and no path, for something that happened outside the model, and then path, old and new are null.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/ground_truth.yaml:record
scenario:
  # Changes the rate and publishes a ground-truth record of the change
  - at: 30
    path: Shop.arrival.orders.rate
    value: 1.5
    record: {fault: order_surge, cause: flash sale}
  # A record with no change, such as a fault planted outside the model
  - at: 45
    record: {fault: label_printer_offline}

add_scenario takes the same steps, record included. A process publishes a label itself with context.env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...).

run_scenario takes the same steps, record included. A process publishes a label itself with env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...).

Labels go only to sinks with when: labels, and those sinks receive nothing else. The labels therefore never reach the pipeline under test, and a scorer reads them apart from the data. Choose What Each Sink Gets shows the sinks of this blueprint.

The labels sink writes one file per batch under labels/, such as labels/labels_1a2b3c4d.jsonl, with one line per label:

{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":30.0,"timestamp":"...","path":"Shop.arrival.orders.rate","old":0.5,"new":1.5,"label":{"fault":"order_surge","cause":"flash sale"}}
{"stream_type":"label","sim_ts":45.0,"timestamp":"...","path":null,"old":null,"new":null,"label":{"fault":"label_printer_offline"}}

In Python, env.publish_label(label, path=..., old=..., new=...) publishes one, and add_egress(sink, when="labels") or setup_egress(..., labels=[...]) makes a labels sink, as the measuring example shows.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Registration. run(), or register_sim_parameter in the low-level API, flattens the SimParameter into the registry. The registry holds one DynamicValue per path, with the value and a change signal. Beside them, it keeps the configuration objects that the paths belong to, such as each DistributionConfig.

An update. registry.update(path, value) applies one change. The checks run in order, and an accepted value reaches the parts that read it:

  • A path that does not exist is logged as a warning, and the update is ignored.
  • A value of another type is converted to the type the path holds, so the string "5" sent to an integer path becomes 5. Python's conversion is used, so 2.5 sent to an integer path becomes 2. A value that cannot be converted is logged as an error and ignored.
  • A distribution parameter is checked on a copy of its configuration, by the rules used at build. One out of range is logged as an error, and the old value stays.
  • A current_cap outside 0 to max_cap, or a container level outside 0 to current_cap, is stored clamped to that range, with a warning. A lower max_cap clamps the stored current_cap the same way.
  • A value equal to the current one changes nothing.
  • Otherwise the value is stored, and the attribute of the configuration object is set too, found by splitting the path at its last dot: Shop.service.packing.mean sets mean on the object at Shop.service.packing. The Sampler reads that object at every draw, so it sees the new value.

Change Signal. Each value has a SimPy Store with one slot as its signal. An update puts a token in it if it is empty, and wait_for_change() waits for that token. The slot holds one token, so several changes before a waiter wakes give one signal, and only one waiting process takes it. Resources, stores and containers already wait on their own paths, and a token that your process takes does not reach them. Wait only on paths that nothing else waits on, such as variables:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Waiting on a change needs process code: a process function listed under processes waits on context.env.registry in the same way, as Processes shows for a process.

A builder process waits on context.env.registry in the same way, as Processes shows for a process.

docs/snippets/pages/registry.py:wait
def watch_speed(env):
    """Logs the conveyor speed every time it changes."""
    speed = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.conveyor_speed")
    while True:
        yield speed.wait_for_change()
        print(f"t={env.now}: conveyor speed is now {speed.value}")


env.process(watch_speed(env))

A container's level also changes with every put and get. The registry keeps that level, so a reader sees it, but does not signal the container again.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
What follows a change:

  • Distributions. The next draw uses the new value. The arrival already being waited for keeps its gap, and a task that has drawn its service time keeps it.
  • Resources, stores and containers. The capacity follows at once, and a container's level follows its path, as Resources and Stores and Containers describe.
  • Variables. The new value is stored, and a process reads it with env.registry.get(path).value.

A change is easiest to see in the telemetry. With stats: minimal, the scenario above shows the second packer land:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 20.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 1}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}

The reading at 30 seconds still shows 1. The resource applies a change within the same simulation instant, but after the step that made it. The reading was taken before that. The builder publishes the same readings with with_stats:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

stats: minimal in the blueprint above publishes these readings every 10 seconds.

docs/snippets/pages/live_parameters.py:telemetry
# The packers' capacity, in use, queue and utilization every 2 seconds
app.with_stats("minimal", interval=2.0)

env.setup_stats("Shop", "minimal", interval=2.0) publishes the same readings, as Statistics shows.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• An unknown path is a warning, not an error, for an ingress message or a process. Only a scenario is checked when it loads.
  • A family is fixed. There is no path that turns a normal into an exponential. That is a new model.
  • Several changes, one signal. A process waiting on a path wakes once for several changes made before it runs, and reads the latest value.
  • Ingress lands on the wall clock. A message's change lands at whatever simulation time the run has reached when it arrives. A change that must happen at an exact simulation time needs a scenario step.

docs.title: Model Parts
docs.text: A model is made of a few kinds of parts. This page is the map: which block models what, and what it is called in each way of writing. Each block has a page of its own.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
An entity is the thing that flows through a model: an order, a visitor, a support call. It enters through an arrival and does the work its task describes. While it works, it holds a resource, and it may take from or add to a store or container. Then it goes on to the next task. What Is DES? explains discrete-event simulation, the kind of simulation these blocks build. Look at how the blocks connect:

Block What it models YAML Builder Low-level Page Arrival how often an entity enters, and what it starts with arrivals add_arrival, @app.arrival_loop a process that waits for a drawn gap Arrivals and Services Service how long a piece of work takes services add_service a DistributionConfig drawn with a Sampler Arrivals and Services Task what one entity does, with its events tasks @app.task a SimPy process Tasks and Processes Resource packers, benches, lanes: whole units held by a task resources add_resource DynamicResource Resources Container an amount, such as a stock of boxes, that tasks take and add containers add_container DynamicContainer Stores and Containers Store items, such as parcels on a shelf, that tasks put and get stores add_store DynamicStore Stores and Containers Task flow the task that follows a finished one, and what the entity carries next, attributes, set next=, attributes=, set= Router, Entity Task Flow Process anything else that runs over time: a break, a drift, a schedule processes add_process env.process Tasks and Processes Statistics what the run measures about itself stats with_stats env.setup_stats, env.stats Statistics Variable any other live value, such as a speed variables add_variable SimParameter(variables=...) Live Parameters

The shop tutorial, in the Learn section, puts them together one at a time, in a small shop.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: A model declares its blocks, and its tasks use them by name. A task names its service and its resource, and an arrival names the task it starts. The table above gives each block's YAML key, builder call and low-level class. Writing a Model shows a whole model in each form.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: When the run starts, run() builds the environment, registers every block's parameters in the registry, builds the resources, stores and containers, and starts the arrivals and processes. What run() Does lists the steps in order. From then on, each block reads its live values from the registry: a distribution reads its parameters at each draw, and a resource follows its capacity path.

docs.title: Arrivals and Services: Sampler and the Distributions
docs.text: Two building blocks set the timing of every simulation. An arrival decides how often a new entity enters the model: an order, a visitor, a support call. A service decides how long a piece of work takes: packing an order, answering a call. Both are distributions of time, and each time one is needed, a value is drawn from the distribution with its current parameters.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Block Answers Used by Example Arrival How long until the next entity? the arrival loop, which starts a task for each one an order every 2 s on average Service How long does this piece of work take? a task, while it holds its resource 3 s of packing, give or take 0.5 s

An arrival draws each gap afresh from its distribution, so the gaps differ and entities arrive at uneven times. Look at the first five orders of the shop in First Simulation:

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
Every distribution is a family, dist, and the parameters that family takes. There are ten families. A parameter outside its range, a missing one, or one the family does not take is refused when the model is built, with the YAML line when it comes from a blueprint. Reference, Distributions lists every family with its parameters, rules, mean and variance. On this page, the table below names each family, the list under it gives each family's rules, and one example shows the form.

Family Use it for Parameters exponential Gaps between arrivals that happen independently of each other: orders, calls, visits. Many short gaps and a few long ones, with mean 1 / rate. rate normal Work with a typical time and a small, symmetric spread. mean, std truncated_normal Work with a typical time and a hard minimum. mean, std, low lognormal Times that are never negative and now and then much longer: repairs, support calls. mean, std constant Fixed times: a conveyor, a setup, a step that takes no time. value uniform Any time in a range, all equally likely, when only the range is known. low, high triangular An expert's estimate: the shortest, the most likely and the longest time. low, mode, high gamma Times less variable than exponential.
