A whole-number shape is the Erlang distribution: that many exponential steps in a row. shape, scale weibull Time to failure: a shape below 1 fails early, a shape above 1 wears out. shape, scale empirical Times taken from real data, when no family fits. values with weights, or edges with counts

The rules for each family's parameters:

  • exponential: rate above 0, in events per second: 0.5 is one every 2 seconds on average, 2.0 is two a second. It is the one parameter that is not a time, so it takes no duration.
  • normal: mean, and std 0 or more (0 when left out). A std of 0 gives the mean every time. A draw can be negative, and every time is raised to at least 0.00001 seconds. In a wide normal, these raised draws raise the mean, so use truncated_normal instead.
  • truncated_normal: mean, std 0 or more, and low, 0 when left out. With std 0, mean must be at least low. A draw below low is thrown away and drawn again, so no draws pile up at the limit. The mean is therefore the truncated distribution's own: 1.29 seconds for mean: 1, std: 1, low: 0. The higher low is above the mean, the fewer plain draws are kept. So when low is more than half a standard deviation above the mean, truncated_normal draws from an exponential proposal instead (Robert, 1995), which stays exact and fast for any low.
  • lognormal: mean above 0 and std 0 or more (0 when left out). Both describe the times you get, not the underlying normal. desflow converts them.
  • constant: value 0 or more. It uses no random number at all.
  • uniform: low and high, with low < high. The mean is halfway between them.
  • triangular: low, mode and high, all required, with low <= mode <= high and low < high. The mean is (low + mode + high) ÷ 3.
  • gamma: shape and scale, both above 0. The mean is shape × scale and the variance shape × scale². From a mean and a standard deviation: shape = (mean ÷ std)² and scale = std² ÷ mean, so a mean of 1.5 seconds with a std of 0.5 is shape 9 and scale 0.1667.
  • weibull: shape and scale, both above 0. The mean is scale × gamma(1 + 1 ÷ shape), where gamma is the gamma function.
  • empirical: either values, each equally likely unless the optional weights give one weight per value; or a histogram of edges and counts, with one count per bin. A histogram draw picks a bin in proportion to its count, then any time inside the bin, all equally likely. Weights and counts are 0 or more and add up to more than 0, and edges increase. The lists are taken when the model is loaded, so an empirical distribution has no registry path and does not change while the run goes on.

desflow dist lists the families, and desflow dist <family> prints one family's parameters and rules. With --mean and --std it converts them to the family's parameters, so the gamma above needs no arithmetic:

desflow dist gamma --mean 1.5 --std 0.5

parameters: shape 9, scale 0.166667
YAML: {dist: gamma, shape: 9, scale: 0.166667}
Python: dist="gamma", shape=9, scale=0.166667

The last two lines are the service in a blueprint and in the builder. Command Line shows the other conversions.

Three of these families in a blueprint: a labelling time of at least 0.2 seconds, a station that fails more often as it wears, a histogram of measured packing times with three bins, and a scanning time of 0.5 seconds four times in five and 2 seconds otherwise:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:families
# under services: a hard minimum, a time to failure, a histogram of data, and
# weighted values
labelling: {dist: truncated_normal, mean: 1 s, std: 1 s, low: 0.2 s}
station_failure: {dist: weibull, shape: 1.5, scale: 10 min}
measured_packing: {dist: empirical, edges: [1 s, 2 s, 3 s, 4 s], counts: [5, 3, 2]}
scanning: {dist: empirical, values: [0.5 s, 2 s], weights: [4, 1]}
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-families
# A hard minimum, a time to failure, a histogram of data, and weighted values
app.add_service("labelling", dist="truncated_normal", mean=1.0, std=1.0, low=0.2)
app.add_service("station_failure", dist="weibull", shape=1.5, scale=600)
app.add_service(
    "measured_packing", dist="empirical", edges=[1, 2, 3, 4], counts=[5, 3, 2]
)
app.add_service("scanning", dist="empirical", values=[0.5, 2], weights=[4, 1])

Each is a DistributionConfig with the same parameters in seconds, such as DistributionConfig(dist="weibull", shape=1.5, scale=600).

An arrival or a service takes the same form for every family: dist, and the parameters in that family's row of the table. An exponential arrival, in the three ways to write it:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:exponential
# under arrivals: an order every 2 seconds on average
orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack}
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-exponential
# An order every 2 s on average, each starting the task pack
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack")
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:low-level-exponential
gap = DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)  # an order every 2 s on average

An arrival draws its gap from data in the same way. Here a batch arrives 1 second after the last one three times in four, and 5 seconds after it otherwise:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:weighted-arrival
# under arrivals: a gap of 1 second three times in four, and 5 seconds otherwise
batches: {dist: empirical, values: [1 s, 5 s], weights: [3, 1], spawn: pack}
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-weighted-arrival
# A gap of 1 s three times in four, and 5 s otherwise
app.add_arrival(
    "batches", dist="empirical", values=[1, 5], weights=[3, 1], spawn="pack"
)

DistributionConfig(dist="empirical", values=[1, 5], weights=[3, 1]) is the gap.

docs.title: Durations
docs.text:
In a blueprint, every time-valued parameter takes a duration as well as a number of seconds: mean, std, low, mode, high, scale and value, and the values and edges of an empirical. A plain number is seconds. rate stays a number per second.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:durations
# under services: every time-valued parameter takes a duration
support_call: {dist: lognormal, mean: 5 min, std: 3 min}

The builder takes seconds: app.add_service("support_call", dist="lognormal", mean=300, std=180).

The low-level API takes seconds: DistributionConfig(dist="lognormal", mean=300, std=180).

docs.title: Seeding
docs.text:
A seed makes every draw the same on every run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/arrivals_services.yaml:seed
# The same draws on every run; leave it out to draw a seed and log it
random_seed: 42

desflow run arrivals_services.yaml --seed 7 overrides it without editing the file.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:builder-seed
# The same draws on every run; leave it out to draw a seed and log it
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0, random_seed=42)
docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:low-level-seed
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # the same draws on every run

In the low-level API you draw yourself, from the current values:

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:low-level-draw
seconds = sampler.sample(packing)  # one draw, in seconds, from the current values

A run without a seed draws one and logs it, so it can be repeated: desflow run logs the command with --seed, and a builder run logs the value to pass as random_seed:

No random_seed was given, so this run uses 3166812249. Pass random_seed=3166812249 to repeat it.

A low-level Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random, as How It Works explains. Randomness and Seeds shows seeds in use.

docs.title: Replay
docs.text:
An arrival can take its times from recorded rows instead of a distribution. Each row of a CSV or Parquet file, or of a list of dicts, becomes one entity at the row's time. The fields named in fields become the entity's attributes. Here each row of local_replay_orders.csv is an order, at its time in seconds from the start of the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/local_replay.yaml:replay
arrivals:
  orders:
    replay:
      # A CSV or Parquet file, relative to this blueprint
      path: ../local_replay_orders.csv
      time: time
      unit: s
      fields: [order_id, items]
    spawn: pack
examples/builder/local_replay_example.py:replay
# A CSV or Parquet file, or a list of dicts
.add_arrival_replay(
    "orders", TRACE, time="time", unit="s", fields=["order_id", "items"]
)

add_arrival_replay takes spawn= as add_arrival does, which starts the named task for each row. This example writes an @app.arrival_loop of its own instead, where wait_for_arrival("orders") waits for the next row.

examples/low-level/local_replay_example.py:replay
def replay(env, sampler, packers):
    """Starts one order at each row's time, carrying the row's fields."""
    rows = read_trace(TRACE, time="time", unit="s", fields=["order_id", "items"])
    for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
        yield env.timeout(row.time - env.now)
        key = f"orders-{number}"
        env.process(pack(env, sampler, packers, key, number - 1, row.fields))

read_trace reads and checks the rows, and returns each with its simulation time, row number and fields.

unit is ms, s, min or h from the start of the run, or timestamp for a date and time, placed on the run's clock from logical_start_time. The rows must be in time order, and the arrival follows these rules:

  • Rows at equal times arrive at that time, in the order of the file.
  • A row before the start stops the run, and rows at or after until never arrive.
  • A row without a valid time stops the run, unless on_invalid is skip, which leaves it out with a warning.
  • After the last row, the arrival stops and logs one INFO line.

A Parquet file needs the parquet extra. A replayed arrival has no registry path. Local Replay compares a recorded morning with a model of it.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
One registry of distributions. Every family is declared once, in desflow.core.distributions.DISTRIBUTIONS, with its parameters, its range rules, how to draw from it, its mean and variance, and what it gives with no random generator. The YAML models, the builder, DistributionConfig, the Sampler and the registry's live paths all read it, so they accept the same families and parameters. These are 200,000 draws from each family:

A draw reads the live configuration. A DistributionConfig holds the family and its parameters. Sampler.sample(config) reads the parameters at the moment it is called, so a change made while the run goes on applies from the next draw. A task draws its service time once it has its resource and has published started. The arrival loop draws the next gap when it starts waiting. Every value is raised to at least 0.00001 seconds, so a time is never 0 or negative.

One random stream per distribution. A seeded Sampler makes one generator for each name: NumPy's SeedSequence(seed, spawn_key=(CRC32 of the name,)). When the registry registers a distribution, it names it by its path without the sim id, such as arrival.orders or service.packing, and every draw from that distribution comes from that stream. Probability routing draws from route.<task> in the same way, as Task Flow describes. Each stream depends only on the seed and the distribution's name. Adding a distribution therefore leaves every other one's draws unchanged. The name leaves out the sim id, so renaming the simulation does not change them either:

In the low-level API, a DistributionConfig that was never registered draws from the Sampler's main generator instead. Your own code can take a stream of its own with sampler.generator("<name>"):

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint and a builder model register every distribution, so each draws from its own stream. Code of your own takes a stream from context.sampler.generator("<name>") once the run is built.

A blueprint and a builder model register every distribution, so each draws from its own stream. Code of your own takes a stream from context.sampler.generator("<name>") once the run is built.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:streams
# Each registered distribution draws from the stream named by its path without
# the sim id; register the parameters, and sample() picks the stream
registry = SimulationRegistry(simpy.Environment())
registry.register_sim_parameter(SimParameter(sim_id="Shop", arrival={"orders": gap}))
assert gap.stream == "arrival.orders"
stream = Sampler(seed=42).generator("arrival.orders")  # the same seed, the same name
assert stream is not None and sampler.sample(gap) == stream.exponential(2.0)

Sampler(rng=np.random.default_rng(42)) draws the same numbers as Sampler(seed=42), because the streams come from the generator's seed.

No random generator. A Sampler() with neither a seed nor a generator draws nothing at random: every sample is the distribution's mean, or a constant's value. A run then uses the mean of every input and gives the same output each time, which suits a test. That output is not the model's average result: variation lengthens waits, so a run on mean inputs gives shorter waits than random runs give on average. A truncated_normal gives its mean or its low, whichever is higher.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

A blueprint and a builder model always have a random generator: the random_seed, or a seed drawn and logged at the start. Draws at the mean are for a low-level test.

A blueprint and a builder model always have a random generator: the random_seed, or a seed drawn and logged at the start. Draws at the mean are for a low-level test.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:no-generator
fixed = Sampler()  # no random generator: every draw is the mean, or the value
assert fixed.sample(packing) == 3.0 and fixed.sample(gap) == 2.0
assert fixed.sample(checking) == 1.5  # shape × scale

SimPy and desflow. SimPy has no distributions: a SimPy model draws its own times, usually with random.expovariate(0.5) for a gap of 2 seconds on average, and writes yield env.timeout(...) with the result. Nothing checks the parameters, a negative draw makes timeout raise, and the parameters are ordinary variables. desflow names each distribution and its parameters once, checks them, keeps them in the registry, and gives each a stream of its own. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
Each scalar parameter a family takes has a path in the registry: <sim_id>.arrival.<name>.rate for an exponential arrival, <sim_id>.service.<name>.mean and .std for a normal service, .low, .mode and .high for a triangular, .shape and .scale for a gamma or weibull, .value for a constant. A scenario, an ingress message or a process changes it while the run goes on, as Live Parameters explains:

  • The next draw uses the new value. An order already being packed keeps the time it drew, and the arrival already being waited for keeps its gap.
  • An update is checked on a copy of the configuration, by the same rules as at build. A value outside the range is refused with an error log line, and the old value stays:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

A scenario step or an ingress message with an out-of-range value is refused in the same way, with the same error log line.

A scenario step or an ingress message with an out-of-range value is refused in the same way, with the same error log line.

docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:refused
packing_path = "Shop.service.packing.std"
registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(sim_id="Shop", service={"packing": packing})
)
registry.update(packing_path, -1.0)  # refused with an error log line
assert registry.get(packing_path).value == 0.5  # the old value stays

Invalid value for 'Shop.service.packing.std': normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0. Update ignored.
  • The family is fixed when the model is built. There is no path that turns a normal into an exponential. An update to a parameter the family does not have, such as .rate on a normal, is refused as an unknown path, with a warning.
  • An empirical distribution has no paths: its lists are taken at load.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Refused at build. The same checks refuse a bad distribution when the model is built. These three are an out-of-range std, a parameter normal does not take, and a mode above high:

    YAMLBuilderLow-level

    desflow run and SimulationContext.from_yaml refuse the same parameters, with the file, the line and the same message: shop.yaml:3: services.packing: Value error, normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0.

    app.add_service and app.add_arrival raise the same ValueError, such as normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0.

    docs/snippets/pages/arrivals_services.py:invalid
    refused: List[Dict[str, Any]] = [
    {"dist": "normal", "mean": 3.0, "std": -1.0},  # out of range
    {"dist": "normal", "mean": 3.0, "rate": 2.0},  # a parameter normal does not take
    {"dist": "triangular", "low": 1.0, "mode": 3.0, "high": 2.0},  # mode above high
]
for parameters in refused:
    try:
        DistributionConfig(**parameters)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(error)


    normal std must be 0 or more, got -1.0
normal does not take rate; it takes mean, std
triangular needs low <= mode <= high, got low 1.0, mode 3.0, high 2.0

  • A wide normal. When std is half of mean, 2.3% of draws fall below 0 and are raised to the floor. When std equals mean, 15.9% are. The raised draws push the average time up: the 200,000 draws of the normal panel in the chart above, with mean 1 and std 1, average 1.08, not 1. Use truncated_normal.

  • Rate against mean. exponential takes a rate per second, not a mean gap: an order every 30 seconds is rate: 0.0333, not 30.
  • A seed and the timestamps. A seed fixes the draws and so the simulation times, but each record's timestamp also depends on when the run started, unless logical_start_time is set, as Time and Pacing explains.
  • Spread lengthens queues. Two models with the same mean times but a different spread have different queues: more spread means longer waits, as Queues and Capacity and Choosing Inputs measure.

docs.title: Example: Local Replay
docs.text:
The local-replay example has one packer and the 40 orders of a recorded morning, which it replays from a CSV file at their times. The last order arrives at 73 seconds. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 120 simulation seconds.

The tutorial page Local Replay teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

uvpip

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get local-replay --api yaml
cd local-replay/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run local_replay.yaml

# 1. Install

# 2. Download the example

cd local-replay/yaml

# 3. Run it

Quick Start

Quick Start

docs.title: Input Fitting
docs.text: A model's distributions should come from data where data exists. Input fitting takes a column of measured times and fits every distribution family desflow has. It checks each result, and also offers the data itself as an empirical distribution. It writes the chosen settings in a form a model loads. This page describes the command and the Python call, every option, each outcome and how to deal with it, and how the fitting is done.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
desflow fit and fit_column fit the families of Arrivals and Services to service durations or to the gaps between arrivals, by maximum likelihood with scipy. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters under which the measured values are most probable. Each family's fit becomes one row of a table, with its parameters in seconds and its diagnostics, and the best is marked. Fitting the Inputs fits the shop's 40 packing times and shows why the best by the numbers still needs checking against the model's answer. Fit a Distribution fits the gaps of an order log.

Fitting needs the fit extra, which installs scipy and matplotlib: pip install "desflow[fit]". A base install runs without the extra: desflow imports scipy and matplotlib only when a fit runs.

docs.title: Fit a Column
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level 
# Fit the packing times, write the best fit and plot every candidate
desflow fit packing_times.csv --column packing_seconds --unit s --lower 0 --out packing_fit.yaml --plot fit.png

The command prints the table, writes the best candidate's settings to --out and the plot to --plot. It exits with status 1 when no candidate is usable, and with status 2 when the input is invalid.

examples/builder/fitting_example.py:fit
times = read_column(DATA, "packing_seconds")
result = fit_column(times, unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
examples/low-level/fitting_example.py:fit
result = fit_column(read_column(DATA, "packing_seconds"), unit="s", lower=0)
print(result.text())  # every candidate, its status and diagnostics
PARAMS = SimParameter(
    sim_id="Shop",
    # An order every 1.25 s on average (rate 0.8)
    arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.8)},
    # The best candidate's settings, such as dist="triangular", low=0.546332
    service={"packing": DistributionConfig(**result.settings())},
    resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=2, max_cap=4)},
)

read_column(path, column), imported with from desflow.analysis.fit import read_column, reads one CSV column as text. fit_column takes any list of numbers or text, where an empty cell or None is a missing value.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Command option fit_column argument What it sets Default --column the CSV column to fit required --unit unit the data's unit: ms, s, min or h; the settings are always in seconds s --candidates candidates the families to try, such as gamma,lognormal; an unknown name is refused every family --lower, --upper lower, upper the plausible range, in the data's unit: a value outside it is invalid, and a family that can draw outside it is flagged none --bins bins offer the empirical distribution as a histogram with this many bins the values themselves --min-count min_count the fewest values a family is fitted to 20 --tolerance tolerance how far a fitted mean and standard deviation may be from the data's, as a share of the data's 0.25 --drop-invalid drop_invalid leave invalid values out, counted, rather than stopping off --out result.yaml() write the best candidate's settings as YAML --plot result.plot(path) draw the data against the best candidate

A value is invalid when it is not a number, is not finite, or lies outside --lower and --upper. The table's first line counts the rows, and the values used, missing and invalid.

docs.title: Read the Result
docs.text:
fit_column returns a FitResult:

  • table: one row per candidate, with family, status, reason, parameters, log_likelihood, aic, ks_statistic, ks_p_value, bounds and best. aic is the AIC, where lower is better.
  • best: the best candidate's family.
  • settings(kind=None): the settings of the best, or of the family kind, for add_service(name, **settings). A family that is not usable is refused, and the error names those that are.
  • text(): the table as the command prints it.
  • yaml(kind=None): the settings as the YAML file --out writes.
  • plot(path, kind=None): the PNG --plot draws: the data's histogram over values generated from the candidate, and a Q-Q plot, which puts each sorted data value against the generated value at the same quantile. Points on the diagonal mean that the two agree.

The settings have six significant digits, the same numbers the YAML file holds, so a script and a blueprint that load one fit draw the same values.

docs.title: How the Best Is Chosen
docs.text:
The best is the fitted family with the lowest AIC among those that cannot draw outside --lower and --upper. When every value is the same, it is constant. When no family within the bounds fitted, it is empirical, which never draws outside the data's range. Only when there is no empirical candidate is a fitted family that can draw outside the bounds chosen. A family that is rejected, did not fit or was skipped is never chosen.

When two families' AIC are too close to tell them apart, as AIC and the KS Test explains, check what the choice changes in the model's answer, as Fitting the Inputs does.

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Each candidate ends with one status. Every one but fitted has a reason, and none stops the fit:

Status Cause What to do skipped fewer values than --min-count collect more data, or use the empirical candidate, which is still offered; lower --min-count only if the values are known to be typical skipped a value of 0 or below, for gamma, weibull or lognormal, which are defined above 0 only find out what the zeros are: rounding (record finer times), a different kind of event (remove it from the data), or real zero durations (use a family with no positive-only support, such as exponential or truncated_normal) skipped every value is the same, so only constant and empirical are fitted use constant, or check that the column is the one meant skipped a value below low, for truncated_normal, whose low is --lower, or 0 set --lower to the true lower bound did not fit scipy's fit raised an error or its search did not settle; the reason is scipy's message the data is far from that family's shape: choose another family; more data can help rejected a fitted parameter is not finite or is out of the family's range as for did not fit rejected the fitted mean or standard deviation is more than --tolerance from the data's look for outliers: correct or remove a value that is a recording error, and keep one that is real. --upper leaves out values above it only with --drop-invalid; without it, such a value stops the fit with status 2. With --upper, only the families bounded above, uniform and triangular, can be chosen as best, then empirical. Or use --bins for an empirical histogram rejected a value lies where the family cannot draw as for the zeros above fitted with a bounds note the family can draw below --lower or above --upper, such as normal below 0 it is chosen only when nothing within the bounds fits; prefer a family with the right support

The command fails only when no candidate is usable, empirical included. empirical is unusable only when there are no values, or when --candidates leaves it out.

docs.title: Load the Settings
docs.text:
YAMLBuilderLow-level

!include reads a mapping from another file, relative to the blueprint, so the file --out wrote is loaded and checked as if it were written in place:

examples/yaml/fitting.yaml:include
services:
  # The fitted distribution, read from the file desflow fit wrote
  packing: !include packing_fit.yaml

An arrival also needs its spawn, so the include names the file and adds keys to it: orders: !include {file: fitted/orders.yaml, spawn: pack}. A YAML syntax error in the included file, or a file that is not a mapping, names that file and its line. A wrong key or value in it is reported at the blueprint's !include line, and so is a missing file. A file that includes itself, directly or through another, is refused at the !include that closes the loop.

examples/builder/fitting_example.py:service
# The best candidate's settings, such as dist="triangular", low=0.546332
.add_service("packing", **result.settings())

DistributionConfig(**result.settings()), as the fit section above shows.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Data first. The values are read, and missing ones are counted and left out. Invalid ones are refused or, with --drop-invalid, counted and left out. They are converted to seconds. Then each family is checked against the data before it is fitted: enough values, positive values where the family needs them, and not a constant column.

Maximum likelihood, location at 0. desflow's families have no location parameter: a gamma or a Weibull starts at 0. scipy can also fit a location, which moves the start of the distribution to wherever the data suggests. For the tutorials' 40 packing times plus one outlier of 120 seconds, a free location puts a gamma's start at 0.70 seconds, the smallest value, with a shape of 0.21 and a scale of 81. desflow has no parameter for that start. So the location of exponential, gamma, weibull and lognormal is fixed at 0, and each fit is converted to desflow's parameters:

Family Fitted with desflow's parameters exponential scipy.stats.expon.fit(x, floc=0) rate = 1 ÷ scale normal scipy.stats.norm.fit(x) mean, std lognormal scipy.stats.lognorm.fit(x, floc=0) the variable's mean = scale × e^(s²/2) and std = mean × √(e^(s²) − 1) truncated_normal the likelihood of scipy.stats.truncnorm with low fixed, maximised by scipy.optimize.minimize mean, std, low uniform scipy.stats.uniform.fit(x) low, high triangular scipy.stats.triang.fit(x) low, mode, high gamma scipy.stats.gamma.fit(x, floc=0) shape, scale weibull scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit(x, floc=0) shape, scale constant every value is the same value empirical the values, or numpy.histogram with --bins values, or edges and counts

Each fit runs on its own, so one that fails is a row, not a crash.

Checks. Every fitted result is checked before it can be chosen. Each parameter must be finite and within the family's rules, the same rules a blueprint's distribution is checked against. The family's mean and standard deviation, from desflow's own formulas, must be within --tolerance of the data's. A result that fails is rejected with the reason. Some bad fits still pass these checks. Fitted to a gamma, the three values 1.0, 1.0000001 and 1.0000002 give a shape of 1.4 × 10¹⁴ and a scale of 7.1 × 10⁻¹⁵, with the right mean and spread. --min-count guards against such fits: no family is fitted to fewer values than --min-count.

Diagnostics. For each fitted family, the table gives the log-likelihood of the data and the AIC. The k in the AIC counts only the fitted parameters: a fixed location does not count. The table also gives the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and p-value from scipy.stats.kstest. The p-value assumes the parameters were known in advance. They were estimated from the same data, so the p-value is approximate and tends to be too high. empirical has no AIC.

Plot. The generated values are drawn through desflow's Sampler, seeded, with the same smallest delay a run applies, so the plot shows what a run draws and repeats exactly.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Size of the extra. These sizes were measured in new Python 3.12 environments on macOS. scipy 1.18.1 takes about 70 MB installed with uv, and about 100 MB with pip, which also compiles bytecode. Its download is 20 to 37 MB, depending on the platform. matplotlib and its dependencies, beyond the NumPy desflow already needs, add about 55 MB with uv and about 70 MB with pip. Fitting is not in the base install because of these sizes.
  • Local files only. The command reads a CSV file. Reading from a database or an object store, and automated selection beyond the lowest AIC, come later.
  • A fit is not a validation. A family that fits the data well can still change the model's answer, and a model whose inputs fit can still answer the question badly. Compare the model's output with the real system's, as Experiment Results does.
  • One column at a time. Each column is fitted on its own, so a dependence between two inputs, such as larger orders taking longer to pack, is not captured.

docs.title: Example: Fitted Inputs
docs.text:
The fitting example fits the 40 packing times of the tutorials and runs one hour of a two-packer shop with the fitted packing time. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Fitting the Inputs teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

docs.title: Stores and Containers: DynamicStore and DynamicContainer
docs.text: A resource is held and given back. Stores and containers hold things that tasks take away and add: items, or an amount. This page shows how to declare them, how tasks put and get, and what a live change does.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• A store holds items, each one a value of its own: parcels on a shelf waiting for a courier, orders in a buffer. A task puts an item in, and another takes the oldest out.
  • A container holds an amount: boxes in a bin, fuel in a tank, a stock level. A task takes some, and another adds some.

Both have a capacity, or no limit. A task that takes waits while there is not enough, and a task that adds waits while there is no room. Stock uses a container in the shop.

docs.title: Declare Them
docs.text:
A container has three settings. current_cap is its capacity, the largest amount it holds. max_cap is the largest capacity a live change can set. level is the amount it holds when the run starts, 0 when left out. A store has a current_cap and a max_cap, in whole items, and starts empty unless it lists items (Start With Items and Serve by Priority). run() builds a DynamicContainer and a DynamicStore for each one the context declares. A store and a container cannot share a name.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:container
containers:
  # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
  stock: {current_cap: 100, max_cap: 100, level: 20}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:store
stores:
  # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
  parcels: {current_cap: 5, max_cap: 10}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-container
# An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
app.add_container("stock", current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-store
# Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=5, max_cap=10)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-container
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An amount: room for 100 boxes, 20 when the run starts
        containers={"stock": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=20)},
        # Items: room for 5 parcels, empty when the run starts
        stores={"parcels": CapacityConfig(current_cap=5, max_cap=10)},
    )
)
stock = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "stock")  # starts at the level above, 20
parcels = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "parcels")

A DynamicContainer built with no init starts at the level its ContainerConfig gives. init= sets another.

A store or container with no current_cap has no capacity limit, as simpy.Store(env) and simpy.Container(env) have: a put never waits for room. current_cap: .inf in YAML, or float("inf") in code, says the same. A max_cap alone gives the current_cap, and a current_cap alone gives the max_cap. A live update can give a store with no limit a capacity. A store's capacity is a whole number of items, so a fractional capacity is rounded down. .inf or the text "inf" sets no limit again. A store or container with no limit publishes capacity as null.

docs.title: Take and Add
docs.text:
A task takes with get and adds with put. For a container, each names the container and an amount. The amount can be a number, or an expression such as payload.boxes for a field of the previous task's payload. In the builder, it can also be a function of the task id and the previous task's payload. The amount is 1 when left out. For a store, each names the store. A put adds the task's finished payload as the item, and a get takes the oldest item and passes it to the task's function as item.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:take
pack_order:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer
  get: {container: stock, amount: payload.boxes}
docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:put
# Adds its finished payload to the store as an item
put: {store: parcels}
payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-take
# Takes the boxes the previous task's payload names, once it has a packer.
# The amount is a number, an expression, or a function of the task id and the
# previous task's payload, such as lambda task_id, payload: payload["boxes"].
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "stock", "amount": "payload.boxes"},
    put={"store": "parcels"},  # adds the finished payload as an item
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


# Takes the oldest parcel, waiting while the store is empty; `item` is that parcel
@app.task(service_id="collecting", get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item["event_type"]}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-take
def pack(env, order_id):
    yield stock.get(2)  # takes 2 boxes, waiting while fewer are left
    yield parcels.put({"order_id": order_id})  # waits while the store is full


def collect_parcel(env):
    parcel = yield parcels.get()  # waits while the store is empty
    print(f"collected order {parcel['order_id']}; {stock.level:g} boxes left")

get(amount), put(amount), put(item) and get() are SimPy events: yielding one waits until it succeeds, and a store's get() succeeds with the item.

A task with a resource gets its unit first and then takes its get, so it waits for stock while holding the unit. A task adds its put after its service time, then publishes the finished event. Tasks and Processes lists every step.

A put or get makes the task wait until it is granted. With wait: false ("wait": False in the builder), the task makes the request and goes on at once, as a SimPy put that is not yielded does. It publishes finished without waiting, and the request stays in the queue until it can be granted. Such a request follows these rules:

  • It is granted first in, first out, together with the requests that are waited for.
  • An interrupt, on_interrupt: abandon and patience never cancel it.
  • A run can end while it still waits, and a drain does not wait for it.
  • A get takes its item later and drops it. So it cannot use item_field or a function that declares item, and its item.<field> can be read only in its own filter.
  • It is refused in a branch of a wait.

The pump task of Example: Fuel Dock puts fuel into a tank this way. The third pump finds room for only 20 units of fuel, so its put stays queued.

docs.title: Start With Items and Serve by Priority
docs.text:
A store can hold items when the run starts, such as parcels left from yesterday. items lists them in the order a get returns them. A store cannot start with more items than its current_cap: the blueprint or add_store is refused with the reason.

A store with priority returns the item with the lowest priority value first, as SimPy's PriorityStore does. Its items are [priority, item] pairs, and a task's put gives each new item its priority. Items of equal priority come out in the order they went in. A priority can be:

  • a number, or an expression such as attr.priority that gives one;
  • a list such as [1, 2], ordered element by element, as a tuple is;
  • any other value that can be ordered against the others, such as a text.

A priority keeps the value it is given, so the text '10' sorts as text, before '9'. In YAML a string is an expression, so a text priority such as 'P1' comes from attr.grade or payload.grade. Priorities that cannot be compared, such as a number and a text, raise TypeError at the put, as in SimPy.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/parcel_store.yaml:store
stores:
  parcels:
    current_cap: 10
    max_cap: 10
    # A courier takes the lowest priority value first, the oldest first among equals
    priority: true
    # Left from yesterday: [priority, item] pairs, held before the first put
    items:
      - [2, {order: standard-0}]
      - [1, {order: express-0}]
docs/snippets/yaml/parcel_store.yaml:put
pack:
  # Each parcel's priority, read when it is put in the store
  put: {store: parcels, priority: attr.priority}
  payload: {order: standard}
  id_field: number
docs/snippets/pages/parcel_store.py:builder-store
app = SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0.0)
# A courier takes the lowest priority value first, the oldest first among equals.
# Left from yesterday: (priority, item) pairs, held before the first put.
app.add_store(
    "parcels",
    current_cap=10,
    max_cap=10,
    priority=True,
    items=[(2, {"order": "standard-0"}), (1, {"order": "express-0"})],
)

A task's put takes the priority the same way: put={"store": "parcels", "priority": "attr.priority"}.

docs/snippets/pages/parcel_store.py:low-level-store
parcels = DynamicStore(
    env,
    "Shop",
    "parcels",
    priority=True,
    # Each pair is held as a PriorityItem, ranked by priority and then by order
    items=[(2, {"order": "standard-0"}), (1, {"order": "express-0"})],
)


def courier_process(env):
    first = yield parcels.get()  # a PriorityItem; .item is the parcel
    print(f"collected {first.item['order']}")
    # A put of your own wraps the item the same way, so ties keep their order
    yield parcels.put(parcels.wrap({"order": "express-1"}, 1))

A low-level priority store holds simpy.PriorityItems. wrap(item, priority) makes one, ranked by the priority and then by a rising number. The builder and YAML use it to keep equal priorities in order. A plain PriorityItem(priority, item) also works, but keeps no order among equal priorities.

A get on a priority store takes no priority of its own and is refused with one: the item's priority decides the order. Priorities compares priority storage with a resource's priority queue.

docs.title: Pick an Item, or Give Up Waiting
docs.text:
A store get can take a filter, a condition that picks which item it takes, as SimPy's FilterStore does. The filter reads the item on offer as item.<field>, and every name that other conditions read, such as attr.area for the entity's own attribute. The get takes the oldest item that matches, and waits while none does. A waiting get that matches nothing does not stop a later get from taking an item that matches it.

A priority store takes no filter, because SimPy has no store that both ranks and filters. The blueprint or run() refuses a filter on one, and names the task.

A task's patience covers its whole wait: for its wait, then its resource, then its get. When it runs out, the task publishes reneged and its get is cancelled, so it takes nothing later. In the low-level API, cancel() on a put or get event that has not succeeded takes it out of its queue, as in SimPy: a cancelled get takes nothing, and a cancelled put adds nothing. In YAML, item_field adds the item that the task's get took to its payload. A builder function receives the item as item:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/filtered_inventory.yaml:collect
tasks:
  pack:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    # The parcel goes on the shelf as the payload, with its area.
    put: {store: parcels}
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    attributes: [area]
  collect:
    # The oldest parcel for the courier's own area.
    get: {store: parcels, filter: item.area == attr.area}
    # A courier leaves without a parcel after 20 seconds.
    patience: 20 s
    # The parcel the courier took, in the finished event.
    item_field: parcel
    payload: {event_type: parcel_collected}
examples/builder/filtered_inventory_example.py:collect
@app.task(
    # The oldest parcel for the courier's own area
    get={"store": "parcels", "filter": "item.area == attr.area"},
    # A courier leaves without a parcel after 20 seconds
    patience=20,
)
def collect(task_id, context, item):
    """`item` is the parcel the courier took."""
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": item}

A filter can also be a function of the item: "filter": lambda parcel: parcel["area"] == "north".

examples/low-level/filtered_inventory_example.py:collect
def collect(env, sampler, shop, key, area, task_id):
    """Takes the oldest parcel for its own area, or leaves after 20 seconds."""

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="collect", instance=task_id)

    flow = key.rsplit("-", 1)[0]
    env.stats.flow_started(flow)  # the courier enters the shop
    publish({"status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("collect", task_id)
    get = shop["parcels"].get(filter=lambda parcel: parcel["area"] == area)
    yield get | env.timeout(20)
    if not get.triggered:
        get.cancel()  # out of the queue, so it takes no parcel later
        publish({"status": "reneged"})
        env.stats.task_reneged("collect", task_id)
        env.stats.flow_ended(flow)
        return
    publish({"status": "started"})
    env.stats.task_started("collect", task_id)
    publish({"event_type": "parcel_collected", "parcel": get.value})
    env.stats.task_finished("collect", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished(flow)

item.<field> can also be read in the task's put and next, after its get. Filtered Inventory uses a filter and patience on a shelf of shirts.

docs.title: Custom Store and Container Types
docs.text:
A store or container of your own class changes how items or amounts go in and out. Subclass desflow.StoreBase (a simpy.Store) or desflow.ContainerBase (a simpy.Container) and override _do_put or _do_get, set PutQueue or GetQueue, or bind put and get to event classes of your own, as in SimPy. The constructor is SimPy's, (env, capacity=inf) for a store and (env, capacity=inf, init=0) for a container. Name the class with type: !python module.Class in a blueprint, type= in add_store and add_container, or type= in DynamicStore and DynamicContainer.

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/advanced/fuel_dock.yaml:dock
stores:
  # A lane of your own type; it holds two trucks
  lane: {current_cap: 2, max_cap: 2, type: !python fuel_dock_types.Lane}

containers:
  # A tank of 100: two pumps fill 80 of it, so the third put waits for room
  tank: {current_cap: 100, max_cap: 100}

arrivals:
  diesel_trucks: {dist: constant, value: 3, spawn: park, attributes: {fuel: diesel}}
  petrol_trucks: {dist: constant, value: 5, spawn: park, attributes: {fuel: petrol}}
  crew: {dist: constant, value: 7, spawn: unload}
  tankers: {dist: constant, value: 4, spawn: pump}
  marshals: {dist: constant, value: 15, spawn: marshal}

tasks:
  park:
    # The truck waits outside while the lane is full
    put: {store: lane}
    payload: {event_type: truck_parked}
    attributes: [fuel]
  unload:
    # The newest truck in the lane, because of the lane's type
    get: {store: lane}
    item_field: truck
    payload: {event_type: truck_unloaded}
  pump:
    # The tank truck starts the pump and leaves; it does not wait for the put
    put: {container: tank, amount: 40, wait: false}
    payload: {event_type: pump_started}
  marshal:
    # Waits until a truck is held outside the full lane
    wait: {condition: putters.lane >= 1}
    payload: {event_type: overflow_bay_called}

The class is in examples/yaml/advanced/fuel_dock_types.py, next to the blueprint, which !python finds first.

examples/builder/fuel_dock_example.py:dock
class Lane(StoreBase):
    """A store that gives back the newest item, like trucks parked nose to tail."""

    def _do_get(self, event):
        if self.items:
            event.succeed(self.items.pop())


app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Dock", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    # A lane of your own type; it holds two trucks
    .add_store("lane", current_cap=2, max_cap=2, type=Lane)
    # A tank of 100: two pumps fill 80 of it, so the third put waits for room
    .add_container("tank", current_cap=100, max_cap=100)
    .add_arrival(
        "diesel_trucks", dist="constant", value=3, attributes={"fuel": "diesel"}
    )
    .add_arrival(
        "petrol_trucks", dist="constant", value=5, attributes={"fuel": "petrol"}
    )
    .add_arrival("crew", dist="constant", value=7)
    .add_arrival("tankers", dist="constant", value=4)
    .add_arrival("marshals", dist="constant", value=15)
)


# The truck waits outside while the lane is full
@app.task(put={"store": "lane"})
def park(task_id, context, entity):
    return {"event_type": "truck_parked", "fuel": entity.attributes["fuel"]}


# The newest truck in the lane, because of the lane's type
@app.task(get={"store": "lane"})
def unload(task_id, context, item):
    return {"event_type": "truck_unloaded", "truck": item}


# The tank truck starts the pump and leaves; it does not wait for the put
@app.task(put={"container": "tank", "amount": 40, "wait": False})
def pump(task_id, context, entity):
    return {"event_type": "pump_started"}


# Waits until a truck is held outside the full lane
@app.task(wait={"condition": "putters.lane >= 1"})
def marshal(task_id, context, entity):
    return {"event_type": "overflow_bay_called"}
examples/low-level/fuel_dock_example.py:dock
class Lane(StoreBase):
    """A store that gives back the newest item, like trucks parked nose to tail."""

    def _do_get(self, event):
        if self.items:
            event.succeed(self.items.pop())


def build(env):
    """Builds the lane and the tank, in the builder's order."""
    return {
        # A lane of your own type; it holds two trucks
        "lane": DynamicStore(env, "Dock", "lane", type=Lane),
        # The tank holds 100, the capacity in the parameters
        "tank": DynamicContainer(env, "Dock", "tank"),
    }

A container type is written the same way, from ContainerBase. This bin counts the puts it grants, and a Transfer gives a task its get as an object, the form the dictionaries above are read into:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

type names the class in a module beside the file, here a copy of the bin in shop_logic.py:

docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:container-type
# A container of your own class, from shop_logic.py beside the blueprint
labels: {current_cap: 10, max_cap: 10, level: 10, type: !python shop_logic.CountedBin}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-types
class CountedBin(ContainerBase):
    """A container that counts the puts it grants."""

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.restocks = 0

    def _do_put(self, event):
        granted = super()._do_put(event)
        if event.triggered:
            self.restocks += 1
        return granted


app.add_container("labels", current_cap=10, level=10, type=CountedBin)

# A task's get or put can also be a Transfer, built once and given to several tasks
one_label = Transfer(container="labels", amount=1)


@app.task(get=one_label)
def print_label(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}

A low-level model builds an instance of the class itself, as the Low-level tab above builds the lane and the tank.

The statistics and the conditions follow every change to a store's items or a container's level made by _do_put or _do_get, whether the override calls super() or not, and each change is reported to them once. ContainerBase compares the level before and after, so an override that returns True without changing the level reports nothing. A change to the length of put_queue or get_queue is reported to the conditions that read putters. or getters.. A queue class must support len() and remove(). A cancel() is reported from the event classes, so it works with a queue class of your own.

A task's put stores its payload as the item, and its get passes the item on, unwrapped, whatever the type. A type cannot be given with priority: a type sets its own order, so subclass StoreBase and simpy.PriorityStore for a ranked store. A get with a filter needs a type that subclasses simpy.FilterStore, and a blueprint or run() without such a type is refused, naming the task. A live capacity update reaches a type of your own as it does the default.

docs.title: Registry Paths, Readings and Conditions
docs.text:
A container has three registry paths, <sim_id>.containers.<name>.current_cap, .max_cap and .level. A store has <sim_id>.stores.<name>.current_cap and .max_cap. With statistics at the minimal level or above, each publishes four readings, such as Shop.stats.containers.stock.level:

Reading Store Container capacity items it can hold largest amount level items held amount held getters_waiting tasks waiting to get an item tasks waiting to take an amount putters_waiting tasks waiting to put an item tasks waiting to add an amount

basic adds level_avg, the level averaged over time. Statistics describes it. Below are the readings of stores_containers.yaml, the blueprint whose parts this page shows. They are taken at 30 and 40 simulation seconds, before and after the stock count that Under Live Changes shows:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 3}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 0.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 30.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.level', 'value': 5}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.stores.parcels.putters_waiting', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.level', 'value': 38.0}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 40.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.containers.stock.getters_waiting', 'value': 0}

At 30 seconds the bin is empty and two orders wait for boxes. At 40 seconds the stock count has put 50 boxes in, those two have taken theirs, and the shelf of parcels is full, with two packed orders waiting for room.

A condition in a task's next reads a level as level.<name>, so an order can go to backorder when level.stock == 0, as Task Flow shows.

A condition can also read how many tasks wait at a store or container, and what a store holds:

Name Reads putters.<name>, getters.<name> the number of puts or gets waiting, not counting one that is granted at once, as the putters_waiting and getters_waiting readings; len(put_queue) and len(get_queue) in the low-level API count(<store>) the number of items the store holds, as level.<store> count(<store>, <condition>) how many items meet the condition, which reads item.<field> of each items(<store>), items(<store>, item.<field>) the list of items, or that field of each; a priority store gives its items unwrapped

in and not in read an items(...) list, as in payload.sku in items(shelf, item.sku), which is true while the shelf holds that sku. The store is a bare name, and count and items cannot be nested inside each other. The names are checked at load: each must name a store, and putters. and getters. may also name a container.

A condition that reads one of these names is checked again when a put or get joins or leaves a queue. A condition that reads none of them, such as level.stock == 0, is not checked again for a queue change. A queue change is not a change of level, so level_avg does not move. The marshal task of Example: Fuel Dock waits on putters.lane >= 1.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A container keeps a level between 0 and its capacity, with a queue of getters and a queue of putters. A get succeeds as soon as the level covers its amount, and a put as soon as there is room for all of it. Until then, each waits in its queue, in the order it arrived:

A store keeps a list of items, up to its capacity. A put adds an item at the end, and a get takes the first, so items leave in the order they came. A get with a filter takes the first item its filter accepts:

SimPy and desflow. desflow builds on three SimPy classes. A container is SimPy's Container. A store is a FilterStore, which serves its gets as Store does while no waiting get has a filter. A priority store is a PriorityStore, which hands out the lowest item first. A full put that waits for room and an empty get that waits for an item or an amount are checked against plain SimPy in all three APIs. SimPy Compatibility lists the checks. SimPy's capacities are fixed when they are created, and desflow's follow the registry. desflow also keeps the registry's level in step with every put and get, and reports each change to the statistics. SimPy and desflow compares the two.

docs.title: Under Live Changes
docs.text:
• Capacity follows current_cap, clamped to between 0 and max_cap. A higher capacity wakes waiting putters. A capacity below what is held destroys nothing: puts wait until enough has been taken.
  • A container's level is set by an update to its level path, as a stock count or a restock from outside would. The new level is clamped to between 0 and current_cap, with a warning, and it wakes both queues: a higher level serves waiting getters, and a lower one can make room for putters.
  • A store or container with no limit can be given a number as current_cap during a run, and .inf or the text "inf" sets no limit again. Lowering it destroys nothing, as the Capacity item above says.
  • current_cap is the capacity, not a level. A model that used a container's current_cap as a level, such as the wear of a roll, moves it to level.

The stock count in stores_containers.yaml, in each way of writing:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/stores_containers.yaml:level
scenario:
  # A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds
  - {at: 30, path: Shop.containers.stock.level, value: 50}
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:builder-level
def stock_count(context: SimulationContext):
    """A stock count at 30 seconds: the level path sets what the container holds."""
    yield context.env.timeout(30)
    context.env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)


app.add_process(stock_count)
docs/snippets/pages/stores_containers.py:low-level-level
def stock_count_process(env):
    """A stock count: sets the level; waiting gets and puts are woken."""
    yield env.timeout(30)
    env.registry.update("Shop.containers.stock.level", 50)

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• A container that never refills blocks its getters for good, and a task that waits for stock while holding a resource blocks the resource too. Supply has to keep up with demand, as Stock shows.
  • Whole items. A store's capacity is a whole number or no limit, and it holds items, not amounts.
  • A put or get with wait: false is never cancelled, so a supply that outpaces its consumers grows the queue without end. A run drops what is still waiting when it ends.
  • A filter checks every waiting get on each put. For a store with many waiting gets and a filter that rarely matches, the work grows in proportion to both, as SimPy's FilterStore does.
  • One store or container per get or put. A task has at most one get and one put.

docs.title: Example: Stock, Parcels and Express Orders
docs.text:
The stock example combines a container and a store. Packing takes a box from a container and puts the parcel in a store, which starts with two parcels from yesterday. A courier collects the parcels. Express orders go first at the packers, and also at the courier, because the parcels store is a priority store. The stock runs out, so packing waits until a restock at 40 seconds sets the level to 30 boxes. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Stock teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

cd stock/yaml

# 3. Run it

    service: packing
    resource: packers

    # Puts the finished payload in the store as a parcel of the order's priority.
    put: {store: parcels, priority: attr.priority}
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    attributes: [priority]

examples/low-level/stock_example.py:pack
def pack(env, sampler, shop, key, priority, task_id):
    """Queued, a packer by priority, a box from stock, packing, then a parcel."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack", task_id)  # counted as in progress
    with shop["packers"].request(priority=priority) as req:
        yield req
        # Waits while the stock is empty
        yield shop["stock"].get(1)
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack", task_id)
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed", "priority": priority}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        # Waits while the store is full; wrap ranks the parcel by its priority
        yield shop["parcels"].put(shop["parcels"].wrap(payload, priority))
        publish(payload)
        env.stats.task_finished("pack", task_id)

The whole file is examples/low-level/stock_example.py.

docs.title: Example: Fuel Dock
docs.text:
The fuel-dock example combines the parts of this page:

  • Fuel trucks wait in a lane of your own type, which gives back the newest truck first.
  • A crew unloads one truck every 7 seconds.
  • A tank truck puts fuel into a tank that holds 100 units, without waiting for the put. Once the tank is nearly full, the put waits in the tank's queue.
  • A marshal calls the overflow bay once a truck waits outside the full lane.

It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 40 simulation seconds.
