docs.title: Replications
docs.text: One run of a model is one sample: another seed draws other times and gives other values. Replications run the same model with many seeds and summarise each built-in statistic with a mean and a 95% interval. This page shows how to run them from the command line and from Python, in each of the three ways to write a model, what they return and send to the sinks, and how the seeds and intervals are made.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A replication is one run of the model with a seed of its own. N replications give N independent values of each built-in statistic, such as the mean wait of a task. Their mean is the estimate, and the half-width of its 95% interval says how precise it is: with 95% confidence, the true value lies within the mean plus or minus the half-width. Trusting Results shows on the shop why one run is not an answer and how to choose the number of replications.

docs.title: Run Replications
docs.text:
Give the model, the number of replications, the seed they are spawned from and the time the arrivals stop:

YAMLBuilderLow-level 
desflow run replications.yaml --replications 20 --measure tasks.pack.wait_mean

--seed overrides simulation.random_seed, and --until overrides run.until, as for one run. --level sets the confidence level (0.95 when it is not given), --workers sets how many replications run at once, each in its own process, and --drain drains every replication, as run.drain: true does. The command prints the summary, the seed of each replication and the command that repeats one. The blueprint's own warmup applies to every replication:

examples/yaml/replications.yaml:seed
# The replications' seeds are spawned from this one; --seed overrides it
random_seed: 42
warmup: 3 min
docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:builder
# shop is a function returning a new SimulationContext, called once per run
result = replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until="1 h", warmup="3 min", measures=MEASURES)

shop is a function with no arguments that returns a new SimulationContext, such as the example's, because each replication starts from a new context. A blueprint path works here too.

docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:low-level
def model(env, sampler):
    """Builds the shop in the environment it is given, drawing from sampler."""
    env.registry.register_sim_parameter(PARAMS)
    env.process(orders(env, sampler, DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")))


def low_level():
    shop = LowLevelModel(model, sim_id="Shop")
    return replicate(shop, 3, seed=42, until=3600, warmup=180, measures=MEASURES)

LowLevelModel takes a function that builds the model, given an environment and a sampler, and the sim_id that the model's statistics are published under. The function registers the parameters, builds the resources and starts the processes. It sets up no statistics, because replicate does, and it sets up no sinks. Its tasks report their steps to env.stats, as Statistics shows.

replicate takes these options:

Option What it sets Default n how many replications, 2 or more seed the seed the replications' seeds are spawned from; None draws one and logs it until where each replication's arrivals stop, in seconds or a duration such as "1 h"; the replication ends there unless stop ends it earlier or drain runs on a blueprint's run.until stop ends each replication when it happens, as for run(): {"signal": name}, a signal's name, or {"condition": "..."}; for a LowLevelModel, a function of the environment that returns the event a blueprint's run.stop drain at until, stop the arrivals and run each replication on until no entity is left: True, or {"limit": "1 h"}; a LowLevelModel is drained when its function returns its arrival processes and reports its entities with env.stats.flow_started and flow_finished a blueprint's run.drain warmup the end of each replication's warm-up the model's own measures the statistics to summarise every statistic the run publishes, at least up to typical level the confidence level of the half-widths 0.95 workers how many replications run at once, each in its own process 1 overrides registry paths and the values every replication starts with, such as {"Shop.resources.packers.current_cap": 3}, set in the order given; a value the registry would refuse or clamp is refused, so a max_cap below the current current_cap needs current_cap set first none

docs.title: Choose the Measures
docs.text:
A measure is a statistic's published name without the sim id and stats, such as tasks.pack.wait_mean for Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_mean. Reference, Statistics lists them. Each replication keeps the statistics level its measures need, whatever level the model sets: basic for counts and time averages, typical for means and maxima of waits and services, and all for percentiles. A higher level the model sets stays.

A name that no replication publishes is refused, with the names the model does publish. A count that is published only once it is above 0, such as reneged, is 0 in a replication without one. A mean with no observation in a replication, such as the wait of a task that never started, is refused with the replication's number rather than left out.

docs.title: Read the Result
docs.text:
replicate, imported with from desflow import replicate, returns a Replications. Its summary has one row per measure: a mapping with measure, n, mean, half_width and level. The interval runs from mean - half_width to mean + half_width. Its table has one row per replication and measure, with the replication's number and seed, and seeds lists the seeds in order:

docs/snippets/pages/replications.py:read
print(result.summary_text())  # each measure's n, mean and half-width
for row in result.summary:  # measure, n, mean, half_width and level
    low, high = row["mean"] - row["half_width"], row["mean"] + row["half_width"]
    print(f"{row['measure']}: {low:.2f} to {high:.2f} ({row['level']:.0%})")
print(result.seeds)  # replication i ran with seeds[i - 1]
for row in result.table:  # one row per replication and measure
    print(row["replication"], row["seed"], row["measure"], row["value"])

The summary of the three replications above:

measure                               n          mean    half-width (95%)
tasks.pack.wait_mean                  3          4.16                2.22
resources.packers.utilization_avg     3         78.51               4.363

Three replications give a wide interval. Trusting Results shows how to choose enough.

docs.title: Repeat One Replication
docs.text: Each replication's seed is a plain integer, recorded in seeds and in every row of the table. Any replication can therefore be repeated on its own, with the same end time, drain and warm-up: desflow run shop.yaml --seed <its seed>, random_seed in a builder context, or Sampler(seed=...) in the low-level API. That run publishes its event records, which replications do not.

docs.title: What the Sinks Receive
docs.text:
When the model has sinks, a blueprint's egress or a builder's add_egress, they receive the result once, as telemetry stamped at the end time: each replication's value, then each measure's mean, half-width and count. A low-level model has no sinks of its own. Below are the records a Console sink receives from the three replications above:

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Seeds. The replications' seeds are numpy.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn(n), each turned into one plain integer. The same seed gives the same list, and a longer list starts with the shorter one, so 40 replications begin with the 10 that n=10 runs. Within a replication each distribution draws from a random sequence of its own, as in any run (Randomness and Seeds).

One replication. Each replication builds the model again: it reads the blueprint, calls the factory, or calls the low-level function with a new environment and sampler. It runs unpaced, at factor 0, with no ingress, no egress and no statistics timer. It applies the warm-up and the overrides before the clock starts, and reads env.stats.readings() at its end. A blueprint's run.before functions run once per replication, and once more when the model has sinks, for the build that sends them the result.

Intervals. The half-width is t × s ÷ √n. Here s is the sample standard deviation of the n values, and t is the Student t quantile at (1 + level) ÷ 2 with n − 1 degrees of freedom. desflow computes the quantile itself, by bisection on the t distribution's cumulative probability, so replications need nothing beyond a base install. The tests check it against a published table.

Workers. With workers above 1, replications run in a pool of that many processes. Each process imports the model. The model must therefore be a blueprint path or a function defined at the top of a module. A lambda, or a function defined inside another function, is refused with that reason. The values are the same as with one worker.

Sinks. When the model has sinks, it is built once more after the last replication, with its sinks, without its ingress, and with the clock at the end time. This build is not run. Its own statistics are switched off, so the sinks receive only the result. A model without sinks is not built again.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• No event records. Replications send no event records: the orders of twenty replications, each with its own seed, would mix in one sink and could not be told apart. Repeat one replication with its seed to get its records.
  • Independent seeds only. Every replication of one call has its own seed. Comparing two designs with the same seeds, and checking that their random streams line up, is an experiment's job (Experiments).
  • Same model each time. A builder factory must return a new context on every call. A context that has run keeps its entity counters and is not a new replication.
  • Built-in statistics only. A replication summarises the built-in statistics at its end. Readings of your own, published with context.publish, are not summarised.
  • Steady state and terminating runs. The warm-up applies to each replication. A run with a natural start and end, such as a shop day, keeps its empty start and needs no warm-up. Output Analysis explains the two kinds of run.

docs.title: Example: Replications
docs.text:
The replications example runs one hour of the shop 20 times, with seeds spawned from 42 and a 3-minute warm-up, and prints the mean and half-width of every statistic up to typical. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Trusting Results teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: Built-in Statistics
docs.text: A run can measure itself: how busy each resource was, how long tasks waited, how many entities finished. This page shows how to switch the statistics on, what each level publishes and costs, how each value is computed, and how to add readings of your own.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: The built-in statistics are measures that desflow keeps while the run goes on and publishes as telemetry, under fixed names such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean. They need no code of yours in the builder or YAML, and they reach every sink like any other telemetry. They are off by default, because most runs only generate data. Measuring a Run reads them on the shop.

docs.title: Choose a Level
docs.text:
A level switches them on. Each level publishes what the levels before it publish, and answers one more question:

Level Question Adds none nothing; the default minimal What is happening now? resources: capacity, in_use, queue_length, utilization, and down for one that breaks down; stores and containers: capacity, level, getters_waiting, putters_waiting; tasks: in_progress basic How much got done, and how busy was it? tasks and flows: finished; flows: started and in_system; tasks: balked, reneged, failed, interrupted, preempted and resumed, and flows: failed, once one happens; resources: utilization_avg, queue_length_avg, and downtime and failures for one that breaks down; stores and containers: level_avg typical How long did tasks take? tasks: wait_mean, wait_max, service_mean, service_max all How long did the slowest take? tasks: wait_p50, wait_p95, wait_p99, service_p50, service_p95, service_p99

They are published every interval of simulation time, 10 seconds when it is not given. The first publication comes one interval after the start, and one more comes at the end of the run. When the timer has already published at the end's time, the end publishes only the values that changed since:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation time and once at the end
stats: {level: typical, interval: 1 min}

stats: typical is the short form, with the 10-second interval. The interval takes seconds or a duration.

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-levels
# none (the default), minimal, basic, typical or all, each adding to the one before;
# published every interval of simulation seconds and once at the end
app.with_stats("typical", interval=60)
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-levels
env.setup_stats("Shop", "typical", interval=60)  # before or after the resources

Resources, stores and containers add themselves to env.stats when they are built. Tasks are your own processes, so each reports its steps:

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-report
# A low-level task reports its own steps to the statistics
env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)
with packers.request() as request:
    yield request
    env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
env.stats.flow_finished("orders")  # the order leaves the shop

docs.title: Read the Names
docs.text:
Every statistic is published as telemetry named <sim_id>.stats.<kind>.<name>.<statistic>, where the kind is resources, stores, containers, tasks or flows. A flow is named by the arrival that started its entities: Shop.stats.flows.orders.finished counts the orders that left the model. Reference, Statistics lists every name with what it measures. Below are the statistics that statistics.yaml, the blueprint whose levels part is shown above, publishes at the end of its two-minute run:

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.capacity', 'value': 2}
[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.in_use', 'value': 2}

[TEL] {'sim_ts': 120.0, 'timestamp': '...', 'path_id': 'Shop.stats.resources.packers.utilization', 'value': 100.0}

The same values can be read by name, during or after the run:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

desflow run --stdout prints the same values as telemetry records, as above.

app.env.stats.readings() gives the same values, by name, during or after the run.

docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:low-level-read
# Every statistic the level publishes, by its published name
readings = env.stats.readings()
print(f"mean wait {readings['Shop.stats.tasks.pack_order.wait_mean']:.2f} s")

docs.title: Which Entities a Count Covers
docs.text:
When the statistics are read, every entity that has arrived belongs to one population. Each population has its own counts, published from basic unless the table says otherwise. A mean wait or service time covers only the instances that reached that step, so report the counts beside it:

Population Which entities Counts completed left the model after their last task flows.<arrival>.finished; tasks.<task>.finished per task still present started and not yet ended when the statistics are read flows.<arrival>.in_system; tasks.<task>.in_progress, the instances queued or started, from minimal rejected refused to join a queue, as their balk held tasks.<task>.balked abandoned left a queue when their patience ran out, or ended by an interrupt under on_interrupt: abandon tasks.<task>.reneged; an abandoned flow leaves in_system without adding to finished or failed, and tasks.<task>.interrupted counts the interrupts failed ended in a failure that no on_fail handled flows.<arrival>.failed; tasks.<task>.failed counts failed instances warm-up-crossing started before the warm-up ended and ended after it in finished, and in the wait and service times with their whole wait, but not in started

An entity a task spawns (Start a Flow Without Waiting) counts as a flow of its own under the spawned task's name. So flows.<task>.* and tasks.<task>.* cover it as they cover any arrival's flow. The spawning entity's key is in attr.parent.

Without a warm-up, started is finished plus in_system plus the entities that balked, reneged, failed or were abandoned. A warm-up starts started, finished, failed and the outcome counts again from zero, and leaves in_system and in_progress as they are. After a warm-up, finished also counts the warm-up-crossing entities, which started leaves out, so finished can be larger than started. End Conditions counts each population of a run.

docs.title: Add Readings of Your Own
docs.text:
Anything else is a custom reading: a function called at an interval of simulation time, which publishes with context.publish(name, value) as <sim_id>.<name>. It can read resources, stores, containers or any registry value.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/statistics.yaml:custom
telemetry:
  # Readings of your own: called as packers_report(context) every 30 seconds
  - interval: 30
    function: !python shop_logic.packers_report

The function is in shop_logic.py, beside the blueprint:

docs/snippets/yaml/shop_logic.py:packers-report
def packers_report(context):
    """A custom reading: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get(f"{context.sim_id}.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate
docs/snippets/pages/built_in_statistics.py:builder-custom
@app.telemetry_loop(interval=30.0)
def packers_report(context: SimulationContext):
    """Readings of your own: orders waiting per packer, and the live arrival rate."""
    packers = context.get_resource("packers")
    waiting = len(packers.queue)
    context.publish("waiting_per_packer", waiting / max(packers.capacity, 1))
    rate = context.env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value
    context.publish("arrival_rate", rate)  # as Shop.arrival_rate

A process that loops, publishes with env.publish_telemetry(name, value) and waits with env.timeout(interval) does the same.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The environment keeps one Statistics object, env.stats, which collects nothing until a level above none is set. Its timer publishes every value at each interval, and the teardown publishes them once more. When the timer has already published at the teardown's time, the teardown publishes only the values that changed since.

Readings now. capacity, in_use, queue_length and level are read from the object at the moment of publishing. in_use counts the units held by tasks, and a capacity drop does not take busy units away. After a drop, in_use can therefore be above capacity, and utilization (in_use ÷ capacity × 100) can be above 100%. A resource with no limit (current_cap: .inf) publishes capacity as null and a utilization of 0. A store or container with no limit publishes its capacity as null too.

Breakdowns. A resource with a breakdown reads down now: 1 while it is down, 0 otherwise. downtime adds the length of each down period, and of one still going on. failures adds one at each failure. Model Breakdowns checks both against the events.

Averages over time. utilization_avg, queue_length_avg and level_avg weigh each value by how long it lasted. Each resource, store and container reports every change, and the statistics add the area under the value since the last change, so the average is exact at any moment rather than sampled:

Counts. finished adds one when a task instance finishes, and a flow's finished adds one when an entity's last task has no next task. A flow's started adds one when an entity's first task instance begins, before its balk check and its queue, whether or not it is then served. An entity that the spawn key or an on: spawn action starts is counted at the spawn when the spawn has no after. With an after, it is counted when the spawned task starts, after the delay. in_system is the number of the flow's entities in the model now: started, and not yet finished, failed or gone. Which Entities a Count Covers shows how started adds up. A task's in_progress is the number of its instances queued or started and not yet ended, now. A low-level process reports an entity's start with env.stats.flow_started(arrival). It reports an entity that leaves without finishing or failing with env.stats.flow_ended(arrival). A task's balked adds one when an instance refuses to join its queue, reneged when one leaves the queue after its patience, and failed when one fails (Failures). A flow's failed adds one when an entity's flow ends in a failure no on_fail handles. interrupted and preempted add one for each interrupt or preemption an instance receives, and resumed when it is served again. Each is published once it is above 0. A balked, reneged or failed instance adds no wait or service time. An interrupted instance that resumes adds one wait, the sum of all its waits, and one service time, the time it was served. A low-level process counts them with env.stats.task_balked(task, instance), env.stats.task_reneged(task, instance), env.stats.task_failed(task, instance), env.stats.flow_failed(arrival), env.stats.task_interrupted(task, instance, preempted=...) and env.stats.task_resumed(task, instance).

Wait and service. The wait of a task instance runs from its queued step to its started step, and its service from started to finished. A task that never queues, such as a timed step, waits 0. typical keeps only a count, a total and a maximum of each, so the memory they use does not grow with the run. all keeps every observation and computes the percentiles exactly with NumPy's percentile at each publication, so its memory grows with the number of tasks.

Warm-up. A run's warmup resets every statistic once, at that time: the averages start again from zero area, and the counts and observations from zero. An instance that was queued before the reset and starts after it counts with its whole wait. Time and Pacing describes the warm-up.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Cost. minimal reads a few values at each publication. basic adds a little work at every change of a resource, store or container. typical adds a little at every task step. all keeps every wait and service time in memory for the whole run. Use it for runs of thousands of tasks, not for a generator that runs for days.
  • One way to get resource readings. Before 0.21.0, a telemetry entry could publish <resource>.<reading> by name. That shortcut is gone: stats: minimal publishes the same readings, under Shop.stats.resources.<name>.<reading>. telemetry now takes only a function, for readings of your own.
  • One run is one sample. The statistics describe one run with one seed. Values from the same run are not independent of each other, and another seed gives other values. Replications give independent values. Trusting Results shows what that means for a result, and Replications run a model with many seeds.
  • A task appears once it has run. At typical and all, a task's statistics are published from the first time it starts. At basic, they are published from the first time it finishes.

docs.title: Example: Measuring a Run
docs.text:
The measuring example publishes every statistic of the packers and the pack task every 5 minutes of simulation time, and leaves out a 3-minute warm-up. When packing slows down, it sends a ground-truth record to a sink of its own. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own.

The tutorial page Measuring a Run teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

desflow examples get downloads the example at the release you install, into a folder of its own. Pick uv or pip:

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api yaml
cd measuring/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run measuring.yaml

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api yaml
cd measuring/yaml

# 3. Run it
desflow run measuring.yaml
examples/yaml/measuring.yaml:measure
# Every level: readings, counts and time averages, mean and maximum wait and service,
# and their 50th, 95th and 99th percentiles, such as Shop.stats.tasks.pack.wait_p95.
stats: {level: all, interval: 5 min}

scenario:
  # Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average. The record is the ground truth.
  - at: 12 min
    path: Shop.service.packing.scale
    value: 1.2
    record: {fault: slow_packing, cause: new packing material}

The whole file is examples/yaml/measuring.yaml.

Quick Start

uvpip 
# 1. Install
uv tool install desflow

# 2. Download the example
desflow examples get measuring --api builder
cd measuring/builder

# 3. Run it
uv run --no-project --with desflow measuring_example.py

# 1. Install
pip install desflow

# 2. Download the example

cd measuring/builder

# 3. Run it

examples/builder/measuring_example.py:fault
def slow_packing(context):
    """Packing slows from 4 to 4.8 seconds on average at 12 minutes, with its label."""
    yield context.env.timeout(720)
    path = "Shop.service.packing.scale"
    registry = context.env.registry
    old = registry.get(path).value
    registry.update(path, 1.2)
    context.env.publish_label(
        {"fault": "slow_packing", "cause": "new packing material"},
        path=path,
        old=old,
        new=registry.get(path).value,
    )


app.add_process(slow_packing)

The whole file is examples/builder/measuring_example.py.

docs.title: Tasks and Processes: SimulationContext
docs.text: A task is what one entity does: an order being packed, a return being logged. A process is anything else that runs over time: packers going on a break every hour, a speed that drifts, a shift plan. This page shows how to write a task, what run() does with tasks, and what a task does step by step. Processes shows how to write a process.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: Both are SimPy generators: functions that yield to wait. The builder and YAML write the common ones for you, and the low-level API writes them by hand. A task waits for what it needs, does its work for a sampled time, publishes an event at each step, and may lead to the next task. A process can do anything a generator can: wait, change values in the registry, publish records or start tasks.

docs.title: Pages in This Section
docs.text:
• Processes: run a generator alongside the tasks, with an example of processes that interact.
  • Signals and Waiting: wait for signals, conditions and child flows, start flows, and run actions when an event happens.
  • Failures: when a task fails, what a failure does, and what happens to one nobody handles.

docs.title: A Task
docs.text:
A task with a service and a resource asks for a unit of the resource, holds it for a time drawn from the service, and releases it. A task with neither takes no time and holds nothing: it publishes its payload at once. Such a task suits a step that only records an event, such as logging a return.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:task
tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing  # how long the work takes
    resource: packers  # what it holds while it works
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}  # the finished event's value
    next: print_label  # the task that follows; Task Flow has the other forms
  return_logged:
    # No service and no resource: publishes its payload at once
    payload: {event_type: return_logged}

payload is a fixed mapping. A payload that changes per entity is a Python function, called as function(task_id, context):

docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:payload-function
# also under tasks: a payload computed by a Python function
pack_with_delivery:
  service: packing
  resource: packers
  # Called as choose_delivery(task_id, context) when the order gets a packer
  payload: !python shop_logic.choose_delivery
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-task
@app.task(service_id="packing", resource_id="packers", next="print_label")
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # Runs when the order gets a packer, before the packing time.
    # The returned dict is the finished event's value.
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task()  # no service and no resource: publishes at once
def return_logged(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "return_logged"}

The function is called with the task id and whatever the caller passes. It also receives entity, upstream and item by keyword when it declares a parameter of that name: the entity, what the previous task handed on, and what a store get took. A function that declares none of them is called without them.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-task
def pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids):
    """What @app.task does, by hand."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        payload = {"event_type": "order_packed"}
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        publish(payload)
    # next: print_label, a new instance for the same order
    env.process(print_label_process(env, sampler, key, next(label_ids)))

This is ordinary SimPy: packers.request() waits for a unit, env.timeout waits the service time, and leaving the with block releases the unit. The env.publish_event call at each step produces the records.

A task can also take from or add to a store or container (get, put), rank its requests (priority), and name the task that follows it (next). Stores and Containers, Resources and Task Flow describe each.

docs.title: A Timed Step
docs.text:
A task with a service and no resource is a timed step: work that takes time but needs nothing that can be busy, such as printing a label or waiting for a supplier. It publishes started at once, with no queued event, waits the sampled time, and publishes its finished event. Its wait is 0. It is SimPy's env.timeout: the tests check that it ends at the same simulation time as a plain SimPy timeout in all three APIs (SimPy Compatibility).

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:timed-step
print_label:
  # A service and no resource: a timed step that starts at once
  service: labelling
  payload: {event_type: label_printed}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-timed-step
@app.task(service_id="labelling")  # a service and no resource: starts at once
def print_label(task_id: int):
    return {"event_type": "label_printed"}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-timed-step
def print_label_process(env, sampler, key, task_id):
    """A timed step: started at once, with no queued event."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.labelling"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="print_label", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
    publish({"event_type": "label_printed"})

docs.title: Arrivals Start Tasks
docs.text:
An arrival starts one task per arrival. The loop draws a gap from the arrival's distribution, waits for that duration, starts a task for the new entity, and repeats. The task runs on its own while the loop waits for the next arrival.

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:arrival
arrivals:
  # Each arrival spawns one pack_order, and one return_logged
  # An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2)
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.2, spawn: pack_order}
  # A return every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
  returns: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.1, spawn: return_logged}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-arrival
# Each arrival starts one pack_order
# An order every 5 s on average (rate 0.2)
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.2, spawn="pack_order")

spawn= starts the named task for each arrival's entity, whose key is the arrival name and a counter: orders-1, orders-2. The record's instance comes from the task's one counter, which next and other arrivals share, so no two runs of the task share an id. A spawn that names a task never added is refused when run() checks the model.

@app.arrival_loop runs a generator of your own. The loop below starts one return_logged for each return, which is what spawn="return_logged" does in one argument, as the YAML tab writes it. A loop is needed only when it does more than start one task, such as choosing the task from the entity's attributes. context.wait_for_arrival returns the new Entity. Pass it to the task with entity=. A task called without one starts an entity of its own, keyed by the task's name and a counter, such as return_logged-1. The task_id becomes the record's instance. Take it from context.next_instance, the task's one counter.

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-arrival-loop
# A return every 10 s on average (rate 0.1)
app.add_arrival("returns", dist="exponential", rate=0.1)


@app.arrival_loop("returns")
def returns(context: SimulationContext):
    while True:
        # Draws the next gap, waits for it, and returns the new entity, keyed returns-1, ...
        parcel = yield context.wait_for_arrival("returns")
        task_id = context.next_instance("return_logged")  # the task's one counter
        context.spawn(return_logged(task_id, entity=parcel))  # the loop goes on at once
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-arrival
def orders_process(env, sampler, packers):
    """What an arrival with spawn does, by hand."""
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")
    label_ids = itertools.count()
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))
        key = f"orders-{task_id + 1}"
        env.process(pack_order_process(env, sampler, packers, key, task_id, label_ids))
        task_id += 1

In the low-level API every loop is started once, before the run:

docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-start
env.process(orders_process(env, sampler, packers))  # start each loop once
env.process(breaks_process(env, "packers", every=50, duration=5))

docs.title: Records of a Task
docs.text:
Every event of a task carries three fields beside its value: key, the entity's key; task, the task's name; and instance, the number of this run of the task, counted from 0 for each task. The first order of the blueprint in A Task, packed and then labelled:

[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'queued'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 3.672, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.packing', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'pack_order', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'order_packed'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 5.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'path_id': 'Shop.service.labelling', 'status': 'started'}}
[EVT] {'sim_ts': 7.369, 'timestamp': '...', 'key': 'orders-1', 'task': 'print_label', 'instance': 0, 'value': {'event_type': 'label_printed'}}

All five events share the key orders-1, so an order can be followed through every task it passes. The finished event's value is exactly the payload. Records and Telemetry describes every field.

docs.title: What run() Does
docs.text:
run() builds everything the context describes and runs it, in this order:

Until run() is called nothing exists but the description, and the runtime helpers that Builder API lists raise RuntimeError. Teardown runs in a finally block, so the last statistics are published and every sink is flushed even when the run stops with an error or Ctrl+C.

docs.title: What @app.task Does
docs.text:
@app.task turns your function into a SimPy process that does these steps, publishing a record at three of them:

  1. If its balk condition holds, it publishes balked and stops.
  2. If it has a wait, a resource or a get, it publishes queued and starts its patience timer, which runs only while it waits. Then it waits until its wait ends.
  3. It asks for the resource, in the resource's queue order, then takes its get from a store or container, waiting while there is not enough.
  4. It publishes started, calls your function, and keeps what it returns as the payload. The payload is computed before the service time, so it can use the state of the simulation at that moment.
  5. It waits the service time, drawn from the live distribution.
  6. It adds its put to a store or container, waiting while there is no room, and checks its fail condition.
  7. It publishes the payload as the finished event, or failed, and releases the resource.
  8. It fires its signal (or fails it) and sends its interrupt action to the tasks it names. It applies set to the entity's attributes. Then it starts the next task that its next chooses, or its on_fail task, as a new instance for the same entity.

A YAML task and its spawn make the same task and arrival loop that the builder code above makes. The code that runs these steps is TaskRun in desflow/core/task.py. In SimPy terms each task run is one process started with env.process, and each arrival loop is another. SimPy and desflow describes processes.

A process outside a task runs as Processes describes.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
• Resources are acquired in one order. A task can hold several resources and hand one to the next task, but tasks that acquire two resources in opposite orders are refused: Several Resources.
  • An interrupt gives back everything. An interrupted task cancels its waits and releases every unit it holds before it follows its on_interrupt, so a resumed task queues again behind the requests already waiting: Interruptions.
  • A finished event is exactly the payload. It has no status or path_id unless the payload includes them.
  • A condition branch checks after every change. In a model with many waits on conditions and many changes, the work grows in proportion to both.
  • Runtime helpers need a running simulation. They raise RuntimeError before run(), as Builder API lists. Call them inside a loop, task or process.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text: This page shows when a task fails and what happens next.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A failure is a task that does not finish its work: an order that fails its check, a wait that fails, code that raises an error. desflow records it, then sends the entity to a task that handles it, or ends the entity's flow.

A task fails in three cases:

  • Its fail condition holds after its service. fail reads the task's own payload as payload.<field>, as next does.
  • The wait it needs fails.
  • Its function raises an exception. The function is a builder task's function or a YAML task's !python payload function.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
run.on_unhandled_failure sets what happens to a failure of a task, child flow or one-shot signal that nobody handles. It has two values:

  • continue, the default in YAML and the builder: the failure is marked as handled (SimPy calls this defused), and the run goes on. A data generator should not stop on one failed order.
  • stop, the default in the low-level API: the failure stops the run, as plain SimPy does. A root task that fails with no on_fail raises an exception, and so does a one-shot signal failed with nobody waiting. The exception reaches the caller of run().

The builder and YAML switch to stop with run(on_unhandled_failure="stop") or run: {on_unhandled_failure: stop}, and the low-level API switches to continue with DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure="continue"). In the low-level API, an exception raised in a process always reaches the process that yields it, and one nobody handles stops the run, as in SimPy.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Under run:

docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:unhandled
# continue, the default: a failure nobody handles is defused and the run goes on;
# stop raises it to the caller of run()
on_unhandled_failure: continue

Under stop, the failure reaches the caller of run() as an exception. TaskFailed names the task and the reason, and this prints pack failed: after the cut-off:

docs/snippets/pages/failures.py:task-failed
# Under stop, the first failure that no on_fail handles reaches the caller of run()
try:
    shop().run(until=60, on_unhandled_failure="stop")
except TaskFailed as failure:
    print(f"{failure.task} failed: {failure.reason}")

stop is the default. DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure="continue") switches to continue.

A run that stops on a signal raises SignalFailed when the signal fails, as Run Length describes:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

run.stop names the signal. When the signal fails, desflow run reports the reason and exits with an error.

This prints closing failed: the till did not balance:

docs/snippets/pages/failures.py:signal-failed
# A run that stops on a signal raises the reason the signal failed with
try:
    shop().run(until=60, stop={"signal": "closing"})
except SignalFailed as failure:
    print(f"{failure.signal} failed: {failure.reason}")

env.run(until=event) on the signal's event raises the exception the event failed with, as in SimPy.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
A failed task then does three things, in order:

  1. It publishes failed instead of its finished payload, with a reason: the condition's text, or its fail_reason.
  2. It fails its signal, so every task waiting for the signal fails too.
  3. It goes to its on_fail task. Without on_fail, the entity's flow ends, and a child flow fails the task waiting for it, with the same reason.

At the basic statistics level and above, each failure is counted as tasks.<task>.failed, and each flow that ends in one as flows.<arrival>.failed. The inspect task of the example in Signals and Waiting fails a gift and sends it to be wrapped.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text: The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in Stability and Limits on the Tasks and Processes page.

docs.title: Processes
docs.text: A process runs alongside the tasks. This page shows how to write one, and an example in which processes and tasks interact.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: A process is anything in the shop that runs over time but is not one entity's work: a break for the packers, a drift in a parameter, a delivery schedule. An arrival starts one task per entity, while a process starts once, when the run starts, and runs alongside the tasks.

docs.title: A Process
docs.text:
This process sends the packers on a 5-second break every 50 seconds:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/tasks.yaml:process
processes:
  # Called as breaks(context, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
  - function: !python shop_logic.breaks
    kwargs: {resource: packers, every: 50, duration: 5}
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:builder-process
def breaks(context: SimulationContext, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """Takes every packer off for a break of `duration` seconds every `every` seconds."""
    path = f"{context.sim_id}.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    registry = context.env.registry
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(every)
        normal = registry.get(path).value
        registry.update(path, 0)
        yield context.env.timeout(duration)
        registry.update(path, normal)


app.add_process(breaks, resource="packers", every=50, duration=5)
docs/snippets/pages/tasks.py:low-level-process
def breaks_process(env, resource: str, every: float, duration: float):
    """What add_process starts, by hand: a plain SimPy generator."""
    path = f"Shop.resources.{resource}.current_cap"
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(every)
        normal = env.registry.get(path).value
        env.registry.update(path, 0)
        yield env.timeout(duration)
        env.registry.update(path, normal)

Setting current_cap to 0 stops new work but not the work in progress: Resources explains what happens to busy units when a capacity drops.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
add_process(func, **kwargs) starts func(context, **kwargs) when the run starts, and a YAML processes entry does the same with a !python function. Inside it, context.env is the DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, so a process can do anything a low-level script does: context.env.timeout, context.env.registry.update, context.env.publish_event. A process is how low-level code joins a builder or YAML model.

context.env.active_process is the running SimPy process. Its name is the task's name, because a task's process is named after the task. Its target is the event it waits on now, or None once it has ended. A condition reads the same three values as process.name, process.instance (the task's instance id, the instance field of its records) and process.target, a string such as timeout, signal.<name>, task.<name>, condition, resource.<name>, get.<name>, put.<name> or service. In a task's own expressions they name that task. In an interrupt or running where, they name each instance tested.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text: The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in Stability and Limits on the Tasks and Processes page.

docs.title: Example: Process Interaction
docs.text:
The process-interaction example combines a child flow, a failure that on_fail handles, and orders that wait for a courier's signal or a time limit. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 300 simulation seconds.

The tutorial page Process Interaction teaches these features step by step.

YAMLBuilderLow-level

docs.title: Signals and Waiting
docs.text:
A task can wait for signals, conditions and child flows, start other flows and run actions when an event happens. This page shows each.

The tutorial page Process Interaction teaches these features step by step.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text: In a shop, work often depends on other work. An order waits until its parts are picked, a courier leaves once an order is packed, and a guard is told when an alarm round ends. desflow models this with four tools: a wait that a task makes before it asks for its resource, signals that tasks fire, flows that a task starts without waiting for them, and actions that run when an event happens.

docs.title: Wait, Signals and Child Flows
docs.text:
A task can wait for something before it queues for its resource: its wait. A wait has one branch, or a group of several named branches: any, all or at_least. A branch can itself be a group, so waits nest. An empty any or all succeeds at once. In SimPy, AnyOf waits for the first event and AllOf for every event, and a Condition with a count rule does what at_least does. Wait for One or All shows the groups. A leaf branch is one of:

Branch Waits for Its value {signal: name} the next firing of a signal declared under signals (builder add_signal) the firing's value, the payload of the task that fired it {task: name} a child flow: that task, started for the same entity with its own instance id, and the tasks its next leads to, until the flow ends the last task's finished payload {timeout: 40 s}, or {timeout: {after: 40 s, value: ...}} a time; value is carried to the waiter, as SimPy's env.timeout(delay, value) None, or the value given {condition: level.stock >= 5} a condition to hold, checked when the wait starts and again after every store or container change, change in a queue that the condition reads, registry update, signal firing and finished task True {request: name} a unit of a resource; a won unit is held through the service and given back when the task ends the request {get: {store: name}} or {get: {container: name, amount: 2}} an item or an amount, as a task get does the item taken {put: {store: name}} or {put: {container: name, amount: 2}} room to add the payload of the task before it, or an amount none {running: {task: name, where: ...}} every running instance of a task, on the waiter's entity and on the entities it spawned, to end, as SimPy's yield process does; where narrows them, read in each instance's scope; when none match, the wait is done at once the one instance's finished payload, or a mapping from instance id to payload for several, in start order

A running branch waits for tasks already running. Here an order waits for the delivery it started, unless the delivery has already left with the van:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/wait_groups.yaml:running
# Wait for the delivery this order started, unless it has left with the van
wait:
  running:
    task: deliver
    where: process.target != 'service'

@app.task(wait=...) takes the same mapping as a dict: wait={"running": {"task": "deliver", "where": "process.target != 'service'"}}.

A low-level process waits for another by yielding it, as SimPy's yield process does.

A single branch is named after its signal, task or resource, or timeout, condition, get or put. After the wait, each branch has three values:

  • wait.<branch>.done says whether the branch happened before the wait ended.
  • wait.<branch>.ok says whether it succeeded.
  • wait.<branch>.value (or .value.<field>) is its value.

next, fail and amounts read these values, and a builder function that declares wait receives them as a mapping.

A task fires a signal with signal: name when it finishes, with its payload as the value. Any condition reads the signal as signal.<name>.count, .ok and .value. The process-interaction example waits for a child flow, then for the first of a courier's signal and a time limit:

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:check
check:
  # Starts the child flow inspect and waits for it to end.
  wait: {task: inspect}
  payload: {event_type: order_checked}
  next: dispatch
inspect:
  service: inspecting
  payload: {event_type: inspected}
  # A gift fails inspection; on_fail sends it to wrap, and the flow goes on.
  fail: attr.gift == 1
  fail_reason: gift needs wrapping
  on_fail: wrap
wrap:
  service: wrapping
  payload: {event_type: wrapped}
examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:dispatch
dispatch:
  # The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first.
  wait:
    any:
      courier: {signal: courier_left}
      limit: {timeout: 40 s}
  payload: {event_type: dispatched}
  next:
    when: [{condition: wait.courier.done, task: by_courier}]
    default: by_post
examples/yaml/process_interaction.yaml:courier
courier:
  payload: {event_type: courier_left}
  # Fires courier_left with this payload; every order waiting for it resumes.
  signal: courier_left
examples/builder/process_interaction_example.py:check
# Starts the child flow inspect and waits for it to end
@app.task(wait={"task": "inspect"}, next="dispatch")
def check(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "order_checked"}


# A gift fails inspection; on_fail sends it to wrap, and the flow goes on
@app.task(
    service_id="inspecting",
    fail="attr.gift == 1",
    fail_reason="gift needs wrapping",
    on_fail="wrap",
)
def inspect(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "inspected"}


@app.task(service_id="wrapping")
def wrap(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "wrapped"}
examples/builder/process_interaction_example.py:dispatch
# The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first
@app.task(
    wait={"any": {"courier": {"signal": "courier_left"}, "limit": {"timeout": 40}}},
    next={
        "when": [{"condition": "wait.courier.done", "task": "by_courier"}],
        "default": "by_post",
    },
)
def dispatch(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "dispatched"}
examples/builder/process_interaction_example.py:courier
# Fires courier_left with this payload; every order waiting for it resumes
@app.task(signal="courier_left")
def courier(task_id, context):
    return {"event_type": "courier_left"}

context.signal(name) returns the Signal, which a process can fire, fail or wait for. context.call(task, entity=...) starts a child flow from a process and returns its SimPy process, which a process can yield. context.spawn returns the process it starts too, so is_alive, triggered, ok and value inspect it, as in SimPy.

examples/low-level/process_interaction_example.py:check
def check(shop, key, arrival):
    """Starts the child process inspect and waits for it to end."""
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("check")
    shop.publish(key, "check", task_id, {"status": "queued"})
    stats.task_queued("check", task_id)
    yield env.any_of([env.process(inspect(shop, key, arrival))])
    shop.publish(key, "check", task_id, {"status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("check", task_id)
    shop.publish(key, "check", task_id, {"event_type": "order_checked"})
    stats.task_finished("check", task_id)
    env.process(dispatch(shop, key, arrival))


def inspect(shop, key, arrival):
    """A gift fails inspection and is wrapped instead; returns the last payload."""
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("inspect")
    path_id = "Shop.service.inspecting"
    shop.publish(key, "inspect", task_id, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("inspect", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(shop.service("inspecting")[1])
    if GIFT[arrival] == 1:
        failed = {
            "path_id": path_id,
            "status": "failed",
            "reason": "gift needs wrapping",
        }
        shop.publish(key, "inspect", task_id, failed)
        stats.task_failed("inspect", task_id)
        return (yield env.process(wrap(shop, key)))
    payload = {"event_type": "inspected"}
    shop.publish(key, "inspect", task_id, payload)
    stats.task_finished("inspect", task_id)
    return payload


def wrap(shop, key):
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("wrap")
    path_id = "Shop.service.wrapping"
    shop.publish(key, "wrap", task_id, {"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("wrap", task_id)
    yield env.timeout(shop.service("wrapping")[1])
    payload = {"event_type": "wrapped"}
    shop.publish(key, "wrap", task_id, payload)
    stats.task_finished("wrap", task_id)
    return payload
examples/low-level/process_interaction_example.py:dispatch
def dispatch(shop, key, arrival):
    """The courier's departure, or 40 seconds, whichever comes first."""
    env, stats, task_id = shop.env, shop.env.stats, shop.next_id("dispatch")
    shop.publish(key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "queued"})
    stats.task_queued("dispatch", task_id)
    courier = shop.courier_left.wait()
    done = yield env.any_of([courier, env.timeout(40)])
    shop.publish(key, "dispatch", task_id, {"status": "started"})
    stats.task_started("dispatch", task_id)
    shop.publish(key, "dispatch", task_id, {"event_type": "dispatched"})
    stats.task_finished("dispatch", task_id)
    task = "by_courier" if courier in done else "by_post"
    env.process(send(shop, key, arrival, task))
examples/low-level/process_interaction_example.py:courier
def courier(shop, key):
    """Fires courier_left; every order waiting for it resumes."""
    task_id = shop.next_id("courier")
    shop.env.stats.flow_started("couriers")
    payload = {"event_type": "courier_left"}
    shop.publish(key, "courier", task_id, payload)
    shop.env.stats.task_finished("courier", task_id)
    shop.courier_left.fire(payload)
    shop.env.stats.flow_finished("couriers")
    yield shop.env.timeout(0)

The low-level API is plain SimPy here: a child is env.process(...), its value is what it returns, and env.any_of and env.all_of wait for the first or for every event. Signal(env, name) is the named event the builder and YAML use. env.watch_changes(check) calls check after every change a condition can read. env.watch_changes(check, queues=True) also calls it after a change in the number of puts or gets waiting at a store or container.

docs.title: One-Shot Signals
docs.text: A signal written as a mapping with once: true (builder add_signal(name, once=True)) fires once, as SimPy's Event does. It does not re-arm, so a task that waits for it after it has fired resumes at once. A second firing is refused. A plain signal keeps re-arming after each firing, so a waiter that starts later waits for the next. A closing-time signal is a one-shot: signals: {closing: {once: true}}.

docs.title: Start a Flow Without Waiting
docs.text:
A task's spawn starts another task as a new entity, keyed <task>-n, and goes on at once, as SimPy's env.process starts a process without yielding it. A courier that leaves once an order is packed is a spawn: spawn: {task: courier} on the pack task, or @app.task(spawn={"task": "courier"}). A process spawns a generator with context.spawn(generator). The spawned entity is an entity like any other:

  • It enters and leaves the model as any entity does, so a drain waits for it.
  • It counts as a flow of its own, under the spawned task's name.
  • Its records carry its own key, and the spawning entity's key is read as attr.parent.

A spawned task cannot share its name with an arrival, because their flow statistics and entity numbers would merge.

spawn: {task: courier, after: 3 s} starts the new entity 3 seconds after the task finishes, as SimPy's start_delayed does. context.spawn(generator, delay=3) does the same for a process. A drain that ends during the delay ends the run before the spawned entity starts, as it does for an arrival not yet due. An after of 0 or less is refused.

A task's interrupt runs when the task finishes, as a spawn does. Here the task that closes the shop interrupts each order still being checked, and starts a sweep 2 seconds later:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:task-actions
# When the shop closes: stop each order still being checked, and start a sweep
# 2 seconds later
interrupt: {task: check, where: "process.target == 'service'", cause: closing}
spawn: {task: sweep, after: 2 s}

@app.task(interrupt=..., spawn=...) takes the same two mappings as dicts.

A low-level process calls process.interrupt(cause) on each process it stops, and starts the sweep with env.process after a timeout of 2 seconds.

docs.title: Be Told When a Flow Ends
docs.text: A task's subscribe asks to be interrupted when something happens, rather than pausing for it. subscribe: {task: charger} starts the charger child flow, and interrupts the task when that flow ends, with the cause {"event": "charger", "value": <charger's payload>}. The task then follows its on_interrupt, as it does for any interrupt. context.subscribe(event) subscribes a process to any SimPy event, a process included, as SimPy's subscribe_at does. It refuses an event that has already happened.

docs.title: Actions When an Event Happens
docs.text:
An on: list runs actions when a signal fires or a task ends, before any waiter, as a SimPy callback runs when its event fires. The list belongs to a task or to a signal. On a task, it runs however the task ends: finish, balk, renege, abandon or failure. Each entry is one of:

  • fire: {signal: name} fires a signal. value fires it with a literal value. from: name copies an outcome instead. For a signal, it copies the signal's latest outcome. For a task, it copies the finished payload, or the failure reason, of the last instance of that task to end on the entity. SimPy's trigger copies another event's outcome in the same way. With nothing to copy yet it fires nothing and logs a warning. value and from together are refused. On a one-shot signal, urgent: true makes the waiters resume before the other events at their time, as SimPy's URGENT priority orders them. after: 5 s fires it 5 seconds from now, as env.schedule(event, priority, delay) does. The signal counts as fired at once, so a second fire is refused. A drain does not count the entity that fired it as waiting for the later firing. On a signal that re-arms, urgent and after are refused at build, with once: true named as the fix.
  • spawn: {task, after} starts a new entity, as the spawn key does.
  • interrupt: {task, where, cause} interrupts running instances, as a task's interrupt does.
  • path with value sets a registry value, as a scenario step does.

The same closing task with an on: list: it stops the packing by hand, makes the orders come every 6 seconds, and fires a one-shot reminder with a value 5 seconds later:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:on-actions
# However the task ends: stop the packing by hand, make the orders come every
# 6 seconds, and remind the couriers 5 seconds later
on:
  - interrupt: {task: pack_by_hand, cause: closing}
  - {path: Shop.arrival.orders.value, value: 6}
  - fire: {signal: reminder, value: last parcels, after: 5 s}

@app.task(on=[...]) takes the same list of mappings.

A low-level model adds a callback to the event, as SimPy's event.callbacks runs one when the event fires.

A one-shot closing signal with an on: action that fires last_call before the other events at closing time:

YAMLBuilderLow-level docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:urgent
closing:
  once: true
  on:
    # Tell the couriers before anything else that happens at closing time
    - fire: {signal: last_call, urgent: true}
last_call: {once: true}

app.add_signal("closing", once=True, on=[{"fire": {"signal": "last_call", "urgent": True}}]) declares the same signal, and app.add_signal("last_call", once=True) the other.

A low-level model schedules the event with SimPy's URGENT priority, env.schedule(event, URGENT).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The task publishes queued when its wait starts, so the wait counts in its wait statistics. Its patience covers the wait as well as its resource and its get. When an any wait ends, its losing signal, timeout and condition branches are dropped. Its losing child flows keep running, as SimPy leaves processes running. Wait for One or All shows ties and failures. A wait for signals, tasks and times holds no resource. Waiting for all of several such things reserves nothing: the task asks for its resource only after the wait.

A drain waits for a task's on: actions and for the on: actions of signals its tasks fire, so a final task that fires a signal with on: actions leaves only after they have run.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text: The limits of this page are listed with those of the whole section, in Stability and Limits on the Tasks and Processes page.

docs.title: Example: Process Events
docs.text:
The process-events example combines the event features of this page:

  • A guard starts an alarm round and is told when it ends (subscribe).
  • A packed order fires the ready signal from its own payload, for a waiting shipper (an on: action with fire ... from).
  • A one-shot closing signal has an on: action that spawns a sweep one second later (spawn with after).

The arrival gaps are set so that each of these happens once. It needs no Docker service and ends on its own after 12 simulation seconds.

YAMLBuilderLow-level examples/yaml/process_events.yaml:events
signals:
  # A plain signal re-arms; the one-shot closing fires once and spawns a sweep
  ready: {}
  closing:
    once: true
    on:
      - spawn: {task: sweep, after: 1 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: constant, value: 6, spawn: pack}
  shippers: {dist: constant, value: 7, spawn: ship}
  closers: {dist: constant, value: 9, spawn: close}
  guards: {dist: constant, value: 8, spawn: guard}

tasks:
  # A packed order fires ready from its own finished payload; a shipper reads it
  pack:
    service: packing
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
    on:
      - fire: {signal: ready, from: pack}
  ship:
    wait: {signal: ready}
    payload: {event_type: order_shipped}
  # Fires the one-shot closing when the shop closes
  close:
    signal: closing
    payload: {event_type: shop_closed}
  sweep:
    service: sweeping
    payload: {event_type: floor_swept}
  # The guard starts an alarm round and is interrupted when it ends
  guard:
    service: guarding
    subscribe: {task: alarm}
    on_interrupt: abandon
    payload: {event_type: shift_done}
  alarm:
    service: alarming
    payload: {event_type: alarm_rang}
examples/builder/process_events_example.py:events
app = (
    SimulationContext(sim_id="Shop", factor=0, random_seed=42)
    .add_egress(ConsoleEgress())
    .add_service("packing", dist="constant", value=2)
    .add_service("alarming", dist="constant", value=2)
    .add_service("sweeping", dist="constant", value=1)
    .add_service("guarding", dist="constant", value=100)
    # A plain signal re-arms; the one-shot closing fires once and spawns a sweep
    .add_signal("ready")
    .add_signal("closing", once=True, on=[{"spawn": {"task": "sweep", "after": 1}}])
    .add_arrival("orders", dist="constant", value=6)
    .add_arrival("shippers", dist="constant", value=7)
    .add_arrival("closers", dist="constant", value=9)
    .add_arrival("guards", dist="constant", value=8)
)


# A packed order fires ready from its own finished payload; a shipper reads it
@app.task(service_id="packing", on=[{"fire": {"signal": "ready", "from": "pack"}}])
def pack(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task(wait={"signal": "ready"})
def ship(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "order_shipped"}


# Fires the one-shot closing when the shop closes
@app.task(signal="closing")
def close(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "shop_closed"}


@app.task(service_id="sweeping")
def sweep(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "floor_swept"}


# The guard starts an alarm round and is interrupted when it ends
@app.task(service_id="guarding", subscribe={"task": "alarm"}, on_interrupt="abandon")
def guard(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "shift_done"}


@app.task(service_id="alarming")
def alarm(task_id):
    return {"event_type": "alarm_rang"}

The low-level version uses plain SimPy for each of these: a Signal, an interrupt handled by env.any_of, and simpy.util.start_delayed. The whole file is in the Low-level tab of the Quick Start below.

Run the example in the form you use:

YAMLBuilderLow-level

Quick Start

# 2. Download the example

cd process-events/yaml

# 3. Run it

# 1. Install

# 2. Download the example

cd process-events/yaml

# 3. Run it

The whole file is examples/yaml/process_events.yaml.
