docs.title: Writing a Model
docs.text: desflow has three ways to write a simulation: a YAML blueprint, the builder API and the low-level API. This page says how they relate and which to choose. If you are new to desflow, start with First Simulation, which shows the same model in all three APIs side by side. Return here to look up a specific component.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
The three are layers, not alternatives. Each layer writes the one below it for you:

  • YAML blueprint: a file. SimulationContext.from_yaml, which desflow run calls, reads it and makes the same builder calls a Python script would make, so the result is an ordinary SimulationContext.
  • Builder API: SimulationContext collects resources, distributions, tasks and connectors through its methods and decorators. Its run() compiles them into a SimParameter, builds the environment, registers the parameters and starts the processes.
  • Low-level API: you write that last step by hand: a SimParameter, a DynamicRealtimeEnvironment that registers it, and SimPy processes that use the environment's resources and publish records.

Because each layer ends in the one below, the layers mix: a blueprint can reference Python written for the builder with !python, and a builder process can use the environment directly.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text: YAML Blueprint Builder API Low-level API Entry point desflow run or SimulationContext.from_yaml SimulationContext DynamicRealtimeEnvironment What you write the simulation, declared in a file; Python only for logic YAML cannot express, referenced with !python what the system looks like, with decorators for each task's steps how every event and resource operates, step by step What it does for you everything the builder does, and no Python to run publishing each task's events, requesting resources, sampling times, routing between tasks, statistics nothing: you queue, start, time out and release yourself Typical use changing rates, capacities, connectors and timed experiments between runs without editing code models whose logic is most of the program, and configuration built in code, for example from a loop what the builder does not do, such as resources created during a run

docs.title: Which to Choose
docs.text:
• YAML blueprint when the configuration is what changes between runs: a new arrival rate, another packer, a different broker, a scripted experiment. A file is easy to review and to diff, a run is one command, and a blueprint has a scenario of timed changes on the simulation clock built in. Logic that YAML cannot express goes in a Python module beside the file, as Call Python from YAML shows.
  • Builder API when most of the program is logic and you want it in one Python file, or when you build the configuration in code.
  • Low-level API when you need what the builder does not do, or full control of every event.

YAML Blueprints, Builder API and Low-level API, the next three pages, describe each way in full.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Whichever way a model is written, it builds the same environment, and one run goes the same way from there. How desflow Works shows that run and each part it passes through.

docs.title: YAML Blueprints
docs.text: A YAML blueprint is a simulation written as a file. This page shows how to run one, how a file is read and checked, how to change settings per environment, and where an error points. YAML Keys lists every key a blueprint accepts.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
A blueprint holds, as data, the builder calls that a Python script would make. Each section becomes the builder call of the same name: resources is add_resource, tasks is @app.task, stats is with_stats, and so on. There is no second way of building: SimulationContext.from_yaml makes those calls, in the order a script would, and returns an ordinary SimulationContext. A blueprint and a script that make the same calls produce the same simulation, and the tests check that the YAML, builder and low-level versions of every example publish the same records.

Use Python for logic that YAML cannot express. Reference it with !python, as Call Python from YAML shows.

docs.title: Run a Blueprint
docs.text:
Run it from a shell with the desflow command, which the package installs. These lines use the local example:

desflow examples get local --api yaml    # downloads local/yaml/local.yaml
cd local/yaml
desflow run local.yaml                   # runs until run.until
desflow run local.yaml --until 10min     # overrides run.until
desflow run local.yaml --seed 7          # overrides simulation.random_seed
desflow examples                         # lists the other examples
desflow --version

--until takes seconds or a duration such as 10 min, 2 hours or 1 week. The command logs at INFO level. ConsoleEgress, in its default log format, writes each batch at that level, so its output is visible. A run with no seed logs the seed it drew, with the command that repeats it. An invalid file prints its errors and exits with code 1.

Or run it from Python:

docs/snippets/pages/yaml_loading.py:from-yaml
from desflow import SimulationContext

app = SimulationContext.from_yaml("local.yaml")
app.run()  # calls run.before, then runs until run.until

run() calls the blueprint's run.before functions first, and uses run.until when no until is passed. The builder methods and decorators still work on the context from_yaml returns.

load_context loads a blueprint or a builder Python file by the same path, so a script that takes either kind of file needs no check of its own:

docs/snippets/pages/yaml_loading.py:load-context
from desflow import load_context

# A blueprint, or a builder Python file that defines a SimulationContext at
# module level, from its folder: the one loader desflow run and explain use
app = load_context(".", "local.yaml")

docs.title: Preview the Records
docs.text:
desflow run FILE builds the blueprint and runs it with its own sinks until --until, run.until or Ctrl+C. It takes a YAML file only. A Python builder file runs with python FILE. Two options print the records instead of sending them to the file's sinks:

Command Behaviour desflow run FILE --sample N Prints the first N events, then stops. N is 1 or more. The run is unpaced: factor is set to 0 and go_live_at is cleared. logical_start_time and random_seed are kept, so timestamps and values look as they would in the real run. Ingress entries and run.before are skipped. Telemetry records print between the events but are not counted, and system.simulation.lag_seconds is not printed. desflow run FILE --stdout Prints every record of a normal run except the system.simulation.lag_seconds readings, which describe the wall clock, not the model. factor, go_live_at, logical_start_time and ingress are kept; run.before is skipped.

Both replace every egress entry with one Console of format: json, and a second one for labels when the file has a when: labels entry. A JSON console writes each record as one JSON line on stdout. The run's log stays on stderr, so desflow run FILE --sample 10 | jq .value reads only the records.

A preview checks the whole file, but not the connectors it leaves out:

  • The structure, keys and names of the whole file are validated.
  • run.before is skipped, because its functions prepare the real sinks, such as creating topics. A warning on stderr says so when the file has any.
  • The connectors a preview replaces or skips are not built, so only their type is checked. Their config is checked only by a run that builds them, such as desflow run FILE without these options.
Combination Result --sample with --stdout Allowed. --stdout adds nothing. --sample with --until, or a file with run.until The run ends at whichever comes first. When until comes first, stderr says sample ended at until with k of N events. --sample on a file with go_live_at A backfill-then-live file prints its first history events. when: history and when: live have no effect, because their entries are replaced. --sample on a file that publishes no events It runs until until or Ctrl+C, printing telemetry. --stdout on a file with several egress entries One console prints each record once. Per-entry batch_size and flush_interval are dropped with the entries, and the batching section applies. --sample or --stdout with --replications Usage error, exit code 2: both print one run. --sample 0 Usage error, exit code 2.

Command Line lists every command and option.

docs.title: Times and Durations
docs.text:
A time in a blueprint is a number of seconds or a duration such as 90 s, 10 min, 2 hours or 1 week: run.until, a scenario step's at, simulation.warmup, a stats interval, and every time-valued distribution parameter. rate is the exception: it is a number per second.

logical_start_time and go_live_at are instants: now, a signed duration from now such as -1d or -10m, or an ISO datetime such as 2026-01-01T00:00:00. Both are read against one moment, when the file is loaded, so -10m and now are exactly ten minutes apart. now, the relative forms and an ISO datetime without an offset are read in simulation.timezone, UTC by default, as Clocks and Pacing describes.

docs.title: Settings per Environment
docs.text:
${VAR} in a value is replaced with the environment variable, so one file can serve several environments. ${VAR:-default} uses the default when the variable is unset or empty, as in a shell, and $${ writes a literal ${. An unquoted value is read as YAML reads it after the replacement, so factor: ${SIM_FACTOR:-0} is the number 0. A quoted value stays a string. An unset variable with no default stops the load, and the error names its line.

docs/snippets/yaml/environment.yaml
# Settings that change per environment, read from environment variables.
# Run it with: SIM_FACTOR=1 desflow run environment.yaml
simulation:
  sim_id: ${SIM_ID:-Shop}
  # An unquoted value is read after the replacement, so this is the number 0
  factor: ${SIM_FACTOR:-0}
  # Read against the moment the file is loaded: a day of history up to now
  logical_start_time: -1d
  # Under simulation: timestamps written in Melbourne time, with its offset; the
  # start and now are read in it. UTC by default
  timezone: ${SIM_TIMEZONE:-Australia/Melbourne}
  # Under simulation: how far the run is behind the wall clock, every 10 s; by
  # default off at factor 0 and every second otherwise, and 0 turns it off
  lag_interval: 10 s
  # Under simulation: raise RuntimeError when a paced step is more than factor
  # seconds behind the wall clock; false by default, and never checked at factor 0
  strict: true

egress:
  - type: Console

resources:
  # Quoted, because ${...} inside {...} would end the mapping early; the check
  # turns the text into a number
  packers: {current_cap: "${PACKERS:-2}", max_cap: 5}

run:
  # A duration, such as 1 week, or a number of seconds
  until: ${RUN_FOR:-1 hour}

The Parquet example switches from the local disk to S3 with five variables, and Queues and Capacity runs one file with several numbers of packers.

docs.title: Include a File
docs.text: !include path puts a mapping from another YAML file in place, such as the settings desflow fit writes: packing: !include fitted/packing.yaml. The path is relative to the file that names it. !include {file: path, spawn: pack} adds keys to the file's mapping, such as the task an arrival spawns. The file is read with the same loader, so ${VAR}, !python and !include work in it. A file that includes itself, directly or through another file, is refused. Input Fitting shows it.

docs.title: Run on Your Own Environment
docs.text:
simulation.environment runs the model on your own subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, named with !python, as SimulationContext(environment=...) does in Python, for example environment: !python my_model.TracingEnvironment.

A subclass that overrides __init__ takes **kwargs and passes them on, because desflow builds it with the arguments it builds its own environment with. One that overrides schedule or step calls super(). When a script steps outside run(), step runs once per model event. Inside run(), it runs once per event, desflow's own events included.

In a blueprint, the class is named under simulation. CountingEnvironment in endings_logic.py counts the events the run processes:

docs/snippets/yaml/task_endings.yaml:environment
# Run on a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment, from endings_logic.py beside the file
environment: !python endings_logic.CountingEnvironment

docs.title: Check as You Type
docs.text: desflow schema prints the JSON Schema of a blueprint, and the same file is published on this site, so an editor can complete keys and mark a misspelt key or a value of the wrong kind as you type. Set Up Your Editor shows the setting, and YAML Keys lists every key.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
from_yaml makes the builder calls for you, so a blueprint gets everything the builder does, and it checks the whole file before anything runs. A file is read and checked in five steps, and any step that fails stops the load with a BlueprintError before anything runs:

  1. Read the file. read_document reads it with a subclass of yaml.SafeLoader. ${VAR} is replaced while each scalar is read, !python module.attribute imports the module and returns the attribute, !include path reads a mapping from another YAML file relative to this one, and every key's line is kept in a source map. Every other node is built as yaml.safe_load would build it.
  2. Check every field. The document is validated against the Blueprint model. Unknown keys are refused, so a misspelt key is reported rather than ignored. Every distribution is built as the builder would build it, so a parameter out of range, or one the family does not take, is refused here. Every relative time is read against one now. A spawn after and a fire after must be above 0. simulation.environment must be a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment. All validation errors are reported at once.
  3. Check the names. Each name in the file must exist and fit where it is used:
    • Every service, resource, store, container and next task that a task names exists.
    • Every task's spawn and on: spawn names a task that does not share an arrival's name.
    • A subscribe names a task or a signal.
    • An on: fire names a signal, and an on: interrupt names a task.
    • An on: fire ... from names a signal or a task. The task must run on the same entity as the on: list. For a task's list, that is the entity of the task that holds the list. For a signal's list, it is the entity of a task that fires the signal.
    • Every level.<name> in an expression names a store or a container, and every users.<name> and queue.<name> names a resource.
    • A store and a container do not share a name.
    • A task's priority needs a resource with queue: priority.
    • Resources and stores have whole-number capacities.
    • An on: fire with urgent or after names a signal with once: true.
    • simulation.environment names a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment.
  4. Build the context. The builder calls are made in the order a script would make them: the simulation, ingress, egress, batching, stats, resources, stores, containers, variables, services, arrivals, tasks, arrival loops, processes, telemetry and the scenario.
  5. Check the paths. The parameters are registered into a scratch registry, with the code that the run uses. Every scenario path, and every registry["..."] that an expression reads, is then checked against the paths the run will have. Every scenario value must convert to the type its path holds.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
An error at any step is mapped back to its line through the source map:

docs/snippets/pages/blueprint_error.yaml
# A blueprint with a mistake, for the YAML Blueprints page: pack_order has a priority,
# but its resource serves its queue in the default order, fifo.
simulation:
  sim_id: Shop
  factor: 0

resources:
  packers: {current_cap: 1, max_cap: 2}

services:
  packing: {dist: constant, value: 1.5 s}

arrivals:
  orders: {dist: exponential, rate: 0.5, spawn: pack_order}

tasks:
  pack_order:
    service: packing
    resource: packers
    priority: 0
    payload: {event_type: order_packed}
docs/snippets/pages/blueprint_errors.py:load
try:
    SimulationContext.from_yaml("blueprint_error.yaml")
except BlueprintError as error:
    print(f"Error: {error}")  # what desflow run prints, before exiting with code 1

Error: blueprint_error.yaml:20: task 'pack_order' has a priority, but resource 'packers' does not set queue: priority; set it, or remove the priority

A blueprint covers configuration, including several resources per task (resource: [picker, bench] and keep), preemption (preempt: true) and breakdowns (breakdown:). These stay in Python:

  • Values computed per entity. A mapping payload is a constant, apart from three values added for each entity: the task id that id_field adds, the attributes that attributes adds, and the item a get took, which item_field adds. Random choices, derived fields and state carried between events are a Python payload or process, as Call Python from YAML shows. A task's priority and a get or put amount can be an expression. next rules read attributes, payload fields, levels, registry values, the item a get took (item.<field>), the wait's branches (wait.<branch>.done) and signals (signal.<name>.count), as Task Flow describes.
  • Entity keys. A blueprint uses the default key, <arrival>-<n>. A key function is builder only.
  • Batching. Collecting several entities into one is a process in Python.
  • One simulation per file. A blueprint has one sim_id. !include puts a mapping from another file in place, such as fitted settings, but not a second simulation.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: A blueprint with no !python references is read entirely by yaml.SafeLoader, and loading it imports only the connector modules its type entries name. An !include reads another YAML file the same way and imports nothing itself. A file that references Python, directly or in a file it includes, runs the imports it names. Such a file needs the same trust as a Python script: run blueprints only from people whose scripts you would run. Call Python from YAML explains.

docs.title: Builder API
docs.text: This page writes a whole simulation as one Python file with the builder, SimulationContext: a shop that packs orders with boxes from stock, prints a label, and leaves the parcel for a courier. It builds on Writing a Model, which places the builder between a blueprint and the low-level API, and on Tasks and Processes, which describes what a task does.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
The builder works in two phases. You describe the simulation with its methods and decorators, and nothing runs. run() then builds the environment and the connectors and starts the clock:

Until run() builds the environment, the runtime helpers context.spawn, context.call, context.signal, context.get_resource, context.get_store, context.get_container and context.env raise RuntimeError. Loops, tasks and processes run only after that, so the helpers belong inside them.

docs.title: Create the Context
docs.text:
The context names the simulation and sets its clock: factor for the pacing, random_seed for the draws, logical_start_time for the timestamps. It also takes go_live_at and warmup, which Time and Pacing describes.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:clock
app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,  # 0.0 unpaced, 1.0 real time
    random_seed=42,  # the same draws on every run
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0),  # what simulation time 0 is
)

docs.title: Declare Resources, Stores and Containers
docs.text:
A task holds a resource while it works. A container holds an amount and a store holds items, and tasks take from and add to both. add_variable registers any other live value. Resources and Stores and Containers describe each.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:resources
app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=2, max_cap=5)  # 2 packers now, room for 5
app.add_container("boxes", current_cap=200, max_cap=200, level=100)  # an amount
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=20, max_cap=50)  # items, waiting for a courier
app.add_variable("conveyor_speed", 1.5)  # any other live value

docs.title: Add Distributions
docs.text:
Each service is a distribution, given its parameters by keyword. Each arrival is a distribution too, and Start Them from Arrivals adds it with the task it starts. A parameter out of range, or one the family does not take, raises ValueError here, before the run. Arrivals and Services lists the ten families.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:distributions
app.add_service("packing", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=2, high=4)
app.add_service("labelling", dist="constant", value=0.5)

docs.title: Write the Tasks
docs.text:
@app.task turns a function into a task: it publishes queued, waits for its resource and its get, publishes started, waits the service time, adds its put, and publishes what the function returns as the finished event. next names the task that follows, and the function receives upstream, entity or item when it declares them. Task Flow covers rules and weights.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:tasks
@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "boxes", "amount": 1},  # one box, once it has a packer
    next="print_label",  # the task that follows
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # The value of the finished event: exactly this dictionary
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task(service_id="labelling", put={"store": "parcels"})  # a timed step
def print_label(task_id: int, upstream):
    # upstream is what pack_order handed on; the payload becomes the parcel
    return {"event_type": "label_printed", "packed_by": upstream.task_id}


@app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "label": item["event_type"]}

docs.title: Start Them from Arrivals
docs.text:
add_arrival with spawn= is the builder form of YAML's spawn: each arrival starts the named task for its entity, keyed orders-1, orders-2 and so on. The record's instance comes from the task's one counter, which next and other arrivals share, so no two runs of the task share an id. A spawn that names a task never added is refused when run() checks the model.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:arrivals
# An order every 2 s on average, keyed orders-1, ..., each starting pack_order
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_arrival("couriers", dist="constant", value=10, spawn="collect")  # every 10 s

@app.arrival_loop runs a generator of your own that waits with context.wait_for_arrival and starts tasks with context.spawn. A loop is needed only when it does more than start one task, such as choosing the task from the entity's attributes. Tasks and Processes shows a loop that does what spawn= does, written by hand.

docs.title: Measure the Run
docs.text:
with_stats switches on the built-in statistics, published as telemetry. Statistics lists the levels.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:stats
app.with_stats("typical", interval=30)  # readings, counts, waits, every 30 s

docs.title: Add a Process
docs.text:
add_process is for anything that is not a task. It calls a generator with the context when the run starts. Here the process is a speed that drifts.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:process
def speed_drift(context: SimulationContext, step: float):
    """Raises the conveyor speed a little every 10 simulation seconds."""
    path = "Shop.variables.conveyor_speed"
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10.0)
        speed = context.env.registry.get(path).value
        context.env.registry.update(path, speed + step)


app.add_process(speed_drift, step=0.1)

docs.title: Attach the Connectors
docs.text:
add_ingress brings parameter changes in, and add_egress writes records out, each with its own batching if it needs it. Ingress and Egress list the connectors.

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:connectors
app.add_ingress(LocalIngress(schedule=[(5.0, "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)]))
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(), batch_size=100, flush_interval=1.0)
app.with_batching(batch_size=1_000, flush_interval=5.0)  # defaults for other sinks

LocalIngress counts its delays in wall-clock seconds, so the change to 3 packers is due 5 seconds after the run starts. This unpaced run ends in under a second, so the change never lands. At factor=1.0, it lands 5 seconds into the run. For a change at an exact simulation time, use a scenario step, add_step(at, path=..., value=...) or add_scenario(steps), which Live Parameters describes. A process that waits and then updates the registry, as speed_drift above does, also works.

compile_parameters() returns the SimParameter that run() will register. Call it to check the registry paths before a run:

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py:compile
paths = app.compile_parameters()  # the SimParameter that run() registers

docs.title: Run It
How It Works
docs.text:
run() takes the steps a low-level script writes by hand, in the same order, which What run() Does lists. It adds these:

  • A seed for every run. It makes Sampler(seed=random_seed), and draws and logs a seed when there is none.
  • Resources, stores and containers. One for each add_resource, add_store and add_container, which context.get_resource, get_store and get_container return. add_resource takes a type, a subclass of ResourceBase to build the resource from (Custom Resource Types). add_store and add_container take a type too, a subclass of StoreBase or ContainerBase (Custom Store and Container Types). A store or container with no current_cap and no max_cap has no limit.
  • Tasks. @app.task publishes queued, started and the finished event with the entity key, task and instance, reports each step to the statistics, takes and adds stock, and routes to the next task with a Router.
  • Entities. context.wait_for_arrival returns an Entity with its key and attributes.
  • Names with the sim_id. context.publish(name, value) puts the sim_id in front of the name. The low-level env.publish_telemetry uses the name as given.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
A mistake stops the script before the clock starts. A method raises ValueError when it is called with a value it cannot take:

  • an environment that is not a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment;
  • a fire action with urgent or after on a signal that is not once=True (raised at start());
  • a negative after;
  • a distribution parameter out of range, or one its family does not take;
  • an unknown queue order;
  • a current_cap or max_cap that is not a whole number or infinity, or a max_cap below 1 given with no current_cap;
  • a type that is not a subclass of ResourceBase;
  • a negative queue_limit, or one on a type with a PutQueue of its own;
  • a task with a resource but no service, or a priority without a resource;
  • an unknown on_interrupt;
  • a second task with the same name;
  • a spawn with an after of 0 or less;
  • a fire action given both value and from.

run() then checks what each task names, before the clock or any connector starts. It raises ValueError for:

  • a resource, service, store, container, signal or task that was not added;
  • a priority on a resource that does not queue by priority;
  • two tasks that acquire resources in opposite orders;
  • a spawned task that shares an arrival's name;
  • a fire action's from that names both a signal and a task, or neither;
  • a level.<name>, users.<name>, queue.<name>, signal.<name>, wait.<branch> or registry["..."] that an expression reads but that does not exist.

The builder's limits are those of its tasks and its resources:

  • Resources are fixed when the run starts. run() creates every resource, store and container before the clock starts, and has no call to add one later. A process can add one through context.env, as Add Resources Mid-run shows.
  • advance() needs a started run. It raises RuntimeError before start(), after close() and after the run's own end, and ValueError for a time that is not after now. Run in Segments shows it.
  • strict defaults to False here. Strict Pacing gives what it does and its default in each API.
  • environment= takes a subclass of DynamicRealtimeEnvironment. The context builds it in start() with the same arguments it would give its own environment, so its __init__ takes **kwargs and passes them on.
  • A subscribe refuses a processed event. context.subscribe(event) raises RuntimeError when the event has already happened, or when it is called outside a process.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Full script

The complete file, which the documentation tests run:

docs/snippets/pages/builder.py
"""The Builder API page: a whole simulation in one Python file, step by step.

Run it with `python builder.py`: it runs unpaced for 2 simulation minutes and prints
every record to the terminal.
"""

import logging
from datetime import datetime

from desflow import ConsoleEgress, LocalIngress, SimulationContext

app = SimulationContext(
    sim_id="Shop",
    factor=0.0,  # 0.0 unpaced, 1.0 real time
    random_seed=42,  # the same draws on every run
    logical_start_time=datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 0),  # what simulation time 0 is
)

app.add_resource("packers", current_cap=2, max_cap=5)  # 2 packers now, room for 5
app.add_container("boxes", current_cap=200, max_cap=200, level=100)  # an amount
app.add_store("parcels", current_cap=20, max_cap=50)  # items, waiting for a courier
app.add_variable("conveyor_speed", 1.5)  # any other live value

app.add_service("packing", dist="triangular", low=1, mode=2, high=4)
app.add_service("labelling", dist="constant", value=0.5)


@app.task(
    service_id="packing",
    resource_id="packers",
    get={"container": "boxes", "amount": 1},  # one box, once it has a packer
    next="print_label",  # the task that follows
)
def pack_order(task_id: int):
    # The value of the finished event: exactly this dictionary
    return {"event_type": "order_packed"}


@app.task(service_id="labelling", put={"store": "parcels"})  # a timed step
def print_label(task_id: int, upstream):
    # upstream is what pack_order handed on; the payload becomes the parcel
    return {"event_type": "label_printed", "packed_by": upstream.task_id}


@app.task(get={"store": "parcels"})
def collect(task_id: int, item):
    return {"event_type": "parcel_collected", "label": item["event_type"]}


# An order every 2 s on average, keyed orders-1, ..., each starting pack_order
app.add_arrival("orders", dist="exponential", rate=0.5, spawn="pack_order")
app.add_arrival("couriers", dist="constant", value=10, spawn="collect")  # every 10 s

app.with_stats("typical", interval=30)  # readings, counts, waits, every 30 s


def speed_drift(context: SimulationContext, step: float):
    """Raises the conveyor speed a little every 10 simulation seconds."""
    path = "Shop.variables.conveyor_speed"
    while True:
        yield context.env.timeout(10.0)
        speed = context.env.registry.get(path).value
        context.env.registry.update(path, speed + step)


app.add_process(speed_drift, step=0.1)

app.add_ingress(LocalIngress(schedule=[(5.0, "Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 3)]))
app.add_egress(ConsoleEgress(), batch_size=100, flush_interval=1.0)
app.with_batching(batch_size=1_000, flush_interval=5.0)  # defaults for other sinks

paths = app.compile_parameters()  # the SimParameter that run() registers

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    app.run(until="2 min")

Low-level API writes the same kind of model by hand. A blueprint makes the same builder calls from a file, as YAML Blueprints describes.

docs.title: Low-level API
docs.text: This page writes a simulation with SimPy and the environment directly: a packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders, every step written by hand. It builds on SimPy and desflow, which describes the SimPy constructs, and on Builder API, which writes the same kind of model for you.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
Use the low-level API when you need what the builder does not do: events and interactions of your own shape, such as a resource created while the run goes on in Add Resources Mid-run. A builder or blueprint model can also start a low-level process with add_process, as Tasks and Processes shows.

A low-level script takes these steps, in this order:

docs.title: Create the Environment
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:imports
import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:environment
env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

factor sets the pacing: 1.0 follows the wall clock, and 0.0 runs as fast as possible. logical_start_time and go_live_at work as Time and Pacing describes.

docs.title: Register the Parameters
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:parameters
env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

One SimParameter holds every parameter of one simulation under its sim_id. Registering it gives each value a path, such as Shop.arrival.orders.rate, and only the registered paths exist. Live Parameters lists the paths.

docs.title: Attach the Connectors
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:connectors
env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

setup_egress starts the egress thread, which writes every record the processes publish. setup_ingress starts the ingress thread for parameter changes from outside, and setup_stats switches on the built-in statistics. Egress lists the arguments of setup_egress, including a warm-up and labels sinks.

docs.title: Create Resources, Containers and Stores
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:resources
packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed

Each one reads its capacity from the registry when it is created, so the parameters must be registered first. Each one also adds itself to the statistics. Sampler(seed=42) gives each registered distribution a random stream of its own, so a run repeats exactly, as Arrivals and Services describes.

docs.title: Write the Processes
docs.text:
A process is a SimPy generator: it yields to wait, and publishes records as it goes. This one does what @app.task does in the builder, with a box from stock and a store for the result. It publishes each event with the entity key, the task's name and its instance id, and reports each step to the statistics:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:order
def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")

The service time is drawn once the order has a packer and a box, from the configuration the registry holds at that moment, so a change made while it waited still applies to it.

The arrival loop keeps the configuration object rather than a copy of the rate. The registry changes that object in place when a new rate arrives, so the next draw uses the current rate. It gives each order its key, orders-1, orders-2:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:arrivals
def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1

A reading of your own is a process that publishes at an interval. publish_telemetry uses the name exactly as given:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:telemetry
def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)

A process can also change the simulation itself, through the registry, as a connector or a scenario would:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:control
def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)

docs.title: Start the Processes and Run
docs.text:
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:start
env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))
docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py:run
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
)
try:
    env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
finally:
    env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads

ConsoleEgress writes each record as a log line at INFO level, so logging is switched on first. env.run is SimPy's, so until is a number of simulation seconds. time_to_seconds converts a duration such as "10 min". teardown in finally publishes the last statistics, flushes the last records and stops both threads, even when the run stops with Ctrl+C or an error.

A script can run the model in segments by calling env.run(until=...) again, as in SimPy. env.schedule(event, priority, delay) is SimPy's own: simpy.events.URGENT puts an event before the NORMAL ones at its time. Run Length covers segments, strict, sync() and env.resume_pacing().

An environment subclass is plain Python: class Traced(DynamicRealtimeEnvironment), whose __init__ takes **kwargs and passes them on, and whose step or schedule calls super(). Inside run(), step runs once per event, desflow's own events included.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The environment does little for you. It paces the clock, holds the registry, writes records on the egress thread and keeps the statistics that setup_stats switches on. Everything else is your code. Builder API lists what SimulationContext.run() writes for you on top of the same steps.

The environment runs on three threads: the SimPy thread runs your processes, the ingress thread runs the sources and the egress thread runs the sinks. Alongside your processes, the environment starts processes of its own on the SimPy thread:

  • The ingress monitor applies the sources' changes to the registry every 0.1 simulation seconds.
  • Each sink has a process that flushes its buffer on the sink's interval.
  • The lag monitor measures how far the clock is behind the wall clock once the run is live.
  • The statistics timer publishes the statistics every interval.
  • One process ends the warm-up.

env.step() and env.peek() do not count these processes. Time and Pacing shows the threads and the switch to real time.

docs.title: Stability and Limits
docs.text:
Nothing is checked before the run as a whole. Each call checks only what it reads, when it runs:

  • An unregistered path raises KeyError when a resource, a process or a registry.get asks for it, so register the parameters before creating anything that reads them.
  • A record without egress is dropped. Until setup_egress runs, publish_event and publish_telemetry do nothing, without an error.
  • A Sampler() with no seed draws nothing at random, as Arrivals and Services explains, so give it a seed.
  • A paced run is strict by default. Strict Pacing gives what it does and its default in each API.
  • An unhandled failure stops the run under stop. DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(on_unhandled_failure=...) is stop by default, as a plain SimPy environment is. Under stop, a one-shot Signal failure that nobody waits for raises SignalFailed, and the run stops. Pass "continue" to defuse such a failure and let the run go on. A re-arming signal's failure is always defused. An exception raised in a process stops the run under both settings. The keyword must be stop or continue.

Beyond those, a process can do anything SimPy can model.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Full script

The complete file, which the documentation tests run:

docs/snippets/pages/low_level.py
"""A complete low-level simulation, as the Low-level API page explains it step by step.

One packing team with a stock of boxes and a store of packed orders. Run it with
`python low_level.py`: it runs unpaced for 10 simulation minutes and prints every record
to the terminal.
"""

import logging

from desflow import (
    CapacityConfig,
    ConsoleEgress,
    ContainerConfig,
    DistributionConfig,
    DynamicContainer,
    DynamicRealtimeEnvironment,
    DynamicResource,
    DynamicStore,
    Sampler,
    SimParameter,
    time_to_seconds,
)

env = DynamicRealtimeEnvironment(factor=0.0)  # unpaced; 1.0 follows the wall clock

env.registry.register_sim_parameter(
    SimParameter(
        sim_id="Shop",
        # An order every 2 s on average (rate 0.5)
        arrival={"orders": DistributionConfig(dist="exponential", rate=0.5)},
        service={"packing": DistributionConfig(dist="normal", mean=1.5, std=0.3)},
        resources={"packers": CapacityConfig(current_cap=1, max_cap=3)},
        containers={"boxes": ContainerConfig(current_cap=100, max_cap=100, level=100)},
        stores={"finished": CapacityConfig(current_cap=50, max_cap=50)},
        variables={"boxes_per_order": 1.0},
    )
)

env.setup_egress([ConsoleEgress()])  # starts the egress thread
# env.setup_ingress([KafkaIngress(...)]) would start the ingress thread
env.setup_stats("Shop", "basic", interval=60)  # readings and counts every minute

packers = DynamicResource(env, "Shop", "packers")  # reads Shop.resources.packers.*
boxes = DynamicContainer(env, "Shop", "boxes")  # starts at its level, 100
finished = DynamicStore(env, "Shop", "finished")
sampler = Sampler(seed=42)  # a random stream per distribution, from one seed


def order(env, key, task_id):
    """One order: queue for a packer, take a box, pack, then store the result."""
    path_id = "Shop.service.packing"

    def publish(value):
        env.publish_event(key, value, task="pack_order", instance=task_id)

    publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "queued"})
    env.stats.task_queued("pack_order", task_id)  # what @app.task reports for you
    with packers.request() as request:
        yield request
        count = env.registry.get("Shop.variables.boxes_per_order").value
        yield boxes.get(count)  # waits if the stock is too low
        publish({"path_id": path_id, "status": "started"})
        env.stats.task_started("pack_order", task_id)
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(env.registry.get_config(path_id)))
        yield finished.put({"order": key})
        publish({"event_type": "order_packed"})
    env.stats.task_finished("pack_order", task_id)
    env.stats.flow_finished("orders")


def arrivals(env):
    gap = env.registry.get_config("Shop.arrival.orders")  # the live config object
    task_id = 0
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(sampler.sample(gap))  # each draw reads the current rate
        env.process(order(env, f"orders-{task_id + 1}", task_id))  # the entity key
        task_id += 1


def telemetry(env):
    """A reading of your own, beside the built-in statistics."""
    while True:
        env.publish_telemetry("Shop.boxes_per_packer", boxes.level / packers.capacity)
        yield env.timeout(10.0)


def refill_and_rush(env):
    """Refills boxes every minute, and doubles arrivals after five minutes."""
    while True:
        yield env.timeout(60.0)
        missing = boxes.capacity - boxes.level
        if missing > 0:  # SimPy refuses a put of 0
            yield boxes.put(missing)
        if env.now >= 300 and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value < 1.0:
            env.registry.update("Shop.arrival.orders.rate", 1.0)
            env.registry.update("Shop.resources.packers.current_cap", 2)


env.process(arrivals(env))
env.process(telemetry(env))
env.process(refill_and_rush(env))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    logging.basicConfig(
        level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s [%(asctime)s] %(message)s"
    )
    try:
        env.run(until=time_to_seconds("10 min"))  # until is in simulation seconds
    finally:
        env.teardown()  # flushes the buffers and stops the threads
    assert (
        packers.capacity == 2
        and env.registry.get("Shop.arrival.orders.rate").value == 1.0
    )
    assert len(finished.items) > 0
